## 2. People

*The age pyramid* is *the population. It used to be a display beside a formula; now nothing else decides how many people live here — and since the long sick and the crime batch, nothing dies of only one thing.*

### Six ages, three ways to die

*The band's own annual mortality. Monthly rates are compounded, not divided by twelve.*

| Band | Ages | Annual mortality | Note |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Babies | 0–5 | 0.10% | almost all of it in the first year |
| Children | 6–12 | 0.0075% | the safest band there is |
| Teens | 13–17 | 0.02% | accidents |
| Adults | 18–69 | 0.225% | averaged over a fifty-two year span — and the entire workforce |
| Seniors | 70–84 | 2.90% | population-weighted from a life table |
| Elders | 85–119 | 12.77% | plus ageing out at 120 |

**The seniors were one band of fifty years until save format 27**, at a flat 4.5%. Senior care asks for a place for everybody over seventy, and in the real world about one in nine of them is in one — 2% of seventy-four-year-olds against 29.6% of the over-85s — and one band cannot hold a fifteenfold gradient, nor a mortality curve that runs from 1.4% a year at seventy to over 30% at ninety-five. The two figures are population-weighted from Canada's 2019 life table, and the split is very nearly aggregate-preserving: total deaths among the over-seventies went from 6.5% a year to about 6.7%, and a seventy-year-old has 14.9 years left against the 15.4 the single band gave. The over-85s keep two household shapes of their own, because *Elder living alone* is the cell in trouble first when senior care is short.

Children, teens and adults were halved when illness started killing people, so that the new cause of death would be a redistribution rather than a surcharge. A month's deaths are now struck from three rates against the same opening balance — the band's own rate (scaled by care, and by who has no home), **illness** from the ring of the long sick, and **violence** from the month's homicides — capped together at 5% a month, with the cap scaling each part alike so the shares survive it. Every one of them is recorded by band, so City History can say what the city has died of since it was founded. Since 0.7.27 the month's dead are summed by cause as well — of age, of illness, killed, and aged out at 120 (`PopulationCohorts.getLastDeathsOfAge()`, `getLastKilled()`, `getLastAgedOut()`) — and saved, so the People page's month reads the same after a load.

Bands drain exponentially rather than on a fixed schedule, so a baby boom smears into a bulge rather than travelling through the city as a wave. Nobody is tracked individually; the bucket only has a mean.

### Migration

The city moves toward a target rather than snapping to one. Housing and jobs say how *attractive* the city is, not how many people are in it.

```
target = (0.75 × jobs × residentsPerJob + 0.25 × housingCapacity) × seniorCarePull × rentPull × crimePull
residentsPerJob = (1 + 0.125) / adultShare        // 12.5% labour slack
arrivals   = min(room, max(0, target − population) × 0.15 × crowding)   // room: what the placement has left, since 0.7.17
departures = population × decliningPressure × 0.05
```

Gross flows, not net, so the screen can say *why* the number moved. Since 0.7.27 the month is kept whole and saved after the wage history: the draw in its two halves, work and homes (`Migration.getLastJobDraw()`, `getLastHomeDraw()`), the pulls, the flows, the leavers by cause (`getLastWorkDepartures()` beside the broke and crime), both skill mixes and the licences; a save from before reads *Not recorded yet* until its first month, where a reloaded page had read *a city this good draws 0*. Crowding interpolates to zero between comfortable households and the point where every flatshare and doubled-up home has already formed — a full city still takes arrivals, just fewer. Since 0.7.17 it reads the households that have a door of their own, so a doubled-up household counts as crowding, Jerus's rule: his year-149 city had doors enough by the count, read 0.63, and had 143,443 households living in somebody else's home because the doors were the wrong size. And a month's arrivals are capped at the room the placement has left (`FamilyModel.roomLeft()`): the free doors by size and what the doubling valve still has, in households of the arrivals' own mix. It replaced a wall that stopped every arrival while a single household was left with nowhere, and then let a month of 25,000 to 32,000 in at once; in his city, run on for 120 months, arrivals came in 115 months where they had come in 18 (0.7.17). Nobody leaves unless a pay tier's *real* pay has been declining **twelve months straight** or has stopped entirely. Four more pushes: a band whose wage is pinned at the floor and still has more workers than posts sheds 2% of the surplus a month — the floor in today's money since 0.7.47 (`LabourMarket.isPinned()` reads `cashMinimumWage()`), where it had been compared with the floor in founding money, so that once prices rose no band at the indexed floor ever read as pinned; over the default run that took departures from 65,805 to 1,090,944 and arrivals from 885,622 to 1,694,356 — bankrupt households leave, rent above the target burden deters arrivals, and **crime deters arrivals** — calibrated off Cullen & Levitt (1999), a tenth of the city's draw gone at twice Canada's crime rate, almost all of it as people not coming rather than people leaving. Arrivals carry a skill mix bought by the wage: at the going rate every arrival has a high-school diploma and nothing more, and every band above it, and since 0.7.18 the band below it, comes only for a premium over the going rate, out of a world that has few to spare. At every band's ceiling 7.5% of a month's arrivals have no diploma, the 2021 Census share of immigrants who landed in 2016–2021 aged 25–54 with no certificate (Ontario's figure, as the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario tabulated it; `WageBand.NONE`'s ceiling, 0.1192). Jerus chose *"Some unskilled migrants"*: *"Allow arrivals without a diploma when the unskilled wage is high."* In his year-149 city, run on for 120 months, 13,168 came (0.7.18).

### Households, pay, and what they remember

**Fifteen household shapes**, from `SENIOR_ALONE` and the over-85s' `ELDER_ALONE` through `COUPLE_TWO_CHILDREN` to `SHARED_ADULTS`. Families are built from the adults who *work*; everyone else has their own books. The mix follows the age pyramid and the job tiers; when homes run short, singles form flatshares first and families double up last.

**The households remember.** The builder keeps last month's households as far as the people still exist for them — 1% of them re-form each month by design — shrinking each shape by the worst shortage among the bands it needs, rebuilding only the remainder, and refitting tiers to the jobs by iterative proportional fitting. Before it, a city redrew every family from scratch every month and wallets moved with the redraw. Eight seeds: orphans at the end **490–633 → 11–19**, hunger **4% → 0%**, unemployment **14.8% → 12.2%**. Everything a cell holds moves with the people when the shapes re-form — savings, debt, shares, the dollars abroad, the student loan, and since 16 September the cars — and the move is clamped so that a pool cannot hand out more than it holds, because the day it could, four retired cells owed minus 2.7e-29 dollars and the *sign* of that decided the exchange rate (see [how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

**Homes have sizes.** A studio takes two, a low-rise flat four, a house six; a household has to fit, largest families into the smallest unit that fits, and a one- or two-person flat refuses a dependant outright. **Rent is two markets** — see [prices](#16-prices-the-currency--the-world). An empty home now costs its owner something to hold, and so does a full one: every building pays 1% of its cost a year to stand.

*Six pay tiers, eleven job types — base wages on NS Job Bank medians*

| Tier | Monthly |
| --- | ---: |
| Unskilled | $3,460 |
| Skilled | $4,500 |
| College | $5,500 |
| Professional | $8,200 |
| Senior professional | $9,600 |
| Elite | $15,600 |

> **Seventy-eight ledgers**
>
> Eleven working shapes × six pay tiers, four retired rows, three kinds of out-of-work, students, orphans by age band, and the prisoners. Each keeps savings, debt, a lockout clock, shares in each of the sixteen listed companies, dollars held abroad, student debt, its cars, the month's investment income, the dinners it ate out, the share of its people who could pay for care, the city's own paper, since 0.7.12 the businesses' bonds, since 0.7.43 its last sale's baskets — got, asked for and needed — and the vouchers on them, since 0.7.45 the investment income the vouchers' means test smooths over a year, and since 0.7.46 the month's income after its fixed bills — thirty-eight slots a cell in the save (thirty-two at 0.7.12), each keyed by name so a new row never shifts an old one, and each new slot appended to the end so that an older save reads as a city that had none of it, which it did not. Since 0.7.12 each cell also keeps its bonds one by one, and trades its shares and bonds with the other cells as a participant of its own, saved by the cell's name.
>
> Since 0.7.2 a cell whose census count falls under half a household (`HouseholdBalance.EMPTY_CELL`) is empty: it keeps its count, holds nothing and is paid nothing, and every stock it held folds to its own row first and then to the city — because a cell of 1e-15 households was still being paid, and one line divided a credit by it.

### The household books, and a balance sheet

Every cell, opened, shows wages, the banded wage tax, pension contributions and pensions, the health premium, rent, tuition, interest, shopping, healthcare fees, the transit fares, since 0.7.49 the fuel, the bank's account fee, and what is left — plus **savings, debt, shares, the city's paper, the businesses' bonds and cars per household**, and a waterfall: payslip, rent, fees, food; short, and they spend savings, then sell the city's paper back to the bank's desk, then bring their paper home from abroad, then sell their bonds, then offer their shares on the book at the price at which the dividend they give up yields what borrowing would cost them, then borrow from the bank — since 0.7.7 at a household loan's four costs plus a spread that climbs with what they already owe, never past 36%, and since 0.7.8 only as far as the bank's capital lets it lend — and only then eat less, which makes them ill. A row six months of income in debt that still cannot cover subsistence **goes bankrupt**: 4% a month discharged, locked out of credit for a year, a quarter of them leaving the city. A row that *can* be evicted and still cannot pay loses the share of its homes the shortfall covers.

**Household money is a page of its own** since 0.7.27: each tier's live wage at its head (`HouseholdAccounts.wagePerEarner()`), the books beside the grid on a wide screen, a verdict that counts every row (it had said every household covered its month over five red rows), the rows outside the families measured against a basket (`Household.subsistence()`, not a saver's plan: the students had read −$29,448 in Jerus's city), the retired on their own statement, and INCOME PER RESIDENT where PER WORKER had divided the population by the workforce. Until 0.7.27 an opened cell printed the fares under *Healthcare and school fees* and the account fee under *Interest on what they owe*; each is a line of its own, and since 0.7.49 an opened cell's fares and fuel are its own row's.

Spending follows income, and since 17 September it follows wealth too. A household plans to spend 80% of what is left above subsistence, which until 0.7.43 it took to the grocer's, so shopping was a budget rather than a headcount; on top of that it spends 0.33% of its net worth a month — four percent a year, the middle of the measured propensity to consume out of wealth — and puts half of the income it does not spend on food over a luxury counter and a quarter of it on a table. That plan still decides what the counter and the table spend out of, and what is left of the month is saved. Dividends and the coupon on its paper abroad are paid home and enter the plan, and so, since 0.7.1, are the coupons on the city's own paper, paid into savings as untaxed investment income, and since 0.7.12 those on the businesses' bonds. A household with no debt, no lockout and more than three months of disposable income in the bank puts 30% of the excess into shares, and sends the rest of its idle savings abroad on the same rule the sectors use. It also takes the city's paper at issue: at the settle the households go first, taking a fifth of an issue for every point it yields over the deposit rate (`HOUSEHOLD_PAPER_APPETITE`) and never more than half (`MAX_HOUSEHOLD_PAPER_SHARE`), out of savings past the cushion, and the bank buys the rest. Pensions are pay-as-you-go, and both the contribution rate and the replacement rate are Policy dials. Contributions follow workers and pensions follow pensioners, so an ageing city buys a structural deficit without changing a single policy.

**And since 0.7.43 it asks for its groceries at a price.** The grocer used to be handed the plan in money, the wealth term in it, so a city asked for fourteen to seventeen times the baskets it could eat and the shelf's price answered a head count. A household asks for what it eats now: a basket a head at most, all of it up to the satiation price, 1.5× the shelf's floor (`Retail.SATIATION_MULTIPLE`), a little less above it at an elasticity of 0.4 (`GROCERY_ELASTICITY`, the middle of the measured food-at-home range), and never more than its money buys — everything its plan can fund, and the city's voucher on top (`HouseholdBalance.groceryDemandOf()`). The city's demand falls as the price rises, so there is one price at which it meets what the shops can hand over, and a shortage is shared out at that price, so the poorest are priced out first ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)).

**And since 0.7.3 saving answers the real rate.** Everything a household plans above a basket a head — the propensity's share, the wealth term, and the surplus the counter and the table spend out of — is multiplied by one factor a month struck on the real deposit rate, the bank's deposit rate less the inflation the city expects (since 0.7.42; the year's inflation until then): ten points of real return cut it by a tenth, ten points of negative real return raise it by a tenth, and it is held between a half and one and a half. Subsistence never moves, and at a factor of one the plan is the old plan to the bit. On the default seed on 22 September savers ended the run earning 3.63% real and the households planned 0.964 of what they would spend above a basket at zero; over 4,005 months the factor ran from 0.835 to 1.131, median 0.993. On 28 September, with a deposit rate the bank now chooses (see [the bank](#14-the-bank)), savers ended the run earning 0.23% real and the households planned 0.998; over 4,002 months the factor ran from 0.921 to 1.060, median 1.000. On 1 October, at 0.7.23, they ended at 0.22% real and planned 0.998 again, and over 4,005 months the factor ran from 0.853 to 1.105, median 1.000; on 5 October, at 0.7.49, they ended at −1.99% real and planned 1.020, and the factor ran from 0.988 to 1.076, median 1.020. Until 0.7.43 what it did to prices was almost nothing, because no price in the index read what anybody would spend; the shelf clears on it now, and what that does is in [the central bank](#15-the-central-bank).

> **Why the households were rich**
>
> Household net worth ran at **45 months of the city's GDP at month 480** — dead on the real world's sixty to eighty-four — and **5,072 by month 3,840**. It did not sit at a wrong level; it diverged. Over one run the foreign coupons came to **$2,649bn against $584bn of every wage the city ever paid**, because the households kept about 79% of their wealth abroad at the world's 2% and the coupon was rolled where it was earned, so wealth compounded at 1.58% a year mechanically, 193× over 333 years. Three changes were ensembled one at a time: paying the coupon home took the ratio from 5,380 months to 3,412; letting investment income into the plan put it back to **5,465**, because investment income is a *flow* and a bigger city pays more of it; the wealth term took it to 2,737 and gave the best city of the four. *A stock that compounds can only be bounded by a drain that reads the stock.* And with the coefficient pushed to nine times the empirical range the stock still rose, while delivery fell from 76% of plans to 57% — the households are not hoarding because they are misers; they are hoarding because there is nothing to buy. The cars, the boutiques and the kitchens are the answer to that, and net worth now oscillates (432 → 137 → 128 → 214 months of GDP) instead of climbing.

### What a household owns, and borrows for

**A car is a household stock**, beside savings, debt, shares and the dollars abroad — it follows the people, it is saved per cell by name, a household that leaves takes it — and it is the first one that is *not money*, so a currency reform does not touch it. It is the first durable a household in this game has ever been able to own: the measurement that decided the shape found an unskilled couple banking \$3,160 of a \$4,880 month and sitting on **\$799,100, a hundred and sixty-four months of income**, with \$17.6bn of household savings in the city against zero household debt. That is not a rich city, it is a city with nothing to buy. So affordability barely binds in a mature city and binds hard in a young one, and the constraint is time: 2% of the households that have never owned one buy a car in a month, a car lasts 180 months and is replaced at once when it dies, one per household is saturation, and a cell buys *whole* cars — because a money ratio that comes out as a physical quantity has to cross at a grain coarser than the dust, or a reformed city wants an ulp more of a car and the two cities' trade balances part company. A city whose transit could carry everybody tops out at **half a car per household, for ever**, where its pass is cheap against a car; a metro built after the cars does not remove them, it stops them being replaced, and the fleet decays to the new ceiling over the life of a car.

**And since 0.7.49 a car costs something to run.** A commute by car burns $2.00 of fuel a journey in the world's money (`Motoring.CAR_FUEL_PER_JOURNEY`: fifteen kilometres at eight litres a hundred and about $1.65 a litre), forty journeys a month, priced at the exchange rate and imported, like the railway's, and paid by the rows that drive; since 0.7.62 it is 1.2 litres of `FUEL` a journey, of `PETROL` since 0.7.76, drawn off the refiners' tanks at the market's price before the rest is imported (`Motoring.drawFuel()`), so with no refinery it was the same $2.00 at the world's price level, and a refinery's fuel stayed at home; since 0.7.78 petrol is priced at wholesale, about $0.73 a journey at par, and since 0.7.83 the rows that drive pay the pump's price on it, about $0.97 at the default sales tax, the grocers drawing it off the tanks and the world ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). Its wear is still the calendar's 180 months and its insurance is sunk. Until then nothing in the household model cost anything to run. And a household without a car weighs a month's pass against a car's full monthly cost — its payment over its life at the household rate, and a month of fuel — before it buys, and the share who would rather ride — everybody at a pass of half a car's cost or less, nobody at twice it (`InfrastructureManager.transitChosen()`) — scales how far good transit lowers the ceiling. Jerus: *"acquiring car costs 500 a month and transit is 250 then they take transit"*. A household holds one car, so most commuters in a big city have none of their own — 73% in the 2,400-month research city — and ride where a line reaches them or walk ([transport](#21-transport--vehicles)).

**And they borrow for it.** Jerus: *"make it so that citizens the car requirements are lowered and instead they finance with the bank."* The rule is *pay what you have and borrow the difference*: a household hands over every dollar it has spare and a lender finds the rest, with a fifth of the price (`CAR_DEPOSIT`) as a minimum in cash and half the household's remaining credit room as the most a lender advances — that second number found by `DenominationCheck`, because every financed household was parked within a whisker of the bankruptcy line. With no credit line the rule reduces exactly to the old cash rule, so it can never refuse a purchase the old one allowed. Since 0.7.7 the bank's one per cent fee on new lending is added to the loan, because a household borrows when it is short of cash. The first draft — a fifth down, four fifths borrowed, compulsory — cut ownership at month 266 from 42% to 11%, because these households are cash-rich and income-poor and the loan moved the constraint onto the thing they have not. Seven of eight seeds are bit-identical over four thousand months; the young city diverges in month eight and has bought twice the cars by month ten. The loan is a bridge, not a note: the grocery waterfall repays it out of spare cash within a month or two. Household debt in this game had been exactly zero in every measured city. It is not any more.

**The car goes last.** Jerus: *"if they are doing bad they cut back expenses, sell their cars or go for cheaper groceries."* Two of the three were already in — the plan shrinks by itself, and a poorer cell already buys more grain and less meat — and the car was in nothing: a family sold its shares, brought its paper home, drew its last dollar of credit and went hungry with five months of take-home parked in the drive. There is a **second-hand market at home** now, and the fleet does not shrink when a household sells, it changes hands. The price is struck the way every market here strikes one: a floor at 15% of new (what a scrapper pays), a ceiling at 70%, a position between them from demand against supply — so a city cannot sell its way out of a general crash: everybody offers, nobody buys, the price is scrap, and the harness asserts it (8,000 offered, 0 sold, pinned at the floor). A household offers when the wage after the fixed bills no longer buys the food *and* half a year of that gap beats everything it has saved and can still borrow; a one-month test found households going bankrupt with the car still in the drive thirteen times for every one that sold it. Over 4,002 months of the default run when it shipped the trigger fired in two cell-months, both fractions of a household, and over 4,005 on 22 September in none, because the households were too rich to ever sell anything — which is the finding above, and the reason the counter and the kitchens exist. On 28 September the same seed offered 8,121 cars over 4,002 months and 362 of them found a buyer, at between 15% and 59% of a new car; on 1 October it offered 4,059 over 4,005 months and 149 found one, at between 15% and 32%; on 5 October, at 0.7.49, it offered 2,887 and 95 found one, at between 15% and 69%.

## 3. Outside the families

*Until this system the city's money was spread across every adult in a pay tier, working or not, so an unskilled single adult took home $1,262 in a month of 40% unemployment and nobody was ever poor. Four groups now keep their own books beside the families.*

```
labour force  = workforce − students − prisoners
the pool      = labour force − filled posts        // an identity, not a second count
```

| Row | Lives on | What is true of them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On EI | 55% of the wage they lost, capped | a claim runs twelve months; the benefit is split among claimants out of a real premium |
| EI run out | savings, then credit | the only row that can be evicted; four in five of the pool end up here |
| Lost their home | nothing | hungry, and **3.7×** as likely to be ill and to die |
| Students | savings, a grant, and a loan, interest-free unless the player sets a rate | out of the labour supply until they graduate; graduates repay over 114 months |
| Orphans | nothing, and they pay no fees | one row per age band; no grown-up, so no credit |
| Prisoners | nothing; debts frozen | out of the labour force, out of the housing match, out of every offender group |

**Employment insurance is a real programme.** A 1.63% premium off insurable wages funds a 55% benefit capped at Canada's maximum insurable earnings scaled to the city's unskilled median — $1,903 a month for an unskilled claimant, $3,158 for anyone at or above the cap. Both rates are Policy dials. The ring is struck on the *inflow* of the newly unemployed, cohort by cohort: jobs lost this month join at the wage they lost, each cohort is thinned monthly by hires, deaths and departures, and the twelfth cohort falls off the end into "EI run out". Arrivals who never found work enter at the unskilled wage and get no claim. Since 0.7.17 the builders' idle crews join it too: a builder with less work than crews lays off the posts the work does not need, down to a core crew of a quarter of them, and those it lays off draw EI ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)). Since 0.7.3 the benefit is paid in the month it is credited: struck again at the top of the month on the pool the month opens with and paid there (`Game.payEiBenefits()`), so the treasury, the ledger and the audit read one figure. For as long as EI had existed the out of work were credited last month's bill while the treasury paid this month's, and nothing saw it because the households are outside the audit's pools; `OutsideCheck` closes every Construction Depot in a small city and asserts that the closing month pays the EI of the pool it opened with and the month after pays the bill the closing struck, each credited the month it is paid; three of its lines fail on the old order. A save from 0.7.2 pays one month's EI twice on its first month, once.

**Eviction is a level, not a rate.** A row that can be evicted and is short loses `households × min(1, shortfall / (rent + fees + interest))` of its homes; a quarter of those leave the city and the rest are on the street. Because a cell is an average, its households run out together — evictions arrive as a cliff. For most of the project's life nobody was ever evicted in the ensemble: an out-of-work adult ended a 333-year run holding millions, because the unskilled tier's savings are what they draw on first. It moves with the run. On the default seed on 18 September, with the wealth term and the counters in, 550 households were evicted over 4,002 months and 137 of them left; on 22 September, at 0.7.3, nobody was evicted over 4,005 months, nobody was left on EI at the end, and an out-of-work adult whose claim had run out ended the run with $303,200 put by; on 28 September, at 0.7.15, one household was evicted over 4,002 months and did not leave, 1,378 people were on EI at the end, and an out-of-work adult whose claim had run out ended with $80,600; on 1 October, at 0.7.23, one was evicted over 4,005 months and did not leave, 4,746 people were on EI at the end, and an adult past EI ended with $235,700; and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, nobody was evicted over 4,005 months, 7,135 people were on EI at the end, and an adult past EI ended with $340.1M put by, in a city whose prices had risen 1,213-fold since its founding. Close the biggest employer in a young city and the path works exactly as designed: **549 evicted in the first year, 440 of them in two months, 384 on the street at the worst, 127 still there four years later** (measured on 11 September; no harness reproduces it since).

Housing serves each group with its own valve: an out-of-work adult alone counts a full door, a flatsharer a fifth, a doubled-up seeker or someone on the street none — so the rent bill is split over the doors actually paid for. The transit fare is a third fee beside the health fee and the tuition: from the day transit was built until 16 September it was credited to the city and debited to nobody, and nobody saw it because no fixture had ever built a bus. Until 0.7.49 it was split across the rows the way the clinic's fees are, so the retired, the out of work and the students paid for buses they never rode. Since then the road counts its commuters by row — the working rows' grown-ups, and the cars they hold — and the fares fall on the rows that ride and the drivers' fuel, a fourth fee, on the rows that drive, each followed by people within the row (`HouseholdAccounts.setCommute()`); the rows outside the families pay neither — see [transport](#21-transport--vehicles).

## 4. Health

*Three classes. `Health` is the effect — a multiplier on output. `Healthcare` is the service — an employer with a payroll and a cemetery with a finite number of plots. `Sickness` is the ring of people who have not got better, and it is the one that kills.*

### Sickness is the fourth utilisation ratio

It sits beside energy, water and roads — and, since 17 September, beside the fifth ratio, the sector's own fleet of vans — multiplies with them, and is carried across a save the same way. The one difference is the whole point:

```
output  = capacity × fill × bEnergy × bWater × bRoad × bHealth × bVans
payroll = Σ wage[job type] × posts filled[job type]   // no bHealth, no ratio at all; per job type since 0.7.17
```

Output falls, payroll does not. **The employer carries it** — a mill with fifty on the books pays fifty wages in a bad flu month and sells four weeks of output in three. The workforce, the pyramid and the wage bill never move. A sick worker still gets paid, still shops, still pays rent. Since 0.7.17 every employer pays each job type's wage on the posts of that type actually filled, and the households receive exactly that: it had been the whole schedule times the sector's average fill, which charged an empty post at the average of the posts beside it, and in Jerus's year-149 city the sectors paid $1,273M a month that no household received, the builders $269M of it. Jerus: *"but sick still get paid right? if yes then good."* They are: a sick worker holds a filled post.

*General-care coverage sets the standing absence rate*

| Coverage | Off sick |
| --- | ---: |
| None | 18.0% |
| Half | 10.5% |
| Everybody | 3.0% |

Five things add on top of that baseline and the total is capped at 45%: an outbreak, the unburied (up to 15 points), hunger (up to 8), the share of the city with no home at 3.7 times the baseline, and **the injured** — half a month off work for every violent crime.

**Outbreaks** land on top: roughly one every five years, peaking 8–25%, decaying 55% a month, with hospitals taking 60% off the peak but never preventing one. The roll is a pure function of the month number, so an epidemic survives a reload without the generator's state going in the save — you cannot save-scum out of one. Measured over 4,005 months on the default seed, 22 September: **52 outbreaks, the city ill for 289 months, worst month 45%** — which is the cap; and the run ends at 15.1% with no outbreak in it at all, nobody unburied and two points of hunger on a baseline of 12.8% that general care covered 35% of. On 18 September the same seed ended at 36.8%, fifteen points of it the unburied; the batches since moved every seed, so the two readings are two cities, not a trend. On 28 September it had 52 outbreaks again, ill for 301 months, worst month 45%, and ended at 19.2%: no outbreak, nobody unburied, five points of hunger on a baseline of 14.1% that general care covered 26% of. On 1 October, at 0.7.23: 52 outbreaks, ill for 324 months, worst month 45%, ending at 20.7% — no outbreak, nobody unburied, 4.2 points of hunger on a baseline of 16.4% that general care covered 10% of. On 5 October, at 0.7.49: 52 outbreaks, ill for 298 months, worst month 45%, ending at 39.7% — no outbreak, fifteen points of the unburied, eight of hunger, on a baseline of 16.5% that general care covered 10% of.

**The history keeps the outbreak** since 0.7.46 (`Health.getOutbreakSeverity()`), and City History names an epidemic only while one runs — at least 0.5% of the workforce off sick over what its care explains (`YearBook.EPIDEMIC_OUTBREAK`, `Health.OUTBREAK_FLOOR`), three months or more. It had named one on the sick rate, so a city short of care was one epidemic for life: 2,213 months of the 2,400-month research city's.

### The people who stay sick

Each band carries a thirteen-month ring of who fell ill when. Past **two months** sick, a share of them dies each month — 4% for babies and seniors, 8% for the over-85s, 2% for adults, 1% for children and teens. General care is what gets people out of the ring: it cures 50% of the sick a month untreated and 90% fully served. Babies and the retired fall ill twice as often as the city rate until their own care takes the excess away.

> **What general care stopped doing**
>
> It used to be a ×3 swing on the death rate of every teen and adult. That is gone: general care now acts *only* through the sick rate and through curing the sick. A fully served adult used to die at 0.15% a year; they now die at about 0.232%, base plus a sliver of illness. The halving of the base rate does not make that back at the good end — deliberately, and it is a live lever.

### What care does to a life

A multiplier on the band's annual death rate, interpolated *geometrically* on coverage — unserved is multiplied by the swing, fully served is divided by it, half-served is exactly the base rate. Log space is the right space for a multiplier: halfway between "forty times worse" and "forty times better" is *the same*.

*Annual mortality all-in: the band's rate scaled by care, plus steady-state illness — struck before the seniors were split at 85, and kept as it was struck; the two bands now start from 2.90% and 12.77%, with swings of 1.35× and 1.80×*

| Band | Care type | Swing | No care | Half | Full |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Babies | Childcare | 40× | 7.96% | 0.77% | 0.017% |
| Children | Childcare | 40× | 0.83% | 0.120% | 0.004% |
| Teens | General | — | 0.56% | 0.133% | 0.024% |
| Adults | General | — | 1.28% | 0.449% | 0.232% |
| Seniors | Senior | 1.35× | 9.96% | 5.14% | 3.35% |

Teens and adults have no swing left; the whole of their column is illness. Senior care's swing is 1.35× on the 70-to-85 band and 1.80× on the over-85s, because that is where the care is worth more. Childcare also **doubles the birth rate** at full coverage — 15 per thousand a year to 30 — and senior care makes the city **30% more attractive** to migrants, which is what turns an ageing pyramid into something to manage rather than endure.

Measured on the default seed on 22 September: **illness is 32.7% of all deaths** — 147,312 of 450,113 over 4,005 months, against 42.7% on 18 September; on 28 September it was 39.9%, 263,361 of 660,761 over 4,002; on 1 October 58.0%, 448,687 of 773,490 over 4,005; and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, 55.2%, 485,059 of 877,961. Two editions ago the same figure read 1.4%, 655 of 46,134, and that difference is not the model: until 17 September the hunger measure was reporting zero in a city that was starving, and the sick rate it feeds was being fed a zero (see [what a household eats](#7-goods--markets)); and the playtest's default player leaves the city alone for fifty-four months at a stretch, so every figure it reports is a city in crisis from neglect. A player who tops up power, water, streets, clinics and stores once a year runs the same seeds at 7.8% sick against 23.1%. Babies take the worst of it: twice as often ill, 4% a month past two months, on top of childcare's ×40.

### The two ways to bury somebody

A cemetery is a *stock*: plots are consumed permanently and the land never comes back. A crematorium is a *rate*: almost no land, a great deal of electricity, breaking even only when busy. Households whose monthly surplus would cover a plot over ten years choose burial; the rest choose cremation; overflow runs both ways. A city with neither leaves people where they fell, and **the unburied make the living ill** — up to 15 points on the sick rate, cleared the month a cemetery opens.

### Somebody pays for all of it

Healthcare carries **2,128 jobs** across its fourteen templates, more than any other category the city pays for — only the railway's three offer more. The treasury pays the staffed payroll plus maintenance, less what patients and funerals bring back — measured at about **20% cost recovery** when the ring was added, 25% on the default seed on 22 September, $5.04M a month, with 246 buried and none cremated in the last month of the run, 30% on 28 September, $5.76M a month, 396 buried and none cremated, 33% on 1 October, $4.28M a month, 400 buried and none cremated, and 12% on 5 October, at 0.7.49, $1.83bn a month in a city whose prices had risen 1,213-fold, with 13,865 lying unburied: a net-deficit business at the founding fees, as designed, and since 0.6.8 the player's to make something else. Fees are charged on people *served*, not beds built, so an empty ward is paid for and collects nothing — and since 0.6.8 served means treated. Since 0.7.41 every care gauge says *served*, higher being better: Build's rings and NEEDS YOU's rows the staffed places over the people who need them, unclamped (`CityNeeds.careServed()`), and the Services cards the month's coverage, held at 100% and cut for the priced out — two figures that can sit far apart in the month after a load ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). **Since 0.7.106 a bed nobody can pay for is not cover** (Jerus's A20, 0.7.27's D16): Build's rings, NEEDS YOU's rows and an order's after read the staffed beds less the people the fee turned away last month, floored at nothing (`CityNeeds.careHave()`, `BuildAdvice.carePlaces()`), as the Services cards have read the month's coverage since 0.7.28, so the advice and automatic building size care to the people who can use it, and Build's ring says how many of those without are priced out, *N people without, M priced out*. The model's own coverage is untouched, and so is the default playtest, whose player reads neither.

*Same 600-house city, 360 months, four programmes — measured before the base rates were halved and the sick ring added, and kept because the* shape *is what it is for*

| Programme | Population | Off sick | Births/mo | GDP/mo |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Nothing | 1,232 | 33.0% | 1.5 | $693k |
| General + death care | 1,496 | 3.0% | 1.9 | $1,298k |
| … plus childcare | 2,813 | 3.0% | 5.6 | $2,214k |
| Everything | 4,461 | 3.0% | 7.9 | $3,305k |

The city is founded with a doctor, a nursery, an almshouse, a churchyard and a constabulary — enough for about 1,200 people, sized off the pyramid's own equilibrium shares, and not a building among them. The churchyard's graves last four centuries for a village and six years for a city of eighty thousand.

### The price at the door

Jerus: *"healthcare should be an adjustable price, all the way to even make it a profitable business or the option to make it an obligatory insurance payment system."* Two dials since 0.6.8. `TaxPolicy.healthFeeScale` multiplies the three care fees — general, childcare and senior; funerals are deliberately unscaled — from nothing to 15× the founding ones, and `healthPremiumRate` takes up to 10% of every wage, employee side, on the EI premium's own base, into the treasury with nothing balancing it. Between them they make the corner the *Promises → Health* page names on a chip since 0.7.36, its sentence behind the chip's (i): *free at the point of use*, paid from taxes; *insurance*, no fee and a premium; *a business*, fees past the city's own break-even, which the page strikes live (`Healthcare.breakEvenScale()`, the gross cost over what the fees would raise at 1×) and marks on the fee's dial; *a mix*, a fee and a premium; or *fee-funded, in part*, a fee and the treasury for the rest. Under the chip WHO PAYS FOR CARE draws the month's cost as one bar in its four payers — treatment fees, funeral fees, the premium and the treasury — and the treasury's share is previewed at full service on both sides of a change; a service that cost nothing says so, where the page had read *Fees cover 0%*. The founding fees themselves are struck at the price level people expect since 0.7.42, like every money constant ([the month](#1-the-month)). The ceiling went from 5 to 15 after the first measurement, because a played city breaks even at ×7 to ×13 — the founding fees were set against founding wages, and the labour market has lifted a clinic's payroll since. The default seed on 22 September breaks even at ×9.85, on 28 September at ×10.73, on 1 October at ×18.84, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, at ×8.43.

**A household that cannot pay goes without care, not without food** — Jerus's rule, and what makes the fee a decision. The share of a household's bill that fits in what its plan says it will have after rent, its other bills and a basket for everybody in it — counting income, savings, the paper abroad and the credit still open, the waterfall's own order — is the share of its people the clinics treat, struck against the bill at full service so that a household that skipped last month does not read an empty bill as affordable and swing between served and starving. The rest go untreated in the sick rate, the swings and the births. A household that can cover its bills is served exactly as before, multiplied by exactly 1.0 and asserted at zero tolerance, so at the founding fee the cliff catches only households with nothing, the out of work past EI and elders on a pension: 0 to 247 people a month across the eight seeds, and none on the default seed on 22 September, 28 September or 1 October; on 5 October, at 0.7.49, two a month over the run and none in its last month. Fees at ×5 recovered about two thirds of the cost and priced out no more people than ×1, because the households the cliff catches are out at any positive fee and the working poor can still find $50 a head — a fee that prices a family out of childcare is a fee the dial cannot yet set. `HealthCheck`'s sections 12–16 walk it: the scale against the constants, the break-even, one household both ways, a poor city three times, a rich one at zero tolerance, and the premium to the penny. Since 0.7.12 the poor city's hunger is read over its last year rather than its last month, which was Jerus's change, and read that way the line is red: on 28 September the city charging fifteen times the founding fees was 30.2% hungry over its last year against the free city's 21.8%, 8.4 points against a tolerance of five. The gap has grown since: 77 points on 0.7.17's tree and 39 on 0.7.18's, as 0.7.18's implementer ran them (20.9% against 98.1%, then 14.5% against 53.5%), and on 1 October, at 0.7.23, the free city was 11.1% hungry over its last year and the dear one 51.1%, 40.0 points; on 5 October, at 0.7.49, with hunger counted in baskets since 0.7.43, it was 2.2% against 12.3%, 10.1 points, and the line now reads *no hungrier than the free one by more than the price of care*, the same five points. Which change of 0.7.17 opened it is not traced. Of the dear city's hungry, as 0.7.12 traced them, a quarter were priced out of care, a fifth were billed care their household row had already paid for, and nearly half had money for food after their fixed bills and still planned less, which is untraced. It shipped red on Jerus's word, *"Ship with it red, flagged"*. **Since 0.7.100 one builders' depot stands with the poor city** (his A14), as round 1 stood theirs at 0.7.17: its first depot had still been on site when the fee was set, and the dear twin's sickness stalled its builders for good. The gap fell from 19.7 points at 0.7.99, 2.2% against 21.9%, to 5.4, 0.1 of it priced out of a basket and 5.3 short on the shelf, both halves printed beside the line, which stayed red by 0.4 against the same five; two or four depots read 1.5 and 3.5, measured and not shipped, because choosing the count by the result would tune the fixture to the line. Since 0.7.102 it has passed at every gate, at 0.7.103 by −1.8 points, 3.2 priced out and −5.0 on the shelf — on the shelves' timing, the fee's rule unchanged — and since 0.7.103 the fixture reads the dear twin's fee in every month it turned somebody away, where it read the last month alone. Whether the shelf's half belongs in it is still Jerus's ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).

## 5. Crime & police

*Crime has reasons. Every adult at liberty is sorted once a month, cell by cell, into a graded list of them — because the cells are the only place the reasons meet: the pool knows who is out of work, the housing match knows who has no door and who is crowded, and the household books know who is going short.*

*The reasons, in order. Where a group overlaps another, the higher weight counts.*

| Reason | Weight |
| --- | ---: |
| No home | 5 |
| Out of work, EI run out | 4 |
| Short of money | 3 |
| Out of work, still on EI | 2 |
| Crowded — doubled up or flatsharing | 2 |
| No reason at all | 0.1 |
| *plus* too few police, per adult | 2 |

```
pressure = Σ adults × weight + 2 × (1 − coverage) × adults
crimes   = K × pressure × (1 − 0.90 × coverage^1.5)
coverage = staffed officers / (360 per 100,000)
```

**K is struck, not typed.** It is solved at startup so that a city with Canada's police coverage and the game's own equilibrium adult share commits Canada's 5,585 crimes per 100,000 a year. Full coverage is twice Canada's 180 officers per 100,000 and takes **90%** off — drastically, and never to nothing, which was the brief.

A quarter of crimes are violent. Each costs its victim **half a month off work**, which goes onto the sick rate as an injury term, and **0.115%** of them kill — calibrated against Canada's 1.61 homicides per 100,000. The rest is theft, worth a quarter of an unskilled monthly wage each, half taken from households and half from the tills, and handed to the offenders in proportion to the weight their own cell carried. Theft leaves a sector's books through a named `stolen` line, so the money identity can see it.

**Arrests scale with coverage**: 9% of crimes at full coverage, pro rata below it. Everyone caught serves six months in a ring of monthly cohorts. A prisoner is out of the labour force, out of the housing match, out of every offender group, has their debts frozen and keeps their own ledger row. **Caught and not held is a real state**: with no cell free, the arrest is recorded and the person walks. The prisons page sets the city's prisoners beside Canada's, 127 per 100,000 (`Crime.CANADA_PRISONERS_PER_100K`, 0.7.28).

*Four buildings, all paid for by the city like the hospitals and the schools*

| Building | Capacity | Jobs | All-in |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Police Station | 120 officers | 172 | $45M |
| Police Headquarters | 500 officers | 750 | $180M |
| Jail | 300 cells | 264 | $360M |
| Penitentiary | 600 cells | 590 | $600M |

Measured over eight 333-year seeds: crime runs at **1.8–2.3 times Canada's rate** in the years before the first station and settles at **about a tenth of it** once coverage is full, with the residue coming almost entirely from the long-term unemployed and the crowded. Between 2,100 and 2,900 people are caught over a run and *every one of them walks*, because the smallest prison in the catalogue is 300 cells for $360M and a city of 15,000 never needs or affords one. Seven to ten people are killed over three centuries; $12.8M to $18.6M is stolen. Those were cities of fifteen thousand. The default seed on 22 September ended at 130,978 people with three police stations, coverage at 46%, crime at 1.22× Canada's, **59,189 caught over the run and every one of them still walking**, 334 killed and $891M stolen — the advisor built a station three times in four thousand months and a prison never, so the lockup question below had not gone away, it had grown. On 28 September the same seed ended at 184,736 people with a station and a headquarters, coverage at 62% and crime at 1.19× Canada's, and this time the advisor had built jails: four stood at the end with 344 people inside, and 35,279 of the 79,592 caught over the run were still not held; 593 were killed and $1.50bn stolen. On 1 October, at 0.7.23, it ended at 163,391 people with three stations and nothing else, coverage at 43% and crime at 1.71× Canada's; it built no jail, so all 69,581 caught over the run walked, and 423 were killed and $1.00bn stolen. On 5 October, at 0.7.49, it ended at 185,111 people with one station, coverage at 15% and crime at 2.23× Canada's, too few police the largest of its reasons; all 62,638 caught over the run walked, 961 were killed, and $763bn was stolen, at prices 1,213 times the founding's.

## 6. Work & output

*Seventeen private sectors, each keeping its own books, its own cash reserve, its own debt, its own share register and, since 0.7.12, its own bonds — and, since 11 September, each of them* one class *extending a single template. Ten of the seventeen have been added since, five of them in the three days to 18 September and the last two, oil and its refinery, in 0.7.62, and the whole point of the template is that each cost an afternoon rather than a week.*

> **Why there is a template**
>
> Jerus: *"we should make a single template, and every single sector just extends it, and adds or overrides, right? cause in the future there will be over a thousand or near a thousand sectors."* Before it, six sectors were five handlers in five shapes, named by hand in about a hundred places — eleven loops in the economy manager, a six-way switch in the books, thirteen enumerations in the interface. A seventh would have been a week of finding them. It is now one class, one constant, one line in the registry. Sixty files changed, fifteen new, eight deleted; save format 21 and a clean break.

Everything a sector has is declared once in the template: its **identity** (a saved key, a label, the build-menu group its buildings sit under), its **buildings** (every template in `buildings.json` names its owner, and the sector reads capacity, jobs, land, book value, power, water and road load off its own stacks), its **production** (what it makes, what it uses, how many months it stocks), its **books** (one statement, one shape), its **credit, listing and money abroad**, its **planning**, and its **save**. A sector class is now a declaration of about twenty lines. Mining is the shortest, and the shape a thousand of them should have; since 0.7.112 it stands on one of two bases the materials chains extend (below), and Materials is the shortest on the template itself. Since 0.7.120 Mining reads as *Iron Mining* and Heavy Industry as *Iron & Steel* wherever a sector is named, their saved keys kept (Jerus's Q2 of 8 October).

| Sector | Makes | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retail | groceries, priced on a floor of what the stock cost and half again, and above it toward the price that clears the shelf (0.7.43) | thirteen foods — local first and imports for the shortfall: bread and bakery goods from the ovens, dairy, eggs, meat, vegetables and fruit from the farms, the five processed goods from the plants; grains and fish only ever off a ship |
| Real estate | housing — one rent cheque per occupied home | houses and apartment blocks from construction |
| Industry | bread and bakery goods | crops from local fields first, imports for the shortfall — it used to make food out of nothing |
| Iron & steel | steel, exported or sold to the fabricators; and since 0.7.123 scrap from the city's old steel, pig iron, coke and ore pellets, its scrap, pig iron and coke to its own works first | scrap, the city's own first, since 0.7.120, where it had taken local ore first and imported scrap for the shortfall; and since 0.7.123 iron ore, coking and thermal coal, limestone and lime, and the old steel the city throws out |
| Iron mining | iron ore, since 0.7.120 twenty thousand tonnes a month a mine | a deposit, which the player must buy as land; and since 0.7.120 diesel |
| Construction | building work, recognised as it is delivered | materials |
| Materials | construction material | power, water, wages |
| Business services | support, back-office and engineering work, by the seat-month, all of it sold abroad | people, almost entirely — and an engineering office needs licensed engineers before it will open at all |
| Manufacturing | fabricated steel and machinery — export only until 16 September, when the assembly plants became their first customer at home | steel, local or imported — 44% of a fabricator's revenue at the world's price since 0.7.120, 61% at the US band before it |
| Agriculture | crops for the mills; and since 16 September dairy and eggs, meat, vegetables and fruit for the shelf and the meat works | land, heavily; labour and power barely |
| Food processing | processed meats, ready meals, snacks, cooking fats, drinks — a third of the shelf by weight | meat, vegetables and grains at the Meat Works, crops at the other two; the first customer the Livestock Farm ever had at home |
| Rail | haulage — the freight that used to leave inside the trade band, billed to the shipper at home as a fraction of the lorry rate | track, wagon sets it buys from the Locomotive Works, and diesel since 0.7.76, off the refiners' tanks first and imported for the rest |
| Automotive | cars for the households and the world; vans for the sectors and wagon sets for the railway, which the world will not buy | fabricated steel and machinery — the first thing in the city that buys either |
| Luxury retail | a counter: watches sold at a margin struck against the buyers at the price it charges | luxury goods, all of them imported, deliberately |
| Restaurants | meals, one ninetieth of a person-month each, at three to eight times what the food cost | the same thirteen foods off the same shelf at the same prices — it imports nothing |

**Materials is the seventh**, and the first sector added under the template. The Construction Materials Plant used to feed the city's yard for free; it is a business now, filling a shed rather than planning to two months of demand, and planning on a thirty-six-month view because a building boom is not a month long. A city that builds hard makes materials dear, and a plant near the builders is the first thing in the game that gets cheaper for the buyer *and* richer for the maker at once.

### The eleventh to the fifteenth

**Food processing is the eleventh.** Jerus: *"now a new sector which makes the ready meals, processed meals, snacks, drinks, and cooking fats?"* Those five are 16.3 kg of the reference basket's 50, a third of what a household eats by weight, and every gram of them arrived by ship. Three plants, each decided by a different number: the Meat Works buys meat, vegetables and grains and makes processed meats and ready meals, with the input bill at 40% of revenue; the Snack & Oils Plant turns crops into snacks and cooking fats at 19%; the Bottling Plant turns crops into drinks at 4%. It took four calibration passes and three of them were not calibration: the generic planner sizes a sector by *one* good and skipped every template that did not make it, so two of the three plants were not refused but invisible; a first plant was valued at the import ceiling its own arrival would end, so processed meat stood at $8.90 the month the works was financed and $7.70 the month it opened, and the sector now prices its own plant with its nameplate in the supply; and the sales tax was not in the estimate, which matters here because an import carries no input credit and a city with no herds imports every gram — month 72 of one run read $35k of revenue, $1k of operating income and $5k of tax.

Then the calibration itself, by revenue per worker, which is the ratio that decides whether a maker survives a city growing up: the first pass ran \$6,000–\$10,700 a head against the two bakeries' \$13,500 and \$17,800 and a foundry's \$33,600, and a Bottling Plant was six people making a tonne a day; the three are \$17,100, \$16,800 and \$18,000 a head now, payroll 21–22% of revenue at mid-band. And one rule no other sector needs: **nobody builds a food plant on exports**, because the world's band is narrower than the processing step — raw meat lands at \$7.00 and processed meat ships at \$5.60 — so a plant is financed only when the city already eats what it would make. What the sector is for, in one measurement: at month 98 of a real city the same Meat Works is worth **\$16,559 a month on meat at a farm's export floor and \$1,678 on meat off a ship**. The building did not change; the farms did. Eight seeds: median GDP up 11%, \$375.8M to \$417.9M a month, population unchanged, the sector ending every seed with \$52M–\$86M of assets and zero write-downs in seven of eight.

**Rail is the twelfth and Automotive the thirteenth**, and both are told in [transport](#21-transport--vehicles): the railway is the business that wants to be paid the freight every price in this game has always had inside it, and the assembly plant is the first thing in the city that buys a beam or a machine — ore, steel, fabrication, and now something a person drives away in.

**Luxury retail is the fourteenth.** Jerus: *"lets add restuarants as well as luxury stores, these two will absorb some spending as well"*, and on the pricing, *"supply v demand, thats the most important thing."* A Boutique and a Department Store import what they sell — the world has no shortage of watches — and what a city can be short of is a counter, so the margin is what gets struck, on the market's own rule with a mark-up in place of a price: 1.25× the landed cost with nobody in the shop, 4.00× with a queue at the door, and the position between them from what is wanted against what the counters can serve. Until 0.7.19 *what is wanted* was the pieces the households would take at the floor price, which nobody is ever charged: in Jerus's year-149 city that queue held the margin at 2.646 while only the shoppers who would pay 2.646 bought, and the sector earned 2.5 times any other's profit. Since 0.7.19 it is the pieces they would buy at the margin the shop strikes — Jerus chose *"The customers actually served"*: *"The markup reads the shoppers who buy at the price actually charged, not a queue counted at the lowest price"* — and since a dearer margin loses buyers, the margin is the one fixed point at which the buyers it leaves put it exactly there (`LuxuryRetail.strikeMargin()`, by bisection on the households' own demand); the boutiques' planner reads the same buyers. In his city it took the margin from 2.662 to 2.263 (0.7.19). Since 0.7.43 the shop charges a sixth of the way there a month, in logs, rather than the fixed point itself (`LuxuryRetail.MARGIN_SPEED`), because a shop's price is sticky; the kitchens' margin moves the same way (`Restaurants.MARGIN_SPEED`). Crowded shops widen the margin, a wide margin makes boutiques worth building, and the investor builds them. What it is for is the hoard: household net worth stops diverging and starts oscillating. It is deliberately an import, so a rich city's spending leaves rather than going round again. It is also a fragile business — on one seed it finishes with 22 write-downs and a 252-month borrowing ban — and the sizing of the two buildings against a city's luxury budget has not been tuned. The swing it showed every other month for a while was a price nobody paid, found by 0.7.12: the shop costed its stock at last month's clearing price, which in a month with no seller at home was half the import price, so its shelf turned round in 98% of months; it reads the import price now, and turns round in 2%.

**Restaurants are the fifteenth**, and the rule Jerus attached is what makes them a different sector rather than a second boutique: *a meal out replaces groceries*. So a kitchen imports nothing. A dinner is the same thirteen foods off the same shelf at the same prices, which makes the kitchens a **second buyer** in a market the city is already short of — where *"let the basket get dearer, not bigger"* actually bites — and a **second door** to the food there is, since Retail's binding constraint is coverage rather than stock. A meal is one ninetieth of a person-month, three a day for thirty days, and the hunger measure counts a dinner at what a person-month of food costs, not at what the kitchen charged, because three to eight times the food is wages, rent and somebody else's washing up and none of it is nourishment. The margin is 3.0× to 8.0×, wider than the trade's own 2.9–3.6× because in this city labour runs at four times food — three centuries of farms and food plants made food cheap while the wage schedule did not move — and at most a third of anybody's meals are eaten out. The harness caught three faults nothing else would have: the sector had no demand at all, because a share of a rich household's *surplus* is a share of zero once the wealth term is in the plan; the kitchens could not pay their staff, because a building pays at 100% and serves at the operating rate, which is about half; and a kitchen that stocked for what it served last month was self-limiting for ever. Eight seeds against 0.6.6: **median hunger 36% to 22%**, sickness 18.1% to 16.6%, the kitchens feeding 11–26% of each city and the shops selling about 5% fewer baskets, which is the crowding-out working. The sector finishes seven seeds of eight with zero write-downs at 2.00% credit, which is the profile of a business that cannot fail, and that is on the list.

### Five ratios, and they multiply

| Ratio | Short of it because | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Energy | generation below draw | a step: output scales with the share delivered, and the bill scales with it too |
| Water | supply below draw | same shape; residents draw 0.3 units a head and nobody bills them |
| Roads | load past 90% of capacity | non-linear, floored at 35% — a gridlocked city still moves, slowly; per sector since the streams were split, because a tram takes one business's staff out of the jam and leaves the one next door's lorries in it |
| Health | the workforce is ill or hurt | cuts output only; the payroll is paid in full |
| Vans | the sector has not taken delivery of the lorries its plant needs | the only one a business *buys*: a fleet is built up at an eighth a month, wears out over ten years, and a firm with none is slowed to 60%, not stopped — it hires haulage; since 0.7.12 it orders only the vans its cash and credit can pay for |

On top of those sits the **job fill rate**, worked out per job type: the allocator spends the workforce across the posts the city offers, and a sector's output is discounted by how much of its establishment it could actually staff, and its payroll is each job type's wage on the posts of that type it filled (0.7.17). Since 0.7.18 **workers take the best-paid job they qualify for** ([labour](#11-labour--schools)), so where a short city's bottom rung would out-pay the one above it the two fill as one market, and the empty posts move up the ladder rather than sitting on its bottom rung. The posts the city offers are every building's, bar the builders' crews their work does not need, which they lay off ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)). The four that arrive from outside are the city's to fix; the fifth is the sector's own capital, and is told with the vehicles in [transport](#21-transport--vehicles). Since 0.7.30 a business's Operations page draws the fill and the five as a cascade whose last step is its operating rate (`SectorFlow.THROTTLES`), and its note, which had said output was cut by whichever of five was thinnest and left the vans out, names six and says they multiply, and since 0.7.105 Refining's names seven, the crude units' run the seventh ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)); a sector with nothing standing reads *no plant standing*, where it had read *Staffed 100%* beside a rate in red.

> **Why it is a ratio basis and not a ratio**
>
> A month's income statement is written at the start of the month, off last month's utilisation. The simulation then moves it. Save after that and a reloaded game would price the month at ratios it was never traded at — which showed up the day roads arrived, as $0.51 of income appearing out of a reload. Every statement carries the utilisation it was struck against.

### Maintenance is an operating cost, and it is demand

Every building in the city pays 1% of its build cost a year to stand — every sector, every city-maintained category, and the bank's branches — in cash, in materials *and* in construction points, placed as a real order with the builders rather than written off as a line. Since 0.7.19 the cash part is the building's cash cost with its labour at today's builders' wages, and the bill carries the builders' sales tax: a business that makes taxable supplies claims it back as an input, and the landlords, whose rent is an exempt supply, and the bank's branch bear it, because no rebate reaches a repair; the tax on the city's own repairs is remitted to the city's treasury and so comes home ([VAT](#12-tax-policy--gdp)). On a forty-year stock that is about **40% of the city's whole construction output**, permanently. Charging it made the city *bigger*: population 74,043 → 77,121, GDP $81.7M → $106.2M a month, unemployment 41.5% → 37.6% — because maintenance here is somebody's order book.

Construction recognises revenue *as work is delivered*: an order adds to unearned revenue and a backlog, each month's points earn their share, and the builders buy their material as they build. Booking it all up front made the sector look enormously profitable in a boom and catastrophic the year after. Until 0.7.17 its payroll had a 25% idle floor, every post kept filled and a quarter of the wages paid with nothing to build; since then it keeps a core crew of a quarter of its *posts*, paid in full, and lays the rest off onto EI, and the shedding spiral is still possible and still worth warning about ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)). Since 0.7.22 an order's unearned remainder can go back — a cancelled order of the city's is refunded out of the order book — and the overtime the city pays on a rushed site is earned beside the work on a line of its own, *Overtime on rushed sites*, and paid out to the crews as wages.

### Two bases, and machinery the chains use

**Since 0.7.112 the template has two bases under it** (batch I2, the materials chains' second; `sectors.ProcessingSector`, `sectors.ExtractionSector`). The chains to come — iron redone, coal, copper, stone and wood, thirty-seven buildings — are each a set of rows if the machinery under them exists, and a rewrite if it does not, so it was built first, and since 0.7.120 the iron chain stands on it. **A processing sector** orders its works as the refinery has since 0.7.82: every works that makes something weighed on what it makes, valued made here — the net import price for as much as the city imports, the net export price past it — less what it uses, valued the other way round (`SpreadPlanner.outValue()`, `inValue()`), less its running and standing costs, its consumables and its own power, past the feed, ground, staff and money gates, the best on its cost ordered, one order in flight; and a kind of works whose last one standing earns below nothing six months running is the kind the shrinking rules may sell (`idleMonths.*`, by template id). Iron & Steel has stood on it since 0.7.120, the first, and since 0.7.123 it weighs a works with the lorries its tonnes need as well, their running cost in what the works earns and their price in its whole cost ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). **An extraction sector** is Mining's rule written once — the ground the limit, a mine on a free site of its resource, the best return on its cost, spare once the ore is out — and Mining moved onto it whole, to the bit, the same arithmetic and the same words; since 0.7.120 it asks the spread planner's money gate on an Iron Mine's whole cost before it sinks one, and its estimate takes the mine's consumables off. Three pieces sit in the template beside them. **Captive use**: a good a sector both makes and uses — coke in a steelworks, anodes in copper — goes to its own need first, the market sees only the rest, and no sale or purchase is booked, so revenue and costs are not inflated (`Sector.captive()`). **A works' own power**: a building may make power (`"gen"` in `buildings.json`); it is billed only for its draw past it, and what it makes past its draw it sells the grid at the tariff, on its statement's revenue and outside its sales, the city's utility paying the statements' figure, the money audit noting the pair (*PowerSold*, *PowerBought*). **Consumables**: money a month at nameplate, in the world's money, for what a works uses up, bought at its operating rate and the exchange factor as a service from the world, an import in the trade by good, as the oil shuttle's freight is (`"consumables"`, `Sector.buyConsumables()`). Until 0.7.120 none of the three was used. Since then the two arc furnaces and the Iron Mine buy consumables, and since 0.7.123 ten works do; Iron & Steel keeps its coke, pig iron and scrap captive, moved on its own rails, so its lorries carry its plant's tonnes less those (`Sector.tonnesMoved()`); and the Coke Ovens, the Blast Furnace and the Oxygen Steel Shop make 8,000, 60,000 and 25,000 kW from their gas, the first two selling the grid what they make past their draws ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). `MaterialsCheck` holds all of it, and at 0.7.112 the playtest's eight traces were 0.7.111's to the byte ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)). What the bases and the planners test an order on is its whole cost since the same batch ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)).

## 7. Goods & markets

*There used to be two bespoke markets, one for food and one for iron, each with its own formula and its own bugs. There is one rule now, and forty-nine goods that obey it or opt out — thirteen of which are the food on a grocer's shelf, three of which are vehicles, two of which the world makes and will not buy back, ten of which are oil: the crude the wells lift (0.7.62) and, since 0.7.76, the nine products a barrel is cut into, where until then a refinery made one good, fuel; and eight of which came with steel: scrap since 0.7.120, split from the ore it had stood in for, and since 0.7.123 the seven the integrated route makes and burns.*

```
supply   = flow + stock / 6              // never the raw stockpile
position = demand / (demand + supply)
price    = exportPrice + (importPrice − exportPrice) × position
```

The symmetric form is load-bearing. `demand/supply` clamped to 1 prices a *perfectly balanced* market at the buyer's worst price — one mine feeding one mill used to clear at $399.40 against a $400 ceiling. Here a matched pair splits the band. Supply is flow plus a slice of the stockpile, never the stockpile itself: pricing off inventory alone is circular — low price, withhold, bigger inventory reads as more supply, lower price — and measured that way food collapsed to the floor in every scenario including a genuine shortage.

Neither end of a band is a constant: both are read off the world's own prices every month, through the exchange rate, so a devaluation is import inflation mechanically — and an incentive to substitute. And since 16 September neither end is a single number either: each is the world's own price plus, or less, the cost of moving one unit, so the band a city faces is three quarters freight and one quarter the world's margin, and the freight is a price a railway can win back — see [transport](#21-transport--vehicles). Since 0.7.29 the market reads its wedge apart (`GoodsMarket.worldMargin()`, `freightInBand()`, `railInWedge()`, `bandByLorry()`), and Infrastructure's Freight page draws it a good at a time. The shops buy local food first and import the shortfall; the mills took local ore first and scrap for the rest until 0.7.120, and since then the arc furnaces take scrap, the city's own first, and since 0.7.123 the pelletising plant and the blast furnaces the ore. One clearing pass runs every month: flow goods are made, seller-priced goods sold, each traded good priced, offered, bid for and allocated **pro rata on both sides**, then imported or exported, then the stockable goods made. Every fill is a trade; nothing in these classes moves money. Since 0.7.12 a seller stocks only what its cash and the credit it can still get will pay for, after the bills it cannot avoid; a maker's inputs are the exception and are bought whole, because what a maker produces does not yet read what it bought, and holding its inputs back would make goods out of nothing. The households are not a sector and cannot bid in a strike: they take cars off the makers' shelf at the struck price and import the rest, through the same door the city uses for building material, and a month's purchases are demand for next month's strike. A good with a floor of zero — a van, a wagon set — strikes at exactly zero when nobody here wants one, and a saved zero is restored as zero, because for one build a guard against a missing figure dropped it and a reloaded city read a mid-band price in its place.

### What the shops charge

Jerus asked why a city whose central bank held every bond, aimed at 20% and charged nothing barely inflated, and most of the answer was the grocer's shelf: it was cost-plus times a scarcity mark-up of at most 1.6, read off the share of a head count the shops delivered, so no price in the city's basket read anybody's money. Since 0.7.43 it clears on money (`Retail.repriceShelf()`):

```
floor    = max(the opening price at the expected price level, what the stock cost × 1.5)
clearing = the price at which the baskets the households ask for meet what the shops can hand over
target   = clamp(clearing, floor, 1.5 × floor)
ln shelf' = (1 − 1/6) × (ln shelf + ln(1 + expected inflation a month)) + 1/6 × ln target
```

What the shops can hand over is their coverage times their operating rate, as far as the shelf holds; the clearing price is found by bisection on the households' own demand at a price ([people](#2-people)), and a shortage is shared out at it, so the poorest go without first. Sticky in logs, the shelf drifts with what people expect while it closes on what clears it, about six months to clear (`CLEAR_SPEED`), and one under its floor closes half the gap a month (`FLOOR_CATCH_UP`). The cap of 1.5× the floor (`CLEARING_CAP`) is the most a shortage can do: a cap of 2 was measured to run the autopilot at 3.2% a year. Rent moves in the same shape at a lease's pace, a twelfth a month, and the boutiques' and the kitchens' margins at a sixth ([prices](#16-prices-the-currency--the-world)).

**And the suppliers wait for their money** (0.7.44; `SupplierCredit`). A grocer restocks only as far as its cash and its credit reach (0.7.12), and since 0.7.43 it sells only what is on its shelf, so a till that ran dry bought nothing, sold nothing and stayed dry: 11.9% of the autopilot's months after month 240 handed over less than 5% of what was wanted, and in 94% of them the city had the shops. A real grocer's suppliers wait about a month, so these do: what the till cannot cover of the month's stock, up to the stock for a month of the sales the shops expect at what it costs to bring in (`Retail.SUPPLIER_CREDIT_MONTHS`), is bought on their credit, with no interest and no fee, and repaid at the next strike out of the takings of its sale. It is on both sets of books — the grocer's payables, its suppliers' receivables, the world's share across the audit as a financial flow in and, a month later, out — and the lender reads each as if it were not there. Total stock-outs fell from 11.9% of those months to 0.1%.

### What a household eats

Until September 2026 one good called *Food* did all of this: a unit was a person fed for a month, everything they ate, and every question about a city's diet had that one answer. The shelf is itemised now, and what goes into the basket is decided by income rather than by a dial.

**Engel's law** is the first half: as a household gets richer the *share* of its money spent on food falls while the *amount* rises. **Bennett's law** is the second: the calories move off starchy staples onto meat, dairy, fish and produce. That is why grains carry a *negative* income elasticity — a staple is an inferior good, and a household eats less rice as it gets richer, not more.

Neither law is told what to do at the top of the ladder. A basket is scaled by the **lesser** of what a household can afford and what it can eat, so a poor household is money-limited and goes hungry while a rich one is calorie-limited and buys dearer food instead of more. The falling food share at the top is something the model *produces* rather than something it is given — which matters, because the first draft typed that share in as a constant and produced households whose calories went *down* as they got richer.

There is a third axis that is not income at all. **Convenience food is bought for time**: a working parent buys it at any income, and an out-of-work parent with the same children and the same money does not, because what they are short of is money and what they have is afternoons.

Income is measured in **multiples of what bare subsistence costs** rather than in dollars, so a currency reform cannot move it and the number means something you can say out loud: *this household can afford four times the calories it needs to survive.* The shops stock one shelf for the whole city, averaged over its households by *headcount* rather than by spending — a shelf stocked for money would carry the rich end's fish and fruit for a city of labourers.

> **The shelf is thirteen pantries**
>
> A shop can sell a basket only if it has all of it: what it can serve is the good that runs out first, which is Liebig's barrel on a shelf. That is also how a units bug was caught — shelf room was still sized in *units of food* when the goods became *kilograms*, and one person-month is exactly 50 kg of them, so every shop in the city delivered 20% of demand for ever. A city with roads and a city without scored identically until it was found; afterwards, **87% against 31%**.

When the shelf was itemised all thirteen were imported. Eleven of them can be made at home now: the ovens bake bread and bakery goods out of crops and export what the city cannot eat; the farms make dairy and eggs, meat, vegetables and fruit; the plants make the five processed goods out of meat, vegetables, grains and crops. Grains and fish still only ever come off a ship. And since 18 September the shelf has a second buyer: the kitchens buy the same thirteen in the reference basket's proportions and sell them cooked, one ninetieth of a person-month a plate.

> **The hunger measure was reporting zero in a city that was starving**
>
> Until 17 September the figure read *sold over the shops' own demand*, and the shops' demand was already the least of coverage, want and what could be afforded — the shops' performance against a queue the shops had themselves decided they could serve. At month 3,840 of seed 0 the households planned 21,446,946 baskets, the shops could serve 177,760 people, and the line said 76%. A basket is one person-month, so the city wanted a hundred and twenty-two baskets a head and was allowed one. Honest: **58% of people short, 1.4% of the groceries asked for**.
