Not a reporting change: the hungry feed the sick rate, which feeds the labour supply, and it had been fed a zero. Turning it on cost the default seed 11% of its population and 14% of its GDP — revealed, not caused — and showed a cascade nobody had seen, sickness 12.9% to 34.5%, of which hunger is eight points and *the unburied fifteen*. The basket count is floored to a whole basket, because dividing money by money and keeping the fraction broke the currency-reform twin 1.5e-06 at a time.

**Since 0.7.43 hunger is counted in baskets**: what each household was handed at the last sale, and the meals it ate out at a ninetieth of a basket each, against a basket a head. It had been the plan times the share delivered, one share for the whole city, so a shortage fell on everybody alike; it falls on the households the price leaves out now. And since 0.7.27 it comes in two halves, both saved: the people who would have gone short with the shelves full, priced out (`HouseholdBalance.getHungryAtFullShelves()`, `getHungerPricedOut()`), and the rest, whom the shelves left short (`getHungerShortOfStock()`), beside the share of what was asked for that the shops handed over (`getDeliveredShare()`), which had read 1 after every load. In the 2,400-month research city at 0.7.27 GOING SHORT read 42.2%, 49 people could not afford a basket, and the shops handed over 3% of what was planned. The default seed's city at 0.7.49 ended 79% short, the shops handing over 5.7% of the baskets it asked for and filling 44% of what their coverage could serve, running at 44% on roads at 71%: a city its player leaves alone for decades.

**And the city can pay toward it** (0.7.43). Jerus: *"yes price rations, with an optional government assistance, defualt zero"*. The food assistance dial on *Promises → Food* (`TaxPolicy.getFoodAssistance()`, 0 to 100%, nothing by default) is the share of an eligible household's baskets a voucher covers at the shelf price, and the voucher is money it bids with. A household is eligible when a basket a head would take more than half of what it has after its fixed bills and its investment income (`FOOD_ASSISTANCE_MEANS_SHARE`; that income smoothed over a year since 0.7.45, because a coupon landing in one month took a whole row in and out), which takes in everybody with nothing after their fixed bills. It is paid only on the baskets actually got, into the household's savings at the till, and by the treasury in the same month on a line of its own (`TreasuryLine.FOOD_ASSISTANCE`), a promise, because the groceries have been eaten.

## 8. The private sector

*Nobody tells businesses what to build. Each of the seventeen sectors measures a different signal, projects it six months out, and expands only if the new capacity would carry the interest on its whole cost, whoever pays for it.*

```
the brake   estimated monthly profit ≥ a month's interest at the real rate on the order's whole cost × 1.25   // the whole cost since 0.7.113
the real rate = max(the rate − the inflation the owners expect, a quarter of the rate)   // since 0.7.42
```

A business test, not a credit limit: the lender is willing, the business should not be, and since 0.7.113 it asks it of the whole cost whether the till or a loan pays (below). Since 0.7.42 it is real (`BusinessInvestment.realTestRate()`, `REAL_HURDLE_FLOOR`): the debt is nominal and the profits grow with prices, so a 6% loan in a city expecting 2% costs 4% in what the profits will buy, and the floor keeps expected inflation near the rate from making borrowing free. Alongside it: one order at a time per sector, bar the landlords, who since 0.7.17 may hold twelve months of the builders' work on their sites ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)); no order larger than would open inside twelve months at the wait it would actually have beside everything on site, where until 0.7.17 it was twelve months of the *whole city's* construction output, as though the order had the builders to itself; and a 5% headroom target so nothing expands into capacity it already has. Since 0.7.8 a plan is judged at the rate the loan would actually be written at, off the default curve at the leverage the loan would leave the sector at, and since 0.7.12 at the blend of a bond's coupon and the loan's rate where a bond carries part of it; 3,452 plans were declined on price over the default eight when the curve went in. A landlord's homes answer to the lender's own test instead (0.7.11): the building's net operating income must cover the mortgage's payment 1.20× — since 0.7.44 a payment struck at the same real rate of the insured rate, though the mortgage is still written at the insured rate and a refusal names the rate it tested. **All three are searched for** since 0.7.54 — the largest order inside the wait, the largest slice of it that carries its interest, and the most a landlord's mortgage buys — where each was counted a building at a time, so that the month grew with the order: a ten-billion copy of city2400 took a median of 7.0 s a month, and up to 143 s. The size and the mortgage halve, because their tests are proved to hold on a run from one; the trim asks the old countdown's first 16 slices and then doubles down and halves (`Game.COUNTDOWN_SLICES`), so an order trimmed by fewer is decided exactly as before, and a refusal still names the rate at the whole order. In every run measured the searches decided what the counts did, that copy's month at a median of 46 ms, and `OrderSearchCheck` holds them to the countdowns.

**And every planner that builds posts asks whether the city could staff it** (0.7.18; `Sector.staffing()`). Jerus: *"Construction, Retail, Restaurants, Luxury and the makers check whether they can staff a building before building it (the check four sectors already use), and the 20% it allows can't be jobs nobody can fill."* A building passes when the city's spare workers could fill 80% of its posts (`MIN_STAFFABLE_TO_ORDER`), each band's spare counted as the best-paid-job fill would place it, and none of the rest is in a band nobody can fill. That last is Jerus's reading of his own words, *"Truly unfillable only"*: a band with no spare workers, nobody above it who could step down into it, and no migrants who come for it. Every band has migrants who come for its wage since the same batch, so in play it never binds — 0 of 2,160 staffing questions in a default city — and stands for a band that ever has no way in, which `InvestCheck`'s section 18 causes. An order of several is held to all of them, and the advisor's hold says *"the city could staff X% of a Y; it wants 80%"*. The literal first reading, no posts at all in a band with nobody spare this month, failed every building with a college post in every city without a college, and the default cities ended at 13,808 people against 162,702. Real Estate's homes have no posts and are not asked, and the city's own buildings are the player's; the bank's branch is asked since 0.7.19. In Jerus's year-149 city, run on for 120 months, it held Retail and Restaurants back in 108 of them, Luxury in 116 and Food Processing and Mining in all 120 (0.7.18).

| Sector | Watches |
| --- | --- |
| Real estate | jobs plus jobs under construction — never population, which is its own echo |
| Retail | baskets, since 0.7.43: the households' demand at the shelf's floor, grown with the population over the order's lead time and capped at housing that exists or is being built, against what its shops can hand over — coverage times the operating rate — so a city whose shops cover everybody on paper and hand over 43% of it builds another; until then people against coverage; and since 0.7.83 a second question each month beside the shops', the drivers' litres of petrol, grown as the people are over an order's lead time, against what its filling stations can sell; and since 0.7.106 what the brake tests of a shop or a station is its margin less its posts at today's wages (`Retail.estimatedMonthlyProfit()`, Jerus's A18), where the grocers at their floor had borrowed for shops whose margin did not pay their staff — the test only, the shelf's floor and the ranking as they were |
| Industry | shop coverage against output; refuses outright if price is below cost |
| Construction | its own backlog over what the sites are left after the repairs, expanding past nine months of it, and only with a depot the city could staff (0.7.17) |
| Iron & steel | since 0.7.120 the spread planner, as the refiners' (below): of its works that pass the gates — feed, ground, staff, money — the one that earns most on its whole cost at the city's own prices; since 0.7.123 each weighed with the lorries its tonnes need, and a Scrap Yard only once the city's old steel past what the yards standing take is six tenths of another's intake (below). Until 0.7.120 spare ore — mines first, mills after |
| Mining | unmined deposits, so geology gates it and the player controls the gate: since 0.7.57 the iron sites of the world's fields in the ground the city owns, one mine a site, and since 0.7.62 counting Iron Mines only (`Game.minesCommitted()`); since 0.7.112 on the extraction base, its rule unchanged ([work and output](#6-work--output)); and since 0.7.120 an Iron Mine asked the spread planner's money gate on its whole cost before it is sunk, its estimate less its consumables |
| Materials | the sites' outstanding orders and the repair draw, on a three-year view |
| Business services | seats it could actually staff — the world's appetite for the work is unbounded, so the brake is people, not demand |
| Manufacturing | the price of steel, its biggest bill — 44% of a fabricator's revenue at the world's price since 0.7.120, its wages 29%, where at the US band steel was 61% |
| Agriculture | the mills' crop bill against the price of the ground a field has to stand on — and refuses while anybody in the city has nowhere to live, unless since 0.7.107 its zone holds ground, and then builds only there and only as far as the zone holds ([zoning](#18-land)) |
| Food processing | what the city already eats of its five goods, less what it can already supply, valued at each good's export floor — never a forecast, and never the export market, because the band is narrower than the processing step; scores every template it owns, not the one that makes its planning good |
| Rail | the freight nobody is carrying — it will not lay a line under 60% used, Materials' lesson relearned the afternoon a spur went up in a town of four hundred houses |
| Automotive | the parts — one new plant may want at most a quarter of everything the city fabricates, because "spare" was the wrong word and cost a fixture three hundred months |
| Luxury retail | the buyers at the margin it charges, against the counters — the queue counted at the floor price until 0.7.19 |
| Restaurants | the queue at the door: meals asked for against the tables there are, and a kitchen values itself, because nothing else can |
| Oil | oil sites the city owns with no well on them and oil left in them: one well a month, a well retired when its oil runs out (0.7.62); since 0.7.84 a land well only on a dry site, retired worn out at 263 months and its site drilled again; and since 0.7.91, after the land well, the sea's: a well into a platform's free slot, a pipeline that pays, a platform on the shallow field with the most sea sites free; and since 0.7.93 a land well on the ground's pool of oil and a platform well on the sea's (below); and since 0.7.113 each kind asked to carry the interest on its whole cost before the planner walks on to the next |
| Refining | since 0.7.82 the spread planner: of its buildings that pass the gates — feed, ground, staff, money — the one that earns most on its cost at the city's own prices, at the margin since 0.7.105, a conversion unit on its spread on the stream it would find spare, and a crude unit only for 60% of the petrol and diesel it would make that the city lacks, or of its run that the wells spare, and then with the units its cuts would feed. Until then a whole plant's worth of the city's own — from 0.7.76 the petrol and diesel the drivers and the railway draw that the refineries standing and on site do not make, 1.98 million litres a plant, or crude its wells lift that no refinery takes — and whether its slate cleared above its cost at nameplate, its crude priced at what importing it would cost past the wells' spare (0.7.62); and since 0.7.105 its crude units run only the barrels that pay (below) |

**What the investors said, in a kind** (0.7.30). Each sector's planner leaves a word a month, its order or what held it, and the screens read the word into one of twelve kinds — building, selling, land, staff, licence, ore, supply, credit, money, enough, none and other (`BuildCard.wordKind()`, off the word's own text, whole words, the first match winning) — and a sector's investors as one record (`BuildCard.sectorInvestors()`), which the Sectors list, every business's frame and its Investors page draw, and Build's market cards beside the first gate that building fails. The words were not saved, so after a load or a founding the list said once that nothing was recorded until a month ran (0.7.34); since 0.7.102 the last word crosses a save (`DataSave.lastInvestment`, Jerus's A22), so a loaded city's investors' line is there before the clock moves, and what is *not counted until a month runs* reads a mark of its own (`Game.hasMonthRun()`), where it had read the word's being empty.

### Every order on its whole cost

**Since 0.7.113 every order is asked to carry the interest on its whole cost, whoever pays** (Jerus's decision A of 8 October, *"test every order on its whole cost, whoever pays"*, and his A13 of 10 October, for the investors' slices and the sea's orders; Game's THE LARGEST SLICE, ON ITS WHOLE COST). Until then a slice was asked to earn 1.25 times the interest on what it would borrow, its cost less the till, so an order the till paid for was asked only to earn something, and a business holding cash built what a borrower would not: on the playtest's city at month 9 the restaurants built a Diner for $1,361.8k out of a till holding exactly that, losing $6,951 a month, and from month 127 the grocers built Filling Stations losing $14k to $43k a month out of the shops' till. Now each slice is asked it of its whole cost, at the one rate the slice is judged at — the loan's at the leverage it leaves, or a bond's blended with the bank's where one is cheaper and raises it all — the till's part priced as the money it stands in for, what the slice would otherwise raise at the margin. The financing is what it was: the till pays first, the bond desk is asked for what is borrowed, and a ban stops a slice that borrows. The rule is one replaceable piece (`Game.orderGate()`), the rule to 0.7.112 kept by name for a check to ask; *at prime* reads the same whole cost; and the words say it — a refusal *Declined Diner - not even one would cover its interest on its whole cost*, with the rate its own risk costs where a slice would have carried it at prime, a trim *could not carry the interest on its whole cost*, the Oil page's note *At sea: a platform and its wells would not carry the interest on their whole cost*, and the Sectors screen's rules *earns 1.25× its interest … on its whole cost, whether its cash or a loan pays*. The refiners' planner was the first to ask it, in 0.7.112 (`SpreadPlanner.ON_ITS_WHOLE_COST`, below), where it moved nothing, the refiners never holding cash when they weigh an order; the sea's orders ask it since 0.7.113, each kind of well and the jacket before the planner walks on to the next (`Game.carriesItsWholeCost()`, below); and the bank's branches ask it with every other order. A landlord's homes keep the mortgage lender's test, and a home bought outright is not asked it ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).

**What it did.** It moved the playtest from month 9, and that run is the baseline since. Over it the new rule refused 2,324 orders the old would have built in the same month's state, every one whole and none trimmed: Filling Stations 1,291 times from month 127, 450 of them losing $14k to $43k a month, Assembly Plants 381 times, Meat Works 204, Snack & Oils Plants 190, Fabrication Works 177, Contact Centres 52 and Materials' plants 26. The young city is smaller for it, 1,513 people and 603 jobs at its checkpoint by month 266 against 2,097 and 1,016, and the grown one bigger: 100,000 people at month 1,857 against 2,031, 400,000 at 3,302 against 3,618, 500,000 at 3,704 where it never got there, and 566,444 at the end against 492,823. There is less credit and fewer defaults — 1,408 bonds issued for $12.6T against 1,985 for $19.6T, $12.7T of debt defaulted against $20.1T, the businesses owing $53.2B at the end against $1.0T and the backstop making $0.6B of money against $228.4B — and more is built that pays: 13,793 homes against 6,043, 33,574 Convenience Stores against 5,698. The one cost is Materials, whose longest spell holding no plant and owing went from 257 months to 488, and its longest run of defaults from 83 to 298 ([open questions](#25-open-questions)). Every month passed the audit and every reload matched. On the ensemble's sixteen seeds 24 of 26 criteria pass where 22 did, the high rate's seeds over a point and the shock's population going from red to green and none the other way ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). On the whole cost an order is built whole or refused: in `OrderSearchCheck`'s long run 1,418 of 1,537 orders were refused and none trimmed, where its copy's twin on the old rule trims 24, 17 of them past the countdown's slices, the deepest by 71,823, so the search stays for the rates that are not fixed.

### The eighth, ninth and tenth, and why they are different

The first seven sectors all sold to the city. **Business services** and **manufacturing** sell to the world, which is what broke a two-hundred-year plateau: a city whose every customer lives in it can only grow as fast as it grows. **Agriculture** is the other direction — it sells to the mills, and it is the only sector whose real cost is the ground it stands on.

| Sector | In | Out | Where the money goes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Business services | almost entirely people; 250 sq ft of lot a head | support, back-office and engineering work, by the seat-month, at $5,500 / $8,600 / $14,600 | payroll 66.3% / 65.2% / 55.2% |
| Manufacturing | steel, local or imported | fabricated steel and machinery, flow not stock; export only until the assembly plants arrived | steel 44% since 0.7.120 (61.0% at the US band), or wages 49.1% at the Machine Works on 16 September |
| Agriculture | land heavily, labour and power barely | `CROPS`, to the mills | labour a seventh of a field's sale, power a five-hundredth |

**The engineering office is gated on a licence**, not on money: it will not open without spare licensed engineers for half its gated posts (`LICENCE_COVER_TO_OPEN = 0.5` — thirty-nine of them; thirty-eight is one short), and the only way to make one at home is an Institute of Technology. **Steel got its first domestic customer** and with it an import ceiling of 1.284 against the mills' export floor of .847, a 1.52× wedge that decides whether fabricating here pays at all: 1.55% of build cost a month on imported steel at the ceiling, 3.28% on steel at the mills' floor. Since 0.7.120 the band is the world's, $650 against $470, and what fabrication and machining make moved with the steel in them, so a fabrication shop still adds about $862 a tonne over the steel it uses (below). **The mills got an input cost** — they used to make food out of nothing, on margins of 72–77% against every other plant's 28–31%.

> **The farmland dial**
>
> `TaxPolicy.FARMLAND_RELIEF` assesses farmland at use value rather than development value, on the land half only — barns are still taxed as buildings. It defaults to full relief and says in dollars what the relief costs. Six grain farms on \$112m of ground: **\$151,496 a month with no relief, \$11,295 with full relief.** Without it a field cannot outbid a warehouse for the same acre, and by month 4,002 at \$66 a square foot there are no fields left — ten greenhouses, and the two founding mixed farms.

### The sixteenth and seventeenth: oil, and its refinery

Jerus's city bought every litre its drivers and its railway burned abroad: US$27M a month at month 1,851, about fifteen million litres. Since 0.7.62 the city can make it. **Oil** (`sectors.Oil`) has Mining's shape: an **Oil Well** stands on an oil site the city owns — the world's oil lies in fields as its iron does ([land](#18-land)) — and lifts 415 tonnes of crude a month, a hundred barrels a day, for $2.0M and 400 points on a two-acre pad with three posts — one, a diploma's, since 0.7.84 — the sector plans one a month while a site is unworked and oil is left, and retires a well whose oil has run out, and since 0.7.84 one worn out (below). With no oil site the order is refused *No oil deposit*, and the refusal's page buys the cheapest offer holding oil. **Refining** (`sectors.Refining`) has heavy industry's: an **Oil Refinery**, a modular plant of 2,000 barrels a day, takes 8,300 tonnes of crude a month, with a hundred posts on twenty acres for $60M, and buys the wells' crude first and the world's for the rest; until 0.7.76 it made 8,300,000 litres of one good, fuel, a thousand litres a tonne, and kept three months of it in its tanks. Crude is a flow good, as ore is: a well ships what it lifts and has no tank. **The refinery is gated** as a mill was on spare ore until 0.7.120: it is planned only for a whole plant's worth of the city's own — what the city draws that the refineries standing and on site do not make, or crude its wells lift that no refinery takes — and then while the investors' estimate clears. Without the gate the playtest's city stood 120 refineries at month 4,002, every one an exporter on imported crude, because a tonne bought at $600 sold abroad as a thousand litres at $0.70 and a refinery's crew and power cost less than the $100 between; with a gate at any fuel uncovered the first stood at month 438 in a town of 800. In the playtest at 0.7.64 the first well stood at month 1,119 and the first refinery at 2,564, and 79.9% of the drivers' and the railway's fuel over the run came from abroad.

**Since 0.7.76 a refinery is a crude unit, and a barrel is nine products.** A barrel is not one thing, and a refinery that made fuel of all of it made nothing a real one does. So `FUEL` is retired, its note kept in `Good`, and nine goods take its place: petroleum gas, naphtha, petrol, jet fuel, diesel, lubricants and fuel oil by the litre, each knowing what a litre of it weighs (`Good.litresPerTonne()`), and bitumen and petroleum coke by the tonne ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)). The Oil Refinery's template now says only the crude it takes, and what that becomes is **the slate** (`Refining.slate()`): a medium crude's straight-run cuts — gas, light naphtha, heavy naphtha, kerosene, diesel, gas oil and residue, 1.5, 6, 12, 12, 22, 24 and 22.5% of a tonne's 1,165 litres — each to the product it is worth with no conversion unit to upgrade it: the gas to petroleum gas, the light naphtha to petrol, the heavy to naphtha, the kerosene to jet fuel, the gas oil to fuel oil, and the residue cut three to one with the diesel into fuel oil, whatever the diesel cannot cut burned at no value. A tonne makes 70 litres of petrol, 169 of diesel, 140 of naphtha, 140 of jet fuel, 17 of petroleum gas and 629 of fuel oil, to the litre; the plant's 8,300 tonnes make 580,170 litres of petrol and 1,402,078 of diesel a month, and 7.7 million litres of the four others. Its capacity, what it has on site and its 25 million litres of tanks are the slate's, the tanks shared as the run is — 1.5 million for petrol, 3.625 million for diesel, 13.5 million for fuel oil — and because a product nobody here buys fills its share to the dump line and stays there, what the tanks cannot hold is shipped at the export price before the template's rule could write it off: oil does not spoil, and a tank farm is emptied before it is pulled down. **Who buys what:** the drivers draw petrol (`Motoring.drawFuel()`, at 6d, 1.2 litres a journey) and the railway diesel (eighteen litres a tonne hauled), each off the refiners' tanks at the market's price before they import, so with no refinery the bill was what it had been at the world's price level; everything else a refinery made was shipped, since nothing in the city bought gas, naphtha, jet fuel or fuel oil, and since 0.7.83 the grocers' forecourts draw the drivers' petrol and the vans, the factories and the builders buy diesel, lubricants and bitumen (below). The tanks are stock the national accounts count as held, petrol and diesel in fuel's place and the seven others after them, and the refiners' sales to the drivers were consumption beside the shops' ([GDP](#12-tax-policy--gdp)), the forecourts' since 0.7.83; the money audit's *PetrolFunded* and *PetrolImports* carried the households' imported part, the domestic part being on Refining's own statement, until the forecourts took the drivers' litres in 0.7.83. **The gate was in petrol and diesel**, from 0.7.76 until the spread planner replaced it in 0.7.82: a plant's worth is the 1.98 million litres of the two its crude makes, where it was 8.3 million litres of fuel, so it opens about four times as early in a city's demand, and the estimate is the investors' own over the slate (`BusinessInvestment.estimatedMakerProfit()` with what the plant makes, `Refining.madeBy()`), what the city will take at the local price and the rest at the export price. In the playtest the first refinery is ordered at month 1,093, where at 0.7.71 the first stood at 1,912, and none of them pays: eleven were ordered over the run and eleven shed by the distress rule, never more than two standing and none at the end, and 99.7% of the drivers' and the railway's fuel came from abroad, against 66.3% at 0.7.71 ([open questions](#25-open-questions)). **Two things were to come next, and both came.** Petrol and diesel kept fuel's band, its import price a journey's $2.00 over the journey's 1.2 litres, until 0.7.78 gave them wholesale prices, a decision of Jerus's; and the refinery's other units — grades of crude, the conversion units that make lubricants, bitumen and coke, and a planner for what its slate is worth — followed from 0.7.79 to 0.7.82 (below). A save from before 0.7.76 had its fuel split into petrol and diesel as it loaded, no money moving, in the builds that read it, to 0.7.119 ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)), and `OilCheck` holds the slate and the split ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### Wholesale, three grades, and the units behind the crude unit

**Since 0.7.78 petrol and diesel are priced at wholesale.** Jerus: *"yes wholesale"*. From 0.7.76 the two had kept fuel's band, its import price a journey's $2.00 over its 1.2 litres — a pump price, a forecourt's margin and the taxes in it, standing where every other good stood at the refinery gate. Now all nine products are on the research's ladder (`Good`, THE PRICES): a product's world price is a ratio to crude's world middle a litre, $550 a tonne over its 1,165 litres, about $0.47 — petrol 1.20, diesel 1.35 — imported at 1.08 of it and exported at 0.92, its freight 0.06 of it, so petrol lands at $0.61 a litre and diesel at $0.69, where both had landed at $1.67 ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)). With no refinery the drivers' litre is 63% cheaper and the railway's 59%. The railway keeps its litres: `Rail.FUEL_LITRES_PER_TONNE` is the literal eighteen, where it had been `WORLD_FUEL_PER_TONNE`'s $30 over the import price, so its bill falls with the price and not its burn. Two things followed. A journey's fuel is what a car owner weighs a ride against ([transport](#21-transport--vehicles)), so at the default fare no owner took the bus on cost alone, where 36 to 46% of Jerus's had, and 29.5% in `CarCheck`'s town, the drive's fuel being under a third of the fare, and transit lost a point or two of the commuters where owners had seats the car-less did not fill — 54.1–55.1% of the 2,400-month city's became 53.4–53.7%. And no refinery paid at wholesale on imported crude: in the same city a medium crude's slate at the net export prices was worth $4,042.9k a month against its crude's $4,074.5k at the net import price, less than the crude before a post was paid, and the playtest built none, where 0.7.76 and 0.7.77 had built and shed eleven. A save from before keeps its market's price for petrol and diesel until its first clearing; `OilCheck`, `CarCheck` and `TradeCostCheck` hold the prices ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

**Since 0.7.79 crude comes in three grades.** Every oil field is light, medium or heavy, a third of fields each (`Deposit.grade()`, drawn from the field's place, so nothing is stored and no tonne moves), and each grade is cut by its own column (`Refining.CUTS`): light Brent's, heavy Maya's, medium the blend the world sells. A tonne of light makes 97 litres of petrol and 252 of diesel; of medium 70 and 169; of heavy 59 and none, its 101 litres of residue burned for want of diesel to cut it. The wells' lift is graded field by field in the order the ground was bought (`LandManager`'s oil runs; oil a fixture holds by fiat is medium), and a refinery's month is a mix: its local crude at the lift's grades and its imports at medium, each a share of what it bought, struck once the month's markets have cleared and saved (`crudeMix.*`), and next month's slate is struck on it; a month that bought no crude, and a save from before, read medium. The tanks' shares stay a medium tonne's. On a world whose sea field is heavy, a town whose refinery took 1,053 t of its own heavy crude and imported 1,300 ran a mix of 0.552 medium and 0.448 heavy, and its plant's petrol fell from 580,170 litres a month to 541,216.

**Since 0.7.80 a refinery is a campus.** A crude unit makes cheap cuts as well as dear ones, and a real refinery has units behind it that turn the cheap into the dear (`sectors.RefineryFlow`; the research's 1.2, its prototype's solve ported). Fifteen buildings came. The **Crude Unit**, 100,000 barrels a day: 415,000 t of crude a month, fifty Oil Refineries' crude, road load and tanks, \$400M, 160 posts on 40 ha. And a small and a large of seven kinds of **conversion unit**, each fed one stream and buying and making nothing of its own: a *reformer* turns heavy naphtha into petrol, 82% of it, and makes the hydrogen a hydrocracker needs; a *cracking unit* turns gas oil into petrol, diesel, fuel oil and the cracked gas alkylation takes; a *hydrocracker* gas oil and hydrogen into diesel and jet fuel; *alkylation* cracked gas into petrol; a *coker* residue into gas, naphtha, diesel, fuel oil and coke; a *lube plant* gas oil into lubricants, 40%, and fuel oil; and an *asphalt unit* the heavy crude's residue into bitumen. Their sizes and prices are the research's — a Small Reformer 240 barrels a day for \$16.2M, a Reformer 12,000 for \$108M — the small ones' capital on a 0.485 power of the size between the two crude units (`buildings.json`'s `"refinery"`: the kind, and its feed in litres a month). **The flow** (`RefineryFlow.solve()`) cuts the crude units' run into its streams grade by grade; counts the reformers' hydrogen, 1,400 cubic feet a barrel, which caps the hydrocrackers at 1,850 a barrel of gas oil, and none from an idle reformer; hands each stream — gas oil, residue, heavy naphtha, cracked gas, in that order — to its units widest spread first, a unit at a spread of nothing or less idling; and sends what is left of each stream to the product it is worth unworked, the residue three to one with the diesel into fuel oil and the rest burned. With no unit it is the slate, to the bit. A unit's spread is what it makes of a litre less what the litre is worth with no unit, at each product's local price, which a save restores: at the world's middle prices a reformer's is \$0.0098 a litre, a cracking unit's \$0.0503, a hydrocracker's \$0.1794, alkylation's \$0.2360, a lube plant's \$0.1719 and an asphalt unit's \$0.1543, and a coker's −\$0.0123, its residue's worth assuming diesel to cut it, so a coker runs only where the city imports diesel or ships fuel oil. The refinery's nameplate is the flow's and its pipeline the flow with its units on site less without, at nameplate, the month's rate on top (and since 0.7.105 its run's share); once a unit stands its tanks follow the flow, each product the same months of its own nameplate, so lubricants, bitumen and coke have room. One Small Lube Plant beside one Oil Refinery made 577,034 litres of lubricants a month, 6.0% of the crude's litres, against a real refinery's 1%, and since 0.7.103 the world takes no more than that 1% of the crude a city's crude units run: a Small Lube Plant beside an Oil Refinery that made 9.6% of its crude into lubricants and shipped every litre ships 0.8% and idles the rest, and the planner weighs a lube plant on what the world and the city would still take (below). A unit's card says *upgrades 1,161,495 litres of heavy naphtha a month*, its value added its spread on that feed, and since 0.7.103 a unit's card with no crude unit standing says it has no feed, where it read a loss. `RefineryCheck` holds the flow ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### The spread planner

**Since 0.7.82 the refiners order by the spread** (`sectors.SpreadPlanner`, shared, the materials chains' works its next clients; Refining's THE SPREAD PLANNER). Until then the investors ordered one building, the Oil Refinery, on 0.7.62's gate and the estimate over its slate, and nothing ordered a unit. Now, each month, of the refiners' buildings that pass four gates in order — the feed, the ground, the staff and the money, every gate asked so that a refusal names the first and the land office hears when ground was all that stood in the way — it orders the one that earns most on its cost at **the city's own price** (`cityValue()`): a good at its net import price, landed and hauled, while the city imports any, else at its net export price, what one more unit fetches — and since 0.7.105 **at the margin** (Jerus's R1): a good nobody here trades at its net export price, where it read its local price, the band's middle; petrol and diesel at the net import price only up to what the city imports of them, past that at the net export price (`Refining.cityValues()`); and an order weighed at the run the campus would take with it standing (`runWith()`), so a unit behind a run that has stopped earns nothing and is refused, where on prices alone the planner had ordered conversion units behind crude units the run had stood down. **A conversion unit** is weighed on its spread at those values on the stream it would find spare in the flow of the units standing — a coker the residue, a hydrocracker no more gas oil than the spare hydrogen treats — at the rate, less its running and standing costs, and only with spare stream for 60% of its feed (`FEED_GATE`, the railway's line under which nothing is built). **A crude unit** is weighed only while the petrol and diesel the city lacks on the trend come to 60% of what it would make of them, or the wells' spare crude to 60% of its run, and then **as a package** with the units of its own size its cuts would feed, added the widest margin first, twelve at most: on imported crude a crude unit alone fails at the ladder's prices in any city, so its units would never come. The package charges its crude at the net import price and the wells' spare at the local price, the wells' at the grades they lift next and the rest medium; only the crude unit is ordered, and its units follow on their own spreads. **The money gate** is one replaceable piece: since 0.7.112, Jerus's decision A, 1.25 times the interest at the real rate on the order's whole cost, whatever the refiners hold (`SpreadPlanner.ON_ITS_WHOLE_COST`), the game's own test too since 0.7.113 (above); until then on what the order would borrow, which asked nothing of an order the till paid, the rule kept by name for a check to ask (`-Dplaytest.moneyGate=borrowing`), and the switch changed nothing measured, the refiners never holding cash when they weigh an order. **Idle, then shed**: a kind of unit with no feed six months running may be sold back while the refiners lose money (`idleMonths.*`, saved); a working unit no rule sells; and since 0.7.105 the crude units' nameplate past the most their run used in the last six months is spare too, which the spare-capacity rule sells while the refiners lose money, a quarter of the units at most and never into what the run used, and no rule sells a Tank Farm. On imported crude the playtest's Oil Refinery with the Small Lube Plant its cuts would feed lost 0.15 to 0.57% of its cost a month every year of the run, and the Crude Unit never passed the 60%, the city short at most 22.8 million litres of the 59 million it asks, so the playtest built none. A player's Oil Refinery in a small town is given a Small Lube Plant at 1.05% a month, and on imported crude the refinery is sold after two years of losses and the lube plant, left with no stream, six months later; with forty wells of the town's own both stand twenty years. The hurdle itself, 1.25 times a month's interest at the real rate on what is borrowed, as 0.7.82 measured it, ran from 0.13 to 1.38% of a building's cost a month over the playtest, a median of 0.44%, and from 0.14 to 1.68% in the research and Jerus cities. **One order in flight**, as every sector has, but since 0.7.105 a crude unit on site, whoever ordered it, does not count against it (R3): while only crude units are on site the refiners may order a conversion unit or a Tank Farm, one at a time, and weigh no other crude unit; every other sector keeps its one order. Jerus's own fourteen Crude Units, on site for want of builders, had held his refiners *already building* whatever any unit's spread; freed of them, his planner ordered a Hydrocracker in a good month, on $19.6B of bonds, and it waits in the same queue.

### The forecourts, the vans, the factories and the roads

**Since 0.7.83 the barrel has buyers at home.** Jerus: *"fuel isnt cheap, we are going to add another building, the pump ... its owned by grocery stores"*. **The grocers sell the drivers' petrol** (`sectors.Retail`, THE FORECOURTS): at 6d, as the drivers' month is struck, Retail draws their litres at wholesale — the refiners' tanks first and the world for the rest — on its own books, and sells them to the households at the pump, wholesale × 1.12 / (1 − Retail's sales tax) (`PUMP_MARGIN`, the research's middle, the tax passed on as a seller that remits its rate passes it), 1.32 times wholesale at the default 15%, as far as its **Filling Stations** can sell, and past them at 1.18 (`QUEUE_MARGIN`, the top of the research's range): the drivers pay more, they do not drive less. Since 0.7.103 the city's fuel duty, nothing by default, rides on the price as the treasury's. A station (id 91) is the research's fuel-only kiosk, the shop beside it being the grocery already built: 350,000 litres a month, $0.5M at founding prices, three posts and an acre. Retail asks for one as a second question each month beside its shops' (`planStations()`, as the bank's branch is asked, so that wanting a station never holds a shop), when the drivers' litres grown as the people are outrun what its stations can sell; a station's estimate is its margin on the litres it would sell, and since 0.7.106 its posts' wages come off it. A journey's fuel, what an owner weighs a ride against, is the price on the sign. **The vans burn diesel**: a van-month 240 litres, forty loads of fifty kilometres at twelve litres a hundred (`Sector.DIESEL_LITRES_A_VAN_MONTH`, est.), drawn at the operating rate with the month's wear, near wholesale and off the market as the railway's is, 0.1 to 0.2% of a city's payrolls. **The factories buy lubricants**, an input bought whole as their steel is: ten litres a tonne of machinery, two a tonne of fabricated steel, eight a car or van. **The paved roads take bitumen**: five per cent of the surface a road lays past a Gravel Road's material \[R18\] — 64.25 t a Paved Road or a paving, 151.75 t an Elevated Highway — bought by the builders as the order is placed and billed in its quote (`Game.drawBitumen()`, `BuildQuote.bitumen`). The money audit's *PetrolFunded* and *PetrolImports*, the households' own imports, read nothing since: the forecourts' import is Retail's, and the drivers' bill Retail's sale. In the playtest at 0.7.83 the first station opened at month 91 and 77 stood at the end, 2,591 cars a station against the research's 1,920 in the United States and 2,340 in Canada; of the five research and Jerus cities four built none in two years, three of them for want of a spare hand for one of a station's three posts, so their drivers paid the queue's 18%. Build files the stations as Shops' *Filling stations*, *sells 350,000 L of petrol a month*; Trade's petrol card says the price at the pump today, and History's petrol price is the pump's.

### Wells that wear out, and crude kept in tanks

**Since 0.7.84 a well declines.** It lifts its 415 t the month it opens and 10% less each year after (`sectors.Oil.LAND_KEEPS_A_YEAR`, est. \[W6\]), and is retired worn out below ten barrels a day — at 263 months, about 41.6 t — oldest first, by the month's retirements at its top; the one-well-a-month rule then drills its site again at the full hundred barrels while the field has oil. The wells are kept as vintages — the month a batch opened, how many and their kind — read against the wells standing, so any other rule that sells a well sells the oldest, struck once at the sector's month end and saved (`vintages.*`; a save from before reads every well new, opened the first month it plays). A platform well's profile, three years flat and then 8.5% less a year, retired at 348 months, came with it for the sea. **A land well stands only on a dry site**, a field whose centre is on land (`Game.sitesFor()`; the order, the card and the investors alike): the sea's wait for a platform, and wells already on them are kept. **A well has one post**, a diploma's, where it had three (the research's 0.2–0.4 workers a well). The Oil page says how many stand *On dry ground* and what they are *Lifting a month* against new, and since 0.7.103 a land well's card counts its sites as dry. In the playtest at 0.7.84 the city's two dry sites gave their oil from month 830 to 3,253, where two new wells would have taken 618 months, and 21 wells were retired worn out and drilled again.

**Since 0.7.85 crude can be kept in tanks.** Crude had been a flow: the wells shipped what they lifted and the refiners ran what they bought the month it landed. The **Tank Farm** (id 92, the refiners'): 500,000 m³ of tanks on 10 ha for \$190M, the research's US\$60 a barrel, ten posts. With one standing the refiners keep a month of their crude units' run on hand, as far as the farms' room holds it (`Refining.crudeKept()`; since 0.7.105 with a tanker's cargo of the room kept free), their products share the rest of the room, and their crude is bought as stock, cut to what they can pay for, where a maker's inputs are bought whole; once crude's market has cleared their rate is held to what the crude on hand and the month's fill will run, so a refinery short of cash runs its tanks down and then runs below its rate. With none, every figure is what it was. The **Strategic Reserve** (id 93) is the city's: the farm's tanks, ground and price — 429,185 t of crude — and no posts, because the treasury pays crews only in its own services. A fill (`Game.fillReserve()`) buys crude in the month's crude market as a buyer, pro rata with the refiners, the wells' first and the world's for the rest, cut to the room and to what the treasury can pay; a release (`releaseReserve()`) offers a tonnage a month into the same market beside the wells, and what the refiners do not take stays in the tanks since 0.7.103, where from 0.7.85 it shipped at the export price; a fill stops a release and a release cancels a fill, so the city never trades with itself. Its money moves at the next strike, beside the businesses it traded with (`Game.settleReserve()`), its book at average cost, and the money audit lists only what crossed the edge, *- city ReserveFill* and *+ city ReserveSales*. Both levers are decisions on the record; they have had a screen since 0.7.96, the Oil page's, and since 0.7.102 the reserve's crude bought and sold are lines of the budget. The crude held, the refiners' and the city's, is the thirteenth good the national accounts count as held, and the city's trade in it is in the trade by good ([GDP](#12-tax-policy--gdp)). Build files both as Industry's *Oil storage*, in litres of room, the reserve's card the city's, with no investors' line. The investors order a farm only where a port holds their crude back for room and none stands, on the freight a ship would save them ([the ports](#21-transport--vehicles)); the player may stand one at any time. The playtest builds neither.

### The oil at sea

**Since 0.7.91 the sea's oil can be lifted.** Since 0.7.79 the world's sea has a depth ([land](#18-land)), and since 0.7.84 a land well has stood only on a dry site, so a field centred in the sea waited. The research's platform, 18,000 barrels a day for D$500M, would drain the largest shallow field near a generated city in nineteen months, so the platform is built from the research's per-well figures, Jerus's answer B. Three buildings stand at sea, the Oil sector's, on none of the city's dry ground (ids 98–100): an **Offshore Platform**, a steel jacket for $18M with twelve posts, on a field the city owns whose centre lies no deeper than 150 m (`PLATFORM_MAX_DEPTH_M`), with slots for twelve wells and at most one a sea site of its field that its other platforms have not slotted; a **Platform Well** in a slot, $14M and one post, lifting 415 t a month, held three years and then 8.5% less a year, retired at 348 months; and a **Crude Pipeline**, counted in kilometres, $4.5M a kilometre at sea and $3M on land, a straight line from the field to the founding site. The jackets are kept as the wells' vintages are, by their field and the month they opened, a new one on the shallow field with the most sea sites free, the nearest on a tie, the wells dealt to their slots oldest platform first (saved, `platforms.*` and `pipelines.*`). **Shuttle tankers**: platform crude sold at home pays crude's band freight a tonne, booked as the Oil sector's imported *Shuttle tankers*; crude shipped abroad pays none. **The pipeline rule**: a field's pipe is built when the shuttle freight it saves, less its repairs and tax, over the months of oil left, at most 480, repays its cost 1.25 times, while the refiners are not losing money and the field's first platform is on its plateau, and then the investors' interest test still asks it to carry its debt, on its whole cost since 0.7.113; a field whose whole pipe stands pays no shuttle. **The planner**, after the land well: a platform well into a free slot, then a pipe that pays, then a jacket weighed as a package with as many wells as its free sea sites give, up to twelve, its share of their earnings by cost as a crude unit's is; since 0.7.113 each kind is asked to carry the interest on its whole cost before the planner walks on to the next, where each had only to earn something; once the oil is worked out the empty jackets and the pipes are decommissioned. Build files them as *Oil platforms* and *Oil pipelines* after the wells', the platform well's card saying it needs a platform's slot. Since 0.7.93 the platform wells lift an offshore pool of their own and the land wells the ground's (below), and since 0.7.97 the map draws all three at sea ([land](#18-land)). In `WellCheck`'s town a jacket's package of eight wells earns 0.50% of its cost a month; the playtest's city, whose oil is two dry sites, never owns a sea field and builds none, and in the ensemble's eighty runs no city owned a free shallow sea site.

**Since 0.7.93 the city's crude is two pools** (`LandManager`'s THE TWO OIL POOLS; Jerus: *"each oil field doesnt keep its oil, but you can split it, two pools, offshore oil and ground oil. pipelines leave it as is"*). The **ground pool** is sized from the city's dry oil fields and any oil a holding lists by fiat, the **offshore pool** from its sea fields — each holding's sea part the lesser of what it listed and its sea fields' tonnes, as its sea sites are — and a land well lifts the ground pool alone and a platform well the offshore pool alone (`extractOil()`, `extractOilAtSea()`): the platform wells ask their nameplate at the month's rate of the sea's, the land wells the rest of the ground's (`Oil.groundLimit()`). A field keeps no oil of its own, so the platforms on the shallow fields lift the deep fields' tonnes too. Each pool is worked out on its own fields in the order they were bought, which the map greys and the refiners grade, and whatever reads the oil left reads its kind's pool: an order's deposit gate and the card's tonnes (`Game.remainingFor()`), the land well's planner — *every oil deposit on dry ground is worked out*, where the city owns sea oil — and the sea's, the pipe's months, the offshore pool over the platforms' lift, and the decommissioning. With one pool worked out and the other not, the wells over the empty one are the spare the shrinking rules sell first (`Oil.mayRetire()`), where their payroll had stood until they wore out, 22 to 29 years. The shuttle tankers carry the offshore pool's share of the month's crude sold at home, what it gave, where they had carried the platforms' share of the nameplate, which with two pools could have billed tankers for land crude. The Oil page's *Crude in the ground* is the ground pool, and its At sea lines, shown too where the city owns only deep sea oil, say *Crude under the sea* and *Lifting at sea a month*; the platform well's card and the sea's no-deposit page say *under the sea*. The sea's tonnes taken are saved apart (`oilDepletionAtSea`, save format 35; [saves](#23-time-saves--logs)), and an older save's one pool is charged to the ground, floored at its tonnes, none to the sea. Jerus's city at month 8,473, with 31 dry sites and 80 at sea and its oil worked out as one pool, keeps its dry fields worked out and has its sea's 11,492,307 t back, 4,233,173 t of it on the sixteen shallow fields a platform can stand on, no money moving: its investors order a jacket at once, at 0.349% of its cost a month, and its builders give it about 1.2 of its 3,600 points a month, 26 of the city's sites owing 3.1 million. Stood by hand in a probe, a jacket's four wells lifted 129,365 t of the offshore pool in ten years, every tonne sold at home, the shuttle about 1% of crude's local price. The playtest's city owns no sea oil, so its traces did not move.

### The slate ships, and the run pays its way

**Since 0.7.98 what the city does not take of the slate ships**, every month, at the export price less the railway's charge (`Refining.getMarginalCostPerUnit()`, THE RUN'S PRODUCTS ALL LEAVE). The crude units bought their crude for the whole run, at nameplate times the rate, whatever any one product's line planned, and then each line idled what the city did not take whenever its net export price failed its marginal cost — the line's power, its water and its share of the month's whole crude bill, shared among the nine products by their value at local prices. On imported crude a slate at local prices is worth about its crude, so each product's share came out 1 to 3% over its net export price and nearly all of it idled, while the tanks sat at the dump line: the crude was bought and turned into nothing. A refined product's marginal cost, which its sale at home and its shipment are both tested against, is its share of the power and water alone since then, the crude being the run's. Jerus's city at month 8,474, five Crude Units and an Oil Refinery on 1.65 million tonnes of imported crude a month, had idled its fuel oil, jet fuel, naphtha and gas and most of its petrol and diesel, and its refiners lost $2.49B in two years on $0.49B of sales; with the fix they shipped 1.77 billion litres a month and lost $0.35B on $2.71B, the railway's haulage of the crude in and the products out, mostly. Lubricants alone ship only so far since 0.7.103, the world's 1% of the crude (above); Jerus's city, whose six Lube Plants make 0.71% of its crude, ships what it did.

**Since 0.7.105 a crude unit runs a barrel only while the barrel pays** (Refining's THE RUN; Jerus's decision on why the refinery loses, A2 (b)). The crude units had run flat out whatever the barrel paid, none of the six throttles being a price, so they bought their whole crude every month and lost on every tonne. Now the run is every barrel, in order, up to the first that does not beat its crude (`Refining.runRule()`). The campus's barrel is its flow at nameplate a tonne of crude, one crew at one rate, the first on the wells' crude; its products fetch the city's own take of petrol and diesel at the net import price, everything past that take and every other product at the net export price, and lubricants past what the world and the city take nothing; its crude costs the local price while the wells lift it and the net import price, landed and hauled, past them; and only what the run moves counts — the crude, the haulage in and out and the vans' diesel — the wages, the power, the water and the capital being paid whether it runs or not. So the run stops at the first barrel, at the city's petrol or its diesel, at the wells' crude, at the world's lubricants, or not before nameplate. It moves a quarter of nameplate a month at most (`RUN_PACE`, the spare-capacity rule's quarter), struck at the month's end on that month's prices, and the next month's operating rate is the plant's six throttles times it, so the crude units buy, and every unit makes, that share. It is saved among the refiners' extras (`run.share`), a save from before reading the whole run, as it ran, and a fixture that holds the refiners holds their run; what it leaves idle six months is spare (above). Refining's page leads with *The run*, *Crude run: N% of nameplate* in green, amber or red, and why — *No barrel pays: the first loses 1.7% of what its crude costs, so the crude units stand*, or which barrels it runs and what the next would earn — the refinery's picture says why a month ran nothing, and the oil page's crude units read *idle* or *part run* ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). `RefineryCheck`'s sixteenth section works the study's margins from the model's own prices to a tenth of a point: a barrel of medium crude through a topping plant loses 9.97% of its crude's cost by lorry and 4.66% by rail at the railway's .60, and earns 2.25% by tanker, and the barrels that replace a city's imports earn 1.36% at the floor. Over 24 months of Jerus's city from month 8,474 the run fell to nothing in four, then followed the prices — the railway's freight easing with the refinery stopped — from nothing to 79% of nameplate, most months the barrels of the city's own diesel or petrol, 13% to 29%: its crude fell from 39.7 to 12.6 million tonnes, its products shipped from 42.6 to 12.1 billion litres, and its refiners' loss from $371M to $190M. Their margins sit within 3% of nothing and the city's own tonnes move the railway's price, so the run swings ([open questions](#25-open-questions)); and his refiners are subsidised, so no loss is counted and nothing is sold. The playtest's city stands no refinery, and its traces did not move.

### Iron at the world's price

**Since 0.7.120 ore and scrap are two goods, and steel trades at the world's price** (batch I3, the first of the materials chains to change the game; Jerus's Q2, Q4 to Q6b, C and D of 8 October: *"split"*, *"move to world prices"*). Until then one good, `IRON`, was *"iron ore, and the scrap that stands in for it"*: its import price, \$410, was the mills' scrap and its export price, \$140, the mines' ore, so a mill on imported "ore" was on scrap, and steel sold at the US band, \$1,284 and \$847, which sits behind tariffs. Now `IRON` is iron ore alone, \$115 landed and \$85 shipped; `SCRAP` is a good of its own, \$410 and \$300, the arc furnaces' feed; steel is \$650 and \$470, hot-rolled coil's world price and what a distant mill nets; and what is made of steel moved by the steel in it, so the plants that buy it kept their margins: fabricated steel \$2,210 to \$1,545, machinery \$14,300 and \$9,000 to \$13,400 and \$8,100, a car \$44,000 and \$36,000 to \$41,312.50 and \$33,312.50, the first car 6% cheaper, a van \$72,000 to \$68,135 and a wagon set \$2.4M to \$2,302,200 ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)). Iron in the ground stays US\$0.40 a tonne, written as 1/212.5 of the new export price where it was 1/350 of the old ([land](#18-land)). **The buildings**: id 11, the Steel Foundry, is the **Electric Arc Furnace**, 1,320 t of scrap in for 1,200 t of steel, and the **Steel Mini-Mill** (id 12) takes 6,600 t for 6,000; the **Iron Mine** (id 14) lifts 20,000 t a month, where it lifted 2,500, with the same sixty posts, on 60,000 litres of diesel, 600 kW and 20 units of water, for \$45.0M, its cash, points and material each 4.632 times what they were; and the three buy consumables abroad, the study's running cost less its wages, power, water and diesel — 24.13, 119.7 and 199.8 thousand in the world's money a month. **The sectors** are labelled Iron Mining and Iron & Steel, their keys kept. Iron & Steel is a processing sector, its furnaces ordered by the spread planner on what pays on their whole cost, its old gate on spare local ore gone; Iron Mining asks the same money gate before it sinks a mine, its estimate less its consumables, which the spec's was not, or the mine's \$199.8k a month would have been invisible to it ([work and output](#6-work--output)). Harnesses, the test player and the build advice find the three by id, not by name.

**Why no furnace pays on imported scrap.** The study scored each building in four cases at parity, as a share of its cost a month: A, its feed imported and its output shipped; B, both at the export price; C, its feed at the export price and its output replacing imports; D, both at the import price. `MaterialsCheck`'s ninth section builds them from the game's own figures (`SpreadPlanner.caseEarns()`) and holds them to the study's rounding: the Iron Mine 2.72, 2.74, 4.07 and 4.06%; the Electric Arc Furnace −0.55, −0.06, 0.66 and 0.17%; the Steel Mini-Mill −0.50, 0.11, 1.01 and 0.41%. Walked by hand, a month of each selling steel at home at the landed price, the furnace clears 8.0% of its sales on imported scrap and the mini-mill 13.8%, and 26.6% and 32.4% on the city's own, the gap the scrap's band times its tonnes (`MiningCheck`). On imported scrap, its steel shipped, a furnace loses about half a per cent of its cost a month and earns a fifth of one replacing imports, under every hurdle the game strikes, so freight, not a gate, keeps a city from importing scrap to ship steel; and until 0.7.123 the city made no scrap and nothing used its ore. So at 0.7.120 neither the investors nor the test player's jobs rule, which had built a Steel Foundry nineteen times and builds Industrial Bakeries instead, ever built a furnace, and no mine stood: steel came in at $650. The playtest moved from month 4, the first car 6% cheaper, and ended at 577,610 people against 566,444, but with 15.6% out of work against 9.3%, its real GDP about a fifth lower and its exports about half, every month audited and every reload matched; on the ensemble the high rate's cities lost the steel chain that had kept its posts through 15%, and three criteria went red ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). Its saves went with the old `IRON`: a save of format 36 or older is refused since 0.7.120 ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)).

### The integrated route, and the city's old steel

**Since 0.7.123 Iron & Steel can make steel from ore, and the city makes scrap** (batch I4; Jerus's Q4, Q6 to Q8, Q19, Q20 and A of 8 October). Seven buildings came, ids 101 to 107 ([the catalogue](#19-the-catalogue)), at founding prices: a **Scrap Yard**, 10,500 t of the city's old steel into 10,000 t of scrap a month, $35M and 40 posts; a **Pelletising Plant**, 150,000 t of ore and 4,500 t of thermal coal into 150,000 t of pellets, $270M and 150 posts; **Coke Ovens**, 54,000 t of coking coal into 40,000 t of coke, $264M and 200 posts; a **Mini Blast Furnace**, 24,000 t of ore, 6,750 of coke and 3,750 of limestone into 15,000 t of pig iron, $54M and 150 posts; a **Blast Furnace**, 387,500 t of ore with coke, thermal coal and limestone into 250,000 t of pig iron, $1.35B and 1,200 posts; an **Oxygen Steel Shop**, 246,500 t of pig iron, 72,500 of scrap and 17,400 of lime into 290,000 t of steel, $1.8B and 1,800 posts; and a **Large Mini-Mill**, 137,500 t of scrap into 125,000 t of steel, $1.2B and 400 posts. Each costs what the study said, buys its consumables abroad and carries a `since` year, the year it first existed, which nothing reads yet: 1900, the start year, for the yard, the ovens and both furnaces, 1952 for the oxygen shop, 1955 for pelletising and 1969 for the large mill. Seven goods came with them, pellets, pig iron, coke, two coals, limestone and lime, the coals, limestone and lime imported until the coal and stone chains make them; the coke and both coals are stockable, the fourteenth to the sixteenth goods the national accounts count as held ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)). The pelletising plant and the furnaces are the first buyers of iron ore the game has had. The four cases come out as the study's to its rounding, and on imported feed shipped no works of the route earns past 0.25% of its cost a month (`MaterialsCheck`'s eleventh): the yard 1.54, 1.54, 4.69 and 4.69%; pelletising 0.06, 1.77, 3.71 and 2.00; the ovens −0.21, 0.72, 2.23 and 1.31; the mini furnace −1.14, 1.66, 3.32 and 0.53; the blast furnace 0.21, 1.91, 3.02 and 1.32; the oxygen shop −2.07, −0.64, 2.26 and 0.83; and the large mill −0.23, 1.03, 2.91 and 1.65.

**Captive, and its own power.** Coke, pig iron and scrap go to Iron & Steel's own works first — the ovens' coke to the furnaces, the furnaces' pig iron to the oxygen shop, the yards' scrap to the shop and the arc furnaces — and only the rest is bought or sold, nothing booked for what a works hands itself, and its lorries move its plant's tonnes less those, which go on its own rails (`Sector.tonnesMoved()`). The Coke Ovens make 8,000 kW against a 2,200 kW draw, the Blast Furnace 60,000 against 51,400 and the Oxygen Steel Shop 25,000 against 51,600, from their gas: the sector buys from the grid only its works' draw past what they make, and sells the grid what they make past it at the tariff ([utilities](#20-utilities--roads)). A works whose own power covers its draw is still slowed by the grid's energy ratio, as every plant is; none stood in any run ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).

**The city's old steel** (`OldMetal`). Until 0.7.123 a car the households scrapped was dropped and a demolished building's steel went with its debris. Now four things the city throws out arise each month as old steel, 85% of the steel in them recovered, each its seller's: a car scrapped at fifteen years, 0.9 t, the households'; a building pulled down, 0.3 t a unit of its material, its owner's, and the builders' when the city pulls one of its own down, as their salvage share is; the fabricators' offcuts, 0.05 t a tonne of fabricated steel made; and a worn-out wagon set, 300 t, the railway's. It is not a good, with no market and no world price: it is a pool, which the Scrap Yards buy once a month as they make their scrap, as much as they take at the rate they run, from every seller pro rata to what each threw out, at 70% of scrap's export price (Jerus: *"pay sellers 70%"*) — the households paid into their savings by the cars each scrapped, a sector in its other revenue, *Old metal sold*, and the yards' purchase on their input line, *Old metal*. What no yard takes goes to landfill that month; nothing is carried. A yard is ordered only once the old steel past what the yards standing take is 60% of one more yard's intake (`FEED_GATE`), and is weighed on the share of its nameplate the pool would fill, paying for it; refused, its investors say *too little old steel for one*. The pool is saved with the city (`DataSave.oldMetal`), and the money audit declares the households' part, *OldMetalToHouseholds*.

**A works is weighed with its lorries** (Jerus's decision A; not in the spec). Since 0.7.123 Iron & Steel's planner adds the vans a works' tonnes need, their wear and diesel in what it earns and the vans in its whole cost (`ProcessingSector`). The study's cases and the spec's estimate leave out the fleet every sector has to buy: without it the first build of the probe was a Pelletising Plant on imported ore whose 2,538 vans cost 64% of the plant, lost within months, and over the run Iron & Steel went under whole seventeen times, the backstop was called 31 times and unemployment ended at 13.8%; with it, once, 16 times and 9.7%. The four cases leave the lorries out, as the study did. Jerus has said he will answer it in a note of his own, a batch after the planned ones; until then it stands as built ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).

**What it did.** The playtest is 0.7.120's to the byte through month 1,535: the new goods' markets, the pool and its hooks move nothing while no works stands. At month 1,536 Iron & Steel orders its first Large Mini-Mill, on imported scrap, to replace the 80,803 t of steel a month the city imports, at 0.52 to 0.77% of its cost a month at the city's prices. The mills are built and run at .6 to .8, the city's power short of a 77 MW draw, its health at .9 and the vans still coming; and once a mill covers the imports, steel's local price falls to the middle of its band, so it earns less than it was weighed at, pays interest past what it clears, and some are lost and ordered again: the spec's valuation kept as written, a mill's steel at the import price for as much as the city imports, the planner seeing neither the price falling nor the rate ([open questions](#25-open-questions)). Scrap Yards come from month 2,127, once the pool passes the gate; near the end three yards and two mills stand. The pool is the factories': offcuts are 95 to 97% of it, the cars never pass 3% and the demolitions show in the odd month — 96 t a month recovered at month 600, 984 at 1,200, 5,494 at 1,800, 6,856 at 2,100, 13,045 at 2,400, a yard buying 8,232 and 4,812 going to landfill, 20,446 at 3,000 and 32,750 at 3,900, three yards buying 20,150, at $186.7k a tonne. The city ended at 659,072 people against 577,610, 393,556 posts against 321,670 and 9.7% out of work against 15.6%, its exports $4.94T a month against $2.61T, and its police outrun, coverage 38% against 84% and crime 1.68 times Canada's against 0.44; every month passed the audit and every reload matched. On the ensemble 21 of 25 criteria pass where 20 did: the high rate's towns, 2,000 to 7,000 people at months 600 to 720, are too small for any works of the route and their runs are 0.7.120's to the byte, and under the autopilot Iron & Steel holds posts only in spells, 400 to 840 at most, for 28 to 464 of 2,400 months ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)).

### How an expansion is paid for

In a fixed order, every month: **sell shares** if the register says the company should be raising equity, **spend the till**, **call money home from abroad**, and only then **borrow**. A company under a year old sells half of what it plans; a company with nine good months raises toward its equity target; a company with a bad year raises nothing and borrows nothing. Since 0.7.12 borrowing is two doors: the sector takes the largest bond whose all-in cost is no dearer than the bank's loan and borrows the rest from the bank, and loan and bond together never pass what the bank would lend. A landlord's homes are bought another way since 0.7.11: at least 15% of the cost from its own till and what it holds abroad, its owners asked for new shares for what those lack, and an insured mortgage for the rest ([the bank](#14-the-bank)).

### Capacity retires, and distress retires it faster

Six consecutive losing months, genuinely spare capacity by a 25% margin, and nothing on site — then the biggest holding is thinned, never past what is actually in use, never more than a quarter in one month. The streak is carried in the save, because forgetting it made scrapping save-scummable.

Separately, a firm that **cannot pay** sheds plant: twenty-four months of losses *and* a negative balance after the credit desk has already refused it. Six months killed every founding plant in testing; two years is the runway a real business gets. Since 0.7.12 it may sell any plant that makes something the sector sells, because the rule could once sell only plant making a sector's main good and a Shared Services Centre lost money for 1,151 months. **What is retired is sold to the builders as material** since 0.7.8 — Jerus: *"sold to construction company just in materials, and land to treasury"* — so Construction pays for the template's material at the day's price as far as its cash goes and builds with it before it buys — since 0.7.106 a quarter of that material (`ConstructionControl.SALVAGE_SHARE`, the player's demolitions' rule; [the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)), and the plot goes back to the city as it always did. Occupied homes and the bank are never scrapped by their owners, though since 0.7.22 the city may buy a landlord's homes out and pull them down ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)); the bank closes its own branches, by its own rule ([the bank](#14-the-bank)). A mine over a worked-out deposit now closes inside a year instead of borrowing to pay its crew for three — which makes the bust when the ore runs out sharper, and lets the bank survive it. And a distressed landlord can no longer demolish a city out from under it: the railway's bigger business cycle pushed Real Estate into distress deep enough that it **sold 5,800 of a city's 13,272 homes in seven months** and left 1,137 households with nowhere for a hundred and forty, because the retirement rule asked whether the segment had spare doors and a segment's slack is spread over four sizes. It is guarded, not fixed: nobody sells a door while the housing match says somebody has nowhere, and the proper fix — slack per size — is on the list.

> **Two banners exist because these fail silently**
>
> **Builders being laid off** — construction with no orders shrinks to fit, and everything you build runs through those crews. **Nowhere to build** — the private sector asks for land every month, is told no, and waits. Measured at 120 consecutive months in one ordinary run.

## 9. The builders & the queue

*Every building in the city is put up by one sector out of one month's output, and until 0.7.17 that output was split equally by building type on site, so a single depot took as much as two hundred blocks of flats. Three batches made it the crew each building can use (0.7.17), a price that keeps up with the wages that build it (0.7.19), and a queue the player can put a hand on (0.7.22).*

### Every building gets the crew it can use

Jerus chose *"Share building work fairly"*: *"Builders' output split by buildings on site (every site gets a crew), and no more parking points on building types with nothing left to build"*. The rule it replaced shared the sites' output equally by building *type*. In his year-149 city four types were on site: the builders' own one-depot order, owed 400 points, took a quarter of the output, about 10,700 points, and carried the other 10,300 as progress on a stack with nothing left on it; the landlords' 219 blocks of flats got the same quarter, about 250 homes a month; and 7.82M points sat parked on stacks with nothing to build.

```
weight = buildings on site × points a building^0.70        // CREW_SCALE_EXPONENT = 1 − Bromilow's B
share  = the month's site output after the repairs, one rate a unit of weight,
         each site capped at what it still owes, and what a capped site leaves shared by the same rule
```

The exponent is Bromilow's time–cost law, T = K × C^B, with B about 0.30 on Australian building contracts and 0.32 on Malaysian public projects (Chan 1999): the crew a building can use is its work over its time, which grows as C^1−B. So a building twice the cost takes about 1.23 times as long, and a university of 26,000 points has about eighteen times the crew of a depot's 400. Only the exponent is taken; K, the pace a building could go at alone, is not modelled, and nothing caps a site's crew at it. The weight is the whole building, never what is left of it, because a crew that shrinks with its work never finishes: the rule was briefly the points each stack still owed, and in Jerus's city twelve sites sat one building from done for years. Output no site can use is idle, read as the builders' utilisation, and never banked; a save's parked points are cleared on load and move no money — 7,801,561 of them in his city.

It took four readings to get there. One crew a building, whatever its size, gave a lone university beside two hundred blocks of flats one block's share, and it took ninety months where it had taken twenty-one. A crew in proportion to its points gave a founding's six shops of 120 points a four-hundredth of the output between them, beside a coal plant of 120,000 and the founding's other big works, and the shops did not open for a decade; those two are the exponent at nought and at one. Jerus's own hybrid, *"every order has atleast one crew, and then spare crews are assigned in ascending or descending order sort of like a pyramid"*, cleared every small building a large order starved in the checks, but the builders bought depots for the small orders that rushed through and then stood laid off: thirteen banks failed over the eight default cities against four, and unemployment moved half as much again in a month. By the rule he left, *"v3 if you think yes, otherwise go for the v that starving small orders is fine"*, Bromilow's weights ship, and a small order waits behind a large one. One wait is read off this rule by everything that asks how long an order would take (`BuildingManager.waitFor()`): the planners' lead times and order sizes, the shops' horizon and the build quote, each the order's points over the share it would get beside everything on site.

### The builders count repairs and staffing

Jerus chose *"Builders count repairs and staffing"*: *"Construction's own planner counts repairs and how well it can staff a depot, both when it adds depots and when it sells them off."* The builders' months of queued work are read against what the sites are left after the repairs, which take about 40% of a mature city's construction output, and at their staffed output; a depot is ordered only if the city could staff 80% of it; and retirement keeps what the repairs and the queue need, in staffed output. In his city the depots stood 36% staffed, because a depot is 70% unskilled posts and the unskilled rung was 8.5% filled, and the planner, reading its nameplate against the queue alone, sold its capacity from 232,000 points a month to 56,800 between months 912 and 1,020, after which homes sat flat for nine years. Since 0.7.19 a depot's profit estimate counts the wages of the posts it would fill; it had counted none, and priced a point at what a unit of material costs.

**The crews the work needs.** Jerus chose *"Lay off idle crews"*. Before the labour market fills the month's posts the builders strike the share of their depots' posts the work ahead needs — the repairs plus every point still owed on site, less what the city's own works department does with no posts, over what the depots would do fully staffed — divided by last month's fill, so that the crews who come are the crews the work needs, and never under 25% of the posts (`Construction.IDLE_PAYROLL_FLOOR`) nor over all of them. The posts not offered are not jobs: the city counts fewer, the workers who held them are unemployed by the ordinary path and draw EI, and the allocator gives them any other post it has. The posts kept on are paid in full. Until 0.7.17 an idle builder kept every post filled and paid a quarter of the wages; once every employer's bill became what its workers receive, that quarter was what the crews took home, and the batch's first build, which kept it, turned `MonetaryCheck`'s reading of the rate over and tripled the bank failures of the city held at 25%. The planners still count every post, because a builder that laid crews off for want of work is not short of crews for a queue. What it costs: unemployment moves about twice as much from month to month, the 95th percentile of the default eight's monthly move from 0.81 points to 1.93 (0.7.17).

### The landlords hold a year of work

Jerus chose *"Landlords hold work, not one order"*: *"Landlords may hold orders worth a number of months of building work, instead of one order at a time sized on the whole city's output."* One order at a time, sized on twelve months of the whole city's output, was delivered at about 250 homes a month in his city, and the next order was held *already building* for fifty months. Since 0.7.17 they keep ordering while what their sites owe, the order being weighed included, is at most 12 months of the builders' site output after the repairs (`BusinessInvestment.MAX_ORDER_MONTHS`, `withinMonthsOfWork()`), read with every post offered, since builders who have laid crews off hire them back for the order. When their best home does not fit they order the next smaller one that does (Jerus: *"Try a smaller home"*), and the homes on site count as their supply. Every other sector keeps one order at a time. In his city, run on for 120 months from month 1,792, 0.7.17 added 118,944 homes where 0.7.16 added 38,052, the city grew to 1,517,361 against 1,284,343, and all 47 of its care complexes were finished, the last at month 108.

### The price keeps up with the wages

Jerus chose *"Builders' prices keep up"*: *"The labour part of building and repair prices rises with wages, materials are paid at the price when they're used, and sales tax is in the builder's quote."* Until 0.7.19 the non-material part of every contract and repair bill was the template's cash cost in founding dollars. In his city at month 1,793 a Low-Rise paid the builders 4.25 a point of work against a full depot's wage bill of 6.59 a point, and they lost money in every one of the decade's 120 months, $46.97B in all.

```
labour = min(cash cost / Pe, points × a depot's founding wage bill a point) × (a depot's wage bill a point today / at founding)
work   = the rest of the cash cost, at its founding value struck at the expected price level Pe, + labour
price  = (work + imports + plant × (1 − rM)) / (1 − rB)     // rB the builders' sales tax, rM the materials plant's
```

A Construction Depot's 35 unskilled and 15 diploma posts cost $188.6k a month at the founding ladder for 400 points, 0.47 a point, and that much of a template's cash cost a point is its labour; the rest — overhead, equipment and margin, all but 1,132 of a Low-Rise's 10,196 — stays at its founding value.
