Since 0.7.42 that founding value is struck every month at the price level people expect, as every money constant is ([the month](#1-the-month)), so the founding labour is read off the cash over that level and put back at today's wages (`BuildingManager.nonMaterialCost()`): labour moves with wages and the rest with expectations, and neither is counted twice; at a level of one both read as they did. Indexing the whole cash cost by the wage index was measured by hand and rejected: in his city it would have been 13.5 times the cash cost, a windfall rather than a price. The split is the model's own, because Statistics Canada's Building Construction Price Index is an output index and publishes no labour and material weights. It reaches the quote, the repair bills and the planners' costing, and not the book values or the assessments, which carry a building at its cash cost as before.

**The material is paid at the price when it is used**, by an escalation clause on the pattern of the US Federal Acquisition Regulation's 52.216-4. The owner still pays the whole quote up front, the material priced at the day's rates as an allowance; as the crews draw it, each owner pays its units' share of what the month's draw cost the builders, less its allowance, or is refunded the difference (`Game.settleSiteContracts()`). The city pays on a treasury line of its own, *Material escalation*, owed to the builders as arrears past the advances ceiling; a sector pays from its till. **And the sales tax is in the quote**, grossed up so that the builders keep exactly the work: until 0.7.19 they remitted their rate on all of it out of the work, and in his city 108.6 of their 150.2 of tax fell on material passed through at cost. Who gets it back is the VAT's ([tax, policy and GDP](#12-tax-policy--gdp)).

In his city, run on for 120 months, the builders went from losing $46.97B before tax to earning $9.03B, with 18 loss months where there had been 120; a Low-Rise paid 10.36 a point against a full depot's labour of 6.59, a margin of 36% of what it paid. The first pass took about 30% off the ensembles' cities — the default eight from 166,607 people at the median to 115,002 — because the landlords bore the tax on every home and the bank's first branch carried its upkeep; the rebates on a new rental home and the charter's exemption ([the bank](#14-the-bank)) took both back, and the shipped default city ended at 169,978 against 0.7.18's 166,607 (p 0.442).

**Sectors › Construction reads the month its statement struck** since 0.7.46. The materials row had read the draws since the strike beside a statement of the month before, two different months on one page; Construction now keeps what its month drew, bought from the plant and imported, as its books close (`Sector.beforeBank()`) and saves it, and the page reads *Last month, as on its statement*, with *Since then, so far* under it. A save from before reads *not counted yet* until a month runs.

### The player's hand on the queue

Jerus wanted a construction panel that is *"not just a blue loading screen"*, and then *"not only repirotize and cancel but also destroy buildings, like you yourself destroy buildings"*. On 30 September he chose the mechanics — priority *"Both"*, cancel *"Keep the half-built shell"*, demolish *"City's, plus buy-outs (Recommended)"* — and since 0.7.22 each is a rule with a source (`ConstructionControl`). None of it runs unless the player uses it: with no order set and no rush, every wait and every quote is the old one to the bit, and the default playtest's traces did not move. A site is what the model keeps on site, one stack per building type and, since this batch, each of the city's demolitions; the city's sites are the stacks whose every order is the city's. A stack it shares with an investor's order cannot be reordered, rushed or cancelled, because its progress is one pool.

*The five hands, with their sources (0.7.22), and a sixth (0.7.70)*

| Hand | The rule | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Priority | the city's share of the crews' rule is split among its own sites top down, in the player's order, each taking what it still owes; nobody else's site gains or loses a point; free; a new city site joins at the bottom, and the order clears itself once none of its sites is left | none needed: an owner choosing which of its own contracts goes first |
| Rush | one of the city's sites on 50-hour weeks: 1.137 times a normal month's work in its first month, 1.024 in its second, 0.938 in its third and 0.9375 after, less than a normal month; the city pays 0.375 of the crews' wage bill on the site's share, with the builders' tax, and the crews are paid it as wages; owed as arrears past the ceiling; the count resets after a month off | Business Roundtable, *Scheduled Overtime Effect on Construction Projects*, Report C-2 (1980), Figure 4; time and a half, Canada Labour Code s. 174 |
| Cancel | at the month's end: the month's work done and billed, and the work not done, the material not drawn and the tax on both refunded out of the builders' book; the shell keeps its work, its material and its ground, to be restarted at today's quote or demolished | termination for convenience, FAR 52.249-2; its settlement costs have no line in the model and none is invented |
| Demolish | a site of 5% of the template's points, priced at that building's own work rate with the tax and crewed by the same rule; the building closes as the next month starts — its staff let go and, if it is a home, its households moved into the homes that stand, whoever does not fit left unhoused rather than deleted — since 0.7.106 a quarter of its material (`SALVAGE_SHARE`), all of it before, is sold to the builders by the 0.7.8 rule when the work is done, and its ground comes back to the city; and since 0.7.123 its steel, 0.3 t a unit of its material at 85%, is the builders' old steel, theirs to sell to the Scrap Yards ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)) | SIGTARP, 26 April 2017: Detroit's average demolition of July 2015, $14,855, over NAHB's 2015 average new home, $289,415, is 5.1%; the quarter, the middle of the 20 to 30% of building-related construction and demolition debris recovered for processing and recycling in the United States in 1996 (US EPA, EPA530-R-98-010, 1998) |
| Buy-out | a business's or a landlord's building: the owner is paid its book value, its ground at the land price, and its share of the owner's operating income for the months a replacement would take; its debts stay with it; then the city demolishes it | Ontario's *Expropriations Act*, ss. 13(2), 14(1) and 19(1); the 5% residential allowance of s. 18(1)(a)(i) does not apply, because no owner in the model lives in what it owns |
| Pave | since 0.7.70, one or many of the city's gravel roads paved to Paved Roads, out of the cash: a Paved Road's work and the take-up of the old surface at the demolition's 5% of the gravel road's work, a Paved Road's material less the gravel road's, which goes into its bed, with the builders' tax; queued on the Paved Road site as the city's order, each gravel road carrying its traffic until its own Paved Road opens and then retiring, the ground between the two freed; a paving site is not stopped ([roads](#20-utilities--roads)) | the demolition rule above for the take-up, and the 0.7.8 rule's value of a building's material for the bed |

*What each hand did in the harness's fixture city, as 0.7.22's implementer probed it at about month 38 with the builders' tax at 15% (0.7.22)*

| Hand | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Cancel | an Elementary School ordered at $35.1M, cancelled at 1,023 of its 1,800 points: $15.17M back — $7.73M of work not done, $5.16M of material not drawn, $2.28M of tax; restarting the shell costs $13.68M at today's quote, demolishing it $0.60M |
| Rush | a University on overtime for three months: 1,377, 1,243 and 1,253 points of work against shares of 1,211, 1,213 and 1,335, for a premium of about $230k, $231k and $254k a month with the tax |
| Buy-out | a landlord's block of Low-Rise Apartments: $17.82M to the landlords — $17.12M for the building, $0.15M for the ground and $0.55M of business loss over 10.9 months — and $0.59M to pull it down |
| Demolish | the city's own Elementary School: $1.05M and about 3.6 months; 48 posts and 600 places close, and its 666 units of material are worth $12.2M at that month's price, of which since 0.7.106 a quarter comes back, about $3.05M |

Four calls were made while Jerus slept. A demolished building closes as the next month starts, because closing it on the spot made a city reloaded between the presses play a different month from the live one. A month whose normal share would finish the site anyway is not worked on overtime. *Short of materials* never shows as a site's status, because the model imports whatever the yard, the salvage and the plant do not cover. And the bank's branches can be neither demolished nor bought, since the bank closes them by its own rule. The docs pass's throwaway audit balanced the money to $0.00 through a rush, a cancel, two demolitions and a twenty-house buy-out.

> **A demolition paid, until 0.7.106**
>
> The 0.7.8 rule sold a building's material back at the day's market price, so the fixture's school brought $12.2M of material against a $1.05M demolition, where real demolition recovers far less than new material costs. Since 0.7.106 a quarter comes back (`ConstructionControl.SALVAGE_SHARE`, Jerus's A23) — the player's demolitions, a stopped shell's and a sector's plant retired alike — bought at the market's price as before, and the demolition card says *25% of its material comes back*, its (i) the source. That is recovery by weight, and what comes back is mostly downcycled, so by value it is still generous. In the playtest the first plant retired, at month 17, is the first trace the change moves, and over the run the builders bought 37,071 units of salvage for $200B where they had bought 151,711 for $987B; `AutoBuildCheck`'s decades city, auto-built, stands a village of about 1,800 people at month 600 where it stood 13,581. The citation was quoted from memory, with no network to hand, and is Jerus's to confirm ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).

### The construction page

The hand is played on a page of its own (`ui/ConstructionScreen`), reached from the construction panel's *Open* — a panel folded since 0.7.24 to a 44 px tab down the stage's right edge, a crane, the count of sites and UNDER CONSTRUCTION, which a click opens over the stage, open or folded kept between sessions and folded by default — from *Construction* at the head of Build, and from a build card's *N on site*, which opens it at that site. **Sites** carries the builders' gauge — BUILDERS, the month's points after the repairs; OWED ON SITE; the QUEUE in months against the landlords' twelve; and the MATERIAL in the yard — and then a row a site: the city's first, in the player's order with a rank to move, then everyone else's, then the stopped shells; who ordered it, the done of the total, this month's crews and the time left, paid and owed, a status (*waiting for crews*, *stops at month's end*, *closes as the month starts* among them) and the hand, which on a paving site says *N paving · no stop* since 0.7.70, where its Cancel would be. **Timeline** draws a bar a site to its finish at today's queue. **Demolish** is a picker — the city's buildings, the stopped shells, and the businesses' and landlords' to buy out — and a staging card that says what would close, what it costs, what comes back, the land and the months, before *Demolish* or *Discard*. Every hand that spends money asks first, with the money in the question, and the clock stands still while any question is up. One clock times a site everywhere (`Game.siteMonths()`), because the docs pass found two: the page read the player's order while the right panel, the build card and the quote read the crews' rule. The inbox gained *Overtime now costs more than it gains*, the month before a rush's third, and *A demolition is done*. None of it has been seen on a screen.

## 10. The owners, the bonds & the exchange

*For most of the project's life the corporate sector had no owners: it made money, held it, and nothing ever moved it out. Eighteen companies have a share register now — the seventeen sectors and the bank — the sectors can sell bonds as well as shares since 0.7.12, and both trade on order books where nobody is obliged to take the other side.*

### The register

Every company is founded with shares issued to the city's households at $1,000 each against its book equity. A company reads its own record before it asks for money: **new** under a year, **good** at nine profitable months and not declining, **bad** at six or fewer or a losing year, normal otherwise. Its **equity target** starts at 30% of assets and rises with how volatile its income has been, capped at 70%; a new company aims at half. Households subscribe first — a cell with no debt, no lockout and three months of disposable income banked puts 30% of the excess in — and the world takes the rest, but only if the yield clears the world rate plus three points. New shares are sold at one price, the last trade or fair value before one, and never through the book, because a plan needs to know in the month it builds what it raised. The city's fund never subscribes (0.7.14). Since 0.7.75 the register also keeps each company's **paid-in capital** in money (`Equity.getPaidIn()`): the book its founders' shares were issued against, what it has raised since at home and abroad, less everything its buybacks paid — the bank's own rule, so a company that has bought back more than it raised has paid-in under nothing. The statements split its equity on it ([the screen](#22-the-screen)); a save from before it is given what each company raised since its founding, marked *derived*, and keeping it is why the save is format 33 ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)).

**Forty percent of a positive month is paid out**, from the till, or from the company's own money abroad if the till is short — since 0.7.11 of what the month's net income leaves once the principal it repaid is taken off, Jerus: *"Pay out after principal"*, and since 0.7.12 of that principal net of the new borrowing that rolled it, which is free cash flow to equity, the figure real companies pay dividends from. The bank pays by its own rule ([the bank](#14-the-bank)). A company's **fair value** is the higher of its book equity and the dividend it actually pays capitalised at the world's required return, per share; its **price** is its last trade, and before its first trade its fair value. The city's own holdings are marked at fair value once a share's last trade is a year old (`Exchange.STALE_MARK_MONTHS`, `cityMark()`, 0.7.48), so a share nobody has traded for years does not value the fund at a price nobody would pay now: in the 2,400-month research city Mining's mark went from D\$1,644 a share to D\$0.59.

### One book for each company

Jerus: *"Order book for both."* Since 0.7.12 every share that changes hands meets its buyer on an order book (`OrderBook`), one per company: price and then time decide who is filled, a trade is at the resting order's price, nobody trades with themselves, and **nobody is obliged to trade** — an order with nobody across it rests, and every order still resting is withdrawn at the month's step and posted again from each participant's view of the new month. Each participant posts from the rule it already followed, in this order:

- **The bank's desk**, if it has capital: a bid one per cent under fair value for what its capital can carry, an ask one per cent over it for what it holds, and an ask at fair value itself for anything past its two caps — 25% of the bank's equity in any one company and 50% in all of them. Its own shares are capital, not trading: it bids for them only with what it holds over its target and sells new ones only while it is under it.
- **Emigrants** sell on the way out, and what nobody bids for stays abroad with them.
- **The world** buys when the dividend yield at the best ask clears its own rate plus a three-point premium by a margin, and sells into strength when it falls short, never into a crash, and never in a company under a year old.
- **Companies** past their first year and not in a bad one, with more equity than their target and six months of their costs and their debt service in the till bid for their own shares at up to 10% over fair value, a tenth of the company a year at most, and cancel what they buy. What nobody sells them **stays in the company**: no special dividend is paid by any path since 0.7.12, because paying the unspent money out left the tills bare and brought the failures back.
- **Every household cell** is a participant of its own (Jerus: *"Each household type trades"*): a cell under its cushion offers a tenth of the shortfall at the market, and a cell past it buys four per cent of its excess a month into the best yield over the bank's deposit rate plus a point, the pace its dollars abroad move at.
- **The city's fund** last, taking what the others left. Its rule asks at fair value and, since 0.7.48, bids for a share at the desk's ask, one per cent over it (`TreasuryFund.RULE_PREMIUM`), because at fair value it met nobody. Then the player's hand (0.7.39), at fair value or a price the player names — the best bid, the best ask, the last trade, or fair value in steps of 1% — a buy going no further than the room under the 10% cap, every order the fund has on the company counted as if it filled and the rule's bid making way for the hand's, and its money held out of the cash the rule's bids settle with from the moment it is placed. A waiting order can be cancelled before the step; one that cannot be posted lapses, and the fund's record says why ([tax, policy and GDP](#12-tax-policy--gdp)).

A household short of money sells in the middle of the month, in its waterfall, at the price at which the dividend it gives up costs what borrowing would, so the rich cells' resting bids are where a poor cell's shares go — a transfer between households that no audited pool sees. A share priced at a hundred times its founding price is split a hundred for one, and one that falls to a hundredth is consolidated, and every holding, every resting order and the last trade move by the factor; a cumulative split factor keeps the price history readable per founding share, and since 0.7.48 the history keeps a share's price to six significant figures (`HistorySave.SHARE_PRICE_DIGITS`), where four decimal places had drawn a consolidated company's line at nothing. On the default seed on 28 September the book traded $39.2bn of shares in 44,049 trades over 4,002 months, a listed company traded in 46% of its months, and the median last trade stood at 0.99 of fair value; on 1 October it traded $92.1bn in 32,065 trades over 4,005 months, a listed company traded in 38% of its months, and the median last trade stood at 0.990; on 5 October, at 0.7.49, $52.6T in 29,333 trades at prices 1,213 times the founding's, a listed company trading in 31.5% of its months, the median last trade at 0.990 again.

### The bank was the dealer, until 0.7.12

From the exchange's first night until 0.7.12 the bank's trading desk was the counterparty on every trade, and quoted nothing when the bank was dead. It quoted around fair value, its own book moved the quote, it never sold what it did not hold, and it marked what it held at the lower of the quote and fair value. Its book was capped at a multiple of the bank's equity, which is money — and until 18 September that cap was the one figure in the exchange a currency reform did not divide. It was re-struck each month *after* the households settled, so for the first half of every month a reformed city's desk believed it had a hundred times the room it had; a household with no savings and a grocery bill it could not meet borrowed in the plain city and sold $1.03 of shares in the reformed one, and from there household debt was 4.2% apart in one month and the exchange rate with it. The bisect blamed the fourteenth sector's inventory term, and the term was right: it had moved GDP, GDP had moved what the desk's book was worth against its limit, and a cancellation that had been landing on one side of zero started landing on the other. A bisect names what perturbed a fault, not what the fault is; a latent member of that family is not a harmless one, it is one nobody has perturbed yet.

```
mid = fair × clamp(1 − 0.25 × (dealerShares − demand) / scale, 0.50, 5.00)     // the dealer's quote, until 0.7.12
bid/ask = mid ∓ half of a 2% spread
```

**The desk foots, since 19 September.** Its opened lines on the bank's statement had left out the term that is usually the largest — the change in the mark on what it holds — so a loss sat over sub-lines that did not add to it. *Re-marked what it holds* (`Bank.getMarkChange()`) is a line of its own now, and when it is the bulk of a loss the note says why, which is Jerus's question — *"explain to me the trading desk, cause a bunch of times it's losing billions"*: with buyers it could not fill the dealer quoted up to five times fair value to draw sellers, and it marked what it held at the lower of the quote and fair value, so a wave of emigrants selling into a bubble cost it the difference the same day. `BankCheck` asserts the lines plus the re-mark equal the total, and on a played city they did in 120 of 120 months. Whether a dealer should bid at a quote it does not believe in stopped being a question when the dealer went; the desk marks at the lower of the last trade and fair value. Since 0.7.1 the same desk also buys back the city's paper from the households, at the month's market value off the curve.

> **What it was worth**
>
> When the exchange arrived, eight seeds against the batch before it: GDP $65M → $77M a month, worst unemployment 46% → 37%, exports $104M → $124M, the currency inside 3.5% of parity, dividends to households $3–18bn → $30–56bn a run, every company home-owned in six seeds of eight — and **bank failures 10 → 0**, because the trading desk was a business and a profitable one, and a sector that has just paid its owners borrows for its next mine.

### The firms sell bonds

Jerus: *"notes are the loans businesses make to the banks, and bonds are debts that they issue to investors… households can buy them, but banks also buy them as, only if it wants, and yes they are tradeable so they have par value and all."* The bank failed 115 times on 0.7.11's eight default seeds, and the cause was concentration: the one bank was every business's only lender, and the sector that broke it owed five to six times its equity. So since 0.7.12 a sector borrows through two doors. A **bond** (`CorporateBond`) is a ten-year bullet with a coupon every month, built at par: the underwriter announces the room, every bidder says what it would take at each yield, the coupon is the lowest yield that fills the issue and the rest is a bank loan, and the bank underwrites it for the city's own charge, $12k plus 0.75%. A sector borrowing for a building takes the largest bond whose all-in cost is no dearer than the loan and borrows the rest; the first reading let bonds raise what a capital-short bank had refused, at coupons up to 16%, and failed the bank more, so loan and bond together never pass what the bank would lend. A sector short in the month can be sold a bond by the shortfall desk the same way.

Every bond trades on a book of its own, and the buyers are the ones Jerus named, each by the rule it already had for the nearest thing it holds: the household cells by their rule for the city's paper, wanting a share of each issue that rises with its expected return over what savers are paid; companies that owe nothing by the rule that sends idle cash abroad, never into their own bonds; the world by hot money's; the bank only on the capital it holds over its target, at the yield that makes the bond earn what an equal loan would; and the city's fund. A household short of money sells its bonds after its dollars abroad and before its shares. A bond that falls due is paid from its issuer's till to every holder at face. When a sector's firms default the bondholders lose too, and since 0.7.12 each instrument recovers what it recovers in the world: 75% of a bank loan and 45% of a bond (`LOAN_RECOVERY`, `BOND_RECOVERY`, the midpoints of Moody's and S&P's long-run averages), and the eight seeds measured 74.8% and 44.9%. On the default seed on 28 September 2,266 bonds were issued for $71.2bn over the run; 44 were outstanding at the end, $2.36bn, the households holding $1.29bn of it, other companies $914M and the world $126M. On 1 October 1,857 were issued for $62.8bn, and 5 were outstanding at the end, $183M, the households holding $40.3M of it; on 5 October, at 0.7.49, 2,834 were issued for $11.2T, and 151 were outstanding at the end, $1.81T, the households holding $899bn of it, other companies $761bn and the world $155bn.

The player does not trade, bar the fund's hand, which since 0.7.39 has a broker's pages: the fund's Search, every listed company and every bond outstanding as the player types, and a page a security — its price chart, a share's split-adjusted with fair value and the fund's average cost as lines and its orders as flags, a bond's the cash it still pays, a column a year; KEY STATS; THE BOOK; its record; YOUR POSITION; and THE ORDER TICKET, an order chosen, then reviewed, then placed. A company's owners are a card since 0.7.30, ITS OWNERS on its Balance sheet page under Sectors, which the Bank's Capital & owners page draws too: who holds it as a bar — the city's households, abroad, the bank's desk — then LAST TRADE and its month, or fair value where there has been none, FAIR VALUE, YIELD, MARKET CAP, TRADED, DIVIDEND, BOOK and BOUGHT BACK, with the order book's five levels a side behind *details* in plain figures and the share chart beside them, and the company's regime, payout rule and what it has raised and paid behind its (i). There is a price chart per company, each household cell's shares at the last trade and its bonds, the foreign share of each register on its owners card and the city's shares in foreign hands on Trade, and under Finances a bond market with every issue, who holds it and each bond's own book, drawn ten levels a side since 0.7.32 with the tables twelve deep behind *details*.

## 11. Labour & schools

*A wage used to be one of six constants, copied in once at startup. Labour is a market now, skill is an axis, and a school is the only way to make a doctor at home.*

### Four bands, one price each

```
NONE < DIPLOMA < COLLEGE < UNIVERSITY       // substitution runs downward only
tightness = posts / qualified supply        // per band, at the fill that gives every worker the best-paid post they qualify for (0.7.18)
target    = minimumWage × ratio[job] × clamp(tightness^0.5, 0.70, 4.0)
wage     += (target − wage) × 0.12          // 90% of a shortage prices in over 18 months
```

The **minimum wage is the base** of the whole ladder, so one Policy dial moves every wage in the city, the treasury's own payroll included. Because the unskilled base *is* the floor, an unskilled glut cannot be priced away — it clears in people instead, which is exactly what a binding minimum wage does. The dial is set in founding money and met in today's: the floor is the dial times the cost of living times the player's nudge (`LabourMarket.cashMinimumWage()`), which Policy's THE FLOOR and the drawer's *Min wage* print since 0.7.36 and the People screen's WORK card since 0.7.38; City History's *Minimum wage, founding money* and the year book's column are the dial itself, because the history keeps neither the cost of living nor the nudge as a series. Since 0.7.36 Policy's Wages page draws the eleven jobs under their bands against that floor, each band's chip off `isPinned()`, and a staged floor's ghosts where each wage would head (`targetWageAt()`); and since 0.7.47 a band reads as pinned against the floor in today's money, not the founding one, which is what lets a glut at the indexed floor leave ([migration](#2-people)). Wages also chase the cost of living in full, both directions. Until 0.7.42 that was a twenty-fourth of the gap to the price index a month, about two years; since then, once the basket is based, half of a wage's indexing is the inflation people expect and the other half chases the index at a forty-eighth of the gap (`EXPECTED_SHARE`, `DRIFT_PER_MONTH`), so the pass-through is still one, with no overshoot, and the tightness curve above stays the Phillips part. A harness has held them to it since 0.6.11: `LabourCheck` runs steady inflation and asserts every month that the wage index moves by the expected month to `EXPECTED_SHARE` and by the chase to the rest — one indexation, not two — and sits inside the lag's window, through a currency reform and a reload. When it went in, every one of 144 checkpoint readings on all eight seeds sat at the level the two-year lag implied, and the one-third overshoot measured on 15 September does not reproduce. Students and prisoners are out of the supply while they are away, and the pool is what is left when filled posts are taken off the labour force — an identity, not a second count.

**Gated jobs carry a licence premium** on top of their band's: posts over licence holders, same elasticity, never below one, the pair capped at 4×. A hospital with no medical school pays its doctors over the graduate band — measured at 1.26× against a band in glut at 0.83× — and that price is what draws licensed arrivals and sends graduates back to school.

**Workers take the best-paid job they qualify for** (0.7.18; `PopulationManager.fillByBand()`). Jerus: *"Workers take the best-paid job they qualify for, instead of skilled jobs being filled first. Unskilled pay could then never pass diploma pay, but hospitals and schools would lose some staff."* The bands used to be filled from the top down, with only a band's surplus passed down the ladder, so a city short of hands put the whole shortage on its bottom rung whatever that rung paid: in his year-149 city every one of 185,132 missing workers was an empty unskilled post, 8.5% staffed at $68.6k a month, more than a doctor's $60.4k, while diploma holders filled diploma posts at $25.5k. The rule people follow is occupational choice with skill downgrading — take the best-paid work you are qualified for, and when the lower rung pays as well the better-qualified move down it and push the shortage up (Beaudry, Green and Sand 2016, *Journal of Labor Economics* 34(S1)); no number is taken from it, only the rule. A worker may hold any post at or below their band. The bands are filled from the top as before, and a band that still has empty posts and would pay more than the band above it is joined to it, one market at one wage, until nobody holds a lower-paid post while a better-paid one they could take stands empty; the allocator, the wage, migration's chance of work and the planners' spare workers all read the one fill. How many are employed does not change, only which posts stand empty, and where the wages already fall with the ladder nothing is joined. In his city, run on for 120 months, 62,132 graduates took unskilled posts in the first month, the unskilled rung went from 8.5% to 39.3% staffed in that month, its empty posts at the end from 29,110 to 2,106, the unskilled and diploma wages became one at $17.41k, and the city's healthcare went from 91.5% to 99.4% staffed (0.7.18). The default cities carry unemployment, so it rarely binds in them; a default city is short of college workers all its life, at a median college fill of 0.57, and only a school or a dearer college wage brings them.

### Nine schools, and a pipeline

| Stage | Takes | Produces | Course |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Elementary, Middle, High | children and teens | a diploma, at the *narrowest* stage's coverage | 4 + 3 + 5 yr |
| Community College | diploma-holders | college graduates | 24 mo |
| University | diploma-holders | university graduates | 48 mo |
| Medical, Law, Business, Technology | university graduates | a licence for one job type — raises nobody's band | 84 / 36 / 24 / 48 mo |

Three things make an adult study, multiplied not averaged: a free seat, a return (nobody spends four years to earn what they already earn — a medical student's alternative is the best *ungated* university job), and the money, with tuition a Policy dial between the treasury and the household. **Students are in flight**: cohorts queue by months remaining, graduate at the front, thin at the adults' own attrition, and are out of the labour supply until they finish — living on savings, a grant worth $525 a month in founding money at the default dial, and since 0.7.19 kept up with prices — since 0.7.42 at the price level people expect — and a loan they begin repaying over 114 months the month they graduate. A university built today is graduates in month 49, not this month. Migration can still bring a licensed professional — some share of arriving graduates already hold one — so a small city imports its doctor and a city of eighty thousand cannot import two hundred at any price. That is the handoff to the schools, by arithmetic rather than by rule.

The school leavers' diplomas are a read of their own since 0.7.28 (`Education.getNewDiplomas()`, gross, *not recorded yet* after a load), because the DIPLOMA band's movement nets off every college and university finisher and can read −18 in a month a high school handed diplomas out. And since 0.7.46 the history's *Graduates* are the month's gains at every level (`Education.gainedThisMonth()`), where the series had summed movements whose every +1 has its −1 at the band left, and recorded nothing but rounding.

**A school above the ladder is asked for the students the city would get and hire** since 0.7.51 (`CityNeeds.wanted()`). Jerus: *"universities and education other than elem middl and high schools tend to be overstated and way too early sometimes"*. Its NEEDS YOU row had read who would come if seats were free — those eligible, times who is willing and the enrolment rate, times the course — and nothing asked whether the city had work for the graduates: a founded city of 118 people with five university posts was told to build a $417M university for 33, and Jerus's city has 11,583 university seats with nobody in them and 1,043 lawyers for 75 law posts. The row now wants the smaller of who would come and the posts the degree fills (`CityNeeds.hires()`): the posts of the band it qualifies for, standing and on site, less the people already qualified for them, plus the posts their holders leave as they age out over one course — for a professional school its licence's posts and the licensed. In the 2,400-month city the college's row reads *0 seats, 1,618 would come and be hired*, and the university, medical and law rows that read 24,395, 381 and 162 who would come are gone. Under a class of 25 there is no row, as before, and a first school of its kind is listed only once those would fill half the smallest that teaches it (`CityNeeds.FIRST_SCHOOL_SHARE`, the businesses' first-plant rule). Build sizes an order for one ahead ([the screen](#22-the-screen)), counting the feeder's graduates by the time it opens: the high schools' diplomas for a college or a university, read off saved state (`Education.schoolLeavers()`, the month's own arithmetic, which a load does not lose as it loses `getNewDiplomas()`), and the university's cohorts in flight for a professional school. Services › Education's school not built says both sides: that city's university reads *not built: 24,395 would come, 133 posts for them*.

### The price of a place

Jerus: *"grants its just a menu where you can choose between a fixed amount, or a percentage of last month's surplus, or a % as it is now of living costs, or a % of tuition. and then another slider which is the interest rate for the student loans … and also make it so that you can tweak the price of tuition as well."* Since 0.6.9 the Policy tab's *Promises → Schools* page — the Tuition page renamed — has carried the students' dials together: on one foot bar, five when it opened and since 0.7.6 a price for each kind of school besides, and since 0.7.36 in the staged tray at the foot of the stage ([setting them](#12-tax-policy--gdp)). **The grant is a basis and an amount** (`TaxPolicy.GrantBasis`): a share of the unskilled wage, which was the founding rule and the default until 0.7.19, and which is what "as it is now of living costs" turned out to be; a fixed sum a student, which since 0.7.19 is a real amount kept up with prices and the default for a new city; a share of last month's surplus, as one pool; or a share of each student's own course fee. Each basis has its own ceiling, and all four are struck by one rule, `TaxPolicy.grantBill`, that the treasury's bill, the save's re-strike, the students' row and the page all call, so a grant on the wrong thing cannot look right on one screen and wrong on another. **Since 0.7.19 the grant follows prices** (Jerus: *"Grant follows prices"*): a new city's is $525 a month in founding money times the month's price index until 0.7.42, and since then times the expected price level the month's constants are struck at (`TaxPolicy.DEFAULT_FIXED_GRANT`, at founding the old default's bill to the cent); a save keeps the basis it was played on (*"Old saves keep theirs"*), and an older save's fixed amount is read as the real amount that pays the same at the load month's index. The wage share had been paying his year-149 city $1,425M a month, $9.72k a student; on the new basis it would have paid $415M, $2.83k a student. **The student loan has a rate**, 0 to 15%, nothing by default: the Canadian shape, nothing accruing while they study, charged on a graduate's balance and paid with the instalment, so the balance is only ever principal and falls exactly as it did. The interest is the treasury's own revenue line, *Student loan interest*; the principal still comes back through the treasury's journal. A prisoner's loan freezes with the rest of their debts, no instalment and no interest. **And the price of a place is the player's**: `tuitionScale`, 0 to 5× the founding table, read wherever a fee is read.

**Since 0.7.6 it is a price per school.** Jerus: *"have it so that not only can you raise prices but also raise the price for a specific university, and beside the dial it shows the current space, the current students, and the current cost and revenue."* The scale is nine, one for each kind of school (`TaxPolicy.tuitionScaleOf(type)`), in the shape 0.7.4 gave the income taxes: *Every school at once* moves all nine, and taking it back unstages every kind's own; each kind has its own dial and four figures off the model — the places its buildings seat, the students in it, what its staff and buildings cost the treasury this month, and the tuition its students paid. Since 0.7.36 the page leads with WHO CAN AFFORD A PLACE, a row a course — a place's fee after the city's share against the best wage of whoever can take it, red at `Education.MAX_BURDEN`, 60% — each row opening into its own price; then WHO PAYS FOR SCHOOL; THE SCHOOLS THIS MONTH, which foots now, staff and buildings less what households paid being the net cost and the tuition the city waives in grey outside the sum; and WHAT A PLACE IS PRICED AT; then the grant and the loan. A kind with nothing standing says *no school* and its dial is greyed. The nine ride the end of the policy array, and a shorter array reads them as the one scale it carried. Building it found the trap 0.7.4 had found for the income tax: the month and the load path told every school the first kind's price, which would have put nine prices back to one on every load, and `Game.tellTheSchoolsTheirPrices` hands each kind its own now.

At the defaults nothing moves, bit for bit. At ×3 the poverty trap the `Education` header describes is back: a one-university city at five years has 1,718 students and 69% of its diploma-holders willing at ×1, 1,173 and 26% at ×3, and 1,756 and 90% at ×0. The default playtest has never built a school, so `-Dplaytest.schools=true` builds them, and eight seeds at tuition ×3, the grant half of tuition and loans at 5% all ran clean, the treasury taking $1.1–3.8M a month of interest and fewer people studying. On the way the schools' books were found never to have been restored on the load path — the sixth sighting of that gap, fixed.

## 12. Tax, policy & GDP

*Four base rates since 0.7.4 — on profit, on sales, on wages and on property — and everything else is an offset in rate points from one of them. Resolution happens in one place, clamped, so no screen can quote a rate the city does not collect.*

| Lever | Default | Max | Offsets |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Profit tax | 15% | 60% | fifteen sectors; the bank is charged retail's rate |
| Sales tax | 15% | 60% | fifteen sectors |
| Wage tax | 15% | 60% | four education wage bands |
| Property tax | 1.5%/yr | 10%/yr | seventeen sectors, each held within ten points either way since 0.7.47, where the others' offsets go to thirty, plus farmland relief, and since 0.7.107 zoned ground assessed at its zone's price; quoted annually, charged monthly |

Beside them: the minimum wage, the policy interest rate, tuition's split and since 0.6.9 its price, the pension contribution and replacement rates, the EI premium and benefit rates, the students' grant on its basis and the student loan's rate, since 0.6.8 the health fee's scale and the health premium, since 16 September the transit fare, since 0.7.14 the city's fund's dial, since 0.7.43 food assistance, since 0.7.48 the fund's withdrawal, since 0.7.103 the fuel duty, and since 0.7.107 the zones and the forest law, Policy's fifth area since 0.7.109 ([land](#18-land)) — each a dial with a stated maximum. The rollover and what happens when the bank fails are the treasury's settings, on Finances ([the city's borrowing](#13-the-citys-borrowing), [the bank](#14-the-bank)), and so are the fund's two dials, the withdrawal leading its Rules & cash page. The fare is a price to a car owner and a charge to everybody else (0.7.49): an owner in reach of a line weighs it against a journey's fuel, and a commuter with no car of their own rides at any fare where a line reaches and a seat is free ([transport](#21-transport--vehicles)). It is set per ride, $2.50 by default and $50 at the absurd end, and charged forty journeys a month, because a rider is a person and for its first day it was charged once a month against a constant that says *a single journey* — Jerus caught it by reading the number. Since 0.7.42 the dial is real, set at founding prices and charged at the level the month's constants are struck at, and since 0.7.47 a currency reform divides its cap by the new unit, so a reformed city's ladder still ends where a founding one's does.

**The fuel duty** (0.7.103; `TaxPolicy`'s THE FUEL DUTY; Jerus's A7) is a duty a litre on the petrol the forecourts sell the drivers, on a page of its own, Taxes › Fuel, staged with the taxes: nothing by default, a cent a step, to a dollar a litre at founding prices (`MAX_FUEL_DUTY`, past the dearest duty the research found, the Netherlands' EUR 0.789 a litre in 2024), and real as the fare is, set in founding money, charged at the expected price level and divided by a reform. The pump's price rises by exactly it, added after the sales tax is passed on (`Retail.pumpPrice()`), so the grocers' sale, their tax and their margin are what they were and the whole duty is the treasury's: in the tax take, and so in EARNED and the budget alike, on a line of its own, Government's *Fuel duty*, and in the money audit as *+ e FuelDuty*. A journey's fuel is the price on the sign, so a duty moves owners toward the bus ([transport](#21-transport--vehicles)). Only petrol is sold at the pump: no driver burns diesel, and the vans and the railway buy theirs off the market near wholesale, so they pay none (Jerus: *"petrol only, as built"*). `PolicyPreview` strikes it on the month's litres (`fuelDutyAt()`); it rides the end of the policy's array and the month's duty the grocers' extras, so an older save reads none, and at nothing the default playtest's traces did not move.

**The policy rate reaches 100% since 0.7.2** (`DebtManager.MAX_POLICY_RATE` 1.00; it stopped at 25% before), a bound that never binds in play and is there so a typo cannot set 2,500%. The slider has chips at 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 75 and 100. The Taylor rule beside it is printed as the rule says it (`ruleRate()`), and where the dial's bounds cut it the page says so: *"the rule would set −4.60%, the dial stops at 0.00%"* was the default seed's last month on 22 September, on −3.1% inflation, on 28 September it read −0.35% on −0.2%, and on 1 October −0.33% on −0.2%; on 5 October, at 0.7.49, the rule asked 2.33% on 1.6% inflation, inside the dial's bounds, so the page had nothing to add. Since 0.7.0 the dial is the price of money, and it has three companions on the same page: the target the rule aims at, a dial since 0.7.4, the holdings dial and the advances ceiling; all four are told in [the central bank](#15-the-central-bank).

### Setting them: five areas, one proposal

**The Policy tab is a hub** since 0.7.36: four area cards, five since 0.7.109 — Taxes, Wages, Money, Promises and Zoning ([land](#18-land)) — each a door with its figure, a small picture and a line, over WHAT IS BITING, alert cards with the month one first bites marked new and a door to where it is undone, and RECENT DECISIONS, the last five tax, promise, central bank, currency and, since 0.7.109, zoning decisions. The areas are chips in the head and their pages tabs, and four figures stand over every page but Zoning's, which has its own, each a door: TAX A MONTH, THE FLOOR in today's money, THE POLICY RATE, and PROMISES, which since 0.7.36 leaves out the tuition the city waives, revenue forgone rather than money out. Promises has six pages since 0.7.45, when food assistance got one of its own: Pensions, Out of work, Food, Health, Schools and Subsidies.

"Income tax" is not one tax. It is three — on profit, on value added, and on every payroll — and until 0.7.4 the three shared one dial, and the screens used to be split by *where the modifier lived* rather than by what the money is. They are split by the tax now: Everything · Profit · Sales · Wage · Property. Jerus: *"sure you can choose sale tax for manufacturing, but what about just increasing sale tax for all at the same time? currently that's a hassle, i want to be able to do that for every type of tax, even wage tax."* Since 0.7.4 each of the three has a base of its own, every offset rides its own tax's base, and each tax page's top dial is that base; the old city rate is *Every tax at once* on the Everything page, which moves all three and shows the three side by side — since 0.7.36 as three chips, the thumb on the profit rate with three named ticks, and *three rates* in grey once they part. Splitting them found the load path reading the old single rate *after* the policy array, which would have put a split back together on every load, and the Government tab printing the bank's profit tax at the income rate while the city charged it retail's.

```
[−]  ══════●══════  [+]        20.25%
0.00% to 60.00% · one step is 0.25 points · it is 20.00%
```

Drag to cross the range; it snaps hard on release, and each button is worth exactly one step. **The step is a quarter point everywhere except property, which gets a twentieth** — the same step has a very different bite: 20.00% to 20.25% of income is one part in eighty of what income tax raises, 1.00% to 1.25% of assessed value is one part in four.

**Since 0.7.6 it is every dial's shape, not the tax pages' own.** Jerus: *"all the dials in the policy in the promises section, make them a slider with steps, and a + − on the ends, basically i think it's better if you create an object or class of slider"*. There had been three shapes of one control, and there is one class now, `ui/Ladder`: a minus, a slider that snaps to the step, a plus, the reading in the accent colour when it is off what the city charges, and an ends line — *x to y · one step is z · it is w*. The sensitivity is the step and nothing else, because a drag coarser than a click would be two dials in one. The reading follows the thumb and the change waits for the release, because restaging on every pixel redraws the screen under the pointer. On it are every tax dial and the farmland relief, the wage floor and the policy rate, the target, the holdings and the ceiling, which apply at once and keep their chips as shortcuts, the pension's two, EI's two, both health dials, the tuition split, every school's price, the grant and the loan, and the fare, on Infrastructure › Transit since 0.7.28; each kept its key, range, step and formatter exactly, and `PolicyCheck` did not notice. The standing subsidies are switches and the currency reform is a choice of three, so neither is a ladder.

**Since 0.7.36 every dial is a dial card** (`Levers`; the fare's since 0.7.38): its paragraph behind its name's (i), its reading, the ladder — with named marks under the track, the three income rates once parted, the rule's rate, the clinic's break-even, and words where a reading would mislead (`Ladder.idle()`) — and beside it WHAT IT WOULD DO, each effect before → after over a pair of bars, following the thumb while it is dragged (`Ladder.onTrack()`), the change still waiting for the release, under one grey line: *Struck on this month's books; behaviour is not projected.* Each tax page leads with its base on a dial card and WHO PAYS as ranked rows, the bank a profit payer taxed at Retail's rate in arrears, each row opening into its own offset's card.

**Changes stage and apply together.** A budget is not one rate moved in isolation, so several dials can be moved and applied as one proposal. On the taxes' pages and Schools they stage, since 0.7.36, into a tray at the foot of the stage — a chip a change with its ×, THE BUDGET before → after, and *Apply all N* or *Discard* — where until then a foot bar listed them in the order they were made, and a dial dragged back to the live value unstages rather than staging a no-op. Each dial registers its own setter, which is what lets one press apply a city rate, three sector offsets and the farmland relief without a switch on the key. THE BUDGET is the model's, not the screen's (`PolicyPreview`, 0.7.36): last month's balance plus every line's move — the four taxes and the bank's, which is next month's because it is taxed in arrears, the contributions, both premiums, pensions, EI on the pool, the care fees, tuition, the grant and the loans' interest — each its owner's read of a detached copy of the policy (`TaxPolicy.copy()`), so a dial at zero previews something and the screen adds nothing up, and `PolicyPreviewCheck` holds that, applied, the preview is the model: a month on, the EI bill and the bank's tax charged are the previews to the cent. It strikes the same arithmetic twice — once at what the city charges, once at what is staged — and says plainly that *both* figures are models: comparing a model against last month's actual would make a batch that changed nothing read as a swing. The difference is the answer. Since 0.7.23 each dial a press applies writes a line of its own to the city's decision log at that month, so a proposal of five dials is one flag of five on City History, and a dial set to what it already reads writes nothing ([the screen](#22-the-screen)).

The wage page totals what a payslip actually loses — wage tax plus the pension contribution plus the EI premium, and since 0.6.8 the health premium — which no screen in this game had ever added up; since 0.7.36 it is WHAT A PAYSLIP LOSES, a bar of the wage in four parts at the wage rate, each band moved off it with its own total (`TaxPolicy.payslipShare()`). The premiums and the contribution are read-only there, with a door to Promises, because a second copy of a lever is how two screens start disagreeing about what the city charges.

### What the treasury actually did

**Earned, surplus, banked** (0.7.31). Jerus: *"the money one has is barely visible to see as well as ones income"*, and in his city the line under the cash said +$1.5B a month while the cash grew $2.3B. Three figures, all of them right, are named apart everywhere since: EARNED, the header's — the tax take less the running programmes plus the utilities' net, at today's dials (`Game.getIncome()`); the budget's SURPLUS; and what the cash BANKED. The Government Overview's FROM EARNED TO BANKED walks the road between them as three tiles with every step named and each a door to where it is decided: from EARNED to the budget, eleven steps from 0.7.49 and fifteen since 0.7.102 (`Game.getEarnedToBudget()`) — land sold and bought, buildings, the fund's transfer, the mortgage insurance's premiums and claims, subsidies, the food vouchers, the central bank's remittance and its interest, the students' loan interest, and since 0.7.102 the repairs, the arrears paid down and the reserve's crude bought and sold — with *Today's dials, not the month's* for what a dial moved between the presses leaves; from the budget to the cash, the paper raised and repaid, every line of the journal below by name, and *Not accounted for*. The fares were a twelfth step until 0.7.49, in EARNED and the cash and not in the budget. The old statement is behind *details*.

The Government tab has a bridge from the budget balance — an income measure — to what the treasury's cash actually did between one press and the next, and until 19 September its last row, *Everything else the treasury did*, was a residual with a name on it: land, buildings, reserves, capital put into the bank, bonds bought back, on any month the player did one of them. Jerus: *"it just says 'everything else' — that should be expandable, cause a lot of times that's where a bunch of important things happen."* It opened, and since 0.7.31 each of its lines is a step of the bridge. `TreasuryJournal` records every movement of the city's cash that is neither a budget line nor paper raised or repaid, where it happens and in the player's words — *Put capital into the bank*, *Bought reserves*, *Bought back a bond*, *Lent to students, net of repayments*, since 0.7.0 *Repaid the central bank* and *Advanced by the central bank (printed)*, since 0.7.6 land bought out of the vault, since 0.7.14 what the dial paid into the fund and what resolving the bank cost, and since 0.7.22 *Sold a demolition's material to the builders* — press to press, for the month that ended and the one in progress, both carried in the save. What the lines do not explain prints under them as *Not accounted for*, and on a month the city borrows it is the first coupon's timing, to the cent. Land and buildings stay on the budget's own line and are deliberately not named twice. Opening the row found that *Raised by issuing paper* had read $0 on every month the city borrowed, because its counter was cleared before the strike; that the city's own repair bill and the transit fares were on the Government screen and not in the budget's totals — since 0.7.31 neither has been drawn as a budget line (the repairs had made Spending's key add to 111%), the repairs are named under the totals as outside the budget's total and on the bridge, and since 0.7.49 the fares are a budget line of their own, *Transit fares*, beside *Transit*, the bill the treasury has paid since then; and, not fixed that night, that the bank had never paid for the city's paper (see [debt](#13-the-citys-borrowing)). The budget gained its own lines in the batches since — the health premium, student loan interest, the central bank's remittance and the interest on its advances, a Subsidies line the Government tab had never had, since 0.7.11 the premiums the landlords pay to insure their mortgages under revenue and the claims the city pays on them under spending, since 0.7.14 *Transfer from the fund*, since 0.7.43 *Food assistance*, and since 0.7.49 *Transit fares* and *Transit*; since 0.7.19 *Material escalation on the city's building contracts* and since 0.7.22 *Overtime on the city's rushed sites*, both discretionary and owed to the builders as arrears past the ceiling, with a cancelled order's refund netted against the capital spending — and since 0.7.6 *Land bought* opens into what was converted, what came out of the vault and what was bought back. And since 0.7.0 every payment the treasury makes goes through one door, `Game.treasuryPays(TreasuryLine, amount)`, which is what lets the central bank's ceiling decide who is paid.

**Since 0.7.102 every monthly flow of the treasury is inside the budget's totals** (Jerus's A15, *"rec plus maintence"*). The repairs to the city's own buildings, the arrears it pays down to the businesses, and the strategic reserve's crude bought and sold are budget lines — *Repairs*, *Arrears paid down*, *Crude for the reserve* and *Crude sold from the reserve*, each with its icon and its door (`NationalAccounts`, saved at the government block's end, an older save reading them as nothing) — so the surplus, the rings, the lists and the surplus series carry them, the journal no longer names them, the walk from EARNED takes them as four more steps, and nothing is named *outside the budget's total* any more; the fuel duty has had a line beside them since 0.7.103. What stays outside, and why, is `TreasuryJournal`'s list: a claim or a debt changing hands — the students' loans, the fund's pay-ins and draws, reserves, the bank's resolution capital and preferred, buybacks, the central bank's advances and repayments — and what is not monthly, a demolition's salvage and land out of the vault. The lower balance left the rollover less surplus to net against what falls due, so it rolls more, which moved the playtest's traces from month 601.

### VAT with input credits

Sales tax is a real value-added tax: exports zero-rated with credits still claimable, imports charged at the buyer's rate and fully creditable, the city exempt both ways, residential rent an exempt supply. One deliberate departure from the real thing — **the rate follows the producer, not the product** — because under a product rate most of the sector dials would be cosmetic.

**And the builders' tax is in their quote** since 0.7.19 ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)), so who finally bears it is the real rules'. A business that makes taxable supplies claims the tax on its buildings back as the work is billed, and on its repairs as an input (CRA RC4022; *Excise Tax Act* ss. 169(1) and 123(1)). The landlords, whose rent is an exempt supply, claim no credit, but get the tax on a new rental home back by a rebate: all of it on purpose-built rental housing, a building of four homes or more held for rent (RC4231; s. 256.2(3.1)), which the Studio and the Low-Rise Apartments are; and on any other new rental home the new residential rental property rebate, 36% of the tax and at most $6,300 a unit, phased out between $350,000 and $450,000 of value, those figures in founding money at the price level the month's constants are struck at (the month's price index until 0.7.42), so a House, about $454k with its plot at founding, gets about nothing. No rebate reaches a repair. The city's own rebate (RC4034) is the tax coming home, because the city is what collects it, so it has no line; and the bank's branch, an exempt financial service, bears it. Jerus chose *"Businesses claim it back"*, then, after the first measurement, *"Both rebates"*, and on the landlords' repairs still being taxed, *"Leave as the law has it"*. In his year-149 city the landlords' rebate came to $20.13B over the decade, 15.1% of what they built (0.7.19).

Net remittance is allowed to go negative and is not floored: under producer rates a sector buying high and selling low genuinely is owed money, and flooring would quietly turn a rate cut into a partial one. When it happens the screen names who is owed. **And the producer pays it** — out of its own cash, as it pays the profit tax on its statement's after-tax line. Both used to be collected by the treasury from nobody; closing the money identity found them.

### GDP

Measured by expenditure, C + I + G + NX, replacing an income-approach figure that went negative the moment firms started paying interest. Profit is not production. Since 0.7.20 a ratio to it says *of GDP, annualised* while fewer than twelve months are recorded and *of annual GDP* after. The screens had already scaled a young city's months to a year; only the words changed, and the Dashboard, which had summed the months there were and called them a year. A founding city's revenue really can be 169.7% of its annualised GDP, as the play-through of 0.7.19 read it in month 7: its revenue is the builders' sales tax on its own orders, large against an economy that is mostly those orders. Since 0.7.31 a loaded city's year is its own at once: every load had reset the record to one month, so a city of centuries read a month scaled up for a year after each load (36.4% for 34.4%; *Months recorded 1*; the header's GDP tile *$0 / yr · first year*), and the load path puts the last ten years back from the graph history now (`NationalAccounts.seedHistory()`). And since 0.7.47 the Government screen's *of GDP* and TAX TAKE read each line's own last twelve months against the year's output, where a busy month's spending times twelve had read 129.81% of annual GDP; health and schools keep the month times twelve, because the history records their net cost and the rows are gross.

```
C  what the households bought over three counters — the grocers', the boutiques', the kitchens' — and since 0.7.62 the refiners' fuel, + rent paid
I  construction work put in place + the change in inventory as a VOLUME, priced today: the food shelf at fixed weights, the makers' materials, the boutiques' stockroom, and since 0.7.58 every other good a sector holds at what one costs to bring in
G  utility payroll + the health service's gross cost + the police's + the schools' + transit's bill   // the last two since 0.7.49
NX everything sold abroad − everything landed: steel and scrap, food, materials, machinery, vans, watches, crude, since 0.7.123 the steelworks' coal and flux, and the drivers' and the railway's fuel
```

Inventory is measured as a volume rather than a value, because valuing it books every price move as production — a rule that had to be re-learned the day food became thirteen goods, since the obvious way to add kilograms of grain to kilograms of fish is to value each at its own price. The thirteen are aggregated at *fixed* weights instead, so the figure is still a quantity. The builders' yard is deliberately excluded from the inventory term — work in progress is at contract value and already embodies it, so counting both subtracted the same brick twice — while the materials plant's warehouse is output made and not yet sold, and counts like a mill's. The boutiques' stockroom is the third term, and it was found by a negative month: a Boutique's three months of stock, 960 pieces at $9,000, lands in one month, NX took the landed cost out and nothing said the city still had the goods, so a city that took up shopping reported negative GDP sixty times over a run. Priced at what the shop paid, the arrival nets to zero and the margin is the only thing that scores; sixty negative months became one across eight seeds and 32,040 months. *Any good a sector can hold and does not consume within the month belongs in that block the day the good is written.* It was learned again in 0.7.58: an ensemble month read GDP of −16,056 because a new railway had bought its twenty sets of rolling stock abroad, 90,460, and nothing said the city still had them, and the farms' crops and every sector's vans were the same gap. Since then every other good a sector holds is the fifth term (`NationalAccounts.HELD`), its change in units priced at what one costs to bring in, so a fleet bought abroad nets to nothing and its wear reads as use; the refiners' fuel joined it in 0.7.62, and since 0.7.76 their petrol and diesel in fuel's place and their seven other products after them, twelve goods, and since 0.7.85 crude, the refiners' kept in a Tank Farm and the city's in its reserve, a thirteenth. The households' cars are named and left out, for the reason below. A household's car is not in C: a household turning money into a thing it owns is a portfolio move, like a share. Land sales appear in the government's books and *nowhere* in GDP: selling a field moves an asset that already existed, and counting it would let a city manufacture growth by trading land with itself. Education's cost was outside G until 0.7.49, which healthcare's and the police's were not, and the transit payroll joined it on the outside when the modes arrived — paid, it turned out, by nobody. Both are in G since, at what they cost, as a service with no market price is valued; G is struck at the top of the month from the costs the month before set, so they come in a month behind.

**And since 0.7.6 it can be drawn in its layers.** Jerus: *"have it so the gdp graph can be a toggle, and if toggled it switches from line to mountain graph is it? layered, aka showing how much is made up of investments, net exports, government spending, aka breaking it down."* The four parts are series of their own — `consumption`, `investment`, `government`, `netExports`, each with its rule in the year book and deflated the way real GDP is — and a *layers* chip on City History, the Reports page until 0.7.21, stacks C, I and G from zero with the real GDP line drawn over them, so the gap between the top of the stack and the line is net exports, above it when the city exports more than it lands and below it when not. A stacked area cannot hold a negative layer, and the caption says so. `HistoryCheck` asserts that the four add up to the month's GDP to the cent. Since 0.7.23 the layers are drawn on City History's new chart, with the rest of its lines ([the screen](#22-the-screen)), and since 0.7.37 the four parts are lines of their own on its picker, *GDP: consumption* to *GDP: net exports*, a month each in the money of the day.

### Standing subsidies

Any sector can be put under a standing policy that covers its losses exactly, uncapped, month after month. It is booked as a *capital contribution*, not revenue — the sector's cash rises and its income statement still says it lost money. The city goes overdrawn to pay it, and the overdraft — the central bank's advances since 0.7.0 — is priced as debt, so an over-generous policy bills you through the interest rate; and once the advances have reached their ceiling a subsidy is paid only from cash at or above zero, and what it is refused is owed to the sector as arrears.

### The city's fund

Jerus: *"Rule plus your hand"*, and *"Home only"*. Since 0.7.14 the treasury has a fund (`TreasuryFund`), a pool of its own inside the city: a market book of company shares, the bank's among them, and company bonds; a rescue book of a resolved bank's shares, the city's preferred and its warrants ([the bank](#14-the-bank)); and its cash. Its holdings live where everyone else's do, as a city holding on each company's register and a city holder on every bond, and it posts on both books by a rule and, separately, by the player's hand. It never subscribes to a new issue and never buys the city's own paper.

**The dial** takes 0 to 300% of the year's surplus, nothing by default, paid in once a year at December's close and before the rollover nets the same surplus, so that the two cannot spend it twice; a deficit year saves nothing, and past 100% the rest comes out of the treasury's cash but never takes it below a month of its own spending, the liquidity rule Canada keeps and the rollover already reads. Yearly, because a monthly pay-in would save in the good months of a deficit year. **The rule** is Norway's Government Pension Fund Global: 70% shares and 30% bonds, never more than 10% of any company — a cap that since 0.7.39 stops a hand buy too, at posting, counting every order the fund has on the company as if it filled — rebalanced when shares pass 74% or fall more than four points under 70%, asking at fair value and, since 0.7.48, bidding for a share at the desk's ask, one per cent over it, where at fair value it met nobody; money that does not fit waits as cash, which earns nothing, as the treasury's does. **The withdrawal** is Norway's fiscal rule since 2017 by default: 3% a year of everything it holds, a twelfth a month, to the budget as *Transfer from the fund*, from its cash only — the rule never sells to pay it. Since 0.7.48 it is a dial (Jerus: *"the city fund, you should be able to click how much to withdraw automatically, even 0 or 10% a month"*): 0 to 10% a month in quarter-point steps, one step the default and Norway's rule to the bit (`TreasuryFund.WITHDRAWAL_STEP`). Over the default the dial spends the fund: what its cash cannot cover is sold from its market book, never the rescue book, pro rata at the step, and paid at the next month's top, and the rule buys nothing meanwhile; since 0.7.102 the withdrawal's part, where it is the step's largest sale, is asked at the desk's bid, fair value less 1% (`RULE_PREMIUM`, Jerus's A21), as the rule bids at the desk's ask, where at fair value in a small city nobody bid — `SaveFileCheck`'s town at 10% a month had asked D\$467k and been paid D\$52k late — and the fund's summary stays neutral while the dial sells, what the step sells for being no warning. It is a full-width card at the top of Rules & cash, with next month's effects and a year on (`PolicyPreview.fundWithdrawalAt()`). At nothing the default playtest ended 13% smaller as the dial went in, 166,409 people against 191,012, because the transfer is real revenue in that city; at 10% the 2,400-month research city's market book went from D\$149.7M to D\$16.0M in eight months. **The hand** places orders at fair value or, since 0.7.39, at a price the player names, good for a month and cancellable before the step, a buy's money held from the rule's bids from the moment it is placed; it may sell any share or bond the fund holds, the rescue book's bank shares included, though not the preferred or its warrants, and each order is a line in the decision log, *Order: buy …*, its fills and lapses on Activity. Paying in and drawing out are transfers between two government pools and stay off the budget. The fund has its own area under Finances, *The city's fund*, in a broker's shape since 0.7.39: **Portfolio** — its worth, its return over the chart's window by Modified Dietz and since it began from its own counters, a chart of its worth against what was put in less taken out, its holdings a row a lot with their average cost and unrealized P&L, and since it began by kind; **Search**; **Activity**, every trade, payment and event, newest first; **Rules & cash**, the withdrawal, the dial, the rescue book's terms, paying in and drawing out, and the orders waiting; and a page a security with YOUR POSITION beside THE ORDER TICKET ([the exchange](#10-the-owners-the-bonds--the-exchange)).

**What each holding cost** is kept since 0.7.39 (`FundLedger`, `FundView`), by Canada's adjusted cost base and the average-cost method: one lot a company's market book, the rule's buys and the hand's pooled; one for the rescue book; one a bond; and the income apart. The hand's sale takes the market lot first. A sale realizes its proceeds less the cost it takes out, a maturity its face less cost, a write-down the cost in the share of face it lost, and a rescue the market lot's whole cost, as a loss, since the fund's own bank shares go with everyone's; a split leaves the cost and divides the average. It is bookkeeping only — the default playtest's traces did not move — and an older save is counted at market value in the month it loads, tagged *cost from*. P&L is green and red, a verdict, and nothing else on the fund's pages is.

At the default dial of nothing the default seed on 28 September still ended with a fund of \$116M, fed by the dividends on the bank shares its one resolution had handed it (\$239M of the \$270M of dividends it took), and paid the budget \$659M over the run; on 1 October it ended worth \$724M, fed by the dividends on its rescue book (\$2.61bn of the \$2.86bn of dividends it took), and had paid the budget \$3.63bn, \$435M short of the rule's 3% because the transfer comes from its cash alone. On eight seeds at a dial of 100% it was paid \$15.3T and held about 94% of it as cash, and the cities ended at 174,264 people on average against 166,717 at nothing (0.7.14). On 5 October, at 0.7.49, the default seed's fund ended worth \$287.9bn, \$222.8bn of it the rescue book from eight resolutions, and had paid the budget \$302.8bn at the default withdrawal, \$646M short of it; its ledger had realized −\$14.1M and stood \$24.3bn up on a cost of \$225.4bn, its identity off in its worst month by 4.7e-16 of what it held.

## 13. The city's borrowing

*Three instruments with genuinely different shapes, priced off their own cash flows rather than off a formula that assumed a bullet — and since 0.7.1 all three off one curve that sits on the policy dial, held by whoever bought them: the households, the central bank, and the bank for the rest. Since 0.7.13 the treasury can roll what falls due without the player's hand. What lends to everybody else is [the bank](#14-the-bank).*

| Instrument | Duration | Granularity | Shape |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| T-Bill | 3–12 months | $1M | zero coupon, sold at a discount, one lump at maturity; the short end of the curve, at the dial |
| Serial bond | 1–10 years | $10M | monthly coupon on a declining balance, annual principal slices |
| Term bond | 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years | $100M | low coupon on full face, whole face at maturity |

> **Why the term bond is solved from present value**
>
> The old simple-interest premium made issue-then-repurchase an infinite money button — $2,145 of free cash at ten years, rising to $28,059 at thirty. Solving the face from the bond's present value makes the round trip neutral by construction rather than by a patch.

### The dial, and the curve on it

The **policy rate** is the player's dial on the Policy tab, 0% to 100% since 0.7.2, and since 0.7.0 it is the price of money rather than a floor under somebody else's: the commercial bank's spare cash earns it at the central bank, and its shortfalls pay it and a quarter point at the window ([the central bank](#15-the-central-bank)). The **city's own borrowing rate** is that dial — never less than what the money costs the bank that buys the paper, plus a point, while the bank and the households hold all of it — walked up by the market's read of the city's books, so a dial at 3% and a debt-free treasury with a bank whose money costs it nothing is a city paying 3%. Until 0.7.7 the bank's strain added up to eighteen points on top of that, and it is gone ([the bank](#14-the-bank)). Since 0.7.15 the floor is split by who holds the paper, Jerus's reading of the backstop: *"if bank is in a pickle, and central bank is at 100% then your debt isnt priced at tge bank, ira proportional"*. Until 0.7.0 it was the dial less a two-point discount, a named constant its own comment called the one number in the file that did not describe anything real; with it went a city borrowing below its own central bank's rate.

```
floor = max(MIN_RATE, policy + (1 − s) × max(0, the bank's cost of funds + MIN_MARGIN − policy))
// s: the central bank's share of all the city's paper, notes included, because the bank holds the notes
```

At s = 0 that is the floor 0.7.14 had, to the bit; at s = 1 the bank's state no longer touches the city's rate. Because the bank's money costs it almost nothing when it is flush, the floor is often the bank's point rather than the dial: on the default seed on 28 September the dial ended at 0.01% and the floor at 1.00%, and on 1 October the same.

Two independent measures move the rest — debt against annual GDP, and debt against annual tax revenue — each a linear ramp to five points of spread and then flat. The city's own overdraft counts as principal, because a city over a million in the red with no bonds was being quoted the floor, and since 0.7.0 so does what it owes its central bank in advances. The cheapest money the market will ever offer is 0.5%. Because face depends on rate and rate depends on face, every quote walks that fixed point six times. The quote *is* the arithmetic: what the screen shows is what gets booked, down to the rate before and after and the points the ask itself cost. A letter grade — AAA to CCC — reports the city's position within the market's own band rather than against typed-in thresholds. Since 0.7.14 a reloaded city's rate is the live city's to the bit: the debt market strikes it from four inputs, and one of them, the overdraft, used to be struck again on load from cash that had moved after the month's strike, up to a basis point away, so the save carries the four and the rate.

**The curve.** Jerus: *"the short term rates, aka the one you choose, those should be basically the tbill rate, the others change just as in real life."* Since 0.7.1 every price of the city's own paper — the quote, the issue, the buyback, the market value and the borrow pages, which since 0.7.32 draw it a column per term — is read off one function at the paper's maturity, `DebtManager.priceAt(debt, months)`:

```
rate(months) = floor + credit spread + termPremium(months) − compression(months)
termPremium  nothing to a year · linear to the ten-year entry · linear between entries · flat past fifty years
compression  what the central bank's holdings take off it — see the central bank
```

*The term premium, in points over the dial — DebtManager.TERM_PREMIUM_10Y … 50Y, provisional, Jerus's numbers to settle*

| Maturity | 10 yr | 20 yr | 30 yr | 40 yr | 50 yr |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Premium | 0.50 | 0.90 | 1.15 | 1.35 | 1.50 |

A note carries no premium, so the short end is the floor and `getRate()` — what every screen means by the city's rate, the header's *RATE* tile's tooltip (the strip's *city* line until 0.7.21) and the year book's `interestRate` — stays exactly that; a five-year serial carries 48/108 of the ten-year entry. The credit spread is the same at every maturity, so a hike moves the whole curve in parallel and a city that over-borrows pays more at every point of it, and paper already on the books keeps its coupon and its months, so locking in fifty-year money before a hike is a real decision. **Term loans are issued only at ten, twenty, thirty, forty or fifty years** (`LongTermBond.MATURITIES`), at home and in dollars: any other term is refused in words — *"Term loans are issued at 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years."* — and Borrow's term columns, chips abroad, step by ten. Issue and buyback read the same function, so `RestructureCheck`'s round trip is still neutral by construction, and `CreditCheck`'s section 11 walks the rest: a debt-free note at exactly the dial, each maturity the dial plus its entry, the interpolation, a hike and a debt both parallel, a 25-year request refused and booking nothing, and a twenty-year bond bought back the same month for what it raised, bar the issuance cost.
