Every money constant in the game is an instance field seeded from its constant and redenominated with everything else, and since 0.7.42 struck every month as its founding figure over the unit times the expected price level, so a reform needs nothing new: the unit and the level are both in the product ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). Foreign prices are the exception, quoted in someone else's money and reached through the rate. Since 0.7.47 a reform divides the month's transit bill and fares too, and since 0.7.49 the households' fuel; and the fare dial is read in founding money through the unit, so a reform no longer moves who rides, its cap being the founding cap in the new unit (`TaxPolicy.maxTransitFare()`) — in the 2,400-month city divided by a thousand, a month on, 41,394.6 riders and 11,077 households eligible for vouchers, the unreformed city's figures exactly, where they had read 43,627 and 49,778. The reform instant is bit-exact and conserves money; the following month is a few percent adrift in the discrete decisions, which is filed and has a plan.

## 17. Founding a city

*Until 0.7.10 every city was the same city at month zero: Danzik, founded on D\$2.5B and US\$1B, with no reason ever to borrow. A player founds a city now — its name, its money, what it starts with and the world's inflation — and the default start is small enough that the city borrows for what it builds.*

Jerus: *"lets reduce the cash the city starts with, both the foreign usd and the starting cash, what do you think makes sense? cause the city should borrow right"*. A trace of 0.7.9 found the treasury never going below D\$2.467B in thirty years: the young city spent \$0.1–2M a month and took in \$0.4–5M, owed nothing for about ninety years, and held a vault of 270 or more months of its imports. The endowment had been sized on 9 September to buy the opening, a coal power plant, and nothing since had asked it to do less. **Since 0.7.10 a city is founded on D\$100M and US\$25M**, Jerus's choice from the options put to him (`Game.FOUNDING_CASH`, `FOUNDING_RESERVE_USD`), sized so that the treasury could pay for the playtest's founding village and one of the first big works, and the city would borrow for the rest, the way towns pay for long-lived works, on bonds repaid over the asset's life — Britain's New Towns were built on sixty-year loans from the Exchequer, not on endowments. The vault follows the IMF's old rule of three months of imports. The endowment is still a game number, and the code says so.

**The village is the playtest's, not the player's.** The playtest places a founding village by hand before its advisor takes over — sixty houses, five shops, two farms and a depot — and the play-through of 0.7.19 found that a player's city gets none of it: after *Found the city* the treasury still held D\$100.0M, and month 3 had one house and thirteen people. A player's city starts with the treasury and the vault, and builds the rest. **The sticker is not the invoice.** What a new city pays for a building is the building and the material beyond its yard at the world's price, and since 0.7.19 the builders' sales tax on both: the water plant's D\$65.8M sticker was invoiced D\$109.6M and is D\$129.0M with the tax. So D\$100M pays for the village, D\$38.8M, and one of the wind farm, D\$36.5M, the school, D\$35.3M, or the police station, D\$52.9M; the option Jerus picked had been described on stickers, and he kept D\$100M once it was described on invoices, so the water plant is a bond from day one. That is why the build screen offers a twenty-year bond sized to the gap ([the city's borrowing](#13-the-citys-borrowing)): as 0.7.10 measured it, a Standard city a year on was D\$26.1M short of the water plant, issued D\$40.3M of face at 4.22%, raised D\$26.13M, paid about D\$56k a month, and had the plant in 57 months; on 1 October the same fixture was D\$58.3M short, issued D\$113.8M of face at 7.19%, raised D\$58.4M, paid D\$253k a month and had the plant in 137 months; and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, it was D\$61.8M short, issued D\$137.6M of face at 9.54% on a 3.45% coupon, raised D\$61.8M, paid D\$395k a month and had the plant in 146 months, with the audit closing every one (`NewGameCheck`, section 11). Since 0.7.42 every price on the page is struck at the price level the city expects, which at its founding is founding's, so the invoices a new city is quoted are the ones above.

### Found a city

Jerus, the same afternoon: *"a small thing at the start of the game where you choose the name of the city and the currency … and perhaps the settings to choose the starting cash and usd cash and offworld inflation rate … (with option to just start at default)"*. From 0.7.10 *Start New Game* opened **Found a city** (`ui/FoundingScreen`): the city's name; its money, named after the city or, with a tick, by hand, a name and three letters that are never USD; the money it is founded with; the world's inflation, moved there from Settings because it acts only at founding; and *Found with defaults*, which founded straight away. Each start showed what it would buy. Jerus, on the play-through: *"even the screen shouldnt say what the money could buy, the start screen should be real simple"*. Since 0.7.20 a start shows only what the founders leave, and since 0.7.21 *New city* on the main menu opens one panel over its dimmed skyline: the name, in a field that opens on *Danzik*; one line for its money, *"Its money: the Danzik dollar, D$ · name it yourself"*, where the link opens the name and its three letters in place; WHAT IT STARTS WITH, four cards, each its money in figures and one line on how hard it is, never what it buys, Standard marked *default*, and *Set your own amounts* for Custom; THE WORLD'S INFLATION, a row of five, with *"A faster world makes your money stronger. It can't be changed later."* and the rest behind an (i); and *Found the city* and *Back*. *Found with defaults* is gone, because the page opens on the defaults. None of 0.7.21's panel has been seen on a screen.

**Since 0.7.56 the panel founds a world as well.** THE WORLD, between the money and the inflation, is a seed: a whole number in a field in the figures' face, rolled when the page opens and again by a dice beside it, from 1 to 999,999,999, over *"The same number makes the same coast, lakes and ore."* Any whole number typed is a world; anything else keeps *Found the city* dark with *"Type the world as a whole number, like 4127, or roll the dice."* The defaults, the presets, the harnesses and the playtest found on world 4127 (`Founding.DEFAULT_WORLD_SEED`), so that they stay deterministic. What a seed makes is in [land](#18-land); since 0.7.99 a founding asks no iron of its site, so a city may start with no deposit and import what it needs, and since 0.7.106 a new city is founded with its lake, one water plant's fresh water. The panel grew to about 710 pixels for it, under the 768-pixel window it is laid out for, and the row has not been seen on a screen either.

*The starts, in the order the page lists them (`Founding`)*

| Start | Treasury | Vault | What it is |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Insane | D$0 | US$0 | *"Nothing. The ground is owed on a 20-year bond."* Since 0.7.14: the ground it stands on owed abroad, a twenty-year dollar bond at 3%, for US\$2,100k until 0.7.106 and since then for the plots it owns, US\$3,811.4k on the default world |
| Lean | D$25M | US$10M | *"Tight. Borrow early."* Two-thirds of the playtest's village at a new city's invoices, three quarters until the builders' tax went into them; the city borrows from its first months |
| Standard | D$100M | US$25M | *"The usual start."* The default, sized on the playtest's village and one of the first big works at their invoices |
| Wealthy | D$2.5B | US$1B | *"Plenty to spare."* The start every city had from 0.6.10 to 0.7.9 |
| Custom | D\$6M–D\$10B | US\$0–US\$4B | for testing, not balanced for play; the floor was D$5M until 0.7.19, and is ten houses and a shop at a new city's invoices with the tax |

The choice is a record on the city (`Founding`), set once, saved under eight keys and since 0.7.56 a ninth, the world's seed, and on the real Earth since 0.7.121 four more — the world's kind, the spot's latitude and longitude and the data it is drawn on — and never changed; the currency is a value per city, read through `game.getCurrency()`, because one process holds several cities — the harnesses', and the playtest's reloaded twin. The window's title and the save lists name the city, and every screen that prints its money names it. A save from before 0.7.10 loaded as Danzik, in the Danzik dollar, founded on D\$2.5B and US\$1B, which is what it was, until 0.7.120 refused every save before its format ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)); and one from before 0.7.56 was given a world made from its name, its founding treasury, its ground and its month (`Founding.derivedWorldSeed()`), the same at every load, which its next save keeps. A new game also founds on the autopilot and with the rollover on *same structure* since 0.7.13, with the bank's resolution automatic since 0.7.14, believing its central bank at 0.80 with prices expected at founding's since 0.7.42 ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)), and with its fund's withdrawal at one step, Norway's 3% a year, since 0.7.48; an older save keeps what it was played with, and one from before the anchor or the dial reads those two defaults. Building the screen found two bugs on the founding path: a new game after a load kept the loaded world's inflation, and a new city's first year was back-cast at the previous city's rate.

### On the real Earth

**Since 0.7.121 a city can be founded on the real Earth** (batch E4, `EarthSite`; Jerus's answers of 10 October to his study of the world as planet Earth, *"all rec"*: Earth for new cities and the default where its data is here, no iron field promised near a site, place names for searching only and no borders; the Earth itself is in [land](#18-land)). THE WORLD is two joined chips, *Earth* and *Generated*, Earth chosen when the Earth's data is here; where it is not, Earth is greyed, its tooltip saying where the file goes, and the panel is the generated world's, the seed and its dice. On the Earth the panel widens to two columns, the city's choices on the left and the world on the right. A search runs over the data's 7,342 place names, accents and case folded — a name whole first, then one it begins, then a word it begins, then anywhere in it, eight at most — each hit its name and its latitude and longitude, never a country; Enter takes the first. *Random spot* rolls the seed and lets it pick: of up to 64 of the data's towns and cities, tried in its hash's order, the first with dry ground near and no ice, so the same seed picks the same place. The globe is the planet seen from space while it is wide, from the whole Earth down to 4 km a pixel, and closer than that the city's own far view, down to 150 m a pixel ([the map](#18-land)); a drag turns it, the wheel or − and + zoom it, and a click picks the spot. Under it is THE SPOT, the card, measured off the screen's thread on the world the city would stand on: where the site is from the nearest place, and how far the snap moved it from the spot; *Within 5 km: N% dry · N% rivers and lakes · N% sea*, counted plot by plot as the land office will sell it; how far away the nearest fresh water and the sea are; *Geology:* the province and its class, and each resource's multiplier under the site; and *The nearest iron field*, how far and which way, or none within 983 km. A spot is **refused**, in the bad colour, which keeps *Found the city* dark, where there is no dry ground within 5 km — *"the spot is in the sea, or on an island too small"* — or the site is on ice: *"no city is founded on an ice sheet"*. It is **warned of**, in amber, which does not, in a desert, or with no river or lake within 5 km — *"the city's first water is from the sea, by desalination"* — or no water near at all. The card's last line is the seed's, which on the Earth decides the detail below the data, the fields and the streets, so the same seed and spot found the same city. The game itself will not found a refused spot (`Founding.problem()`), and Insane's tooltip prices the bond for its ground on the spot's own world (below). A card takes 0.25 to 0.9 s; on the fixture Rotterdam's reads 91.2% dry, 6.7% rivers and lakes and 2.1% sea, fresh water 0.08 km away and the sea 3.03 km, oil ×2.58, and the nearest iron 24.1 km north. Of the panel only the globe's and the ground's pixels have been looked at, rendered headless; the globe's height is set so the tallest card fits the 868-pixel window.

**The Earth's file**, `data/earth-1.bin`, 52,757,374 bytes, is not in the repository: it is the asset of the GitHub release `earth-1`, and `tools/earth/get-earth.bat` makes sure it is in place and whole, checking it against `earth-1.sha256` and downloading it when it is missing or bad. `Play CityBuilderSim.bat` calls it first, and `Build EXE.bat` calls it, carries the file into the built game and zips the release with it (the commit after 0.7.122; Jerus: *"when it goes in the zip it must have the earth file as well"*). **Without it the game runs**, on the generated world: the Earth chip is greyed, its tooltip saying *"The real Earth needs its data, earth-1.bin (about 53 MB), which is not here. Put it in a folder named data beside the game, as data/earth-1.bin, and open this page again."*, it is looked for again each time the page opens, and a city already founded on the Earth is refused at its load in words that say so ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)). A save names the Earth it was drawn on, so a later one will be a new file, a new release and a new name, and a city keeps its own. `LongPlaytest --earth rotterdam` founds the playtest's city on the Earth through the screen's own search, on the whole file: 4,005 months, every month audited and every reload matched, ending at 515,136 people, its own baseline beside the default's.

### Insane

Jerus: *"on game start, add a new difficulty called Insane, which is just you start with 0 cash, 0 vault, and a 20y bond 3% for the initial land cost … if easier the starting debt is abroad in usd"*. Since 0.7.14 it is the first start on the page: D\$0, US\$0, and a twenty-year dollar bond at 3% owed abroad for the starting land — until 0.7.106 3,000,000 square feet at the land market's opening price of US\$0.70 a square foot, US\$2,100k, the figure, where since 0.7.67 a new city owned the 3,051,569 its whole blocks draw; since 0.7.106 the plots it is founded on, priced as the land office charges ground — dry whole, fresh water at 45% and sea at 8% — at the opening dollar price (`Founding.landBondUsd()`, `LandMarket.groundKm2()`; Jerus's B): US\$3,811.4k on the default world, its founding lake with it ([land](#18-land)), and US\$3.8M to US\$6.9M on the seventeen worlds measured, the card's tooltip pricing it on the world typed when it opens, and since 0.7.121 on the Earth on the spot picked, once one is. No cash moves, because the founders' land was bought on it, and on the world's curve the old US\$2,100k was worth US\$375k on day 0. On day 0, as `FundCheck`'s section 12 prices it, a city with no revenue and no output pays the full spread: the founding card quoted the village's twenty-year bond at 13.90%, \$85,500k of face to raise \$32,978k, the six-month note at 13.00%, and the window abroad shut, until 0.7.20 took every figure off the founding screen. Since 0.7.21 Insane's card reads *nothing* for its money, and what is owed abroad for its ground is in its tooltip. 0.7.14 made the clock refuse to run until such a city had borrowed (Jerus: *"Borrow first"*); since 0.7.15 it runs on the central bank's advances from its first month instead ([the central bank](#15-the-central-bank)).

Of 0.7.14's eight Insane seeds, three became cities of 148,000, 206,000 and 148,000 people, and five spiralled on the city's own paper, ending with 3,686 to 10,118 people and \$420T to \$6,416T of it; the playtest's player borrows exactly the village's invoice, so every seed ran on the advances from month 3. Lean is hard too: D\$25M covered three quarters of the village then, and two-thirds since the tax went into the invoices; every seed borrows by month 4 to 14, and on 0.7.10 half of them ran out of cash around month 140 and lived on the advances for 450 to 500 months.

### What the smaller start did

As 0.7.10 measured it, making the founding a choice changed nothing else: founded Wealthy, the city reproduced three old ensembles byte for byte, all 24 seed-runs. The default playtest never borrows on D\$100M; its treasury bottoms out at D\$61–67M in its first two years and then grows. What the default run does show is the vault, half gone by month 141 against 739 and empty by month 374 against 987. Under the autopilot the bank failed 76 times against 49, and all of the rise was the vault's: D\$100M with the old US\$1B vault gave the old counts, and D\$2.5B with US\$25M the new ones, because without dollars to steady the currency a rule-held rate sees more imported inflation in the city's middle years. Held at 10%, every seed now runs dry in years 185 to 253, where three of eight did before: a city held at that rate loses money for centuries, and the D\$2.4B had been paying for it. And 42 fixtures in 25 harnesses had been living on the old treasury without saying so — ten went red and three were green only because they ran on a short calendar — and each funds itself explicitly now, with no premise and no tolerance moved.

## 18. Land

*A city stands on a world of its own: an Earth-sized square made from one number, its sea, coast and lakes and seven resources in finite fields, every one of them there to be seen — or, since 0.7.121, on a spot of the real Earth, its ground drawn from the Earth's own data and its fields laid on its geology. It starts with the dry ground of thirty of the old 100,000 sq ft blocks, drawn in whole 120 m blocks of that world, so that a power station and a water plant leave two spare — land is taught on turn one — and since 0.7.106 with its lake's blocks, one water plant's fresh water, and buys the rest a rectangle of whole blocks at a time, from six offers on each side that are never rerolled; and since 0.7.107 it may hold what it owns for the industries it chooses.*

### The world

Since 0.7.56 every city stands on a world of its own (`World`): a flat square the size of the Earth, 368 cells a side of 61.44 km, 511.2 million km² against the Earth's 510.1, with the city founded at its middle. It is made from one number, the seed chosen on the founding page ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)), and the same seed makes the same world on every machine: every value is a SplitMix64 hash of the seed and the place, and every sine and logarithm is `StrictMath`'s. It is measured in **plots** of 30 m, nested by powers of two — a tile is 32 plots, 0.96 km; a district 256, 7.68 km, which is what the map keeps (below); a cell 2,048 — and its ground is value noise in octaves: sea below a level each world finds for itself, so that 71% of it is sea, as the Earth's is; lakes on 3.7% of the land and forest on 31%, the measured shares of each (Verpoorter 2014; FAO 2020); and beaches at the shore. The founding site is the first point, spiralling out from the cells 25–75% land nearest the middle, that is dry at its centre and 600 m round, at least 60% land within 5 km, has the sea within 2.1 km but not within 1.35, and until 0.7.99 had an iron field within 2 km: a coast, with a lake beside it and a river that runs from a lake 64 to 90 plots away past the site to the sea. Since 0.7.99 a founding asks only the first three (Jerus: *"a city doesnt require a deposit"*), so a city may start with no deposit and import what it needs, while the conversion of an older save still asks the fourth, of the old world's fields, and converts as before (`World.searchSites()`). The default world's site is where it was; of the 659 sites a city could be founded on within 100 km of it, 2.3% find iron in their centre or first offers, where 21.5% did, and none coal or oil, where 0.2% and 1.7% did. A world is built the first time it is asked for, in about half a second, and `WorldCheck` holds three of them to the design ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)). Two of the design's levels moved before it shipped: its percentiles had been taken at lattice points of every fine octave, where the noise is a bare lattice value, and made 5.0% of the land lakes and 24% forest, so the lake level went from 0.695 to 0.7092 and the forest's from 0.595 to 0.5676, the shares being the intent.

**Seven resources lie in it, in finite fields, and every one of them can be seen.** Iron, oil, stone, coal, copper and uranium lie in fields (`Resource`, `Deposit`): a cell holds a Poisson count of them by its land, each field a place with a number of sites — most small and a few huge, the floor of (1 − u)^−2/3 capped at 512, 2.52 on average — and whole tonnes that add up exactly to the cell's own total, which is drawn first; a field centred in the sea is drawn again, up to eight times, bar oil, because offshore oil is real. **Since 0.7.99 they are fewer and bigger** (`World`'s FEWER AND BIGGER DEPOSITS; Jerus: *"the world has too many deposits, a city doesnt require a deposit, you can just make a deposit deeper or in very big clusters"*). Every cell's count and total are drawn as before, so the world's totals are what they were to the tonne, and the fields a city sees are drawn from them a pool of cells at a time — a square 2 cells a side for iron, 4 for oil, 6 for stone, 12 for coal, 24 for copper and 37 for uranium, the fewest whose land holds ten clusters (`POOL_CLUSTERS`): a tenth as many fields as the old draws (`FIELD_SCALE`), each ten of their sites added, 10 to 5,120 and 25.2 on average, at the same tonnes a site, so that a mine or a well lasts as it did and its ground costs what it did a site; ten fields to a cluster (`CLUSTER_FIELDS`), its centre in a cell drawn by its share of the old count, off the sea bar oil, with that cell's richness, and its fields anywhere in a disc that holds them as thickly as the old world held fields everywhere, 4.0 km round for iron, 12.6 for oil, 17.8 for stone, 39.9 for coal, 79.8 for copper and 126 for uranium. So a tenth of the land holds them, a field's nearest neighbour lies about where it did — 1.16 km for iron, against the old world's 1.18 and the 3.43 a tenth spread evenly would be — and a pool's fields share its cells' totals to the tonne. A field is listed in the cell its centre is in, numbered from 65,536 (`FIELD_INDEX_FROM`), so that the two worlds' fields can stand in one city. Within 50 km of the default site iron's fields went from 357 to 36, oil's from 31 to 19, stone's from 15 to none and copper's from 2 to none. **An older save kept its ground**, from 0.7.99 until 0.7.120 refused it ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)): every holding it brings holds the old world's fields, as saved (`World.legacyFieldsInCell()`), what it buys after is the new world's, and its standing offers are measured again once, as it loads (`LandMarket.remeasureStanding()`), its books and what it has taken out as saved (save format 36, [saves](#23-time-saves--logs)); Jerus's city at month 8,473 keeps 455 holdings on the old world, and its offers, measured again, hold iron in 4 where 19 did and oil in 1 where 10 did. Forest is the forest of the terrain. Nothing has to be surveyed or found: the fields are in the world from the seed, the land office counts every one centred in an offer when it lists it, and the map draws them. The world's totals are counted once, in about 30 ms, and kept with the city, so that for each resource the world = what no city owns + what the city has left + what it has taken out, to the tonne through every purchase and every tonne lifted (`LandCheck`). What the city takes out is worked out in the order it bought the ground, the centre first, and forest grows back a 240th a month, though nothing cuts timber yet; and since 0.7.107 a building on open forest clears it, and cleared ground never grows back (below).

*The seven, as the world lays them (`Resource`): the fields a km² are the old world's draws, which since 0.7.99 a field gathers ten at a time; an offer's price counts only those with a good*

| Resource | Fields a km² of land | A site | A site holds | In an offer's price |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Iron ore | 0.2 | 0.0372 km² | 15 Mt | 1/212.5 of its world price since 0.7.120, the $0.40 a tonne the office always charged, against the floor of $85 (1/350 of $140 until then); a site is an Iron Mine's own ground, and a km² of land carries 7.59 Mt, the old listing's ore on a quarter of its sites |
| Oil | 0.02 | 0.0405 km² | 150,000 t | 5% of crude's since 0.7.62, by iron's rule of about a year and a half of a working site's profit; a site is a well's ten-acre spacing and thirty years of its 415 t a month |
| Stone | 0.01 | 0.1 km² | 13.5 Mt | free until it has an industry; a quarry 50 m deep |
| Coal | 0.002 | 1 km² | 6.5 Mt | free; a seam 5 m thick |
| Copper | 0.0005 | 0.5 km² | 300,000 t | free; the metal in 120 Mt of ore a km² at 0.5% |
| Uranium | 0.0002 | 0.1 km² | 200 t | free; 1 Mt of ore a km² at 0.2% |
| Forest | — | — | 13,700 m³ a km² | free; the terrain's forest, 31% of the land (FAO 2020) |

**Since 0.7.79 the sea has a depth, and an oil field a grade.** The pass that finds each world's sea level sorts its samples, and the shallowest 8.86% of the sea is the shelf, down to 140 m at its break, the rest deeper below it at the same slope (`World.depthAt()`, `SHELF_SHARE`, `SHELF_BREAK_M`, the research's prototype to five places): a plot has a depth where its ground is under the sea's level, and none on land, in a lake or in the river. A city's sites of a resource are dry or the sea's by where each field's centre lies (`LandManager.getSites(r, dry)`), the two adding up to all of them, so that since 0.7.84 a land well stands on a dry site and since 0.7.91 a platform on a sea field no deeper than 150 m ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). And every oil field is light, medium or heavy crude, a third of fields each, drawn from the field's place and never stored (`Deposit.grade()`); `WorldCheck`'s seventh section holds both.

**Since 0.7.110 a field has a type** (batch I1, the materials chains' first; `Deposit.type()`, `Resource.typesOf()`). Iron is hematite or magnetite, coal thermal or coking, copper sulphide or oxide and stone limestone or hard rock; oil, uranium and forest have none. A field's type is drawn from its place as its grade is, so nothing is stored and no tonne moves, the first type a set share of its resource's fields (`Deposit.TYPE_SHARES`: hematite .75, thermal .85, sulphide .80 and limestone .70, the materials study's), on the old world's fields and the new. The ground counts the city's sites and tonnes by type, adding up to the whole exactly and the world's totals to the tonne (`LandManager`'s THE GROUND BY TYPE); what has been dug of each type is read off what was dug, every tonne until now having come out in the order the ground was bought, as oil's grades are, and is saved only once a works digs by type. A building says what it stands on — a resource, a type of field or any, how many sites and what a unit takes (`"site"` in `buildings.json`): the Iron Mine, the Oil Well and the Platform Well one site of any, the Offshore Platform none — and `LandManager.fits()` answers whether one more works fits beside those standing, its sites packed biggest first into the city's fields of its type in the order it bought them. **Nothing in play reads a type yet**: every building stands on any, nothing digs by type, and the playtest's traces were 0.7.109's to the byte; the chains' mines will, iron's first. On the real Earth, since 0.7.117, a field's type leans on the ground under it (below). What was measured for them: on four worlds every type's share came within 0.63 points of its constant by fields and 1.20 by tonnes; a city holding the nearest iron fields to 25 sites holds one type on 72% of two hundred seeds of the new world, against 6.5% of the old, hematite alone on 60% and magnetite alone on 12%, so a magnetite works would find no field in most cities and a hematite one none in about one in eight; and within 50 km of a founding site coal, copper and stone are rare, so those chains will lean on imports. `WorldCheck`'s ninth section and `LandCheck`'s twenty-sixth hold it ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### The real Earth

**Since 0.7.121 a city may stand on the real Earth** (Jerus's study of the world as planet Earth, answered *"all rec"* on 10 October: Earth for new cities, real river courses, no iron field promised near a site, place names for searching only and no borders, no elevation). The Earth's coasts, lakes, rivers, land cover, geology and places were baked on 8 October into one file of 52.8 MB, and five batches built on it, from 0.7.111 to 0.7.121. Since 0.7.111 the game reads the file and flattens the Earth round any spot with an equal-area projection, so that a square kilometre on it is a real one (`EarthProj`, `EarthData`); since 0.7.115 a world has a key — a seed, or a spot on the Earth and the data it is drawn from — and an Earth world's ground is drawn on the same 30 m plots from the file's shares, its sea, lakes, forest, small lakes, rivers and beaches, the seed's detail below what the data can say, and a founding moved to the nearest dry plot (`World.Key`, `EarthTerrain`). A generated key is the world its seed made, to the byte, and the playtest stands on one. How a spot is chosen, and where the file comes from, are in [founding a city](#17-founding-a-city); how an Earth city's save is read, in [saves](#23-time-saves--logs).

**Its fields follow its geology** (0.7.117; `Geology`). Every geologic province in the data is one of seven classes — ocean, shield, fold belt, rift, shelf, basin or other — first by the name rules of the study's `geology.py`, then by a hand table of 287 rows laid over them, each saying why: of the 219 provinces the rules leave *other* it places 211, 104 fold belts, 47 basins, 24 ocean, 23 shields, 11 rifts and 2 shelves, eight staying other — the Ethiopian and Columbia flood basalts, the Canaries and five basement highs under the Kara, East Siberian and Okhotsk seas; and it corrects 68 the rules misfire, among them Mesopotamia's foreland basin, 343,993 million barrels of oil equivalent, which the rules made ocean, the Lufilian Arc of the Copperbelt, which they made a basin, and Olympic Dam's Stuart Shelf, on dry land. Each resource has a weight by class — iron four on a shield and nothing on a shelf, oil three on a shelf and a twentieth on a shield, copper four in a fold belt, coal two in a basin — and a constant, Z, that keeps the Earth's fields as many as a generated world's density gives: a cell's field land is the land at each of its sixteen points times its province's weight times Z, and oil's times its petroleum too, one plus the logarithm of one plus its known oil over 1,000 million barrels, with the sea over shelves, basins and rifts on top. So geology moves where the fields are, not how many. Z is built as defined, measured on the file with the hand table and the ground south of 60 degrees left out — iron .7219, oil .6033, coal .7884, copper .7322, uranium .7518 and stone .6915 — and not the study's figures, whose iron, copper and uranium do not follow from its own table; so its spots come out under what it printed, Rotterdam's oil 2.58 times a generated world's density where it said 2.99 and the Yilgarn shield's iron 2.89 where it said 3.55, and at its own Z they reproduce to its rounding. A field's type leans on the class under its centre: coking coal's odds three times as long in a fold belt and half on a shield, limestone's twice in a basin or on a shelf, half in a fold belt and a quarter on a shield, so a stone field is limestone .892 of the time in a basin and .507 on a shield, the Earth-wide shares held at a generated world's; iron and copper are flat. `EarthTerrainCheck`'s tenth to fourteenth sections hold it.

**Its sea has a depth** (0.7.121). The file carries no heights, so the depth is the generated world's rule with the distance from the coast for the elevation: 140 m at the shelf's break, 54,167 m out — the width within which 8.86% of the Earth's sea lies, measured on the file as a generated world measures its shelf — and on at the same slope, at least 30 m from the coast, the coast the nearest 15-second cell under the coast's level (`EarthTerrain.depthAt()`, `SHELF_WIDTH_M`). A platform, which stands no deeper than 150 m, stands within about 58 km of a coast. It is crude, as the generated rule is — Rotterdam's North Sea reads 16 m 40 km out and 84 m at 80, the real one about 30 m — and without it an Earth city whose ground held oil at sea would have stopped at its first purchase off the coast, the platforms' rule and the count of its sea fields asking a depth the game could not give.

**And the map draws it** (0.7.119). Zoomed out, each pixel of a far view is classed at its centre from the data's shares and its forest dithered; the rivers are stroked from their real courses while their median width is at least 30/2,500 of a pixel, every river at 2.5 km a pixel and closer and only the widest — the Nile, the Amazon, the Ob, the Lena — at the whole world's 30.7 km, because every river a pixel wide drew Siberia 45% fresh water, where the data has 0.5%, and took 9.1 s; small lakes are discs of their own area; and past the rim of the flattened planet the map paints the void (`EarthTerrain.farTerrain()`, `MapTiles.nodeTerrain()`). A far view over Rotterdam draws in 4.7 to 7.9 ms from 2 to 512 plots a pixel and 20.2 ms at 1,024, and the whole world in 1.6 s. The hover card adds, after whose the ground is, where the pointer lies from the nearest of the data's places, by its name alone — *4.1 km south-west of Rotterdam* — and the province under it with its class, *Geology: Anglo-Dutch Basin, a basin*; past the rim, *Off the planet: the map runs on past the antipode, the point opposite the city* (`LandMap.earthWords()`); 59,760 such lines were measured to fit the card at 1,389 × 868, none over. `MapCheck`'s tenth section holds it, and `EarthCheck`, `EarthTerrainCheck` and `EarthFoundingCheck` the rest, on a 332 KB fixture cut from the file — Rotterdam, Perth, Paris and Fiji's date line — and on the whole file where it is named ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### Blocks, four sides and six places

**The ground is whole blocks** (0.7.67; `LandGrid`, `CityLand`; Jerus's design of 7 October). A block is a square of one grid lined up with the world, 2^k plots a side: 120 m at level 2 (`LandGrid.MIN_LEVEL`, 0.0144 km², the smallest block that holds one of the old 100,000 sq ft blocks, Jerus's *"one block smallest"*), doubling to 983 km at level 15 (`MAX_LEVEL`), so that blocks nest in the world's tiles (level 5, 960 m), its districts (8, 7.68 km) and its cells (11), and the world, 23 × 2^15 plots across, divides into whole blocks at every level. **The city's level** is the largest block of which six fit across a square of everything it owns (`LandGrid.levelFor()`, `FACE_BLOCKS`), so each of a side's six places is one block wide or two: 120 m until the city's whole area passes 2.07 km², 240 m to 8.29, 480 m to 33.2, 960 m to 133, and a district's 7.68 km from 2,123 km², on up to 123 to 246 km at ten billion people. **The centre** is the ground a city is founded with: rings of whole blocks of its level round the site's block until their dry plots reach the 3,000,000 sq ft of the founding figure (`CityLand.found()`) — on the default world 21 blocks of 120 m, 0.3024 km² in all, 0.2835 of it dry and 0.0189 a lake, 315 dry plots where the figure is 309.7 — and the city owns what is drawn, 3,051,569 sq ft, 1.7% more than the figure, because the books follow the map; since 0.7.106 its founding lake's blocks are the centre's too (below). Nothing rolls into it. What the city owns in square feet is its dry ground; the water inside its land is its own too, the lake its water plants draw on and the sea a desalination plant needs ([utilities](#20-utilities--roads)). **What it owns** is a region quadtree over the world's plots, each node unowned, owned whole by one holding, mixed, or owned whole by several, holding the centre's blocks and then each purchase's rectangle in the order bought. A purchase claims only the plots no holding owns yet, so the tree is the same whatever its history, given its rectangles in order: it is never saved, and is rebuilt from them at load (`LandGrid.replay()`). It names a plot's owner in 18 to 49 ns, where the lanes took 47 to 56, and a city of ten billion bought evenly is three to four thousand nodes.

```
the city's level   the largest k, at least 2, such that six blocks of 2^k plots fit across √(every plot it owns)
a block            2^k plots of 30 m a side: 120 m, 240 m, 480 m, 960 m, 1.92 km … 983 km, lined up with the world
an offer           w blocks across and 2w deep against the city's edge, w = round(√plots owned / 6 / 2^k): one or two
                   // clipped by the offers standing, trimmed of what the city owns, held to 2:1; its ground the plots of it not yet owned
```

**Four sides, six places each.** A block's side is read from its centre, seen from the founding site: the larger of its distances east–west and north–south, a tie — a corner block on the diagonal — going to North or South; and its place is which of six equal ranges, left to right facing out, the ratio of its distance across to its distance out falls in, from −1 to 1 (`GridOffers.sideOf()`, `sidePlace()`). Each of the 24 places has one offer standing, or none while its side has no room for it (`LandMarket.OFFERS_A_SIDE`, six; Jerus: *"six offers a side"*). **An offer is a rectangle of whole blocks against the city's edge**, listed in four steps (`GridOffers.list()`). Its seed is the free block of the city's frontier — the side's blocks not wholly owned that hold or touch owned ground — in the place's lane and nearest the site, ties to the lane's middle; with none, the side's free frontier block nearest the lane's middle; with none at the city's level, the same one level finer. Round the seed it is w blocks across and twice that deep, the long side outward, which the level makes one block by two, or two by four where the side has room (`DEPTH_OVER_WIDTH`), and never wider than a sixth of the side's frontier. Where it meets a standing offer, the columns on that offer's side of the seed go, or the rows from it out; then outer rows and columns the city already owns whole are trimmed, and it is held to 2:1 either way. Its ground is the rectangle's plots the city does not own yet, so a coarse offer takes in the finer steps beside it and no gap is left that cannot be offered. A new default city lists 19 offers, four or five an edge, each 1 × 2 blocks of 120 m and 0.0288 km², nearly a tenth of its rings, with five places waiting — twenty since 0.7.106, North 6 standing against its lake's blocks — and all 24 stand within its first four to twelve purchases, as the design measured it on three worlds. From a square kilometre on, the offers bought average 2 to 3% of the city, and by the design's count Jerus's old city's size is 195 to 344 purchases and ten billion people 512 to 785, where the lanes took 411 to 444.

**Never rerolled.** An offer stands at its rectangle, its contents and its price until it is bought, and buying it claims exactly its rectangle's free plots, as one more holding, and lists that place again before any other: its next is the innermost free ground of its lane — a notch the purchase left beside the city first, otherwise the next rectangle straight out. The other 23 never move, because standing rectangles never meet. A place with no room waits empty and is tried again after every purchase and every month, the place just bought first and then North 1 to West 6 (`LandMarket.listMissing()`), and none waits while its side has room for it, which `LandCheck` and the playtest's audit hold. **Corners** fill out the same way: a corner block on the diagonal is North's or South's, and the notches a corner leaves are nearer the site than anything farther out in their lane, so they are offered first and the city grows compact rather than in fingers — bought evenly, the design's cities filled 60 to 80% of their bounding box at every size past 75 purchases, and bought on one side only they grew as a stepped fan, 46 to 58%, where a plain straight-out rule had filled 42% on one side. Ids go out in the order places are listed, so the same city listing the same places sees the same offers, and the offers are saved whole. One over 70% sea stays listed, because sea is cheap, but is tagged MOSTLY SEA and is never the best.

**The books are the plots, exact at every size.** What an offer holds is counted once, as it is listed, plot by plot on the world (`CityLand.groundOf()`): its km² in all, dry, fresh, sea and forest, every field whose centre plot lies on its free ground, whole, and its forest's timber at 13,700 m³ a km². Nothing is sampled, where the lanes read 64 by 64 samples of a band, and the map counts the same plots, so the books and the map agree to the plot; the design had proposed sampling past blocks of 7.68 km, at up to 1.6% of an offer's dry ground on land and a few km² on a coast, and the decision of 7 October was the exact count. Three things keep it affordable: a tile the city owns whole is passed over; a whole tile it owns none of is counted once a world and kept, up to 65,536 of them (`CityLand.TILE_COUNTS_KEPT`); and a rectangle of 2,048 tiles or more is counted over the machine's cores in whole-number sums, the same on any machine (`PARALLEL_TILES`) — `LandCheck`'s 2,116 tiles in 130 ms on two cores and 189 on one. An offer's ground cannot change while it stands.

Until 0.7.57 nine plots were on offer at any time (`LandMarket.LISTING_SIZE`; earlier editions said ten), generated deterministically from the plot's own id, so parcel 47 was the same plot in every session and in every reload. Sizes were multiples of a floor that rose with how much the city already owned; 15% of plots were enormous tracts, and the tract was what made the listing worth reading. **From 0.7.57 to 0.7.66** the land was a square centre sized to the square foot and four sides of ten lanes, wedges fanning out from the site, an offer a lane's next band, forty in all, each sized by a multiple drawn from its id of a block or of 1% of the city, a mean of 3.81, and measured from 64 by 64 samples of its band. A lane bought often grew a finger out of the city, its curved bands were never whole plots, and testing a plot meant testing forty frontiers. That geometry is kept, read-only, to put a saved city on the grid (`LegacyLand`; below).

### A city founded with its lake

**Since 0.7.106 a new city is founded with one water plant's fresh water** (Jerus's A24; `CityLand.found()`, `LandManager.FOUNDING_FRESH_UNITS`). Past the rings, which are what they were, the centre takes whole blocks of the founding lake — from the fresh block nearest the lake's centre, each next the block edge to edge with those taken that holds the most fresh plots, the nearer the lake's centre on a tie and then the northern and the western, and a step toward the nearest fresh block where none beside holds any, all within 107 plots of the site (`CityLand.FRESH_REACH`), which the lake's far shore never lies beyond — until its lake and river hold 0.4934 km² (`FOUNDING_FRESH_KM2`), what yields one Water Treatment Plant's 60,000 units a month at 121,600 a km², going on along the river that leaves the lake where the lake is small. The world is untouched, and the lake's blocks are an island of the city's own ground, open water. On the default world the city owns 54 blocks where it owned 21: 33 of open lake 2.4 km off, 0.4941 km² of lake and river where the rings held 0.0189, 60,083 units of water a month against 2,298, so its first plant, which stood 96% idle until the city bought lake or river, idles nothing ([utilities](#20-utilities--roads)); and the same 3,051,569 sq ft of dry ground. On seventeen worlds measured the dry ground is unchanged on five and 3 to 100% larger on the rest, where a small lake takes the river that leaves it, banks and all, and a world with no lake finds only 408 fresh plots within its reach. The river beside the rings was tried first, and gave the default city 21% more dry ground from its banks; the rings trimmed for the banks split a district's streets in two on world 35; the lake keeps the city's dry ground, its land prices and its map what they were. Build's Water Treatment Plant card and Services' water (i) say a new city is founded with one plant's water; an older save keeps the centre it was founded with. In the playtest the change first shows at month 484, its first water shortage met on the lake where the wells had carried it until then.

### Whole fields

Jerus: *"Yes whole iron fields as one offer, yes that means significant investment."* A field — every one of its sites and all of its tonnes — belongs to the one piece of ground that holds the field's centre plot, wherever its sites lie: the centre, one purchase, or while it is listed one offer. The holdings and the offers never share a plot, so they hold every field exactly once and the world's totals stay exact whoever lists what when. It was the design's rule at 0.7.57; from 0.7.58 to 0.7.63 a field was shared site by site among the ground its sites lay under, so that a new city could buy a single site of its founding field for about US\$5.3M; since 0.7.64 it is whole again, for every resource alike, and since 0.7.67 by the plot that holds its centre. A city converted from a save of 0.7.58 to 0.7.63 keeps exactly the sites it held of a field it held only in part, and that field's other sites go a site at a time to the ground that holds each (below). On the old world, to 0.7.98, the default world's founding field was 35 sites and 449 Mt, its centre 26 plots south and 13 east of the site, a few blocks past a new city's edge, and none of a new city's nineteen offers carried any iron: bought toward, the offer nearest it each time, South 2 listed the field whole after six purchases, one offer of about US\$180M against a founding treasury of D\$100M, and the land office's funding page sized its bond to it. Since 0.7.99 the default world's nearest iron field lies 12 km out, in a lake, and a new city sees no deposit at all in its offers or on its map, whose far views mark only the fields within the offers' reach; on world 35 (`MiningCheck.IRON_SEED`) a dry field of 36 sites lies a kilometre out and is listed whole after a few purchases toward it. An offer's row says so — *"Iron ore: 35 sites, 449 Mt in the ground: every field of it centred in this offer, whole, paid for in its price."* — and the map's hover names whose a field is, since its sites can lie under another offer. The playtest's player buys its iron the same way since 0.7.64, and since 0.7.67 only when the field pays for itself (`LongPlaytest.ironWhenNeeded()`): when an Iron Mine would pay and every iron site the city owns has a mine, it takes the cheapest offer holding iron if the mines it could carry — no more than the field's sites and than the city could staff, each paying what the mining sector's screen says one earns — earn a month the level payment that would repay its price over the funding page's twenty years at the market's rate (`fieldEarnings()`, `fieldPayment()`), out of the cash when that covers it and on that bond when the player's test for borrowing passes. On the grid without that test it bought the founding field at month 356 with 2,759 people, US\$206.2M on a D\$251.6M bond, and ended the run with none of its 199 iron sites under a mine; with it, its first iron was West 2 at month 359, a six-site field of 76.9 Mt for US\$37.05M out of the cash, and over the run it bought four fields, none on a bond, and passed thirteen looks whose cheapest field would not pay back. Since 0.7.99 no offer near its city holds iron: at 0.7.99 it looked 202 times over the run and found none listed, stood no mine and no oil well, bought its ground elsewhere and ended 13.5% smaller ([open questions](#25-open-questions)). And since 0.7.101 the rule is the game's as well: Build's no-deposit page says under its Buy whether the cheapest field pays back for a city this size (`BuildAdvice.ironPayback()`, the test player's rule moved whole) — *It pays back: the N mines the city could staff on it would earn \$x a month, over the \$y a month that repays its price over 20 years*, or that it would not. At 0.7.64 its first had been East 7 at month 485, a one-site field 33 plots out for US\$6.16M, and at 0.7.62 a shared site in month 32.

### Two prices, moved by different things

```
what the world asks   US$0.70 a sq ft × the world's price level × the crowding premium      // since 0.7.55; the player reads US$7.53 a m² since 0.7.68
an offer's price      that on its dry ground, 45% of it on fresh water and 8% on sea, + its fields' tonnes × their share of the world price × the world's price level, to US$5k, fixed at listing
what the city pays    the offer's dollars at the day's rate
what businesses pay   the local base × the crowding premium × a scarcity multiplier from 0.65 to 1.90 on allocated/available
                      // the local base struck at the expected price level since 0.7.42 (LandMarket.getBasePricePerSqFt()); the dollar base is the world's
the crowding premium  1 + 119 × s,   s = 1 / (1 + (4,000 / d)^5.3),   d = people a km² of the land the city owns
```

The multiplier passes 1.0 at about 61% built — below that the city sells land at a loss, which is the intended cost of over-annexing. The earlier version multiplied by utilisation, which sat between 86% and 100% for 2,400 straight months, so "scarcity" was decoration. From 9 September the city was founded with a **\$3.5B endowment** — D\$2.5B in the treasury and US\$1B in the vault from 0.6.10 — enough for a coal plant at 41% of it, a works department at 400 points a month, a shed of material, and a bank standing on day one. Since 0.7.10 it is D\$100M and US\$25M, and the big works are borrowed for ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)).

**The premium is crowding, not size** (0.7.55). Jerus, of the scale study's proposal: *"Yes for land price do that"*. Until then it was 1 + .008 a block owned + .05 a thousand residents, linear in the city's size: a copy of his city ten times over saw its rents rise 3.9 times and lost 18% of its people in thirty months, and at ten billion people a square foot would have cost about 19,500 times what it cost him. A city's size is not what makes its ground dear; how hard it presses on it is. So the premium reads the city's people a square kilometre of the land it owns (`LandMarket.peoplePerKm2()`), through a curve fitted to the three cities held so that each was quoted on the day about what its size had given it — city600 3.67 to 3.74, city2400 35.07 to 35.99, Jerus's 103.39 to 104.00: 1.65 at 1,500 a km², 60.5 at the midpoint of 4,000, 117 at 8,000, and never past 120, where the size premium had no ceiling (`CROWDING_MIDPOINT`, `CROWDING_STEEPNESS`, `CROWDING_CEILING`). A copy of a city K times over, K times the people on K times the land, is quoted exactly what the city is. **And the dollar price follows the dollar's own inflation** (Jerus: *"usd inflation not domestic inflation"*): the base times the world's price level (`WorldEconomy.getPriceLevel()`) times the premium, so the city's own inflation reaches it only through the rate — in Jerus's old city the dollar price rose 14.4% on the day, US prices having risen 1.137 times since his founding. What businesses pay keeps the domestic anchor, because ground inside the city is a domestic thing bought with domestic money: one price would have put every swing of the rate into every business's ground, and would have cut his businesses' by 47% on the day, his currency standing about 1.9 times above parity. The two prices meet at parity, so the city's margin on land is the currency's distance from parity and the scarcity, nothing else, and the land office names the price's parts. Crowding is a consequence and not a cause, as 0.7.58 measured: a city kept short of ground is crowded and quoted dear, but with the premium held at one the playtest's city grew slower, not faster.

### Zones, and the forest law

**Since 0.7.107 the city can hold its ground for an industry** (batch Z1; `Zoning`, `LandManager`'s ZONES AND THE FOREST LAW). Jerus: *"in policy zoning will now exist, and basically the default is free, anything everywhere, but with zoning, you can allocate a % of total land or a specific km² for a specific industry, and even provide the land at a lower rate, or free"* — *"so that some industries can build even tho land is expensive and property tax would kill them"*. A city zones nothing until its player does, and with nothing zoned every figure is what it was. **A zone** is one sector's — any of the seventeen, the landlords' for homes among them — and an amount, not a place, the model having no positions: a share of the city's dry ground, read again as the city buys land so that 2% stays 2%, or a number of square kilometres. It holds free ground for its sector alone, bare ground first and then open forest, up to its size less what its sector has built in it; a zone bigger than what is free holds what is free and fills as land is bought, and when several want more than is free each holds the same share of what it wants. Every other business sees the free ground less what the zones hold, *free for anyone*, and so do the city's own works; a zoned sector sees its zone's too, and builds there first. **Its price** is a share of the going business price, 0 to 100%: the city is paid it when the sector builds there and pays it buying a plot back, which goes back to the zone; and the property tax's roll assesses the zone's ground at it, as farmland is assessed at its use, while the books and the statements keep the going price. An order's ground, its standing cost and a landlord's carry read the zone's price while the zone holds the whole plot. **Its taxes** are the sector's own profit, sales and property offsets — one dial, two doors, Jerus's word: a rate moved in the zone is moved on Policy › Taxes for every building of the sector (`Game.setZoneTax()`). Taken off, a zone's held ground goes back to everyone, and what was sold in it stays with its owner at what it paid, assessed at the going price from then on. And zoned fields do not yield to homes: while anybody has nowhere to live the farms plan only where their zone holds ground, and only as far as it holds ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)).

**The forest law** is two shares of the city's forest ground, nothing by default: what is kept from building, and of that what is kept from cutting too. So the forest is three kinds — *protected*, never cut and never built on, its wood taken from the fullest forest first; *working*, cut but never built on; and *open*, cut or built on — and what may be cut is what stands less the protected wood (`LandManager.cuttableForest()`), which Forestry's crews will read when they come. **Building on open forest clears it.** Forest was dry ground a building could take and nothing cleared it; the map painted a building on forest as grass. Since 0.7.107 the built ground lies on bare ground first, less the bare ground the zones hold for others, and past it on open forest, which it clears, cut-over ground first and then standing forest, whose wood is counted as taken out — Forestry's salvage once Forestry exists, and lost until then — and cleared ground never grows back, so the world's totals still hold to the cubic metre. It is cleared as ground is allocated, and at the month's end for ground set by hand. Played twelve months on copies of five cities with nothing zoned, city600 cleared 0.996 km² of its forest in its first month, 13,647 of its 14,216 m³, Jerus's old city all its 11.83 km² in its first, and his city saved on 8 October none of its 376.6; all five loaded as before. Nothing priced reads the forest cleared, and the playtest, which zones nothing, wrote 0.7.106's traces to the byte. `ZoningCheck` holds the model in nine sections ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### Policy › Zoning

**Since 0.7.109 zoning is Policy's fifth area** (batch Z2; `ui/ZoningScreen`, its figures `ZoningView`, pure): a chip beside Taxes, Wages, Money and Promises and a fifth card on the hub, in Policy's own shape — its dial cards, its staging and its tray, nothing applied until *Apply it* or *Apply all N*, and *Leave it as it is* to discard ([setting them](#12-tax-policy--gdp)). **The ground** leads with four figures of its own, each a door — ZONED, in km² with its share of the dry ground and how many zones; HELD FOR THEM; PRICE GIVEN UP, on what the zones hold, with the month's tax relief; and FOREST KEPT, *none* at the law's 0 and 0 — over THE CITY'S GROUND, the dry ground as one bar: what is built, each zone used solid and held hatched, the bare ground free for anyone and the forest in its three kinds, its parts adding up to the dry ground and each a door to its zone or the law, with a closer bar of the zones and the bare ground under it. Then THE ZONES, a row each — the sector, *holds less than it wants* when short, its size and share, used against held, its price, its three rates as chips with an offset marked, and the month's relief — THE FOREST LAW's bar and sentence, and *Zone ground for an industry*, a picker of every sector with no zone. **A zone's page**, Policy › Zoning › its sector, has HOW MUCH GROUND, *A share of the dry ground* or km², with what it would carry and hold, what stays free for anyone and what its ground would fetch at the going price; ITS PRICE, 0 to 100% in five-point steps, with a plot's ground at the zone's price against the going one, the price given up, the month's relief and THE BUDGET; ITS TAXES, the three offsets on the keys Policy › Taxes moves, each the city's rate, the offset and what results with last month's money, under *The same dials as Policy › Taxes: a move here moves it for every … building*; and *Take the zone off*. A share moves in half points and square kilometres in about a two-hundredth of the dry ground, and a new zone is staged at the going price. **The forest law's page** draws the forest under the staged law, two ladders on one card — protected, and kept from building — and WHAT IT WOULD DO: the forest standing for ever, the most that may be cut, the forest a building may take and the ground free for anyone. THE BUDGET in the tray is the staged policy's taxes with the staged zoning's change. **Elsewhere**: the land office's THE CITY line adds *· 3.2 zoned* (below); Build's LAND FREE says *free for anyone*, with a door under it, *zoned for Iron Mining 1.6 km² ›*, the sector named by its label, or for several industries the area; NEEDS YOU's GROUND, when it is listed, names what the zones hold for others than the homes; the build card's land gate, an order's quote and the investors' *no land* count the sector's own zone and add *… is zoned for others* whenever another zone holds ground ([the catalogue](#19-the-catalogue)); and a zone set, resized, repriced or taken off, and the law, are decisions of a kind of their own, flagged on City History in the ground's sand with a plot's icon, where 0.7.107 had logged them as tax ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). None of it has been seen in the game's window; 95 of its strings were measured to fit at 1,389 × 868, none over. `ZoningViewCheck` holds every figure it shows, in eight sections ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### Land is bought in dollars

Jerus: *"when you buy land, make it so that it costs USD not domestic currency, and basically how it would work is a little toggle at the top to choose, when you buy land, to use up your USD reserves or to convert cash into usd exactly to buy the land, and the default is that you convert."* Since 0.7.6 the land office prices every parcel in US dollars — the same base and premiums, so at the founding rate of 1.00 every number is what it was — fixed when it is listed, and the treasury pays usd × rate on the day it buys: a weak currency makes land dear and a strong one cheap. What businesses pay the city stays local money, struck exactly as before, so the city's margin on land carries the currency, and a currency reform no longer clears the office's board. There are two ways to pay, a chip pair at the top of the office. **Converting**, the default: the treasury buys exactly the dollars and hands them over in one movement, and the vault ends where it began. **From the vault**: the dollars leave it and no local money moves, a capital transaction like the defence's, and the treasury's journal carries the land back against the budget's land line. A vault too short for the plot spends what it holds and converts the rest, and the receipt says so. On the default seed on 28 September the advisor paid US\$10.2B abroad for land over 151 months, none of it out of the vault, and it cost D\$6.15B at the day's rates, 39.6% less than it would have at the founding rate; on 1 October it paid US\$10.6B over 149 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$5.95B, 44.1% less; and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, US\$14.7B over 166 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$3.99T, 26,961% more than at the founding rate, its currency having drifted with prices that rose 1,213-fold; and at 0.7.64, on the world's land, US\$33.1B over 141 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$3.91T, 11,704.5% more, prices having risen 775-fold; and at 0.7.68, on the block grid, US\$30.3B over 84 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$8.17T, 26,870% more, prices having risen 1,001-fold.

Since 0.7.13 the office speaks the paying currency and square kilometres — Jerus: *"for the land … instead of blocks, say km^2, and add a button to buy multiple"*. A plot's large price is in local money when converting and in US dollars from the vault, with the other as a caption beside it; areas read in km² on the exact international foot, to three figures, so a block is 0.00929 km², and so do the build screen's *Not enough land* page and the time-skip report. Since 0.7.26 the office leads with square feet, to three figures (*9.68M sq ft*), with the km² after them, and the left panel's LAND header reads *N free · D\$x/sq ft*, only its Owned and Free lines in km²; since 0.7.61 it reads square kilometres again — the city's size, each offer's and its price a dry km². **Since 0.7.68 every area the player reads**, here and on every screen, notice and line of the log, is in square metres under a hundredth of a square kilometre and in square kilometres from there, three figures, grouped from a thousand (`LandManager.areaWords()`, `M2_WORDS_BELOW`): a House's plot *743 m²*, a new city's offer *0.0288 km²*, ten billion people's dry ground *1,760,000 km²*. The unit is picked after the rounding, so nothing reads *10,000 m²*, and a part reads in its whole's unit, *0.0288 km², 0.0273 dry* (`partFigure()`). Ground prices read a square metre — THE WORLD ASKS about *US\$7.53/m²* at founding, where it read US\$0.70 a square foot — and so do INVESTORS PAY, the margin, the price's parts, History's Land line and the city panel, while an offer keeps its price a dry km²; the farms' ground under cultivation, which read acres, reads the same way, and the investors write *no land - needs 5,570 m², 3,900 m² free*. The model keeps square feet and prices a square foot, so nothing it decides moved: the playtest's figures stayed byte for byte, and only its houses' words changed. The year book's land price stays a square foot, labelled, as the model's own series. A plot the city cannot afford no longer refuses: its button opens a funding page — converting, the twenty-year bond sized to the gap and the six-month note; from the vault, a twenty-year dollar bond or a six-month dollar note sized to the dollar gap, whose dollars are held in the vault, or the old top-up from cash as a third card; with the window abroad shut, a red card across two columns with the reason, and only what remains. Since 0.7.26 the page is the office's own, *Land office › Funding*, with the rail lit, a summary bar of what is held against the gap and a *short by* pill, and the offers as cards (`Pieces.offerCard()`, which Build › Funding took up in 0.7.40), and it goes back to the office when a month lands and nothing needs funding. And *Buy the next N plots*, five by default, buys the office's first N, cheapest ground a square foot first, and since 0.7.61 is *Buy the best N*, from every side; because a listed offer's price is frozen, buying them at once costs exactly what buying them one by one does. **Since 0.7.34 every Buy is a button that says its price** in the money the toggle pays in, the card's width: *Buy · D\$1.0B*; outlined, *Buy on credit · D\$1.0B*, when only a loan pays; from the vault and short, *Buy · US\$200.3M* with *the vault is short: ways to pay* under it; *Buy the next 5* the same in its line, and not drawn with nothing listed; and the funding page's offers *Buy 5 plots · D\$9.8B* over *issues the 20-year bond, then buys* — or *issues it abroad, then buys from the vault*, or *takes what the vault has and converts the rest*. A double-click buys one plot: until 0.7.34 the second click bought the card that had slid into the first one's place. Converting for land has never pushed the currency, which is on the list. Since 0.7.22 the player's hand on the queue reaches the ground too ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)): a stopped shell and a demolition on site hold their ground, a finished demolition's ground comes back to the city as free land, and a buy-out pays the owner for its ground at the price businesses pay the city, recorded as a buyback. Land purchases are not on City History's lane of decisions, as build orders are not; a big one the treasury borrowed for shows as the borrowing.

**Ground is what a mature city runs out of** — land sits at 88–90% for the last decade of most long runs, and the 2,400-month playtest city measured at 0.7.26 was 95% used or more in 120 months of 120 with no sector waiting, which is why no screen colours the share used any more — and the newest sectors are the hungriest for it. A Rail Terminal is 5,500,000 square feet, nearly three times a Coal Power Plant and the largest footprint in the catalogue; a Livestock Farm is 120 acres, the dearest ground of any farm at $108k an acre; a Metro Line is 30,000 square feet for thirty thousand journeys a month, five hundred times a gravel road's capacity per acre. That ladder is the whole reason the modes exist — see [transport](#21-transport--vehicles). Every sector's planner assumes the ground is free and none of them can see they are bidding for the same land; that is on the list, and since 0.7.107 the player can hold ground for the ones that need it (zones, above).

### The office redrawn

Jerus, of the screens still to be done after Build: *"the others are still full of text and the design could be more intuitive and fun"*. The land office was the first redrawn in Build's style (0.7.26), and it answers top down whether the city has room to grow and which ground to buy. **THE GROUND** is four cells — the ground free, who is waiting, what the world asks and what investors pay — over the ground as one bar, the free ground solid and the next N plots as numbered ghosts, on a scale of the two together so that the bar always reads. GROUND FREE takes NEEDS YOU's GROUND row's colour, amber at 9,290 m² or less, an old block of 100,000 sq ft, and red at none (`CityNeeds.ground()`), and so do Build's LAND FREE and the left panel, whose *Land* alert shows only at none: never the share used, which sits at 95–100% for centuries with nothing wrong, so a red USED at 90% went. What the world asks is the going rate, the listing's median a square foot, read a square metre since 0.7.68 (`LandMarket.goingUsdPerSqFt()`), and who is waiting is read from the sectors the month found blocked (`Game.getLandBlockedSectors()`), where it had matched the words *no land* and missed a sector whose ground went between its plan and its purchase. **ON OFFER**, until 0.7.61, was the nine as a three-by-three of wide cards — from 0.7.57 the best nine of the forty — the next N numbered with a pink edge, each with tags of its own: BEST VALUE on the first, the cheapest ground a square foot with any ore inside its price, which is not `bestValue()`; MOST ORE on `richestDeposit()`, since 0.7.57 `richest(IRON)`; ORE and NEW; and one card can carry BEST VALUE and MOST ORE. Prices are neutral, red only when no way pays without debt. Under them four cards say what the ground is worth — the margin, the ground on top of the build, the ore and who is waiting — and behind *details* the world's price of ground over the city's life. The receipt is in the screens' money, *for US\$101.8M, converting D\$72.0M of cash at D\$0.7072*, where it printed *US\$101,800k*. Nothing the office said is gone: what is not on a card is behind an (i). `LandCheck`'s last section, since 0.7.26, holds the model reads it rests on: the going rate the median, the upper middle on an even count and nothing with nothing listed; the GROUND row's level its free ground's, word for word the row NEEDS YOU lists, a city 90% used still fine; and the receipt.

### The office round the map

Since 0.7.61 the office is laid round the city's map. The hero row is the map, 600 by 400, the city's land and its offers hatched over the world, with *Expand* to lay it over the whole window (below); and beside it **THE CITY**: its size in km² — in Jerus's old city as 0.7.61 read it, *107.8 km² · 89.6 dry · 0 fresh · 18.2 sea*, and since 0.7.109 with a zone standing what the zones hold, *· 3.2 zoned* — and its share of the world's iron, *of the world's 1.12 Pt of iron, the city owns 0.0000452%*; the four sides as chips, each with its cheapest dry ground a km² and BEST VALUE on the best's side, and since 0.7.69 a side that lists fewer than six naming its count, *North · 4*; and the chosen side's six places as rows of 28 pixels, each its place, 1 to 6 under *#* where it said *lane*, its km², its dry ground, fresh water and sea as one bar, its deposits as *8 · 136 Mt*, its price in the money the toggle pays in, its price a dry km², one tag — BEST VALUE, then NEW, MOST ORE and MOSTLY SEA, the first that holds — and *Buy*, or *Fund* when only a loan pays. Since 0.7.69 its size's tooltip gives its blocks, *1 × 2 blocks of 120 m · 0.0288 km² · 0.0273 dry, 0.0015 fresh*, and opens the row's; a place waiting for room is one muted row, *no room on this edge yet: it lists when the city grows here*; and the (i) gives a block's side in kilometres from one, *245.76 km*. A row lights its rectangle on the map, and a click on the map picks a side or an offer. Under them THE GROUND and its ghosts, *Buy the best N*, the worth cards — the ore card is *Ore and oil* — the details and the funding page are as they were, the funding page sized to the offer: converting, its bond is quoted for exactly what the chosen offers cost at today's rate less the treasury's cash (`Game.landCashGap()`), and from the vault for what the vault is short of their dollars, and once it is issued the Buy buys them. The 0.7.26 value bar went for want of room in a row. **Build buys from the same office** (`Game.bestOffer()`). LAND FREE reads its area, since 0.7.109 *free for anyone* when a zone stands (zones, above), with *Buy the best: West 1 · 0.0288 km² · US\$215k ›* under it on a new city, naming its place since 0.7.69 where it read *Buy the best land*: the most dry ground a dollar among the offers the city can afford that are not mostly sea, the nearer on a tie. The no-land page's *Buy the best* takes the cheapest offer that covers the shortfall with bare ground, no ore to pay for, and says so — *"West 1, bare ground with no ore to pay for, covers the 743 m² short"* — or, with none, the best value, and asks again; a building short of ground has not asked for ore, and on the literal rule, the cheapest offer that covers it, the playtest's village was sold two sites of iron for US\$11.4M where bare ground cost a tenth of that, and stood still for two hundred months. The no-deposit page's *Buy the cheapest* takes the cheapest offer holding the ore, since 0.7.64, as the playtest's player does, where from 0.7.61 it took the most sites a dollar; and the no-coast page the cheapest offer with sea. Short of cash, each opens the office's funding page sized to that offer. And since 0.7.77 automatic building buys by the no-land page's rule for its own orders, bare ground only, paid as the toggle says ([automatic building](#22-the-screen)).

**Iron is a pooled resource.** Until 0.7.57 a parcel carried a deposit *count* and a tonnage the office drew for it, and roughly 28% of ore parcels carried more than one site; since then the sites and the tonnes are the world's fields in the ground the city owns. The sites cap how many mines can stand, one a site, and every mine draws from one reserve, what the city's fields held less what has been taken out (`LandManager.getIronReserveTonnes()`), worked out in the order the ground was bought. Ore in the ground is worth a fraction of what it fetches once it is out — the value is in getting it out, which is why it sells at 1/212.5 of the world's floor since 0.7.120, US$0.40 a tonne, as 1/350 of the old floor was — and a deposit that is worked out closes its mine inside a year, which is what makes the bust when a mining city runs dry a real event rather than a slow leak. Oil is the same since 0.7.62, a well a site: since 0.7.84 a land well a dry site, and since 0.7.91 a platform's well a sea site in its slot; and since 0.7.93 the city's oil is two pools, the ground's and the sea's, each worked out on its own fields ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)).

### The map of what the city has

Since 0.7.60 the city keeps a map (`CityMap`), and since 0.7.61 it is on screen. **What it stores** is not a picture but a count: each type's buildings in each 7.68 km district of the city's land, with the district's free plots and the iron and oil sites the city owns in it. Each month, once the month's construction and demolitions are done, each type's change goes into the first district with room — nearest the founding site first, but farms, utilities, mines, the railway and the car plants farthest first — removals the other way round, and nothing placed ever moves; mines and wells stand on the city's own sites of their resource, the first not worked out in the order the ground was bought. The map is drawn the first time anything asks for it, so a city nobody looks at pays nothing, and it is saved beside the city as `slot-NN-map.bin`, deflated, with its stamp in the save; a load whose sidecar is missing or stale draws it again, and the picture shifts once. **What it draws is what the city has, no more and no less** (0.7.64). Jerus: *"a brand new city shows that it has a few houses and a shop when it doesnt"*. A new default city holds one building, the Commercial Bank it is founded with (`Game.foundingBank()`), and no road, where 0.7.60's map had drawn homes from its people and workplaces from its jobs, the bank as a shop, beside two highways of the world's. Every building the model has is drawn once, as its own type, on whole plots sized to its type's land — the square root of its plots across and the rest down, a House one plot, Low-Rise Apartments two by three, an Iron Mine six by seven, a Livestock Farm 23 by 23 (`BuildingVisual.footprint()`) — turned to face its road, a mine on its own site; and the model's roads are laid as their own plots by kind, a Gravel Road 46, a Paved Road 26 and an Elevated Highway 7, and no others. A tile is painted from the seed, its ground, what is owned, what it was dealt and its neighbours' roads (`TilePainter`), so it looks the same every time it is drawn: from 0.7.64 to 0.7.71 buildings of sixteen plots or more first, then the roads, grown from ports the next tile agrees on and bridging fresh water but never the sea, then the rest, each from its own hashed place beside a road; from 0.7.72 to 0.7.87 its roads one network dealt to its road tiles, and since 0.7.88 its district's street plan (below). One that no free box on its tile can hold is drawn smaller, and counted: 7 of 2,340 in Jerus's live city at month 416 at 0.7.64, and at most a tenth on the densest screen `MapCheck` draws — 9.30% of it at 0.7.69; 16.72% at 0.7.71, the resized childcare having taken away the one-plot daycares that filled it; and 7.18%, 1,107 of 15,422, from 0.7.72, a tile dealt buildings to no more than 90% of its room while another tile had some (`CityMap.TILE_FULL_MOST`, gone with the deal in 0.7.88), so that a tenth is kept for the shapes buildings come in, and a large building laid on the grid's blocks near a road. A year on, a new city's map is its eleven houses, its store, its diner and its bank.

**From 0.7.72 to 0.7.87 the roads were one network** (Jerus: *"to make the map generation prettier"*), planned once a deal for each district (`CityMap`'s THE NETWORK, whose highways and track 0.7.88 still drew and which is gone since 0.7.89, the names below with it). Its road tiles were grown from the tile nearest its core, its mines' tiles joined first, while its main streets took no more than half its road (`MAINS_SHARE`), the rest the grid among its buildings. A tile's main street ran on its first or its last grid line, 4 or 28 plots in, by its column's own hash (`TilePainter.MAIN_AT`), leaving 27 plots open beside it, room for a Rail Terminal or a Livestock Farm; its mains crossed at its hub, and an arm ran from the hub to each edge's crossing — the plot nearest the main line where it, the plot inside it and the two across the edge were dry, owned and no mine's, so both tiles read the same pair, one crossing an edge where one to three hashed ports had been. Inside a tile the grid's streets lay eight plots apart, so a + junction was eight houses from the next, Jerus's *"about 8 houses' length"* (`JUNCTION_APART`, the street plan's lattice since); lanes left them in T's, and a fill came last. Every road plot was laid before the small buildings, a rail yard or a large building was placed only where it left the network the room its roads still needed (`keepsNetwork()`), and a building stood within four plots of a road (`REACH`) unless its tile had no room for it near its own roads. A district's highway was one straight run from its hub along its main row, turning only at the sea, the city's edge or a mine, four times at most, and crossing once, at the hub. **The railway was drawn**: the Rail Spur and the Freight Line as track, plot by plot, on its tile's edge away from the main, one line a district, crossing a street but never running along one, in openstreetmap-carto's rail grey, #707070, dashed white, on decks over fresh water up to a highway's fourteen plots; a Rail Terminal was a yard beside it on the track's tile nearest a mine.
