On Jerus's old city of half a million, laid on the design's square city, `MapCheck`'s eighth section drew 19,995 road plots in one piece, 135 + junctions none nearer than eight plots, each district's highway one straight run, 7,644 of 7,700 buildings within four plots of a road and none of the rest where its tile had room, and every one of its 792 plots of track. The sidecar was format 4 from then, an older map drawn again once. **Since 0.7.77 gravel bridges rivers** (Jerus: *"gravel road bridge rivers sure"*): a street crosses fresh water gravel as paved, up to six plots, 180 m, the mockup's paved bridge (`STREET_BRIDGE`, the street plan's since), a gravel bridge drawn as every bridge is, the road in its own colour over the deck; the hover says *Gravel road, a bridge*. The sea is still bridged by nothing. On the network Jerus's live city at month 416 drew its roads in two pieces, where 0.7.71 had drawn 27 and 0.7.72 four, and the playtest's at month 1,000 in one, where they had drawn 34 and four, and at 4,000 in seven, where they had drawn 295 and eight, the rest a sea channel and slivers. Its checks passed on the city Jerus's screenshot of 0.7.86 showed — a tile of buildings with no road beside a tile that was a maze of road with a shop in each hole, walls of buildings along every tile edge, and a district's highway crossing itself — because they measured an intermediate list, the road tiles, and not what was drawn; so it went (below).

**On screen** it is one canvas (`ui/MapView`, its arithmetic in the model as `MapFrame`, `LandMap` and `MapTiles` so that `MapCheck` holds it): small in the land office and, with *Expand*, over the whole window, where a drag pans, the wheel zooms by 1.25 a notch at the pointer from the whole world to 16 pixels a plot, + and − zoom, 0 fits and Esc closes, with a legend, the Railway in it since 0.7.72, Track since 0.7.88 and since 0.7.97 nine more, the works on the shore and at sea and a line for the ships, thirty-three in three columns, and a hover card — the ground, whose it is, an offer's size and price, the fields under it and their tonnes, the building, the road or the railway, and whether it is a bridge; since 0.7.88 a street's kind, width and role, *Paved street, 15 m · arterial*, or *Track: the city has bought no road here*, and a building *packed without a street*; since 0.7.89 *a ramp* and *the railway over it* on a highway; and since 0.7.97 a quay, *a terminal's berth, where its ships come alongside*, a jacket, its safety zone and a pipe, *the platforms' crude ashore without tankers*; and since 0.7.119, on the real Earth, where the pointer is from the nearest place and the province under it (the real Earth, above). It draws at the mockup's levels: painted tiles from 3.2 pixels a plot, at 4 pixels a plot and at 8 past 6; blocks of four plots from 1.4; blocks of eight below that while the view holds no more than 1,024 tiles; and past that the districts as tinted nodes over the world's ground, on the real Earth since 0.7.119 the far view drawn from the data. Tiles paint a few a frame, at most 8 ms of it, the middle of the view first and another level's picture standing in; a month or a purchase stamps the tiles in view again and repaints only those whose stamp moved; and its caches together stay within 48 MB at the design's size, 47.8 measured at 0.7.69, and 47.6 since 0.7.88, when the painted tiles kept went from 64 to the hover's one, and 47.7 since 0.7.97 drew the sea's works (`MapTiles.PAINTED_KEPT`) — a tile paints from its plans in about 0.1 ms — and the 48 MB holds the plans instead. The first draw is made off the screen's thread, on a copy of the city's land and counts, and taken back on it caught up to the month (`Game.mapDraft()`, `adoptMap()`). **Its cost follows the screen, never the population**: a 198-tile screen paints and rasters in no more than 80 ms with Jerus's old city as it is and at 9,814, 10,000 and 19,629 times it — five and ten billion people — 59.5 ms at worst at 0.7.64, 63 to 68 on 0.7.72's network, and 24 to 30 since 0.7.88 paints from the plans, about 0.13 ms a tile, each within 1.5 times the five-billion copy's, and a month's change at five and ten billion costs no more than 5 ms. Room is counted plot by plot, about 8 ms a district, and only in the districts a purchase touches, but a large save loaded without its sidecar counts every district once. **On the grid** (0.7.69) every line of the overlay is on whole pixels: the city's edge is one shape of whole straight runs, crisp and stepped, a pixel inside its ground; its block lines are faint, white at 8%, where a block is 6 pixels or more (`MapFrame.BLOCK_LINES_FROM`); each offer is hatched and edged on its free ground only, because a coarse rectangle takes in the city's finer steps beside it and those had read as ground on offer — 16 of the 24 round Jerus's converted city hold some of his ground — and numbered by its place on its freest square at least 11 pixels each way (`PLACE_LABEL_FROM`), and since 0.7.79 the land office opens at its fit, or closer while the smallest offer standing would be drawn under 12 pixels across, to that on the fit's centre (`LandMap.open()`, `MapFrame.OPENING_OFFER_PX`), so that every offer it shows whole is numbered — `MapCheck`'s ten-year town had opened at 2.74 pixels a plot under 0.7.78's growth, its smallest offers drawn 10 or 11 pixels across, and opens at 3.0; Jerus's city and the research cities open where they did, and a town whose own ground is far taller than its smallest offers opens on its middle rather than all of it; and an offer larger than the view is drawn over all of it, where 0.7.61's test of its corners had dropped it. The outline and the cut-outs are found once a purchase or a listing, not every frame, and `MapCheck` holds the arithmetic. The view has not yet been seen in the game's own window; what has been looked at is the painter's renders, and for 0.7.69 a mirror of the overlay drawn in Java2D — a new city, the playtest's at months 1,000 and 4,000, and Jerus's autosave converted — and for 0.7.72 and 0.7.77 the painter's renders of the network, the track and the bridges on the same cities and Jerus's live one, and from 0.7.88 to 0.7.92 the painter's renders of the plans, the runs and the estate cells on his city at month 8,473 and the playtest's at months 1,000 and 4,000, before and after each batch, and at 0.7.97 a mirror of the view's boats over the painted tiles, with the campus, the shore and the oil at sea.

### Streets by need

**Since 0.7.88 a district's streets are a plan** (`DistrictPlan`, 0.7.87, a port of the project's prototype, `proto2.py`; drawn since 0.7.88). No street grid that reaches every building fits in a paved city's 12% of road at 30 m plots, so the plan lays the streets the buildings need — one network, + junctions on a grid, every building within reach — and draws the model's road plots exactly, as what those streets are made of: streets by need, road by surface. Nothing in the model reads it. **A district is 8 by 8 cells**, a cell a tile, its west column and north row the cell's arterials, its interior 31 plots square. Its cells with room — at least 120 of the 961 plots dry, owned and off the highways (`CELL_ROOM_LEAST`) — open outward from its cell nearest the founding site, each next the nearest touching one taken, with a hashed nudge, so they are one piece. Its buildings go in three bands — what follows people, industry, and the outer kinds, a farm, a utility, a plant or the rail — each band largest first, each building at the first spot it fits in its band's open cells, touching a street first and else within four plots of one (`REACH`), a cell opened when none holds it: a **homes cell** of long blocks, a street every 8 plots across them and every 16 along, for the first band, two or four blocks merged for a building wider than one; an **estate cell** for the others. The street pieces are joined to the largest along the lattice, and since 0.7.88 to the streets of the districts before it in the map's order where they meet its edge. **The road is the surface**: the model's gravel and paved plots are laid on the streets as their surface, every street at half width, arterials first and then by its cell's rank, then at full width; a street the surface does not reach is a *track*, which the city has bought no road for. A district with road left over climbs a ladder — square blocks in its homes cells nearest the hub, 56 plots of road a cell (`SQUARE_PLOTS`), then boulevards of its arterials nearest the hub, 100 a cell (`BOULEVARD_PLOTS`) — a step not taken that would leave a building without a place. The game's rules on top of the prototype's: a street bridges fresh water up to 6 plots and an arterial up to 14; where water or the city's edge cuts a cell, a dead end is joined along the cut, and a piece shorter than a block touching nothing is not laid (Jerus: *"no stray roads"*); no building touches a highway plot, corners included, and streets pass beneath a highway and cross a railway, never along either; a resource's sites are fields, taken by a building only when it has no other place, and a mine or well stands on its own; and a building wider than an estate's strip both ways takes a whole estate cell. With the prototype's own hashes and rules (`Input.asPrototype`) the plan is the prototype's, box for box and plot for plot. A shared edge's arterial is surfaced by the district first in the map's order and laid by the other as a seam with no surface of its own, so no plot is paid for twice, and since 0.7.88 one the surfacing district leaves unlaid is surfaced by the other from its leftover. A plan takes about 2 ms a district on Jerus's city and the playtest's. **Since 0.7.94 the same plans cost less** (DistrictPlan's SPEED): each planning thread keeps its arrays from plan to plan, held softly, about 4 MB and 0.4 MB a step of the ladder, so a dense plan leaves 1.2 MB for the collector where it left 11.6; a building starts its look where its shape may still fit; rows of plots are read as bits; a merge's split is settled near the box; and the long loops run a row, a building or a step a call, so they compile early and recover from a deopt at the next call, where the planner had fallen back to the interpreter on inputs it had not seen while the compiler was busy. Every plan is the same, hashed against 0.7.93's before each change — the 1,050 `PlanCheck` makes, the 88 `MapCheck` makes and 274 more; the dense screen's slowest district, ten runs of `PlanCheck` alone, took 26 to 43 ms at 0.7.93, three over its 40, and 17 to 26 ms since; and a month's change at ten billion, which walked 38,109 districts in its first month after a step, walks 8,488, a later walk of the month passing the districts an earlier one found full for its size (`CityMap`'s WALKS PASSED) and the districts lacking road kept in a heap of their own (THE LACKING HEAP).

**The painter draws the plans** since 0.7.88 (`CityMap`, THE DRAWN PLANS; `TilePainter`): each tile from its district's plan, kept packed — a tile's rows a pattern, four bytes a building — for 64 districts (`PLANS_KEPT`), drawn on the view's worker while another level's picture stands in. The deal, the road tiles, the lanes, the fill and the edge ring are gone. **What a district cannot hold is carried** to the next district in the map's order, a chain whose links are kept, and what the last cannot hold is packed at the city's edge, spread a building a tile over its edge districts' free ground, the farthest tiles first, drawn dimmed (`TileRaster.PACKED_DIM`, 0.35) and smaller where no whole box is left, and counted in the legend's note: *n buildings packed without a street: the city is short of ground for streets*, and *n plots of road more than its streets carry*, the road the ladder could not hold, counted rather than drawn. Streets are verge and surface — gravel tan, paved grey, a track brown and dashed — with arterials and boulevards, highways cased with a centre line, and forest under a building cleared. Since 0.7.89 the chain runs in bands of 128 districts (`CHAIN_BAND`), so a screen at the edge of a ten-billion city plans one band, 50 plans in under a second on the worker, where it would have planned all 14,898, and a city of 128 districts or fewer, Jerus's 93 among them, is one band and drawn as before. The sidecar was format 5 from 0.7.88, writing the runs (below) from 0.7.89, and is 6 since 0.7.97; format 4 loads.

**Since 0.7.89 the highways and the railway are the city's** (`CityRuns`), laid city-wide, month by month, where each district had laid its own: a highway on the street line through the middle of a cell, 16 plots in, never an arterial's row (`HIGHWAY_AT`), and the railway on the line a quarter in, 8 plots (`RAIL_AT`). Each net grows from a hub — the highways' at the founding site, the railway's at the city's mine nearest it — in four arms, and more corridors a district apart when every arm is stuck, straight by preference: a step costs a plot, a 45-degree turn 40 and a junction 200 (`TURN_COST`, `JUNCTION_COST`, the prototype's `hw.py`), so an arm turns 45 degrees only along the sea or the city's edge, turns home where the way home pays for it, crosses its own net only where the ground beyond pays for the interchange and otherwise meets it in a T. Laid plots never move, and a demolition takes up the newest end first. Ramps come down at every other arterial and at each arm's end — on the screen only since 0.7.98, when the view's kept copy of a tile's inputs stopped dropping the runs' marks (`MapTiles.copy()`), which had taken the smooth bands of a highway's 45-degree stretches with them, every plan the same hash for hash; the railway crosses streets level and bridges the highways; Rail Terminals are yards on the track, in the cell along it nearest a mine with room. Each district's plan is drawn round them, a verge a plot wide either side of a highway, corners included; what no corridor has ground for is counted, and the legend says so, *n plots of track with no ground left for the railway's lines*. The runs grow over owned dry ground reachable from the hub, so on Jerus's city, about three quarters water, 1,863 of its 3,336 plots of track wait for the islands. The highway that floated inside a block of his city at 0.7.88 is gone. A district's plan was made about 30% sooner in the same batch, the same plan.

**Since 0.7.90 an estate cell's streets fit what it holds** (DistrictPlan's ESTATE LINES). The prototype's estate cell had one spine across its middle, which left rows 4 to 10 and 20 to 26 out of a street's reach. Now its streets run one way across the cell, meeting the arterials in T's, on lines 7 to 23 plots in and 8 or more apart, so a + where one meets a neighbour's street across an arterial is still 8 from the next; the cell takes the spine or strips two rows of the building that opens it deep, whichever holds more of it, a cell the ground cuts trying the other way too. Each estate-band type alone on flat ground fills 71% of its cells' ground where the spine filled 60%: a 4 by 4 works 44 to a cell, not 32, a 9 by 9 plant 9, not 6. **Since 0.7.92 the outer kinds share industry's cells** (SHARED ESTATES; Jerus: *"sure they can share"*): an outer kind its district's own cells cannot hold, with no cell left to open, takes the leftover ground of its industry cells in the order they opened, an empty one whole, before it is carried on; a district that does not run out of cells is drawn as it was, box for box. Packed at the city's edge: Jerus's city 177 at 0.7.88, 156 at 0.7.89 and 148 at 0.7.90 and 0.7.92 — Wind Farms and Assembly Plants, 13 by 14 plots, four to a cell at most, for which his full districts have no cells left — and the playtest's at month 4,000 420 at 0.7.88, 413 at 0.7.90 and 345 at 0.7.92, at month 1,000 48 and then 28. The road his streets cannot carry, counted and not drawn, was 188,507 plots at 0.7.88 and 183,991 at 0.7.92. `PlanCheck` holds the plans and `MapCheck` the painted map ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### The map at the water

**Since 0.7.97 the refinery is a campus on the map** (`CityMap` and `DistrictPlan`, THE CAMPUS): the city map deals all its units to one district, the one holding most of the refinery's ground while it has room, and that district's plan places them first of its industry, each in a cell of the campus's or one touching it, side or corner, drawn in a dark violet of their own; a sidecar older than its format 6 has its units gathered there once, as it is read, so Jerus's sixteen units came together in district (−4, −1) once. **The sea terminals, the tank farms and the reserve's tanks stand on the shore** (`CityShore`, new): each laid once, city-wide as the runs' yards are, district by district from the founding site and tiles nearest first, near its cell's ring, on owned dry ground inland of a shore plot, inside one cell's interior and off every run and highway, and a terminal only by owned salt water that opens to the sea 10 km out (`SeaRoutes.opensToSea()`), its quay straight out over it, 6 to 14 plots by its cargo (`QUAY_PLOTS`); never moved, the newest taken first when one goes, kept in the map's sidecar, and drawn round by the plans as fixed yards. The playtest's 23 General Cargo Terminals at month 4,000, which had gone to a salt lagoon behind a sand bar, sit on its open south coast. **At sea** each platform's jacket stands two plots square amid its slotted sites, its wells on them, its 500 m safety zone dashed, and the pipe runs buried from the field toward the founding site as far as its kilometres stand (`Game.mapAtSea()`). **The boats**: each terminal's route out to the world is found once, on a 480 m grid of the sea whose cells are the sea's where 12 of their 16 samples are salt, and pulled straight (`SeaRoutes`, new; the prototype's `islands.py`) — to the offing, on the bearing with the most sea past the city and 10 km more, or out of a bay by a flood, and on 3 km into the abyss, less where land comes first, each call's last leg turned up to 3 degrees by its hash; and the month's calls (`BoatSchedule`) sail it on the game's clock, a month of ships over a minute of it at 1× and standing while it is paused — imports blue, exports orange, empty legs grey, box ships white — each hull its class's length, 245 m times the cube root of its cargo over 75,000 t (`ShipShapes`, new), drawn larger until close in, a dart under 7 pixels, and fading past the offing. The lanes show at every view but the farthest and the boats close in. Nothing in the model reads any of it. At ten billion, with 20,000 lanes, a frame's boats are found in 0.04 to 0.16 ms against a bound of 0.5, and the playtest's 23 routes at month 4,000 in 0.7 s on the view's worker. Where the campus or the shore moved them the plans differ from 0.7.96's, 5 of Jerus's 93 districts, and the rest are the same hash for hash. `MapCheck`'s ninth section holds all of it ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### Older cities on the grid

Since 0.7.120 a load reaches none of this: every save before format 37 is refused ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)), and what follows is what the builds to 0.7.119 did, the code kept for the day old saves must load again. Every save written before 0.7.67 was put on the grid once, as it loaded (`LandConversion`, `GridConversion`), and no money moved for it. **A save of format 31** (0.7.57 to 0.7.66: a centre and forty lanes) has its old ground read as it was, through the lanes' geometry kept read-only (`LegacyLand`), and snapped to whole blocks one level finer than the city's offers — 240 m for Jerus's live city, whose offers are 480 m. Its fields decide first: each whole field's centre plot and each site of a field it held only in part, a save of 0.7.58 to 0.7.63, marked as the city's or not. A block holding both kinds is split into its four, down to the plot if need be; otherwise a block is the city's when a point in it is the city's, not when a point in it is another's, and else when the save owned half its plots or more. What comes out is one holding, the converted centre: its sites and tonnes the save's to the bit and what it has taken out as saved, so no field changes hands, and a field held in part keeps exactly its own sites (`landPartFields`); its five areas the plots drawn, so the books follow the map and the city's square feet become its dry plots; its purchase records kept as history, what it paid on record — Jerus's, 133 purchases, US\$125.2M listed and D\$164.3M paid — and nothing charged for ground the snap adds or refunded for ground it takes. Then 24 offers are listed round it, the one time offers are listed afresh, at the prices the save last struck, after the load has put back the prices, the buildings and the allocation, so they are priced on the converted city's crowding. Jerus's live city, his autosave at month 416 and slot 3 at month 212, gains 0.130 km² of dry ground, 1.8%, and 0.015 of lake, and loses 0.078 of sea; three blocks are its for its fields, one split; the two fields it held in part keep their 6 of 8 sites; and its 13 iron sites and 160.6 Mt are the save's to the bit, its cash unchanged. Played twelve months, saved as format 32 and loaded, both come back to the bit in every pool the money audit reads, and play their next month alike.

**A save of format 30 or older** (before 0.7.57: one figure, a pool of iron and nine parcels with no place) is given a world as it always was: its seed, if it has none of its own, made from its name, its founding treasury, its ground and its month ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)); its site found as a new city's is, with one test more — the square holding its ground must be at least 80% dry, with the sea within half its side and 2 km — over the 64 coastal cells nearest the middle, failing all of which the driest site found. Since 0.7.67 its centre is rings of blocks of the city's level round that site, the last split down to the plot, holding its dry ground to within a plot and never less; its iron is its own, the sites it had or at least its mines standing and on order, and exactly its tonnes, none invented and none yet taken out, with a field laid at least 1 km out on its own dry ground if the world put no iron there; and the other resources are the world's fields centred on it. Jerus's old city holds its 89.63 km² of dry ground in 960 m blocks to within a plot, with 2.1% more sea and 12.6% less forest than its 0.7.64 centre, and keeps its 155 iron sites and 508 Mt; city600 holds its 3.03 km² in 240 m blocks with a legacy field of ten sites, and city2400 its 33.29 in 960 m blocks; and the old city, played twelve months to 514,354 people, saves as format 32 and reloads to the bit. Since 0.7.59 a save with no water rights is given what its fresh plants already pump less what its lakes yield, so that loading idles nothing it had — Jerus's old city 300,000 units, having no lake in its centre, city2400 960,000 and city600 none ([utilities](#20-utilities--roads)). A save whose square feet disagree with its land by more than a plot — a copy of a city K times over, or ground set by hand in a harness — has its land drawn again round the same site to hold them, as an older save's is, its iron and what was taken out kept (`LandConversion.restate()`).

## 19. The catalogue

*One hundred and eight buildings in `buildings.json`, hot-editable next to the game, every one on a sourced real capital cost at the size the game actually builds it. Edit a number, restart, look — no rebuild. Ids are permanent, because saves are keyed by them; the next is 108. Eighteen were added in the three days to 18 September; three from 0.7.54 to 0.7.62, the Desalination Plant (0.7.59), the Oil Well and the Oil Refinery (0.7.62); and twenty-five from 0.7.80 to 0.7.91, all of them oil's and the sea's: the Crude Unit and fourteen conversion units (0.7.80), the Filling Station (0.7.83), the Tank Farm and the Strategic Reserve (0.7.85), four sea terminals (0.7.86), and the Offshore Platform, the Platform Well and the Crude Pipeline (0.7.91); and seven in 0.7.123, ids 101 to 107, Iron & Steel's integrated route. Since 0.7.71 three old ids are childcare centres of new sizes (below), and since 0.7.120 three are iron's as the world prices it: id 11, the Steel Foundry, is the Electric Arc Furnace, it and the Steel Mini-Mill (12) melt scrap, and the Iron Mine (14) lifts eight times what it did ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)).*

| Category | Templates | What it does |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Residential | 3 | House (six), Studio Apartments (two), Low-Rise (four) — a home has a size and a household has to fit it |
| Commercial | 4 | Convenience Store, Small Grocery — coverage is how many people can shop — and the Commercial Bank; and since 0.7.83 the grocers' Filling Station, 350,000 litres of petrol a month at the pump, three posts on an acre |
| Industrial | 5 | Industrial Bakery and Bakery, which buy crops and bake bread and bakery goods out of them (until September 2026 they were a Textile Mill and a Food Processing Plant making a good called Food out of nothing); and the eleventh sector's Meat Works, Snack & Oils Plant and Bottling Plant — five, six and four posts, among the smallest investor-built job steps in the catalogue |
| Heavy industry | 30 | Electric Arc Furnace (the Steel Foundry until 0.7.120) and Steel Mini-Mill, on scrap since 0.7.120, and since 0.7.123 the integrated route — a Scrap Yard, a Pelletising Plant, Coke Ovens, a Mini Blast Furnace, a Blast Furnace, an Oxygen Steel Shop and a Large Mini-Mill, from $35M to $1.8B — plus manufacturing's Fabrication Shop, Fabrication Works and Machine Works — the first domestic customer steel ever had — and since 0.7.62 the seventeenth sector's Oil Refinery, 8,300 t of crude a month cut since 0.7.76 into 580,170 litres of petrol, 1.4 million of diesel and 7.7 million of four products it ships, where it made 8.3 million litres of fuel; since 0.7.80 the Crude Unit, 100,000 barrels a day for $400M, and a small and a large of seven conversion units — reformer, cracking unit, hydrocracker, alkylation, coker, lube plant and asphalt unit — from a Small Asphalt Unit at $2.2M to an Alkylation Unit at $115M, each fed one stream of the crude units' run; and since 0.7.85 the refiners' Tank Farm and the city's Strategic Reserve, 500,000 m³ of tanks each |
| Business services | 3 | Contact Centre, Shared Services Centre, Engineering Services Office — seats sold abroad; the last needs licensed engineers before it will open |
| Agriculture | 4 | Mixed Farm, Grain Farm, Greenhouse Complex and, since 16 September, the Livestock Farm — 13.8, 55, 3.4 and 120 acres; the glass is the one that survives expensive ground, and the herd is the dearest of the farms per acre — $108k against the Grain Farm's $22k — and sells 6.5% of its build cost a month against the Grain Farm's 18% |
| Mining | 5 | Iron Mine — sixty jobs, a quarry lifting 30,000 t a year until 0.7.120 and 20,000 t a month since, on diesel, for $45.0M — and since 0.7.62 the sixteenth sector's Oil Well, lifting 415 t of crude a month new and 10% less a year since 0.7.84, with one post since then where it had three; each stands on a site of its own resource that the city owns, a well on a dry one; and since 0.7.91 the oil at sea's Offshore Platform, Platform Well and Crude Pipeline, which stand on none of the city's dry ground |
| Construction | 2 | Construction Depot, and the Construction Materials Plant — the seventh sector's only building |
| Electricity | 2 | Coal Power Plant — 280 MW at $1.43B, far more than a city of 74,000 needs — and a Wind Farm, the first small plant beside it |
| Water | 2 | Water Treatment Plant, which treats no more than the city's lakes and river yield since 0.7.59, and the Desalination Plant, the same water from the sea at twice the cost and 10,880 kW |
| Infrastructure | 6 | Gravel Road, Paved Road, Elevated Highway — each the cheapest per trip over its life across a band of land prices, and since 0.7.70 a gravel road can be paved, and since 0.7.103 each keeps its own repairs, 3%, 2% and 1.25% of its price a year, where every other building's are 1% — and since 16 September the Bus Network, Light Rail Line and Metro Line, the same ladder two rungs on: 2,500, 8,000 and 30,000 journeys a month, and the first things in this category that ever had a payroll |
| Ports | 4 | since 0.7.86 the city's sea terminals, a category of their own (`BuildingType.PORTS`): the Tanker, Bulk, Container and General Cargo Terminals, each one berth of one kind of cargo — 3.25, 27.5, 6.75 and 0.45 million tonnes a year, from $70M to $2.31B — ordered only where the city owns sea |
| Rail | 3 | Rail Spur, Freight Line, Rail Terminal — 50,000, 200,000 and 500,000 tonnes a month across the city boundary at $140M, $520M and $1.24B, owned by the twelfth sector and financed like a steel mill; a terminal is 1,482 jobs on 5,500,000 square feet, the largest hiring commitment and the largest footprint in the game |
| Automotive | 4 | Vehicle Works and Assembly Plant (120 and 500 cars a month), Commercial Vehicle Plant (150 vans), Locomotive Works (four wagon sets) — all fed on fabricated steel and machinery, and anchored on heavy manufacturing's revenue per head rather than the food plants', because the first draft never cleared the interest test |
| Luxury | 2 | Boutique and Department Store — 320 and 4,200 pieces a month over a counter, importing every one of them |
| Hospitality | 2 | Diner and Restaurant — 13,500 and 40,500 meals a month, each buying the Convenience Store's basket scaled to the person-months its meals come to, to the kilogram |
| Healthcare | 14 | childcare, general, senior and death care, on Build since 0.7.24 as four rings, the picked ring's buildings as cards; since 0.7.71 childcare is three centres, 80, 220 and 360 places |
| Education | 9 | three basic stages, college, university, and four professional schools that each license one job |
| Safety | 4 | two police buildings and two prisons — the city pays for all four |

Every building declares a cash cost, construction points, materials, maintenance, capacity, lot footprint in square feet, electricity and water draw, road load, its job mix across eleven types, and — since the template — **which sector owns it and what it makes and uses**. A healthcare building also declares what it treats, a school what it teaches, a safety building whether it is a station or a cell block, a transit line the journeys it can carry and a rail building the tonnes; since 0.7.110 a building on a resource the site it stands on (`"site"`: its resource, a type of field or any, its sites and what a unit takes; [land](#18-land)), and since 0.7.112 a building may declare the power it makes (`"gen"`) and the consumables it buys abroad a month (`"consumables"`), which the arc furnaces and the Iron Mine first did in 0.7.120, and since 0.7.123 ten buildings do, three of them making power ([work and output](#6-work--output)); and since 0.7.123 the year it first existed (`"since"`), which nothing reads yet, and the old steel a Scrap Yard takes a month (`"oldMetal"`). The road load is one number and it is read as three: fitted to the catalogue itself, 0.726 × jobs + 0.878 × homes + 0.0386 × tonnes a month, so a mine keeps its road load and learns what share of it is ore — 68% of 420 at 2,500 t a month, and 94% of 3,360 since 0.7.120 at 20,000 — a university is all commuters, and a shop's freight is a van at a back door. Money throughout is in thousands: a cash cost of 30 is $30,000, at founding prices, and since 0.7.42 struck every month at the price level the city expects ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). Every building prices itself — sticker and all-in, from the same method that charges, since 0.7.19 with its labour at today's builders' wages and their sales tax in it — on a card that explains it from its own numbers.

**The Build tab files it differently.** The table's categories are `BuildingType`'s, and since 0.7.24 Build files the catalogue in fourteen of its own (`BuildAdvice.categories()`): the city's five — Utilities (electricity and water), Roads & transit, Healthcare, Education and Safety — then, after a rule, the market's nine — Homes, Shops, Industry (industrial, heavy industry, mining and construction, and since 0.7.86 ports), Offices, Farms, Rail, Vehicles, Luxury shops and Restaurants. Five were renamed as Jerus chose, *"Yes, rename them"*: Residential is Homes, Commercial Shops, Industrial Industry, Infrastructure Roads & transit and Business services Offices, on Build's strip alone. Since 0.7.25 the market's pages draw their buildings in their owning sectors' groups: Industry's seven, nine since 0.7.62 and thirteen since 0.7.91 — food mills, food processing, iron and steel, fabrication and machinery, iron mining, oil, oil platforms, oil pipelines, refining, oil storage, ports, building materials and the builders, the city's reserve and terminals among them on cards of their own with no investors' line — and Shops' two, three since 0.7.83: the groceries, the filling stations and the bank's branches. Since 0.7.120 two of them are named for their sectors' labels, *Iron & Steel* and *Iron Mining*, where they read *Steel* and *Iron*. `BuildAdviceCheck`'s first section holds that every building sits in exactly one of the fourteen.

### One card for every building

Jerus: *"also the build card for every building, i think the card itself needs a redesign dont you think?"* Since 0.7.25 every one of the 73, 76 since 0.7.62, 101 since 0.7.91 and 108 since 0.7.123, is one card, 300 pixels wide (`BuildCard`), the city's five and the market's nine alike: the head, an icon square in the colour of who builds it, *you have N* and what is on site with its wait and a link to the site; the tags; a hero that says what the building gives the city in its own verb and unit, with a detail line; *$X all in · sticker $Y*, always both; two bars scaled within its group — the first the price a unit of what it gives, or for the makers, farms, mines and vehicle plants how many months of value added at today's prices it takes to pay for itself, an office's months of its exports, and since 0.7.70 a road's its cost over its life a trip it takes off the road, and the second the land a unit on market cards and on a road's since 0.7.70, the posts it could not fill per 10,000 served on the city's, and of 100 posts how many the city could not staff on offices — with no track in a group of one; the investors' line, on market cards; the needs line — posts, *the city could staff N%*, the land and its share of what is free, *runs $X/mo*; the stepper with +10 and +100; the quote and its verdict; and the (i) with its stat cover. A tag goes only to the strictly best on a bar, and only in a group of two or more. Each group's note reads the sector's own figures — the doors, the shops' coverage, the counters, the kitchens, the rail's trade, each maker group's demand and nameplate. The quote warns of a missing deposit, *no iron deposit* and since 0.7.62 *no oil deposit*, a missing coast, *no sea owned to draw* (0.7.59), or a licence, *nobody licensed*, before the click.

**The investors' line** says *on site* when an investor's order is on the site, and otherwise the sector's word for the month, read since 0.7.30 into one of twelve kinds ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)), then in amber *this one:* and the first gate this building fails now, in the order the build path asks them — the deposit, the licence, the staffing test, the land — since 0.7.109 counting the sector's own zone, and naming what is zoned for others — a loss in the estimate — and since 0.7.122 the investors' own test, the interest on its whole cost (below); a click opens the owner's Investors page. The words are the month's, and since 0.7.102 the last of them crosses a save, so after a load the line is there before the clock moves; after a founding it says nothing was recorded until a month runs. **Build is a button that asks to be pressed** since 0.7.34 — Jerus: *"everywhere you have build, like the build button, it should be more intuitive aka like an actual button that is basically asking to be pressed, cause currently its a tiny text"*. It is the card's width under the stepper and says the order, *Build 3 · $37.5M*, the count and the quote's all-in total; outlined, *Build 3 on credit · $37.5M*, when the treasury is short, a press opening Build › Funding ([the city's borrowing](#13-the-citys-borrowing)); grey and saying why when it cannot go ahead — *No land free* or *Short 743 m² of land*, *No iron deposit* or *No oil deposit*, *No sea to draw*, *Nobody licensed to work in it* — with the way out under it and a press opening the page that explains; and at none *Build · choose how many*, where a press chooses one and prices it and never orders. A double-click is one press. It had been a small grey button beside +100, disabled at none. Since 0.7.41 a city card's figures are served, supply over demand, under one verdict ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). `BuildCardCheck` holds the cards in ten sections, without a screen: every building has a card and a unit; the hero and the bars are the model's; the tags; the notes; the investors' line and its gates, each caused by a fixture in the build path's order; the verdict; since 0.7.30 the word's kind; since 0.7.40 a run of orders priced as placing them in turn would be; since 0.7.41 served; and since 0.7.122, in an eleventh section, the interest gate (below). The cards have not been seen rendered.

### The card's interest gate

**Since 0.7.122 the card's last gate is the investors' own test** (batch C1; `BuildCard`'s INTEREST gate, `Game.interestTest()`). The gates had ended at the loss, whether the investors' estimate earns anything, while since 0.7.113 the investors ask every order to earn 1.25 times a month's interest on its whole cost, at the rate it would be judged at, whoever pays ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)); so a card could pass every gate the investors declined, and in `BuildCardCheck`'s town an Industrial Bakery earning \$97.6k a month against a bar of \$154.7k, and a Meat Works, showed no gate at all. Now the card asks the game's own question and gives its figures — *"earns \$97.6k a month, under 1.25× its interest on its whole cost (\$123.8k a month at 5.03%)"*, the rate the real one the test reads, what people expect prices to do taken off — on the card's *this one:*, on the Investors page's first gate and on the Sectors screen's every-gate report ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). A building that loses money *"would lose \$X a month, so not 1.25× …"*, behind the loss, which stays the first gate; and under a borrowing ban the gate is the investors' own words, *"borrowing ban, N more months - it would need credit"*. The question and its figures are one computation, the one the investors' brake answers from (`Game.carriesItsWholeCost()`), so the card cannot disagree with the order: `BuildCardCheck`'s eleventh section asks all 56 market buildings in its town and finds each gate the investors' own answer to an order of one, four of them earning over nothing and under their interest. A landlord's home is not asked it, a dash, because the investors ask a home the mortgage lender's test instead, which the card does not yet ask ([open questions](#25-open-questions)). It is advice: no month reads it, and the playtest's traces were 0.7.121's to the byte. 661 of its strings were measured to fit at 1,389 × 868.

### Childcare in three sizes

Jerus: *"one city had 5k daycares and 2k residential buildings, hilarious, the numbers children and housing wise make sense ... i think we need to resize those, daycares are childcares and childcares are even bigger"*. A Home Daycare, eight places for $147k, was the cheapest place to put up, so the advice ordered them by the hundred and Build's cards tagged it the cheapest a child; his live city held 629 of them beside 1,521 home buildings, and the test player, which builds no childcare, had never shown it. Since 0.7.71 the three childcare buildings are centres on the same ids (`buildings.json` and the built-in twins, which `BuildingDataCheck` holds equal), each figure on the model's own scale curve through its two old centres — price, upkeep, power, water, land, road load and posts — with ten points a place and 40% of the price material, so a place costs less to build, keep, stand on and staff the bigger the centre:

*The three centres (0.7.71); a place's price is its cash and material at founding prices*

| Building | Places | Was | Posts | Land | A place | Children an adult |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Small Childcare Centre (15) | 80 | Home Daycare, 8 | 20 | 2,917 m² | $27.4k | 4.0 |
| Childcare Centre (16) | 220 | Neighbourhood Daycare, 60 | 53 | 6,503 m² | $24.9k | 4.15 |
| Large Childcare Centre (17) | 360 | Childcare Centre, 220 | 84 | 9,606 m² | $23.7k | 4.29 |

The sizes are sourced: 80 is the most a Quebec childcare installation may take (*Educational Childcare Act*, CQLR c. S-4.1.1), about Ontario's largest groups one room each (O. Reg. 137/15, Schedule 1: 79); 220 is the model's own old centre, figure for figure; and 360 is China's guide for a kindergarten (Kindergarten Work Regulations, 2016, art. 11: generally not more than 360 children). Every centre's staffing lies between Ontario's three adults to ten children and one to eight. A save holds its buildings by id, and Jerus's word was *"keep them as they are"*, so a Home Daycare loaded as a Small Childcare Centre with its places, posts and ground, ten times what it had, in the builds that read such a save, to 0.7.119 ([open questions](#25-open-questions)); id 16 is called a Childcare Centre because it is that building now, so an old log line naming one still reads true, and nothing maps names back. The advice sizes the order to the need, the whole order over the places lacking ([the screen](#22-the-screen)), while a card's first bar, the quote for one with the yard's material free, still tags the Small centre the cheapest a child where the yard holds material. The map draws a centre as care, where it drew a Home Daycare as a home. The test player builds no childcare by default; its rule, the advice's card whenever NEEDS YOU lists childcare, is a flag (`-Dplaytest.childcare`), and with it on the playtest's city at month 4,000 held 2,951 Home Daycares and 183 Centres for 2,123 home buildings at the old sizes, and 12 Centres and 235 Large ones for 2,379 at the new. `ChildcareCheck` holds the three ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

> **Both halves of a price are sourced now**
>
> A unit of construction material was \$2,000 and is **\$18,000**, defined by the House: ten units against a real house's \$180,000 of structure. Every template's split was re-derived at a real material share — 40% for a building, 25% for a plant, 60% for a road — with every total held to the dollar. It also found that the builders' material import bill had never been paid: \$2.75bn crossed the border over 4,000 months and the expense struck at zero, so Construction ended every run holding the money and the balance of payments never saw a unit move. Range runs from an Oil Well or a Platform Well with one post — an Oil Well had three until 0.7.84, as a Mixed Farm and a Filling Station have, and a Home Daycare two until 0.7.71 — to a Rail Terminal with 1,482 jobs, the Regional Medical Centre's 996 the largest the city pays for, and the terminal's 5,500,000 square feet the largest footprint in the game, ahead of the Livestock Farm and a Municipal Cemetery's 2,000,000.

## 20. Utilities & roads

### Power and water

The grid starts with 10,000 kW free and the reservoir with 8,000 units of 10,000 gallons. Both are gated by the same utility workforce. Power is $10 a kilowatt a month and water $50 a unit — the model's .01 and .05, in thousands, as the Services books print them, and about $5 per thousand gallons. Since 0.7.28 power reads in kW, MW and GW (`Money.power()`) on Services and Build, and the console's utilities report in kW, where earlier editions and the report said watts.

**Only businesses are invoiced.** Houses, depots, roads, the water plant's own 900 kW and the city's own buildings all draw power nobody pays for, and since 0.7.28 that unbilled draw is split into the homes' (`UtilitiesHandler.getHomesElectricityDraw()`, `getHomesWaterDraw()`) and the city's own buildings'. Booking revenue on the whole city's draw was money from nowhere scaling with the housing stock — 73% of it, measured. The utility books exactly what its customers' statements charged them, not a recomputation at the end-of-month ratio. The plants are the city's own: what they sell less their wages goes into the city's cash each month, and a loss is paid as the city's services promise (`TreasuryLine.CITY_SERVICES`). **Since 0.7.41 both read served**, supply over demand, unclamped, under one verdict: green at 100% or more and off NEEDS YOU's list, which for the networks means past 133%, the inverse of the 75% the dashboard has always called tight; red at or under 100%; amber, *tight*, between ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). A city drawing 43% of its plant reads 233% served, enough, and one at 124% of capacity 80% served, short. **A works may make its own power** since 0.7.112, and since 0.7.123 three do, Iron & Steel's Coke Ovens, Blast Furnace and Oxygen Steel Shop, from their gas: a sector is billed only for its works' draw past what they make, and what they make past it is added to what the grid generates, unscaled by the utility's staffing since the works' own crews made it, the utility paying for it at the tariff out of its takings ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)).

### Roads

The city starts with 400 units of capacity — the streets that already exist. Traffic flows freely to 90% of capacity and degrades after that, floored at 35%. Three roads, and the land ladder was in the catalogue before anybody pointed at it: a gravel road is 500 square feet per unit of capacity, a paved road 208, an elevated highway 42 — twelve times the capacity per acre for two and a half times the money. Since 16 September the load is three streams and the network can be relieved by a highway, a tram or a train, but never deleted; that is [transport](#21-transport--vehicles), and this is the baseline it is measured against. Since 0.7.70 each is weighed over its life, and a gravel road can be paved (below).

```
throughput = 1                      if load ≤ 0.9 × cap          // FREE_FLOW .9
           = max(0.35, 0.9/util)   otherwise                  // MIN_THROUGHPUT .35
served     = cap / load the curve reads                  // since 0.7.41: flow is 1 from 111% served, and 0.9 × served under it
```

The road is written as one pair everywhere since 0.7.29, in whole per cents, and since 0.7.41 as served rather than full: *62% served · 56% flow* where it read *161% full · 56% flow*, the same fraction the other way up. Its red line is the curve's own, 111% served, where the flow starts to fall, so a road 100–111% served is red and *tight* where the networks go red at 100%. Since 0.7.29 the room before it slows and its spare capacity read the load the curve reads, where they read the raw trips: 585 trips of room on a road 161% full.

Congestion slowing the sites is the pointed part: a jammed city builds the roads that would unjam it more slowly, and the floor is what keeps that from being a trap.

### A road over its life, and a gravel road paved

Jerus: *"the game still recommends gravel roads, even when i think paved roads are better, also ... make it an option to upgrade from gravel to paved, but not from paved to highway, and that the build menu allows and recommends this if better, total cost is higher than just building paved"*. What had recommended gravel was not the advice, which has priced a road's ground since 0.7.51 and in his city picked paved roads, but Build's road cards, whose price a trip left the ground out, so that *cheapest per trip* went to gravel in every city — in his, 17.9 D$k a trip against paved's 31.5 and a highway's 45.6 — and the test player, which ranked the roads by their founding cash cost a trip and built nothing but gravel in the 0.7.69 run, 123 orders. Since 0.7.70 one figure decides all three: **a road's cost over its life, a trip it takes off the road** (`BuildAdvice.lifetime()`).

```
over its life      its quote + its ground at the land office's price + a month's running × the annuity
a month's running  repairs at its share a year of what it costs to build today (1% until 0.7.103; gravel 3%, paved 2%, a highway 1.25% since), the builders' tax in, + its power and water
                   at the utility's prices + a line's posts and upkeep − a month of fares from the riders it adds
the annuity        240 months, the funding page's 20-year bond (LIFE_MONTHS), at that term's real rate
a trip             over its life, over the trips it takes off the strained line, its freight grade in them
```

The advice ranks its six road candidates by it, the three roads and the three lines; a road card's first bar is it, *cost per trip over 20 years, with its land*, and its second the ground a trip, tagged *cheapest per trip over its life* and *least land per trip*; and the test player picks its road by it. **Over its life gravel gained, not lost**, while every road's repairs were the house's 1% a year of its price: the cheaper road was the cheaper to keep, and the life moved the line toward gravel. In the cities measured at 0.7.70 a paved road beats it where a gravel road's 450,000 sq ft of ground is worth about 1.4 to 1.7 times its quote, and a highway farther out. In Jerus's city at month 416 that line sits at 0.95 of what his land office charges, so paved already wins there, six Paved Roads at 56.7 D\$k a trip against gravel's 57.8; in city2400 it sits at 1.05 and gravel wins, 18.30 against 18.60; the playtest's city at month 4,000 would need its ground 1.89 times dearer, at month 1,000 5.55 times, city600 11 times and a new city 15. So gravel stayed a young city's road. In the playtest the road move ordered paved roads from its look at month 3,422, 8,074 D\$k a trip over their life against gravel's 8,627, and the city ended with 592 gravel roads and 77 paved, where at 0.7.69 it stood 661 gravel and none. **Since 0.7.103 each road has its own repairs** (Jerus's A11; `BuildingsTemplate`'s A ROAD'S OWN REPAIRS, `buildings.json`'s `"repairs"`): a Gravel Road 3% of its price a year, a Paved Road 2% and an Elevated Highway 1.25%, the Canadian Infrastructure Report Card 2016's target reinvestment rates — roads and sidewalks 2.0 to 3.0% of replacement value a year, bridges 1.0 to 1.5%, *"informative only"* — which Jerus checked, where every road had the house's 1%. They are charged by the month's maintenance and read by the advice's road over its life, which a trip on gravel now costs more to keep; every other building keeps its 1%. Jerus's city at month 8,473 pays \$22.0B a month for its roads' repairs where it paid \$9.8B. **And the test player orders roads by need** since the same version (Jerus: *"Fix the test player too"*; `LongPlaytest.roadsByNeed()`): the advice's own card for the road — its road, ranked by its order over its life for each trip it will take off, the city's gravel roads paved among them, and its count, the least that keeps the road ahead at its projection — where it had ordered a count set by the share of its output the road cost, of the road it chose, whatever the trips, and none when what is on site keeps the road ahead; its transit lines stay its own moves. At month 32 the old rule had ordered ten Gravel Roads, \$56.5M of its \$71M; the card asked \$2.7M. With the rule and the repairs together its city ended at 617,942 people at 0.7.103, where 0.7.102's had 544,232, with 230 gravel roads, 291 paved and 161 highways standing against 683, 56 and none, its roads' throughput 86 to 100% at every checkpoint past month 1,700 against 74 to 78%; but its young town is smaller, its roads at 70 to 73% from month 265 to 617, because the card is sized for the advice's horizon and the player looks every 6 to 120 months ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).

**A gravel road can be paved** since 0.7.70, one or many at a time, and a Paved Road is not raised to a highway, as Jerus asked (`ConstructionControl`, F; `Game.paveRoads()`). The price is a Paved Road's work and the take-up of the old surface at the demolition rule's 5% of the gravel road's work, and a Paved Road's material less the gravel road's 193 units, which go into its bed, and since 0.7.83 the 64.25 t of bitumen its surface binds, bought by the builders with the order ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)), the builders' tax in (`Game.quotePave()`), paid from the treasury's cash with no loan page. So a gravel road and its paving cost more than a Paved Road built outright — 17.6% more in Jerus's city and 22% in the playtest's with the yard empty — while paving one costs 75 to 79% of a new Paved Road where the material is bought; on a day the yard holds a gravel road's material and not a Paved Road's, the two quotes can sum lower, because a quote takes the yard's material free. The pavings queue on the Paved Road site as the city's order, standing on the gravel roads' ground: each gravel road carries its 900 units until its own Paved Road opens, first in first out, and then retires, its Paved Road carrying 1,200 and the 200,000 sq ft between their grounds coming back free. A paving site is not stopped while it paves ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)), and the hand is saved with the rest of the queue's, an older save having none. It is recommended only where it beats a new Paved Road over its life a trip, the ground it frees taken off at what the next road would pay for it (`BuildAdvice.pavingBeatsPaved()`): the Gravel Road card's PAVE TO A PAVED ROAD block tags it *paving beats a new Paved Road*, the Overview offers *Gravel Road, paved* as a card of its own and leaves it out of *Build all three*, and the test player paves where paving is the least of its roads. In the default playtest at 0.7.70 it never was: of 0.7.69's 140 road orders with gravel to pave, it would have beaten a new Paved Road at none; at 0.7.99 the playtest paved 87 gravel roads in 14 orders, and at 0.7.106, its player ordering roads by need, 10 in 2. `RoadCheck` holds the life, the crossovers, the cards, the price, and paving played, saved and refused ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### Fresh water has a limit, and the sea can be drunk

Since 0.7.59 the Water Treatment Plants together treat no more than the city's lakes and river yield: 121,600 units a month a km² of fresh water the city owns (`UtilitiesHandler.FRESH_UNITS_PER_KM2`), plus its water rights. The yield is the world's renewable river runoff, about 42,700 km³ a year (Shiklomanov), over the world's river and stream area, 773,000 km² (Allen & Pavelsky 2018): 4.6 million m³ a month a km², which is 121,600 units of 37.854 m³. So a water plant's 60,000 units need about half a km² of lake or river. The reservoir's 8,000 units are groundwater, the old wells', and stand outside the limit. Past it the rest of the fresh plants' nameplate idles and the water is rationed through the same ratio as any shortage, which throttles the businesses that draw it; under it, what the plants make is the old formula to the bit.

```
the limit    121,600 × owned fresh km² + the city's water rights
water made   (8,000 + desalination's nameplate) × fill + min(the fresh plants' nameplate × fill, the limit)
             // fill: the utility workforce's, as before; at no fill at all the wells still give their 8,000
```

The Services page says so in amber under the water bar — *"fresh water limit: 62% of the plants' nameplate idle · buy lake or river, or desalinate"* (`CityNeeds.freshLimitLine()`) — and holds its *at full staff* to the limit, and the build advice values a fresh plant at the water left under it, so a capped city is offered desalination. **The Desalination Plant** (id 73, `"source": "SEA"`) makes what a water plant makes, with the same crew and ground, at twice its cost, the low end of seawater reverse osmosis's two to five times a conventional plant; and it draws 10,880 kW, 3.5 kWh a cubic metre against the water plant's own 0.29, the biggest single new draw on the grid, 1.34 wind farms of it. The limit does not reach it, and it needs the sea: an order with no owned sea is refused, *No sea to draw* (`BuildResult.NO_COAST`), and the refusal's page buys the cheapest offer with sea ([land](#18-land)). **Rights** keep the old cities whole: a save from before the limit is given what its standing fresh plants already pump less what its lakes yield, so that loading idles nothing; a new city has none. A new default city owned 0.0189 km² of lake from 0.7.67, its whole blocks taking in a little more of it than the old centre's 0.011, a limit of 2,298 units, so its first water plant, 60,000 at nameplate, would idle 96% until it bought lake or river; since 0.7.106 it is founded with its lake, 0.4941 km² of lake and river, 60,083 units, and its first plant idles nothing ([land](#18-land)); at 0.7.59 the playtest's city had 1.1 km² of it by its first shortage, bought with its ground, and at 0.7.64 it was never offered a move past the limit, ending with 16.68 km² of lake and river, two water plants and none for the sea; nor at 0.7.68, ending with 69.16 km² of lake and river and 197.01 of sea, two water plants and nine desalination plants. The playtest's player orders a water plant only while the water left under the limit covers it, and then desalination on owned sea, the offer with the most lake or river a dollar (`LandMarket.bestFresh()`), or the cheapest with sea.

### Construction output

```
round(working capacity × construction fill rate × road ratio × health work ratio)
working capacity = the city's own 400 points + the depots' capacity × the share of their posts offered   // since 0.7.17
```

One definition, used by the screen, by the sites, and by what the sector is paid for. The three had to be the same number: a copy that drifts books revenue for work nobody did, and very nearly did when roads arrived. What reaches the *sites* is what is left once the standing stock has had its repairs — about 40% of the total, permanently — and since 0.7.17 it is shared among them by the crew each building can use ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)). The depots count at the share of their posts the builders kept on that month, and the city's own works department, which has no posts, counts whole; whoever is weighing an order reads the same figure with every post offered (`getConstructionOutputAtEveryPost()`), because an order is work and work hires the crews back. Since 0.7.22 a rushed site's crews work longer hours on top of it, more points in their first two months and fewer from the third, and the builders count them beside the output.

## 21. Transport & vehicles

*Until 16 September the entire transport model was one scalar: a road network with a capacity and a load, one throughput ratio between 0.35 and 1, and three road types that were the same road at three prices. Jerus:* "decomposing the existing import/export bands into world price + transportation cost… then later, transportation efficiency can make that freight component smaller or larger." *Nine batches followed in three days under the same version number, each one there to make the next possible: the band decomposes, the load splits, the modes and the fare, the railway, the vehicles, and the screen that finally shows a player any of it.*

### The band was a freight bill

Every traded good carried two constants and the gap between them was the whole local market — and nothing in the game said why the gap was the width it was. Each good carries a third number now, the cost of moving one unit, and the two ends split into four:

```
worldImportPrice = worldBuyPrice  + baseFreight     // the world's own ask, plus getting it here
worldExportPrice = worldSellPrice − baseFreight     // the world's own bid, less getting it there
```

Three quarters of the wedge is freight and one quarter the world's margin, and the split is a game decision rather than a measurement: it sets how much of the band good logistics can ever win back. At three quarters a 23% band bottoms out near 6%. **The price table was already a freight model and nobody designed it that way**: freight as a share of the world price sits at 21–25% for fifteen of the seventeen goods that had both ends, and the two outside that band are iron at 49% and materials at 43% — the two lowest-value-density things in the game, where real freight genuinely is half the delivered cost. The delivered prices are the stored literals and the world band is derived, which is the opposite of how it reads and the only way round that is exact: storing the world band and adding the freight back gives 0.8470000000000002 for steel and 0.27999999999999997 for crops, and an ulp in this codebase is never nothing. Not one price moved on the day it shipped, and eight seeds over 333 years came back byte-identical; `TradeCostCheck` asserts every delivered price against a table of what it was that morning, because a test that reads its own subject proves nothing.

### One road load is three

`Traffic { COMMUTERS, GOODS, BULK }`, and which mode can carry what falls out of the classes rather than needing a table of exceptions: commuters can ride a tram and nothing else can; goods — a shop's bread and milk — are a van at a back door however many rails a city lays, and take the train only across the boundary; bulk — ore, steel, crops, grain, aggregate, beams, machines, a locomotive on a low-loader — is what a railway is for. The shares were fitted rather than guessed, by least squares against the catalogue itself:

```
roadLoad = 0.726 × jobs + 0.878 × homes + 0.0386 × tonnes a month        // R² = 0.74 over the 56 templates that loaded a road when the fit was struck; eighty-two do today
```

The implied rate is one worker per nineteen tonnes a month — a truckload — and nobody set out to encode that. The residuals are all explainable and all one way: an Iron Mine 280 over the fit (heavy vehicles), a Penitentiary 288 under and a Long-Term Care Complex 136 under (their occupants do not commute), a University 258 over (students travel and the fit counts only wages). None of it matters, because the fit supplies the *share* and the stored road load supplies the *magnitude*: a mine keeps its road load and learns what share of it is ore — 68% of its 420 when it lifted 2,500 t a month, and since 0.7.120, at 20,000 t, 94% of 3,360, the old load a tonne carried over.

*Commuters / goods / bulk, as the fit reads the catalogue*

| Building | Road load | Split |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Steel Mini-Mill | 500 | 17% / 0% / 83% |
| Grain Farm | 18 | 14% / 0% / 86% |
| Iron Mine | 3,360 | 6% / 0% / 94% |
| Bakery | 40 | 53% / 16% / 31% |
| Small Grocery | 55 | 87% / 12% / 1% |
| University | 520 | 100% / 0% / 0% |
| A played city | — | 86% / 3% / 11% |

A real city is 86% people, which is what urban traffic actually is. And the ensemble found a defect whose fix is the better design: the first version summed the three streams to get the network's total, and eight seeds came back subtly different from the build before them — a thousand dollars in three trillion, one person in forty-eight thousand — because every building's three loads add to its own road load to the bit, and what does not survive is adding them up in a different *order*. So the total keeps the exact sweep it always had and the breakdown is read alongside it. The demand did not change; only the ability to see what it is made of.

### The modes, and a fare that is a price

*The land ladder, per unit of capacity — a journey a month for the transit lines*

| Mode | Capacity | Land | Sq ft a unit | Cash a unit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Gravel Road | 900 | 450,000 | 500 | $2,584 |
| Paved Road | 1,200 | 250,000 | 208 | $4,500 |
| Elevated Highway | 1,500 | 63,000 | 42 | $6,400 |
| Bus Network | 2,500 | 20,000 | 8 | $4,800 |
| Light Rail Line | 8,000 | 45,000 | 6 | $8,000 |
| Metro Line | 30,000 | 30,000 | 1 | $10,667 |

A metro is five hundred times a gravel road's capacity per acre for four times the price a journey. A city that has run out of ground and not out of money builds one; a city with ground to spare never should — which is the first real answer this game has had to its own late-game wall. **Every mode is a relief on an unchanged baseline**, and that is the design rather than an implementation detail: a city with no highway and no transit computes exactly the load it computed yesterday and degrades on exactly the curve it degraded on. A highway relieves freight, not by carrying more but because a tonne of ore on a grade-separated road does not share a junction with a school run — bulk by 40%, goods by 15%, commuters not at all. Transit takes people off the road entirely, and three things stop it being the answer to everything: a city's lines reach 65% of each group of commuters, the car-less and the car owners alike since 0.7.49 (`TRANSIT_MAX_SHARE`), so no more than that ever ride, whatever is built; what transit can carry is capped at twice the road capacity under it, because buses are road vehicles and a metro station needs a street outside it — *a city that builds a metro and no streets gets a metro nobody can reach*; and it never touches freight. Measured on a load of 10,000 in the played mix: 5,590 riders with room to spare, 4,800 with fewer streets, 800 with none, and with the best of everything **the road still carries 39%** of what it would. The road can be halved and it can never be deleted. It is also why the stream split matters to a business: an office and a mill on the same jammed road read 74% and 47% against the road's own 42%, because the mill beats the road by exactly as much of its own traffic as rides the tram, and a lorry in a jam is in a jam. A sector with nothing standing reads the city's own blend rather than a clean road, because the planner costs a first plant at the sector's operating rate and a congested city was cheerfully building plants a 38% road said it could not afford.

**A fare was a price, not a charge**, from 16 September to 0.7.48. Nobody chooses to be policed and a patient in a clinic is not shopping; the person on a bus chose to be, and can choose a car instead. So the ridership ceiling was what a *free* system would carry and the fare walked it down on a straight line to nobody at the maximum: free, 5,590 riders; at the default, 5,311; at the ceiling, none. And the two lines moved against each other, which was the whole decision — six times the fare took $58,695 a month instead of $13,276 and put 1,398 more cars on the road. Jerus asked for a dial that can be made profitable *"by alot"*; it can, at a ridership the city may not want. The fare is money, so a reform moves it — the twenty-third of that family and the first caught in the same edit that created the field — and since 0.7.47 the curve reads the dial in founding money through the currency's unit, so a reform moves nobody's mind about the bus; until then it did, by about 5% of the riders in the 2,400-month city divided by a thousand, and its cap is the founding cap in the new unit (`TaxPolicy.maxTransitFare()`). Since 0.7.42 the fare is real: the dial is set in founding money and charged at the price level the city expects (`TaxPolicy.chargedFare()`), so it keeps its worth, and the screens show it in today's money. Two things were found on the way: nothing in the infrastructure category had ever had a job, so nobody had written a line to pay one, and a Metro Line is 828 posts; and the fare was charged once a month against a constant that says *a single journey*, so a monthly pass cost $2.50 against a $3,460 wage, seven hundredths of one percent, and the buses could not have paid for themselves at any fare a player would set. That was the transit loss the list had carried as a balance problem. It is 40 journeys a month now — out and back, twenty days — a pass is $100 or 2.9% of an unskilled wage, and the dial stays per ride because that is the number a person on a platform recognises.

**Since 0.7.49 it is a price to car owners and a charge to everyone else.** Jerus: *"households shouldnt check the transit price alone to determine if they use it, they should determine the cost of their own transportation ... if one household category has 3k workers and 2k cars, then well, 1k has to take transit cause they have no choice ... but if they already have car they look at oil costs"*. So the commuters are split by whether they have a car of their own, counted per worker in the working cells (`HouseholdBalance.captiveShare()`): a household holds one car at most, so a couple's second earner and four of five flatmates have none. **The car-less** ride whatever the fare, if a line reaches them and there is a seat: 65% of them are in reach, the seats go to them first, and the rest walk, at no money cost but on the street at today's car factor, so the jam is what it costs them. A dearer fare takes more of their money and does not empty the buses. **The owners** weigh a ride, the dial at the expected level, against a journey's fuel, \$2.00 in the world's money at today's rate (`Motoring.CAR_FUEL_PER_JOURNEY`) — since 0.7.62 its 1.2 litres at the price fuel lands at, petrol since 0.7.76, the refiners' while they have it on offer, at wholesale since 0.7.78 and since 0.7.83 at the pump's price on it (`Motoring.journeyFuel()`) — and a cell splits rather than flips: all of it on the bus at half the drive's cost, all of it in the car at twice it, the straight line between (`InfrastructureManager.transitChosen()`), because a cell is thousands of households with commutes of every length. The jam still puts more of them on the bus, walked down by the old fare curve, so an owner who chose the car rides exactly as before; 65% of the owners are in reach too, and they take the seats the car-less left. The ceiling did not move — the car-less and the owners in reach are never more than 65% of the commuters, and the stock and the road under it cap both — and the road reads what is not on a bus at the car factor, as it did. Because the dial is anchored and the fuel is today's, a weak currency puts owners on the bus. At wholesale, from 0.7.78, a drive's fuel came to under a third of the default fare, so no owner took the bus on cost alone where as many as 46% had, and at the pump since 0.7.83, 1.32 times wholesale at the default sales tax, still none does at par, and since 0.7.103 the fuel duty rides on the sign, so a duty moves owners toward the bus ([tax](#12-tax-policy--gdp)); the owners who ride are the jam's ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). In the 2,400-month city 73% of workers have no car of their own; the old rule, which read cars per household, had left 21,000 seats empty there while the streets jammed, and at 0.7.49 56,775 ride: 48,716 car-less, every one in reach, and 8,059 owners who chose the bus, while 26,232 car-less walk and 19,498 drive. Raising the fare loses owners and keeps the car-less, so revenue rises almost in line with it: at \$50 a ride, the dial's cap, the riders bottom out at the car-less, 48,716, and the fares at D\$97.6M a month, a pass 27.6% of an unskilled household's take-home. It is a tax on people who cannot leave, and the fare card says who is paying it. The fares fall on the households' riding rows since 0.7.49, and the fuel, a fourth fee, on their driving rows; the retired, the out of work and the students pay neither ([people](#2-people)).

> **The fare was collected from nobody**
>
> From the day transit was built until 16 September the city credited itself the fare and debited no household. Nobody saw it because **nothing had ever built a bus**: the playtest's advisor answered every jam with tarmac, so four thousand months a seed, eight seeds a run, not one city ever carried a passenger, and every fixture that needed a road bought a road. The first ensemble in which the advisor bought a Bus Network failed the money audit on all eight seeds, and the residual was the fare to six decimals — 2,186 riders at $2.50 is $5.47, and the audit said 5.465207. *A harness cannot check a thing nobody does.* `MoneyCheck`'s own header says every money bug this codebase has had was a flow with one side, and the twenty-ninth harness could not see this one because its city had no buses. It builds three now. Fixing it found its sibling at once: `setTransit` was missing from the load path, the fifth sighting of that shape, invisible until the fare became real money.

> **The bill was paid by nobody**
>
> Transit's wages and upkeep were struck every month and paid by nobody. The crews drew their pay and the lines their upkeep, the fares came in, and no line of the treasury, the budget or the audit carried the bill — D\$23.96M a month in the 2,400-month city against D\$4.12M of fares, measured at 0.7.47. The Government screen's bridge had found it in 0.7.31 as a bill on no budget line that, as far as the bridge and the audit could show, nobody paid, and it went on the list. **Since 0.7.49 the treasury pays it** as a promise, after the police (`TreasuryLine.TRANSIT`), and the budget, EARNED, the audit and G carry it, the fares a budget line beside it ([tax, policy and GDP](#12-tax-policy--gdp)); the bill is carried across a save. Paying it taught the playtest's player to count it: its advisor had 25 bus networks at month 1,000 in a city of 15,740, a post for every ten seats, and at the design study's checkpoints their bill, unpaid, came to as much as 54% of a month's output. Since 0.7.49 it buys a line only while the output the road gives back with it standing and the fares of the riders it adds pay its crews (`LongPlaytest.linesThatPay()`) — the police station's rule, with the fares counted — and with that rule the playtest's treasury never fell below its own earlier low.

### The railway

Rail is the twelfth sector, and the business that wants to be paid the freight every price in this game has always had inside it. Jerus: *"the freight cant reach zero cause freight needs profit, its its own sector… it wants and will do everything possible to stay profitable and maximize profits. freight money goes to that sector."* There were two ways to write that and only one keeps the audit honest. Paying the railway out of the band would have a payment the books record as going abroad in fact going to a company in the city. So **the band carries only what the lorries still move, and the railway bills the shipper at home**, like any other supplier of a service — the invoice goes on the shipper's input line, where freight belongs in anybody's accounts, the money never leaves the city, and the VAT falls out for free because the ledger already credits a purchase at the supplier's own rate.

```
what a shipper pays a unit  = (1 − share) × baseFreight     // still to the lorries, inside the band
                            + share × quote × baseFreight  // to the railway, on its invoice
allowed  = what a month costs to run + 1.2% of the track it has sunk
quote    = clamp(allowed / what it would bill at the lorry rate × scarcity, 0.30, 1)
```

**A shop's pricing rule cannot price a utility**, and the measurement is what said so. Written first as Retail's shelf — cost plus a quarter — it quoted 32% of the lorry rate, earned $4.5m a month on ten billion of track, and was written down six times: a railway's running cost is a fraction of its capital, so a mark-up on running costs allows a return of nothing on the track. It prices like a regulated network now, running costs plus 1.2% a month on the rate base, floored at 30% of the lorry rate because rail is cheaper than a lorry and not free, capped at one because nobody ships by rail at more than the lorry charges, lifted up to 1.6× by what it cannot carry. It settles at 38–43%. Building too much rail does not make freight cheaper; it makes a railway that cannot pay for itself, and `RailCheck` asserts that a network with four times the track it needs pins at the lorries' price and earns less on four times the capital. The link that falls out of it is real and welcome: **a railway earning 1.2% a month on money that costs it 1% is barely a business, so dear money is what keeps a city's trade band wide**. And the band alone was lying to the sectors: at a 92% quote on 92% of the traffic it said steel's wedge had fallen from 52% to 11% when the shipper had saved eight per cent, because the railway's invoice was not in it. Every place that asks *is this worth exporting* reads a net price now; every place that settles a trade reads the band; with no railway the two are the same number to the bit.

**Track is half a railway.** Capacity is the lesser of the track laid and the wagon sets to run it, at 2,500 tonnes a set and a twenty-year life, so track with no locomotives carries nothing: a Rail Spur is twenty sets, $48m of rolling stock on a $140m spur, and a mature city's million tonnes of track is 420 sets and about 1¾ sets a month of replacement for ever, which is half a Locomotive Works running. Rolling stock is a *pantry* rather than an input — that one line is what makes a bought set accumulate into a fleet instead of vanishing into a month's production — and a save from before trains has trains, because it was hauling, so it had locomotives. The railway will not lay a line under 60% used, Materials' lesson relearned the afternoon a spur went up in a town of four hundred houses and a bank failed over it. It relieves 75% of the bulk it carries off the road, never all of it, because the last mile off a siding is a lorry and a spur reads as 94% trucks; bulk goes before goods, which decides almost nothing today because bulk is 99.7% of the tonnage crossing the boundary. Every tonne it hauls burns $30 of fuel in the world's money, a real import before there was any oil good, so that the day oil became a good nothing else had to change; and since 0.7.62 the railway draws `FUEL` as a buyer, and since 0.7.76 `DIESEL`, eighteen litres a tonne (`Rail.FUEL_LITRES_PER_TONNE`, the $30 over fuel's import price, a literal since 0.7.78, when diesel's price fell to wholesale and the railway's bill with it, by 59%), off the refiners' tanks first, keeping among its extras what came from abroad, where it had booked an imported service with no good (`Sector.bookImportedService()`, gone). Since 0.7.29 the lorry bill is told three ways — billed at home, paid abroad and kept — and what the railway was allowed to bill and what went abroad are kept across a save among its extras, with no format change; a save from before reads them as not known until a month runs, bar a railway that billed nothing at home, which sent the whole bill abroad. Since 0.7.46 the month's trade in units is saved too, so a reloaded railway bills its first month as the city that never reloaded does, where it had billed almost nothing and its quote had jumped ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)).

> **What a railway is worth**
>
> Eight seeds, four thousand months each: population **113,178 → 178,975 (+58%)**, GDP **$416.8M → $711.2M a month (+71%)**, per seed 32–91% and 14–113%. On the default seed steel's net wedge goes from 51.6% of the world price to 25.9%. And it is a healthy business in all eight: zero write-downs, zero loss months, the best credit rate in the game, and in seven of eight no debt at all.
