PICK WHAT TO DRAW has an icon a group and every series the history keeps, 217 lines where it offered 148: GDP's four parts, M0, M2, the reserves, the advances and the remittance, the bank's provisions, dividends, allowance, capital ratio, target and return on equity, each band's dead a month, a SECTORS group with each sector's net income and workers, and each company's fair value beside its shares; since 0.7.35 a Parity line beside the exchange rate (`fxParity`, empty in an older history), since 0.7.45 23 more with the basket's links drawn as dashed marks, and since 0.7.46 the bank's leverage ratio and its target, graduates as gains and Health's outbreak. PRICES THIS MONTH counts the goods by how each is priced — with the world, at what it charges, between, at what it pays, open on one side, set by a seller — over every good on its band behind *details*, a seller-priced good naming its seller as a door to Sectors. The episode lane's colours read `YearBook.isSevere()`, which RUNNING NOW's order reads too, and since 0.7.46 an epidemic is named only while an outbreak runs, so the 2,213-month epidemic of the 2,400-month city is gone. The founding month's decisions, older than the history's first month, stand on that month with each decision's own month on its card (`ChartModel.onAxis()`).

**The other charts are City History's own** since the redraws: Finances' OWED AND THE RATE, the public debt and the borrowing rate on two axes with the borrowing decisions as flags (0.7.32), and Money's M2 with M0 and the advances; the Bank's ITS RATES and its six small charts (0.7.33), which show the last ten years and do not pan, *Over the years* opening City History; Trade's currency beside parity, with the currency's crises and the city's currency decisions as flags and no full-screen button (0.7.35, `TimeChart.withoutFullScreen()`); and the fund's worth on Portfolio and a security's price, with the fund's decisions as flags (0.7.39), the fund's three series kept but not on the picker. Since 0.7.38 a small chart draws the decisions it is handed on a smaller lane under its years, a hover giving the flag's card, and the founding month's decisions stand on the first month of every lane.

### The decision log

The plan Jerus agreed asked for the player's own decisions on the timeline — *"taxes to 17%"*, *"central bank cut to 0%"*, *"bank rescued"* — and nothing in the game kept them: a tax rate is saved as what it is, not as when it moved, so the month a player cut it could be guessed from a step in a line and the reason for the step could not be. A decision is a flow, and a flow cannot be reconstructed from the state a month ended in, so since 0.7.23 it is recorded as it happens and saved (`DecisionLog`): a month, a kind and a line — *Taxes to 17%*, *Central bank rate to 0.00%*, *Bank rescued for its shares*, *Rushed University*. It is written in the one place each policy is applied, never in the interface, so a decision made from any screen or by a harness is recorded the same way, and a value set to what it already was writes nothing. What is logged: every tax and the farmland relief; every promise — the wage floor, the pension's two dials, EI's two, tuition, the grant and the student loan's rate, both health dials, the fare, a standing subsidy and since 0.7.43 food assistance; the central bank's dials and the hand taking or handing back the rate; the bank — a rescue, marked *(automatic)* when the treasury's setting made it, the preferred offer and the rescue setting; the fund's dial, since 0.7.48 its withdrawal, what is paid into it or drawn from it, and each order of its hand, since 0.7.39 written as the order it is, *Order: buy D\$4.0M of Construction shares at D\$111,490*, and a cancel as *Cancelled: …*, where it had read *Fund to buy …* of an order that might buy nothing — its fills and lapses are the fund's Activity, not decisions; an issue or a buyback of the city's paper, the rollover's setting and a default chosen abroad; a currency reform, reserves bought or sold and how land is paid for; and every hand on the construction queue; and since 0.7.107 a zone set, resized, repriced or taken off and the forest law, a kind of their own since 0.7.109, where 0.7.107 logged them as tax, a zone's tax rows staying tax. A proposal of several dials applied together is one flag with its count. What is not: ordinary build orders and land purchases, which a city places every month and which would smear the lane — a big one the treasury cannot pay for shows as the borrowing that paid for it; the rule moving the rate each month; the rollover's own issues, a foreign default the treasury could not avoid and the reserves a dollar issue buys as part of itself; and anything while a city is founded or loaded. Flags are coloured by their area — money blue, promises teal, the queue pink, and since 0.7.109 zoning the ground's sand. A label is fixed text in the money of the day, and a later reform does not rewrite it; the log has no cap and is saved whole under one key. It was shown nowhere but the chart until the redraws; since, it is on City History's lane and in its lists, on the smaller lanes of the Bank's rates, Finances' OWED AND THE RATE and Trade's currency chart, each with its own kinds, and in Policy's RECENT DECISIONS.

### The interface is a package

Until 18 September every screen was one class: `UserInterface.java`, 25,098 lines, 492 methods, a hundred banner sections, and a session working on the bank had to carry the policy tab's text in the same window. It was nineteen files in `ui/` then and is twenty-eight now, with `Ladder` (0.7.6), `FoundingScreen` (0.7.10), `ConstructionScreen` (0.7.22), `TimeChart` (0.7.23), `InfrastructureScreen` (0.7.28), `FundScreen` (0.7.39), `MapView` (0.7.61, [land](#18-land)), `StatementView` (0.7.74) and `ZoningScreen` (0.7.109), and the model never imports it. `UserInterface` is the window — the stage and its theme, the header with the clock, the money block, the five tiles, the *Needs you* chip, the rating and the inbox, the rail, the City overview's drawer and the construction panel's tab, the main menu and its backdrop, the panels and the dialogs, the time-skip dialog, the scroller every screen draws into — at about 6,100 lines, where it was about 4,000 at the split; its debt bar went in 0.7.24. Every tab is a class of its own, `BankScreen`, `PolicyScreen`, `PeopleScreen` and so on, its banners moved verbatim with a scripted `ui.` prefix wherever it reaches the window, the Infrastructure tab drawn by `ServicesScreen` until 0.7.28, and the City overview's content — the summary, the dashboard, the problem list — is `SummaryScreen`, though since 0.7.24 the problem list is measured in the model (`CityNeeds`). What every screen shares is four toolkit classes of stateless helpers, `Money`, `Statement`, `Pieces` and `Levers`, reached through an `import static` so that not one of their call sites changed, with `Palette`, `Icons`, `Ladder` and `TimeChart` beside them; the redraws put their shared parts in `Pieces`, the dial card in `Levers` (0.7.36), and the marks, the tracking and the idle words in `Ladder`. Twelve model members and two imports were the whole cost of the boundary. The move was mechanical — a dry run prints the couplings and the compiler catches what the script missed — and the one thing the compiler cannot check is the standing rule of this interface: **the month arrives on a clock, so every panel is rebuilt under the player and must restore its own scroll position**. Opening every tab on the split found three small things: the fare dial carried the player to the Policy tab the moment it was let go, because the staged-lever slider redrew the policy screen by name; the Build tab scrolled twice as fast as every other, because it is the one screen whose content sits straight in the page and a wheel floor meant for a notch was raised on every delta of a burst; and the Reports tab, City History now, moved under the pointer when a line was ticked, because the legend grows a block per line, so that one page keeps its position as pixels from the bottom.

### The statement opens

Jerus: *"can you make it so in the UI when you click on revenue or cogs, it expands and shows the individual items."* One figure that is really ten is a figure a player can read and cannot act on. Four lines on every sector's income statement open now — **Revenue** by good, split city and abroad; the **cost of sales** by good, split city and imported; **Wages** by pay tier, with posts; and **Sales tax remitted**, charged, at the border and credited — and underneath them is a `Sector.Split` per good, booked from the trade rather than reconstructed from units times price, because a local sale and an export clear at different prices in the same month. The first thing it showed was that the city's own bakeries were shipping 62% of what they baked at the world's floor while the shops bought imported meat, fruit and fish by the half-million. A disclosure that discloses nothing is worse than none: a line with one good and nothing shipped does not open, because the caret would promise a breakdown and then repeat the figure above it — and the rule about how many rows there are has to count the rows, since Construction sells no goods at all and fell straight through a rule about goods to draw a caret onto one row that repeated its total. That *other revenue* turned out to be two businesses under one label, work recognised off the order book and this month's repairs billed to every standing building, and a city whose building work has stopped and whose repair income is still growing is a city that has finished growing. Since 0.7.19 the material escalation the owners paid is a third part of it, and since 0.7.22 the overtime on rushed sites a fourth. The parts are frozen into the statement when it is struck, like the per-good money, because a screen reading a working field late describes a month the statement above it is not about.

The same disclosure reached two more statements on 19 September. The Government tab's bridge from the budget to the treasury's cash opened its last row into the treasury's journal, and since 0.7.31 every journal line is a step of the bridge, with what the journal cannot explain printed under it as *Not accounted for* ([tax, policy and GDP](#12-tax-policy--gdp)); and the bank's trading desk, whose opened lines had never added up to its total because the re-mark was left out, foots ([the owners and the exchange](#10-the-owners-the-bonds--the-exchange)). A row with nothing to disclose stays a plain row. Because the panel is rebuilt every month under the player, a line drawn closed every time snapped shut each month while the player was reading it; since 0.7.9 a screen can keep a set of the lines it has open (`Statement.opens()`), and the Bank tab was the first that did. Since 0.7.30 the Sectors screen keeps each business's opened lines, its waterfall's Revenue, Bought in, Wages and Sales tax bars opening their lines, and since 0.7.31 the Government tab keeps its opened lines, folds and bridge columns through a month.

### A summary and a statement

Jerus: *"both a summarized and a detailed actual statement ... the income statement, balance sheet, cash and debt, and investor ... a banks income statement is different, cause interest income"*. Since 0.7.74 a business's Income, Balance sheet, Cash & debt and Investors pages, and the Bank's Profit and Balance sheet ([the bank](#14-the-bank)), carry one switch at the right of the page strip, *Summary | Statement*, one choice for every business and the bank, kept for the session and not saved; Operations has none. **The Summary** is the pictures, their subtotals the statement's, with IN SHORT, this month against last, and the ratios: Income's waterfall, each bar opening its note in the Statement, and OF EVERY DOLLAR IT TOOK, a bar of cents; the Balance sheet's two bars, its equity's month as a bridge and its ratios — current, quick, debt to equity and to assets, the owners' share, return on equity, book a share; Cash & debt's bridge in three steps, free cash flow, what it paid its owners, its cash in days, CAN IT CARRY WHAT IT OWES and WHEN IT FALLS DUE; and Investors' FOR ITS SHAREHOLDERS, with the owners card since 0.7.75 and a door to it on the Balance sheet. **The Statement** is the formal statements (`SectorStatements`, drawn by `ui/StatementView`): a title block; columns for the note, this month, last month, the change and a common-size share, the last two of which the toolbar turns off; negatives in parentheses, a rule over a subtotal and two under a bottom line; in $ thousands, the model's own unit, until a figure passes seven digits and then in $ millions (`THOUSANDS_UNTIL`), so the landlords' $1.2B a month does not run to ten; and a note number opening its line in place, or every note at once. The statement of profit or loss runs from revenue, the sales tax under it and revenue after it, through the cost of sales to GROSS PROFIT, the operating costs, property tax among them, to OPERATING PROFIT, the finance costs by instrument, PROFIT BEFORE TAX and the business tax, to PROFIT FOR THE MONTH, every bottom line the model's own to the cent; then, outside the trading result, the flows that move a business's equity and reach no statement — the city's subsidy and arrears, the interest on its bank balance and the coupons it is paid, the interest abroad rolled into its holdings, an overdraft forgiven, loans written off and the theft, and since 0.7.75 the bonds its holders wrote off and what its borrowing cost it up front, twelve lines — and the TOTAL RESULT. The sheet is classified, current and long-lived, its debt by kind and by when it falls due; the cash flow is in three sections, operating, investing and financing, *Not accounted for* shown only from a dollar, and never in a city measured; and the statement of changes in equity names what moved it. **Six formats** change the words and the middle line (`Sector.statementFormat()`): the makers, the default; the merchants — Retail, Luxury Retail and the kitchens — with *Sales*, *Cost of goods sold* and GROSS MARGIN; the landlords with *Rents and charges*, no gross line and NET OPERATING INCOME; the builders' *Contract revenue* and GROSS PROFIT ON CONTRACTS; the carriers and services, the railway and the offices; and the bank's own, interest income to NET INTEREST INCOME. Each reads the ratios its kind has: stock turns, rent over the mortgage's payments, months of work booked, revenue a worker.

**Since 0.7.75 the statements say what the first batch could not read.** The sheet's equity is *Share capital, paid in*, the register's paid-in ([the owners](#10-the-owners-the-bonds--the-exchange)), its parts as note 10, and *Retained earnings and revaluation*; the statement of changes in equity is in three columns, share capital, what it kept and revalued, and the total, share capital closing on its own lines, and a save from before says *derived* where it was derived. What the prices did to the stock, the land and the buildings it began the month with, and what it holds abroad revalued, are named before *and the rest*. Cash & debt's statement has ITS DEBT THIS MONTH, BY KIND: bank loans, bonds, mortgages and interim loans, each from last month's sheet to this month's — borrowed, repaid, written off — with its rate and the month the last of it falls due, the suppliers as a memo, counted where each moves (`BusinessDebtManager`), and, until the sheet was read at the close (below), what was lent after the sheet was read named under it, because the sheet read the debt before the month's building loans. And the investor report has **every building at every gate** (`BuildCard.appraise()`): ore, licence, staff, land, whether it pays and, since 0.7.122, whether it carries the interest on its whole cost, a sixth column, *interest* ([the card's interest gate](#19-the-catalogue)), each ticked, crossed with why on hover, or a dash where the gate is not that building's, with what one would earn a month, cost to build and take to pay back, how it would be paid for — its owners, its till and borrowing, as the investors' own rule splits it (`Game.financingOf()`) — and a *So:* line, because the first gate alone hid a second: in the two cities `SectorStatementCheck` plays, 57 of 78 buildings fail at some gate, and with the ground taken 44 stop first at land, two of which would lose money with the land as well. Since 0.7.122 a building that passes them all *passes every gate*, where it read *passes all five*, and one that fails the interest alone says *at today's rates it would not build however the other gates stood*; the grid is 1,098 pixels wide with its sixth column. Nothing in the model reads any of it, and the playtest's traces were byte-identical at both versions. What a statement needs from a month only memory has — the interest by instrument, the debt by kind and how it moved, the stock's revaluation — is not counted the month after a load, and the debt's movements for two, and the page says so. The statements have been drawn here only through a mirror in Java2D; none has been seen in the game's window.

**Since 0.7.102 the sheet is read at the month's close** (Jerus's A16; the statements' F-S1-2): the books' sheet is pushed again as the month is recorded, so a business's debt, land and buildings are as they stand when its cash is read, the debt's schedule runs close to close and nothing is lent after the sheet — none of 8,194 schedules in `SectorStatementCheck`'s cities, where city600 had shown 47 of 408 sector-months apart by more than $1k. And what borrowing costs up front is expensed over each debt's life ([the bank](#14-the-bank)): the statement of profit or loss carries *Borrowing costs, over each debt's life* before the tax, the sheet *...still to expense* among its assets and the cash flow *...paid when it borrowed*, and the three leave the lines outside the trading result, which hold nine on a month they are deferred; the Sectors waterfall and the dollar bar show them. The register and the exchange read the same equity, so a listing's book and a buyback's assets moved with the close, which moved the playtest's traces from month 10.

### The refinery as a picture, and the oil on one page

**Since 0.7.95 Refining's Operations page opens on its refinery**, OPERATIONS · THE REFINERY (`RefineryView`, a new model class, pure; the research's mockup, Jerus's idea): the month's crude in on the left, from the city's land and platform wells, its reserve, the world or a Tank Farm's store, credited by what each was bought that month; the column filled with its cuts in boiling order; the conversion units, the first rank fed from the gas oil and the residue, the second — the reformers and alkylation — from what other units make, a cut no unit takes running through both as a band; the furnaces, where the residue no diesel could cut is burned; the tank, filled by product, with what was taken out of the refiners' tanks and the imports, hatched, under it; and on the right who took each product — the cars' petrol at the pump, the vans' and the railway's diesel, the factories' lubricants, the roads' bitumen, the tanks, the world, and what idled — every ribbon to one scale, the height's, bitumen and coke drawn at 1,010 litres a tonne so that every node balances. Under it a strip of the products: made, imported, exported, in or out of the tanks, and the price here; and a unit's line reads its run, its spread at the local and at the city's own prices and what one more would need under the pointer. It is the month as the products were made on it — the flow, mix and rate the refiners keep at the month's end before they strike the next (`Refining.monthsFlow()`, not saved) — traced cut to unit to product with each pool kept by origin, the takers off the buyers' own rows and the railway's diesel off its haul (`Rail.getFuelLitres()`), so a city just loaded says *Not drawn until a month runs*. **Since 0.7.96 Oil's Operations page opens on the whole chain** (`OilView`, new, pure): four figures — what the wells lifted, the crude left in the two pools and the years it lasts at this month's lift, the crude bought abroad, and the products across the edge as the Trade tab books them; THE WELLS by kind, the land wells' lift, decline and ground pool and each platform's depth, distance, plateau and lift, the offshore pool and how its crude comes ashore, beside LOCAL CRUDE, a bar a year of what the wells standing would lift over the next ten years if nothing new were built, each pool lifted no further than its oil — solid this month and pale ahead, no history of the lift being kept; THE REFINERY's units, every kind with what it turns into what, its run, its spread at the city's prices and as a pill the planner's first failed gate — feed, ground, staff, money, or *would lose* — the whole reason under the pointer, and since 0.7.105 the crude units' *idle* or *part run*; PRODUCTS, crude and the nine with their prices, the world's over crude's, and the month made, used, imported, exported and where it went; and THE STRATEGIC RESERVE, whose Fill and Release are dial cards (`Levers`): Fill orders crude for the next clearing up to the room left or what the treasury can pay at crude's import price (`Game.reserveFillMost()`, which `fillReserve()` reads, the same arithmetic), Release sets the tonnes a month, a step a hundredth of the reach, each applied as a decision. The units and products are the refinery picture's month, so the two pages cannot disagree. Every figure, word, colour and shape of both is the model's, held by `RefineryViewCheck` and `OilViewCheck`; the screens only paint, and neither has been seen in the game's window — they were drawn here through Java2D mirrors, every word measured to fit at 1,389 × 868.

### The summary is a problem list

The summary panel used to be six fixed rows — economy, tax, labour, health, land, people. Of the sixteen problems a player can actually build their way out of it could show exactly one, health, and only as a sick rate. A city with no water, no cells and nowhere to bury its dead read exactly like a city with none of those problems.

It is two lists now, and since 0.7.24 a drawer, the City overview, behind the header's *Needs you* chip: the chip opens it on NEEDS YOU, *Pin* keeps it across screens and outside clicks, and Esc closes it pinned or not. Since 0.7.24 the list is measured in the model (`CityNeeds`), so the chip's count, the drawer and Build's Overview read one list. **NEEDS YOU** carries the conditions that have a lever — twenty-one with 0.7.24's FALLS DUE, and twenty-two with 0.7.45's PRICES — each row a door to the screen that owns the fix, and each disappearing when it is solved; when it is empty it names the condition closest to its yellow line instead, so it is never blank. FALLS DUE is red whenever any of the city's paper matures within three months, *\$X in N mo, the rollover's*, or *by hand* with the rollover manual, its door Finances: the old strip's red maturity, kept red on Jerus's word. An amber TREASURY row reads *\$X, under a month's tax (\$Y)*, where it read *in hand*; PRICES says whether the city still believes its central bank ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)); and since 0.7.32 the three Finances rows land where they say, whatever page the tab was left on. Since 0.7.20 a row whose fix is already a building on site, for anybody's order, says so and how long it will take. The served rows — power, water, the road, care and the schools — read supply over demand since 0.7.41, *233% served* or *62% served · 56% flow*, the road as one pair since 0.7.29; they are listed on the same lines as before, power and water from 75% of capacity, but coloured by one verdict, and keep it while their sites are on the way (above), and the drawer's RESOURCES line counts *1 short · 1 tight* and can be red. **HOW THE CITY IS** carries seven readings with no dial — out of work, off sick, hungry, people a month, doubled up, ground used, the currency — always present, coloured when bad, and its door goes to the screen that *diagnoses* rather than the one that fixes: OFF SICK to Services' health overview since 0.7.28, on the model's lines (`CityNeeds.SICK_YELLOW` 6%, `SICK_RED` 12%), where it had opened whatever Services last showed; *hungry* the share of people since 0.7.27, where it had read Health's points beside a page showing the other figure; and the currency on the one parity rule since 0.7.35, its door opening The currency. Since 0.7.20 the Dashboard's GDP, and the ratios read off it, are annualised before a year is recorded; it had summed the months there were and called them a year.

Writing it turned up a model bug that no harness had: `getEnergyRatio()` and `getWaterRatio()` both return min(supply / demand, 1), so a row keyed off them could not appear until the lights were already out. They read load — demand over supply — now, against the 75% the dashboard has called "tight" all along, and since 0.7.41 the rows print it the other way up, served.

## 23. Time, saves & logs

*There is no* next month *button: the month arrives on a clock, a save has to be the city it was to the cent, and everything the game says goes to a file.*

### Time runs on its own

The city runs on a clock at five seconds a month (`SECONDS_PER_MONTH`) and a speed the player picks off a snapping ladder — 0.1× · 0.25× · 0.5× · 1× · 2× · 5× · 10× · 20× · 50× — with the space bar as play/pause and the arrow keys moving the ladder; since 0.7.21 the ladder is the header clock's *‹* and *›* rather than a slider. The day inside the month is painted so the city looks alive between the ticks, even though nothing in the model moves until the month turns.

Three things that only matter once the month arrives unasked. A frame that takes a long time is **clamped at a quarter second**, so a stalled window cannot swallow thirty months while it was away — the worst a single frame can advance is 2.5 months. Redraw is capped at one in every 120ms, because at 50× a month lands every 100ms and the screen cannot usefully be redrawn faster than it can be read; and since 0.7.40 it waits while a mouse button is down and is drawn after the release (`UserInterface.holdPresses()`), because a click needs the press and the release on the same node, at 20× a month lands every 250ms, and a rebuild between the two swallowed it — Jerus had to click a button several times to have it go through. The clock runs the months meanwhile and marks the redraw pending, and a slider or a chart drag is no longer rebuilt under the hand. And a panel is now rebuilt *while the player is still looking at it*, so every scrolling page has to hold its own position across the rebuild rather than snapping to the top — which took seven attempts and a trace file to get right, and is written up on its own.

The game can pause itself when something happens, and by default it does not: the setting exists, and it is off, because a clock that stops without being asked is worse than a notice that waits. Since 0.7.22 the clock stands still while any question is up — a cancel, a demolition, a buy-out, the Quit dialog — so that nothing changes under a decision being made.

### The calendar

Month 1 is January 2000. Purely presentational, with deliberately no reverse function — nothing should derive a month from a date string.

### Skipping time

A skip takes a snapshot before, samples *every month* during, and diffs a snapshot after. Episodes cannot be reconstructed from endpoints: a city that starved for fifty months and recovered looks identical at both ends to one that never had a problem. The report counts months short of power, water, land and road capacity, months nothing was built, epidemics and their worst month, and the peak unburied — then writes plain sentences ordered by how much each should worry you. Since 0.7.8 it says what lenders wrote off, amber only past a sound book's loss, and since 0.7.15 a skip no longer stops at an empty treasury: it stops only when a month throws, and says what the central bank advanced over it and what is owed at the end. On the default seed on 1 October no skip refused to run, so the playtest never had to step a month by itself instead, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, none did either.

### The year book, as text and as CSV

Jerus: *"csv if its cheaper token wise to read than xlsx, also keep the txt"*. Since 0.7.16 the export writes six files: `year-book.txt` and `decade-book.txt` as before, the same bytes 0.7.15 wrote bar the version on their first line, and beside each its main table and its WITHIN table, each year's worst and best month, as CSV — `year-book.csv`, `year-book-within.csv`, `decade-book.csv` and `decade-book-within.csv`, in the game's folder beside the log (`GameFiles.yearBookCsv()`). A CSV is plain text, so it is never dearer to read than an xlsx, which is zipped XML; Excel opens it as columns without an import step; and it needs no library. Each table is built once (`YearBook.Table`), and the text's block and the CSV are both written from it, so the two files cannot disagree. The format is RFC 4180: CRLF line ends, a field quoted only for a comma, a quote or a line break, the text's own column names as the header, the text's own strings in the cells — three significant figures and a point for the decimal whatever the locale — a blank left empty, and no BOM. Since 0.7.37 the button is in City History's head and its result a card under it — *Written to* the folder, a line of file names a book, anything that failed in red, and a × — where a message named the folder once and then each book's three files. The books have gained columns since: `fxParity` (0.7.35); the fund's worth and what was put in and taken out (0.7.39); expected inflation and credibility (0.7.42); the food assistance paid and the baskets it bought (0.7.43); 0.7.45's expected level, each of the index's five parts with its own level and weight, the month the basket in force was struck, the shelf price and its floor, the kitchens' and counters' margins with their targets, the baskets asked for and handed over, the households assisted, and the hunger with its priced-out share; and 0.7.46's `bankLeverageRatio`, `bankLeverageTarget` and `outbreak`, with graduates counted as gains. Since 0.7.46 the books name an epidemic on Health's outbreaks, where they had read the sick rate, and so named one that lasted 2,213 months ([health](#4-health)). Its first locale test passed a writer that formatted by locale, because it wrote the CSV after restoring the locale, and was fixed. Left small for Jerus: an episodes CSV, full precision, a friendlier message when a CSV is open in Excel, and an Excel set to a comma decimal, which opens a comma CSV as one column.

### History past five hundred years

A history keeps its newest six thousand months, five hundred years, a month to an entry (`HistorySave.MONTHLY_KEPT`), and since 0.7.55 a calendar year all of whose months are older than that folds into one entry at its last month, each series by the year book's own rule for it (`YearBook.kindOf()`), so that a folded year is exactly the book's row: a flow added — GDP and its parts, the births and deaths, revenue and every tax — a level taken at the year's end — cash, debt, the population, the money stock — and a rate averaged — the policy rate, the exchange rate, the price index. The history keeps how many months each entry holds, and its readers weigh by it: a folded flow reads a month at a time as its monthly average (`aligned()`), totals and running totals read what was stored, a rolling year counts twelve months and not twelve entries, the year book's rows and the fund's return weigh each entry by its months, and City History's crosshair names a folded entry *the year Y, kept whole*. The first fold comes at month 6,012 of a history begun at month 1, and the newest six thousand months are always kept one to an entry; only the months inside the old years are given up. Where nothing has folded every reader is what it was to the bit, and the default playtest's 4,005 months never fold. An older history reads all its entries as months, and `HistoryCheck` grows one to 6,041 months and holds the fold, the totals, the save and every reader across the seam.

### Saves

Ten numbered slots plus an autosave, under `%APPDATA%` on Windows and the platform equivalent elsewhere — chosen because Steam Cloud syncs from known roots and a bare home folder is not one. Writes go to a temp file, back up the existing save, then atomically move; the worst case is a stray temp file and a save one autosave old. History graphs are per slot. Autosave fires every twelve months, before any skip, and on quit, and since 0.7.20 Quit asks first. Since 0.7.52 the twelve-monthly one is written at the month's end, once the month is recorded. It was written at the top, after the calendar turned and before anything ran, so the file said month N on a city that had finished N − 1, and a city loaded from it never ran N — Jerus's, saved by 0.7.49 at month 1,851, held its history to 1,850 and went on to 1,852. An autosave written before 0.7.52 still loads that way, its month gone and a one-month gap left in its history, because its month's top had run and would run again; the next one, twelve months on, holds a whole month. The two others were always written between the presses. `SaveSlotCheck` loads all three and plays on. The load list names each city and slot and the autosave once, *Autosave · month 13*, and since 0.7.21 the main menu's *YOUR CITIES* reads the three newest slots' headers.

The save format is at **38**, and its changelog is the best history the project has. Older saves load back to format 37, the floor (`GameVersion.OLDEST_LOADABLE_FORMAT`, since 0.7.108, at 21 until 0.7.120 raised it); what is refused is a save from a newer build and one below the floor, one gate since 0.7.108 where it was a check on the sector template's break (below). So every save written before 0.7.120 is refused by this build, and what this section says an older format does at its load is what it did in the builds up to 0.7.119, which still open it: the conversions stay in the code, held by their harnesses on their own, for the day old saves must load again. Nineteen carried the household balance sheet, twenty the repriced unit of material — an old yard read at its old value — and twenty-one the sector template, which was a clean break. Twenty-two was business services, twenty-three manufacturing, twenty-four the farms, twenty-five the bank's own cost of funds, twenty-six the price index's water-marks and twenty-seven the sixth age band — which also made every band-indexed array save its band *names* beside its values, so the day a seventh band arrives no existing file is read at the wrong offsets. **Twenty-eight is the player's hand on the queue** (0.7.22), under one key: a format-27 build handed such a save would load it wrongly, not merely incompletely, because a stopped shell and a demolition on site hold ground and are off their stacks, and an older build would come back with the ground free, the work gone and the money spent. **Twenty-nine is the decision log** (0.7.23), under one key: a format-28 build would load the city, play on, and write it back without its decisions at its next autosave, and a decision is a flow nothing else in the save can give back. Both are safe the other way: a 27 save loads with no order set and nothing rushed, stopped or being demolished, and a 28 with an empty log, which is what each city had. **Thirty is the month the People page draws** (0.7.27): Migration's last month — the draw and its two halves, the pulls, the arrivals and the departures and who made them up, the mixes and the licences — after its wage history, the pyramid's dead by cause after its flows, and the share the shops handed over and the hungry at full shelves after the households' row array. A format-29 build handed such a save would load it wrongly: each of the three arrays is a length it refuses whole, so it would come back with no wage history, nobody able to leave for a year, and a pyramid of nobody. A 29 save loads with those figures at nothing until a month runs, which is what a reloaded People page showed before. **Thirty-one is the land on the world** (0.7.57): the city's centre, its forty lanes, every purchase in its order, the forty offers standing, what has been taken out of its ground, and the world's totals and sea level. A format-30 build handed such a save would load it wrongly, with no ore under a city whose mines stand on it and nine fresh parcels; the other way, a format-30 save is converted onto its world once, as it loads ([land](#18-land)). **Thirty-two is the land on the block grid** (0.7.67): the centre's record 24 wide and its blocks, each purchase as a rectangle 31 wide, the fields held in part, a converted city's purchase history and the 24 offers 29 wide, with no lanes and no purchases in the old shape (`landCentre`, `landCentreRects`, `landHoldings`, `landPartFields`, `landConverted`, `landOffers`). A format-31 build handed such a save would load it wrongly: the centre's record is the wrong width there, so it would draw a new centre from the figure alone and list forty fresh offers, dropping every purchase and the offers standing. The other way, a format-31 save is snapped onto the grid once, as it loads ([land](#18-land)). **Thirty-three is each company's paid-in capital** (0.7.75): every company's register entry three numbers longer — the book its founders' shares were issued against, what its buybacks paid, and whether the two were derived — and the books' months a dozen fields longer: the paid-in and the founders' shares issued in the month, its loan fees, premiums, bonds' issuing costs and bonds written off, and its ground and buildings' material at the month's prices ([the owners](#10-the-owners-the-bonds--the-exchange)). A format-32 build handed such a save would load it wrongly: its register refuses whole an array of a width it does not know, so it would come back with no shareholders at all — no shares, no record, no dividends. The other way, a format-32 save's paid-in is derived at the load as what each company raised since its founding, marked *derived*, and its books' two months are put on it, so that the equity statement closes. **Thirty-four is the fuel split** (0.7.76): no `FUEL` anywhere — its market, the sectors' stock and books and its slot among the goods held are petrol's and diesel's, and the goods held are twelve. A format-33 build handed such a save would load it wrongly: knowing no petrol or diesel, it would drop the refiners' tanks, the month's fuel sales and both markets' strike, and read the goods held at the wrong width. The other way, a save of format 33 or older is converted once as it loads, before anything is restored (`FuelSplit`): every `FUEL` figure becomes petrol at the share of the month's litres the drivers burned against the railway's, and diesel the rest, each pair summing to the figure to the bit; the railway's own purchases all diesel, because it burns nothing else; the market's price kept for both; and the seven other products at a known zero. No money moves, petrol and diesel being on fuel's band. **Thirty-five is the oil in two pools** (0.7.93): the depletion's oil is the ground pool's alone, and the sea's is saved beside it (`oilDepletionAtSea`). A format-34 build handed such a save would load it wrongly, reading the depletion's oil as the one pool's, so every tonne the platform wells had lifted would be back in the ground. The other way, a format-34 save's one pool is charged to the ground once the land is in place, floored at that pool's tonnes, and none to the sea, the tonnes the floor cuts given back to the world (`LandManager.restoreOilPools()`); no money moves, the crude having been sold when it was lifted. **Thirty-six is the old world's ground** (0.7.99): how many of the city's holdings, the centre and then its purchases in the order made, hold the fields the world had to 0.7.98 (`landOldWorldHoldings`), none for a city founded since. A format-35 build handed such a save would load it wrongly, knowing only the old world's fields, so the ground bought since would hold other fields than the ones its books and its mines and wells were counted on. The other way, a save with no such key holds the old world's fields on all the ground it owned, and its standing offers are measured again on the new (`LandMarket.remeasureStanding()`); no money moves, the books as saved and the world's totals the same to the tonne, and at a load the save's own key decides, the format number only where it has none. **Thirty-seven is scrap split from ore** (0.7.120): `IRON` iron ore alone, priced on its own band, and `SCRAP` a market of its own, keyed in the sectors' maps, the ledgers and the statements. A format-36 build handed such a save would load it wrongly, knowing no scrap: it would drop the furnaces' feed, their month's purchases and the market's strike, and read ore's price against the old band. The other way is refused, not converted: a format-36 save's `IRON` holds the mills' scrap and the mines' ore as one good, one price and one line in the mills' books, and would load wrongly here, the scrap read as ore at a price outside its band, so the floor went to 37 in the same batch (below). **Thirty-eight is a city on the real Earth** (0.7.121): the world's kind, the spot's latitude and longitude and the data's identity, written on an Earth city and on no other, so a generated city's save is format 37's but for its number. A format-37 build handed an Earth city would load it wrongly, putting it on its seed's generated ground, another coast with other fields under its holdings; the other way loads rightly, a save with no kind being the generated world every city before 0.7.121 stands on, read byte for byte as 0.7.120 read it, so the floor stays at 37.

The thirteen foods went in *without* a bump, because goods have been saved by name since the sector template: a good this build does not know is dropped and says so in the log, which is what happens to an old city's warehouse of `FOOD`. And so did everything the batches of two editions ago added — five sectors, the freight band, the three streams, the modes and the fare, the railway's quote and its locomotives, every sector's fleet, the households' cars, their investment income, the luxury baseline and the dinners they ate — because a sector is keyed by name, a market is keyed by name, and every new figure in a household cell is appended to the end of an array whose reader checks its length. A city saved before them opened with no cars, no fleets, no kitchens, and the rolling stock its track implies, which is exactly what that city was; an eleven-sector build was proved to load a ten-sector save to the cent before the first of the five shipped. **The central bank went in without a bump too**, and so did everything around it: the treasury's journal for both months and its raised counter; the two health dials, the coverage each month used and a cell slot for the share of a cell's people who could pay for care; the grant's basis and amount, the loan's rate and the tuition scale on the policy array's tail; the vault in dollars and its revaluation (slots 22 and 23 of the foreign accounts), the debt's revaluation (24), the defence (25–27) and the real rate differential with its two inflations (28–30); what the bank still owes for paper sold between the presses, under two keys; the central bank's books, the arrears, the autopilot, the policy rate boxed so that a 0% dial reloads at 0%, the holdings dial and the advances ceiling, each under its own key; who holds every bond, saved with the bond; the households' paper as the thirty-first slot of a cell, with its book ratio; and a buyback's holders outside the pools. The fold and the spend factor added nothing: the first is a rule about counts, and the second is struck again on load. A city saved by 0.6.7 opened in 0.7.3 with an empty central bank, the vault it had bought if it bought one, the bank holding all of its paper and nothing in arrears — exactly what that city was — and a city saved by 0.7.2 pays one month's EI twice on its first month, once. Between them the long sick, the people outside the families, the household record and the whole crime system went in *without* a bump, deliberately: Gson leaves a missing key alone, and a format-21 city loads with each of them empty, which is correct for that city. A big saved city comes back with only its founding constabulary and shows the crime notice until it builds a station.

The batches from 0.7.4 to 0.7.15 went in without a bump as well, each batch's new figures under keys of their own or on the end of an array whose reader knows its older widths: the inflation target's key, the three tax bases and then a tuition scale for each of the nine kinds of school on the policy array's tail, each school kind's month on the end of the schools' array; the history's new series — two a sector, GDP's four parts, the dial, the bank's prime, deposit rate and fees, and six of its capital — with an older history's strain premium skipped on load; the land office's choice of how to pay, its listing behind a marker that says its prices are dollars, the office's dollar ground price as a fourth slot, and the land's dollars as slots 31–36 of the foreign accounts; the bank's pricing record and its late profit, its allowance, its capital record, its month's lines and a year of them, its year of balance sheets and its equity's two parts; every borrower's last quarter, the builders' salvage and a statement's stock paid for earlier; the households' account fee on the end of their statement; the eight keys of the founding record; the mortgages, saved among the business debts under their own type with the insurance's three counters and two lines on the government's month; the bond market, each cell's bonds as the thirty-second slot and bond by bond by name, the exchange's books, and the interim loans under a type of their own; the rollover's setting, ledger and record; the city's fund, the bank's preferred and its record, three slots a company on the register for the city's holdings and a city holder on every bond, and the four inputs the debt market's rate was struck from; and what the central bank has paid the households for their paper and paid at issue rolling its own. A 0.7.15 save with the holdings dial past half, opened in 0.7.14, loads at half.

**And from 0.7.16 to 0.7.21 nothing needed one.** 0.7.16, 0.7.18, 0.7.20 and 0.7.21 put nothing in the save: the year book's CSV is a file it writes, the best-paid fill is a function of the posts, the workers and the licences, all saved already, and the remembered build category, the receipts, the toasts and the fonts are the window's. 0.7.17 put the builders' share of their posts, its need and the fill it was struck on in their sector's extras; 0.7.19 each payer's contract on site with the material its quote allowed for and the share of the tax it gets back, the sectors' capital purchases in the month's ledger, the builders' escalation in their extras, the bank's customers and its operating cost in its month's lines with two slots on the end of its last month, and the grant's marker that its fixed amount is real on the end of the tax policy's state. The pins on City History are a preference in `settings.json`, not the city's. A city saved by the build an earlier edition described, 0.7.15 at format 27, opened in the builds up to 0.7.119 as the city it was, bar the construction points it had parked on stacks with nothing left to build, which are dropped on load and move no money (7,801,561 in Jerus's city): its builders offering every post until its first month strikes their crews, each contract on site read as its owner's with the escalation starting at the load, its grant on the basis it was played on, no order set on the queue and nothing rushed, stopped or coming down, and an empty decision log. From its first month this build's rules apply to it.

**Nor has anything since.** 0.7.24 to 0.7.26 put nothing in the save, and from 0.7.28 to 0.7.52 every figure went under a key of its own, among a sector's extras, or on the end of an array whose reader knows its older widths, and a missing key or slot seeds. 0.7.29 put the railway's allowed bill and what went abroad in its extras, written only when known; 0.7.31 puts the last ten years of GDP back from the history on a load, so a loaded city's year is its own, where every load had reset it to one month; 0.7.39 the fund's ledger and the hand's posted orders inside the fund's own state, and three series on the history, an older save's ledger seeded at its load with one row saying so. The price model went in the same way: 0.7.42 the anchor under its own key, a save from before it seeded at a credibility of 0.80 and an expected level of 1.0 because its constants are still at founding money; 0.7.43 the chained basket behind a marker an older array lacks, the food assistance dial on the policy's tail and the shops' extras; 0.7.44 the suppliers' credit among the shops' extras; and 0.7.45 each part's own chained level. Then the model fixes saved what a reloaded city had read as nothing or struck again: 0.7.46 the month's trade in units, the balance of payments' month on the foreign accounts' slots 37–44, care's fees by kind, each cell's income after its fixed bills as a cell slot, and Construction's struck materials; 0.7.48 the fund's withdrawal and what it sells for and paid late; and 0.7.49 transit's bill, the share of workers with no car of their own, a journey's fuel and the households' fuel by row; and 0.7.52 how strictly the rule holds the target, by name under its own key. A save from before each loads as the city it was: Trade's month *not counted yet* and care's fees unsplit until a month runs, the fund at Norway's 3%, transit's bill derived at the load, the rule at Standard. 0.7.53 and 0.7.54 put nothing new in it, and 0.7.53 widened what was there: the population, in the save and in its header, the workforce, the businesses' population trend and ten of the history's series — the posts, the workforce, the out of work, the population, the births, deaths, arrivals and departures, the homes and the builders' capacity — can pass 2,147,483,647, which a JSON number does not notice, so an older save loads into them as it did, and the save of a city past it is one an older build marks unreadable rather than loading it wrong. `ScaleCheck` saves one of five billion and loads it back figure for figure. The fixes moved no trace on their own: 0.7.46's eight traces were 0.7.45's to the byte. A newer save is not safe the other way: a 0.7.45 build handed a 0.7.49 save refuses its cells, its care and the households' statement whole, at widths it does not know, which is the downgrade the number guards and is on the list.

**From 0.7.55 to 0.7.64 one thing needed a bump, the land.** 0.7.55 put the land price's parts — the crowding, the premium and the world's price level — on the end of the office's price state, an older save reading its premium back from its price, and the months each folded entry of the history holds, an older history having none; 0.7.56 the world's seed under a key of its own, a save without it deriving one; and 0.7.57 the land on the world, which is format 31 (above), the old listing, iron pool and tonnes read only to convert. Then nothing needed one again. 0.7.58 put the goods the sectors hold on the end of the national accounts' slots, an older save's first month booking no change in them; 0.7.59 the water rights, a save without them given what its plants already pump; 0.7.60 the map's stamp, the map itself a file of its own beside the save, `slot-NN-map.bin`, written through the same swap, whose format 2 since 0.7.64 has an older sidecar drawn again once; 0.7.62 the drivers' fuel as 6d drew it — the bill, its imported part and the litres — a save without it importing every litre, as it struck, and the railway's imported fuel among its extras; and 0.7.63 the graduates waiting for the next census to carry their loans and the four ratios each sector's month was run at, two figures only the month sets: without them Jerus's city came back 7,447 units short a month after a load, its graduates' loans left with the students, and city2400, short of power, billed its saved month 0.02% dear. A save from before 0.7.46's units has them derived on load (`Sector.deriveCarriedTrade()`), and every save writes them now, empty or not. 0.7.61 put nothing in it. Jerus's two 0.7.63 saves, his autosave at month 416 and slot 3 at month 212, load in 0.7.64 with every key of the file read, play twelve months, and save and reload to the bit in every pool the money audit reads and in their people. A city saved by 0.7.54, at format 30, the build an earlier edition described, opened in the builds up to 0.7.119 on its own world: its seed derived, its ground a centre of whole blocks holding its dry ground to within a plot and twenty-four offers listed round it, its water rights what its plants pump, its drivers' fuel all imported until its first month draws it, and its map drawn when the land office first asks for it.

**From 0.7.65 to 0.7.69 the land needed a bump again, and nothing else went in.** 0.7.65 and 0.7.66 built the grid and the conversion beside the game, which read neither; 0.7.67 is format 32 (above), the quadtree never saved but rebuilt from the rectangles at load, and the map's sidecar its format 3, stamped by the land's rectangles, so an older sidecar is drawn again once; and 0.7.68 and 0.7.69 changed words and screens and put nothing in the save. Jerus's two 0.7.63 saves, his autosave at month 416 and slot 3 at month 212, load in 0.7.67 onto the grid with their cash unchanged, play twelve months, and save as format 32 and reload to the bit in every pool the money audit reads, in their people, their land, their offers and their figure, and a month on alike; his old city, saved by 0.7.49 at format 30, does the same at 514,354 people; and nothing 0.7.68 and 0.7.69 changed is read on the load. A city saved by 0.7.64, at format 31, the build an earlier edition described, opened in the builds up to 0.7.119 on the block grid: its ground snapped one level finer than its offers, its books its drawn plots, its sites, tonnes and what it has taken out as saved, its purchases kept as history, 24 offers listed afresh and its map drawn again ([land](#18-land)). The other way is shut: a build of 0.7.66 or older refuses a format-32 save as one from a newer build, so a city once saved by 0.7.67 cannot go back.

**From 0.7.70 to 0.7.77 two things needed a bump, and the rest went in without one.** 0.7.70 put the gravel roads being paved, in their batches, with the player's hand on the queue under its key, an older save having none; 0.7.71 changed no field, a save holding its buildings by id, so a Home Daycare comes back a Small Childcare Centre with its places, posts and ground ([the catalogue](#19-the-catalogue)); 0.7.72 made the map's sidecar its format 4, so an older map is drawn again once; 0.7.73 put automatic building under a key of its own, an older save loading with it off, and 0.7.77 its ground under the same key, an older one having bought none; and 0.7.74 put nothing in it, the statements' reads kept in memory and not counted the month after a load. 0.7.75 is format 33 and 0.7.76 format 34 (above). Each was proved as it went in: at 0.7.75 city600 and city2400 at format 30, Jerus's autosave at month 416 and slot 3 at month 212 at 31, and a save of his at month 418 written by 0.7.74's own build at 32 all load with every listed company's paid-in derived and said so, their equity statements closing, and saved as format 33 come back the same; and at 0.7.76 saves of every format from 30 to 33 — among them the playtest's city at month 4,002, whose 6.58 million litres of fuel split at 32% petrol, and his month 418, all petrol — load with every pair summing to the bit, their cash to the bit and nothing written off, play a year, and saved as format 34 reload the same and play their next month alike to the cent. A city saved by 0.7.69, at format 32, opened in 0.7.77 with its paid-in derived, its fuel split by the month's litres, its daycares centres of the new sizes, its map drawn again and automatic building off, and a build of 0.7.75 or older refuses a format-34 save as one from a newer build.

**From 0.7.78 to 0.7.92 nothing needed a bump**, the format staying at 34, each new figure under a key of its own or among a sector's extras, which an older save reads as nothing: the refinery's crude mix (`crudeMix.*`, 0.7.79; an older save's medium); automatic building's limit over GDP and its toggle, under its key, and the year of GDP exactly (`DataSave.gdpRolling`, 0.7.81; an older save's limit the default, its toggle off and its year seeded from the graph as before); the refiners' idle months by kind (0.7.82); the forecourts' month (`pump.*`, 0.7.83; none sold); the wells' vintages (0.7.84; every well read new, opened the first month it plays); the city's reserve (`DataSave.reserve`) and the refiners' crude on hand in their pantry (0.7.85; an empty reserve and none kept); the ports' shares and month (`DataSave.portMonth`, 0.7.86; nothing at sea); and the platforms and pipelines (0.7.91; none). The map's sidecar was its format 5 from 0.7.88, writing the runs from 0.7.89 (6 since 0.7.97), a format-4 one and 0.7.88's, which wrote none, laid from their counts as they are read ([land](#18-land)). Each oil batch loaded the research and Jerus cities — city600 and city2400 at format 30, Jerus's autosave at month 416 and slot 3 at month 212 at 31, his old city at month 1,851 written by 0.7.49, and from 0.7.91 his city at month 8,473 — and played them one or two years, every month's audit within its tolerance and nothing written off.

**From 0.7.93 to 0.7.106 two things needed a bump, and the rest went in without one.** 0.7.93 is format 35 and 0.7.99 format 36 (above). 0.7.94 to 0.7.96 and 0.7.98 put nothing in the save: the plan's speed, the refinery's picture and the oil page read what was saved already, the month's flow and the railway's litres kept in memory and drawn only once a month has run; 0.7.97 made the map's sidecar its format 6, keeping the works on the shore, a format-4 or 5 sidecar laying them from its counts and gathering the refinery's units once, as it is read. 0.7.100 changed no model. 0.7.101 put nothing new in, automatic building's year of revenue being 0.7.100's, and a save at the old default limit of 60% reads the new one, 240%. 0.7.102 put the budget's four lines at the government block's end, what each business's borrowing cost it still to expense and when, and the investors' last word (`DataSave.lastInvestment`), an older save reading none of them, which is what its month carried; 0.7.103 the fuel duty on the end of the policy's array and the month's duty among the grocers' extras, an older save reading none; 0.7.104 what a resident paid the city at each of automatic building's last twelve passes, an older save reading the month's figure until a pass records a year; 0.7.105 the refiners' run and its last six months among their extras, an older save reading the whole run, as it ran; and 0.7.106 nothing, an older save keeping the centre it was founded with, the bond it owes and a demolition on site at the salvage it was quoted. Two fixes to the load went in beside them: since 0.7.103 a stack emptied — every gravel road paved, the last one retired — keeps its place in the list the month shares the crews over, the load standing an empty stack for every building the save's stack order names, where a city saved with one had parted from its twin within months; and since 0.7.106 a load puts back the central bank's lines and the fund's transfer in the month's accounts, which only the government block had carried, so a refresh of the books before a loaded city's first month no longer strikes its interest on its advances as nothing. Each batch loaded the research and Jerus cities — city600 and city2400, his autosave at month 416 and slot 3, his old city at month 1,851 and his city at month 8,473 — and played them for months or years, every month's audit within its tolerance and every reload the same. A city saved by 0.7.69, at format 32, the build an earlier edition described, opened in the builds up to 0.7.119 with its paid-in derived, its fuel split by the month's litres, its daycares centres of the new sizes, its map drawn again, automatic building off, its ground on the old world's fields with its offers measured again, and its oil, if it has any, one pool charged to the ground. The other way is shut: a build of 0.7.98 or older refuses a format-36 save as one from a newer build. And since 10 October the house rule is that an older save need not load until the game is published (Jerus: *"old saves do not matter, only once we publish to old saves matter"*): no conversion is written for one any more, and a change that would make one load wrongly bumps the format and, since 0.7.108, raises the floor to it in the same batch (below), where until then the loader refused only a format newer than its own or older than 21, so a bump alone refused no older save.

**Since 0.7.108 an old save is refused cleanly** (batch P7). The house rule has its mechanism: `GameVersion.OLDEST_LOADABLE_FORMAT`, 37 since 0.7.120, the oldest format this build loads, which a batch that bumps `SAVE_FORMAT` because an older save would load wrongly raises to the new format in the same batch, writing no conversion. It replaced the sector template's own check, so one floor holds both. A save below it is refused as a newer build's is: nothing of it applied, and its file, its history and the folder left exactly as they were. The slot list's line under it is the refusal, its Load button off — *This city was saved by build X, and build 0.7.123 can no longer read it. Build X still opens it.*, or *an older build* where the save carries no stamp — and the log says *Slot N not loaded (save format F; this build reads formats 37 to 38), its file left as it was*; *Continue*'s autosave and YOUR CITIES pass such a slot by, as they pass a newer build's. The floor was 21 until 0.7.120, so nothing that loaded at 0.7.107 was refused then; 0.7.120 was the first batch to raise it, and stopped every city saved before it loading, by design, the build that saved each still opening it (below). `SaveFileCheck`'s section on the floor writes a city at the floor, below it, unstamped and from a newer build, and checks each answer and every file in the folder byte for byte; with the floor set to `SAVE_FORMAT` on a copy, the same harnesses stayed green.

**From 0.7.107 to 0.7.115 nothing needed a bump**, the format staying at 36: the city's zones, its forest law and the forest it has cleared, under a key of their own that a city with nothing set and nothing cleared does not write (`DataSave.zoning`, 0.7.107); what has been dug of each type of field, written only once a works digs by type, which none does yet, a save without it reading as the order its tonnes came out in (`depletionByType`, 0.7.110); and the power a works sold the grid, on its statement, an older save reading none, which is what it sold (0.7.112). 0.7.108, 0.7.109, 0.7.111, 0.7.113 and 0.7.115 put nothing in it; an Earth world's key is for the batch that founds one to save, with a format of its own ([land](#18-land)). Copies of five saves — city600, city2400 and three of Jerus's — loaded as before through the zoning and the types, and the types' were saved to slot 10 and loaded again with the same figures. A city saved by 0.7.106, the build an earlier edition described, opened in the builds from 0.7.107 to 0.7.119 as the city it was: nothing zoned, the law at 0 and 0 and no forest cleared until its first month clears what its buildings stand on, its fields typed by their place and what it has dug read by type off the order it bought them, and nothing sold to the grid. The other way is shut as it was: a build of 0.7.98 or older refuses a format-36 save as one from a newer build.

**From 0.7.116 to 0.7.123 two things needed a bump, and the floor went up for the first time.** 0.7.120 is format 37 and 0.7.121 format 38 (above), and 0.7.120 raised the floor to 37 in the same batch, as the house rule asks: every save written before it, at format 36 or older — Jerus's cities in slots 1 to 9 among them — is refused by 0.7.120 and every build since. Nothing of such a save is applied and its file is not touched; the slot list marks it, its Load button off, in the words above, naming the build that saved it, and the log says *Slot N not loaded (save format 36; this build reads formats 37 to 38), its file left as it was*. **To open an old city**, run the build that saved it, or any build after it up to 0.7.119, the last that reads format 36 — the repository's commit b4ba4c2 is 0.7.119 — in a folder of its own beside the live game, since the PC's copy follows the repository's main line; the city plays on there, and cannot come forward. Whether Jerus keeps it so, or has the iron batch's merge reverted and the batch brought back with the conversion written, is his ([open questions](#25-open-questions)). **A city on the real Earth** is refused in words of its own, nothing of it applied and its file as it was: by a build before 0.7.121, as a newer build's save; by a build whose Earth is not here, *"This city stands on the real Earth, and the Earth's data is not here: put earth-1.bin in a folder named data beside the game, as data/earth-1.bin."*; and by one that reads another Earth, whose coasts and rivers would not be the ones it was built on, *"The build that saved it still opens it."* (`EarthSite.loadProblem()`); the map's sidecar names an Earth world's whole key, a generated world's seed as before, with no change to its format. 0.7.123 put the city's old steel under a key of its own (`DataSave.oldMetal`): the steel arisen since the yards last bought, by seller and source, and the yards' last month, a save from 0.7.120 to 0.7.122 reading none, which is what that city had thrown out that a yard could buy. 0.7.117, 0.7.119 and 0.7.122 put nothing in the save. A save of 0.7.120 loads in this build, its generated world read byte for byte as it was written; a city saved by 0.7.115, the build the last edition described, at format 36, does not, and 0.7.115 still opens it. The other way is shut: a build of 0.7.119 or older refuses a format-37 save, and 0.7.120 a format-38 one, as a newer build's.

A city saved by 0.7.23, at format 29, the build an earlier edition described, opened in the builds up to 0.7.119 as the city it was, bar four things: its People page's month reads nothing until a month runs; its anchor is seeded and its basket waits a month to link, the first month stepping the year's rate as the shelf turns sticky; its fixed grant, new-home rebates and account fee come back about 10% lower, because they are struck at an expected level of 1.0 where the old city had indexed them, 1.11 in the 2,400-month city; and its fund draws at Norway's 3% and its treasury pays transit's bill from the first month. And a load since 0.7.25 hands the investors' planner the bank, as a month does: until then the planner had no bank for the first month after every load, and its word read *Holding: no bank*.

### Logs

Every `println` in the game already goes to a rotating log file, because a logging system that needs a thousand edits does not get adopted. In a packaged build there is no console, so all of it previously went nowhere. Reports and graphs to the log default off, so the 2 MB log holds the crash rather than three centuries of ASCII graphs. The decision log prints nothing: it is in the save and on the chart.

## 24. How it's checked

*Ninety-seven self-hosted harnesses plus a 4,000-month playtest that audits every month, asserts money is conserved to the cent, and reloads the city repeatedly to prove a saved game and a played one agree. `AllChecks` runs all ninety-eight, one JVM each, in about twelve minutes — 318 seconds on 5 October, 381 at 0.7.52, 21 of them `CentralBankCheck`'s with its new probe city, 408 at 0.7.54, 28 of them `OrderSearchCheck`'s and 7 `ScaleCheck`'s, 628 at 0.7.62, 546 at 0.7.64, 94 of them the playtest's, 24 `ScaleCheck`'s and 12 `MapCheck`'s, 516 at 0.7.69, `GridCheck` 2.3 of them and `ConversionCheck` 3.5 when they went in, 634 at 0.7.76, 711 at 0.7.106, 717 at 0.7.115 and 882 at 0.7.123, in a cloud session where the one that needs JavaFX, `BuildMenuCheck`, is skipped: at 0.7.76 eighty-four green and one red, `HealthCheck`, and at 0.7.106 all ninety-one green, `HealthCheck` among them since 0.7.102, at 0.7.115 all ninety-six, and at 0.7.123 all ninety-seven; the three Earth harnesses and `MapCheck`'s Earth section run their whole-file sections only where the Earth's file is named, and say so in a line where it is not. At 0.7.77 the suite took 1,073 seconds with another agent's jobs holding both of the machine's processors, and under that load `MapCheck`'s timing labels went red beside `HealthCheck` — its functional assertions green in every one of eighteen runs, alone or in the suite, and its timings red on one to six labels a run while the load lasted; that edition's own run of it read the same, one timing label red; since then `MapCheck` times a month's change on the main thread's CPU (0.7.100) and `PlanCheck`'s planner is steady alone (0.7.94), though both have read red now and then in suites run while another batch held the processors, `PlanCheck`'s slowest plan up to 85 ms against its 40 at a load of four, the work unchanged. There were sixty-six at the edition of 0.7.23; the thirty-one since are `BuildAdviceCheck` (0.7.24), `BuildCardCheck` (0.7.25), `SectorFlowCheck` (0.7.30), `PolicyPreviewCheck` (0.7.36), `FundLedgerCheck` (0.7.39), `ExpectationsCheck` (0.7.42), `GroceryCheck` (0.7.43), `SupplierCreditCheck` (0.7.44), `ScaleCheck` (0.7.53), `OrderSearchCheck` (0.7.54), `WorldCheck` (0.7.56), `MapCheck` (0.7.60), `OilCheck` (0.7.62), `GridCheck` (0.7.65), `ConversionCheck` (0.7.66), `RoadCheck` (0.7.70), `ChildcareCheck` (0.7.71), `AutoBuildCheck` (0.7.73), `SectorStatementCheck` (0.7.74), `RefineryCheck` (0.7.80), `WellCheck` (0.7.84), `PortCheck` (0.7.86), `PlanCheck` (0.7.87), `RefineryViewCheck` (0.7.95), `OilViewCheck` (0.7.96), `ZoningCheck` (0.7.107), `ZoningViewCheck` (0.7.109), `EarthCheck` (0.7.111), `MaterialsCheck` (0.7.112), `EarthTerrainCheck` (0.7.115) and `EarthFoundingCheck` (0.7.121). `BuildMenuCheck` had failed 73 checks since 0.7.19, because its price check was older than the builders' sales tax; since 0.7.21 it checks the taxed price, worked from the price rule's own inputs rather than read back off the quote (Jerus:* "Update to the taxed price"*), and it runs in the cloud on its own against the Windows JavaFX jars, where at 0.7.23, at 0.7.49, at 0.7.51, at 0.7.52 and again at 0.7.54 it read* PASS, 73 of 73<em>, and since the catalogue grew,</em> 74 of 74 *at 0.7.59 and* 76 of 76 *at 0.7.62 and at every build from 0.7.64 to 0.7.77, then 91, 92, 94 and 98 of the same as the oil's buildings came (0.7.80 to 0.7.86), 98 of 98 to 0.7.90,* 101 of 101 *from 0.7.91 to 0.7.122 and* 108 of 108 *since 0.7.123. `HealthCheck`'s red line reads the hunger of a city charging fifteen times the founding fees for care against a free one's over their last year, and from partway through 0.7.12 the dear city was hungrier by more than the price of care — 8.4 points against a tolerance of five on 28 September, 40.0 on 1 October, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, with hunger counted in baskets since 0.7.43, 10.1: 2.2% against 12.3% ([health](#4-health)); it shipped red on Jerus's word,* "Ship with it red, flagged"*; since 0.7.100 a builders' depot stands with the poor city, which took the gap from 19.7 points to 5.4, and since 0.7.102 it passes, at 0.7.103 by −1.8, on the shelves' timing ([health](#4-health)). The line that stood here before it, `InfrastructureCheck`'s* "and its shops can actually be supplied"*, which Jerus put down to roads —* "its fine, we will balance later." *— went green by accident on one build of 0.7.2 and red again on the next, and has passed on every suite since 0.7.7; the fixture is sensitive to the young city's rates, so it stays on the list. Every count and constant on this page is struck from the tree at 0.7.49, in the passages 0.7.50 and 0.7.51 changed, at 0.7.51, in 0.7.52's at 0.7.52, and in 0.7.53's and 0.7.54's at 0.7.54, in every passage 0.7.55 to 0.7.64 changed at 0.7.64, in every passage 0.7.65 to 0.7.69 changed at 0.7.69, in every passage 0.7.70 to 0.7.77 changed at 0.7.77, in every passage 0.7.78 to 0.7.106 changed at 0.7.106, in every passage 0.7.107 to 0.7.115 changed at 0.7.115, and in every passage 0.7.116 to 0.7.123 changed at 0.7.123; every measurement carries its date or its batch, and "the default seed on 5 October" is the plain playtest at 0.7.49, as "1 October" was 0.7.23's and "28 September" 0.7.15's. `RealismCheck`, a probe outside the build, is the rebalance's instrument and the thing to run first if any real-world figure is questioned. And since 18 September the playtest is the gate for a refactor as well as for a mechanic: it is deterministic, two baseline runs are byte-identical, and every move out of `Game` and every comment-only pass was proved by a run that compared equal to the morning's, bar its wall-clock line. The four interface batches proved the same way that they left the model's default run alone: the default playtest's eight trace files — the month, the borrowing, the houses, the people, the bank, the bonds, the building and the labour — came out byte-identical to 0.7.19's at 0.7.20, 0.7.21, 0.7.22 and 0.7.23, so a reading of the default seed taken at 0.7.19 still held at 0.7.23, and so they did at every batch to 0.7.41, the redraws among them. The price model was the first to move them on purpose: they were re-baselined at 0.7.42, 0.7.43 and 0.7.44, each harness premise the new design made wrong listed for Jerus and changed, and no tolerance loosened; 0.7.45 and 0.7.46 left them byte-identical; and they were re-baselined again at 0.7.47 for the floor in today's money, at 0.7.48 for the fund and at 0.7.49 for transit, each new assertion shown to fail on the build before; 0.7.50 to 0.7.54 — the chart crash, the build advice, the autosave's month and the bank's strictness, the counts that can pass 2.1 billion, and the order searches — left them byte-identical. On the world's land they moved again, each move explained before the next batch began: re-baselined at 0.7.55 for the crowding premium, at 0.7.57 for the land on the world, twice at 0.7.58 for early iron and then for a test player that keeps its ground ahead, at 0.7.59 for the water limit, at 0.7.62 for fuel and at 0.7.64 for whole fields; on the block grid at 0.7.67, twice, for the grid and then for a test player that buys no ground it does not need, and at 0.7.68 for the houses' words alone, every figure byte for byte; 0.7.56's world, 0.7.60's map, 0.7.61's view and 0.7.63's save fixes left them byte-identical, as did 0.7.65's grid and 0.7.66's conversion, built beside the game, and 0.7.69's office and view; after the grid they moved twice more, at 0.7.70 for roads chosen over their life, the test player's first paved roads ordered at month 3,422, and at 0.7.76 for petrol and diesel, its first refinery ordered at month 1,093, while 0.7.71's childcare, 0.7.72's map, 0.7.73's automatic building, 0.7.74's and 0.7.75's statements and 0.7.77's bridges and ground left them byte-identical, the childcare and automatic building reaching the test player only behind flags it leaves off; and since 0.7.60 the playtest keeps its city's map up every month and reads it back the same at every reload. From 0.7.78 to 0.7.92 they moved four times — at 0.7.78 for petrol and diesel at wholesale, at 0.7.83 from the first van's diesel, at 0.7.84 from the first well, which wears out, and at 0.7.86 from the first sea terminal — and from 0.7.93 to 0.7.106 four more: at 0.7.99 for the fewer and bigger fields, from month 360, its player finding no iron; at 0.7.102 for the budget's four lines, the sheet at the close and the borrowing costs, from month 4; at 0.7.103 for the road rule and each road's own repairs, from month 32; and at 0.7.106 for the demolition's salvage, the grocers' staff and the founding lake, from month 17; each move explained before the next batch began, and every other version byte-identical, the oil's because the playtest's city owns no sea oil and stands no refinery. From 0.7.107 to 0.7.115 they moved once, at 0.7.113, for every order on its whole cost, from month 9, its first move a Diner refused ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)), and every other version was byte-identical: the playtest zones nothing, loads nothing older, reads no field's type, builds nothing that makes power, and stands on a generated world. From 0.7.116 to 0.7.123 they moved twice, re-baselined each time: at 0.7.120 for iron at the world's price, from month 4, the first car 6% cheaper and no furnace ever built; and at 0.7.123 for the integrated route, from month 1,536, its first Large Mini-Mill ordered. 0.7.117, 0.7.119, 0.7.121 and 0.7.122 were byte-identical: the Earth's geology and map reach no generated world, the default playtest founds on one, and the card is advice. A playtest founded on the real Earth is its own baseline since 0.7.121 ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)). The test player plays by rules of its own that moved with them: since 0.7.58 it keeps about 5% of its dry ground free ahead of six months' growth, the build advice's own line, spending at most a tenth of its cash a look (`LongPlaytest.keepGroundAhead()`), because on the world's smaller offers a player that bought only when it was full grew a city half the size; since 0.7.59 it orders water plants only for the water its lakes yield; since 0.7.64 it buys its iron a whole field at a time; and since 0.7.67 it keeps three rules a sensible player keeps, found where ensemble seed 14 collapsed on the grid, 70% out of work by month 600 and never recovering. It weighs room to grow only past that same ground-ahead line, where at months 477 to 490 it had spent all six moves of its looks on ground it did not need while its power and roads ran short; it orders no more transit lines than riders would fill, a cap that had been twenty-five times too loose, after the crash's sixteen Bus Networks ran their crews' wages up to all of its revenue; and it buys an iron field only once the mines it could staff would pay its price back ([land](#18-land)). Since 0.7.70 it asks the advice which road to build and paves where paving is the least of the roads, which in its own city it never is ([roads](#20-utilities--roads)); its childcare rule (0.7.71) and its hand-over of the works to automatic building (0.7.73) are flags it leaves off; since 0.7.86 it orders a sea terminal where a kind's trade that could go by sea passes its berths by 60% of a berth's month; and since 0.7.103 it orders the advice's own card for the road, its road and its count ([roads](#20-utilities--roads)).
