With those rules the playtest's city ended at 469,591 people at 0.7.69, half as large again as 0.7.64's 305,172, because its player builds power and roads where it had bought ground; at 477,358 at 0.7.70, its roads chosen over their life; at 484,273 at 0.7.76; at 630,290 at 0.7.86, its ports among it; at 545,179 at 0.7.99, finding no iron; at 544,232 at 0.7.102; at 617,942 at 0.7.103, its roads by need; at 492,823, at month 4,003, at 0.7.106; at 566,444, at month 4,002, at 0.7.113, its investors asked the interest on every order's whole cost; at 577,610, at month 4,000, at 0.7.120, no furnace ever paying; and at 659,072 at 0.7.123, its mills and yards standing. Since 0.7.42 a change to the model is also scored on an ensemble, sixteen seeds under five policies against criteria written as code before the first number was seen ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). Scored like for like, it passed 21 of its 26 criteria at 0.7.55, 16 on the world's land before the test player kept its ground ahead, 21 again after, and 22 at 0.7.62 and at 0.7.64, the same four failing at both; on the block grid 21 at 0.7.67, a fifth failing and seed 14 collapsing, and 23 once its test player was mended, three failing, and 23 again at 0.7.71, the same three, its roads chosen over their life; 23 of 25 at 0.7.86 and at 0.7.93, one vacuous; 22 of 25 at 0.7.99, the boom's spell red again; and with S1 and H1 restated and H2 counted ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)), 24 of 26 at 0.7.100 and 0.7.101, 23 at 0.7.102, 22 at 0.7.103 and at 0.7.106, 24 at 0.7.113, every order on its whole cost; and, the hot young city's second criterion having no burst to judge, 20 of 25 at 0.7.120 and 21 at 0.7.123 ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).*

> **Rules the harnesses are written to**
>
> **A fixture must cause the condition, not wait for it. Assert against the model's own constants, never a literal** — a check pinned to 0.06 or 2.25 tests that nobody edited the harness. **Assert the shape of a distribution, not only its total** — an aggregate cannot see a missing category. **Count how often a new mechanic actually fires in a real run** — out-migration once shipped fully tested and fired zero times in 4,002 months, and foreign borrowing had to be told to happen. **A quantity in one unit tested against a rule that assumed another** is the shape that keeps recurring. **A fixture has to cause the condition under test, not stand next to it** — fifty-odd sightings now, the latest a fixture that measured an oven's revenue on one of its two products and reported it losing money. **When a fix is safe because some case is exactly unchanged, assert that case at zero tolerance** — a sector making one good must carry exactly 1.0 of its own cost, and that is a check rather than a comment. **A harness cannot check a thing nobody does** — the fare was collected from nobody for as long as no fixture had built a bus. **When a harness goes red on your change, ask the same question of ten fixtures before believing it is your change** — one fixture said the farms broke the currency reform; ten said the model had been carrying a coin-toss for months. **A sentinel is a value for the code to compare, never a value to print**, and the place it leaks is the screen, which was the one layer with no harness behind it — and the plainer rule beside it: play the game, because fifty-one green harnesses and a ten-fixture sweep did not find a nine-quintillion-dollar unit cost that clicking on Agriculture found in ninety seconds. **Assert the premise the whole suite stands on** — a `month++` left twice at the top of the month passed every harness in the suite, and only the playtest's month numbers gave it away; `CalendarCheck` asserts one press is one month now. **Is the field money? Then it belongs in the reform the day it is written** — a rule cheaper than the twenty-five constants of the family before it. **A held sector is held in both directions** — a planner that could demolish a harness's fixture scrapped six spurs of an over-built railway, and an assertion whose subject is decided by a planner is an assertion about the planner. **A fixture says what it lives on** — when the founding treasury went from D\$2.5B to D\$100M, forty-two fixtures in twenty-five harnesses turned out to have been living on it, only ten went red, and three were green because their calendars had quietly run short; each is handed its treasury explicitly now (0.7.10). **Compare mechanisms, not counts** — a last-bit rounding difference moves an eight-seed count of bank failures by about three and the amount written off by about \$60bn (0.7.8).

> **Decided by dust**
>
> The money-constant family — a bound written in absolute money that a currency reform walks past — is past twenty-five sightings, and since 16 September it has two relatives that are not constants at all. **The sign of a residue.** Four retired households owed minus 2.7e-29 dollars, out of the monthly rebuild handing a cell `weight × g / g`, which can come back an ulp above `weight`. The magnitude is not money and nothing reads it as money; one thing reads its *sign* — `investAbroad()` asks `debt <= 0` to decide who may keep money abroad — so four cells flipped, their paper came home at a tenth a month, the financial account moved by thousands, and the exchange rate, which is every import and export price in the city, moved with it: a city and its reformed twin ran together at 1e-13 for 158 months and were 2–4% apart a decade later. The fix is four clamps and no numbers, because a ratio cannot go stale in a new unit. *A zero-crossing test is a threshold, and a threshold on a residue is decided by luck.* **A money ratio that comes out as a physical quantity.** The car affordability test is money over money and the answer is cars, which the road, the market and the trade balance all read; `(a/100)/(b/100)` is not `a/b`, so a reformed city wanted an ulp more of a car, bought it somewhere else, and `DenominationCheck` went red on sixteen assertions. Scale-invariant in arithmetic and not in floating point, and the cure is a grain: a cell buys whole cars, and the shops sell whole baskets. The playtest flags any household position below zero at zero tolerance, every month of every seed, and was seen to fail 216 times before it was trusted.
>
> Two more sightings since. **A hair of borrowing is a discrete state** (0.6.8): the waterfall clamps a negative remainder, but a positive 1e-21 becomes a debt, and `investAbroad()` gates on `debt <= 0`; the first draft of the price at the door re-split a row's bill by its paying heads, and the reform twins parted a decade later over *interest 2.36e-21 against 0.0* in one cell. The re-split was dropped rather than touch the waterfall. **A ghost household** (0.7.2): a cell whose census count had fallen to a residue — 1e-15 households, or a real 0.3 — still held savings and was still being paid, a household to some lines and not to others, and one line divided a credit by it; `DenominationCheck` went red at a floating-point knife-edge and the trace found it. The cure is a grain again: under half a household a cell is empty, and `DenominationCheck` looks 202 times over both cities and finds no cell under half a household holding anything. And one in the harness itself: its own two dust thresholds were fixed dollar amounts until 0.7.12, and scale with the currency now.

### The tree, and the prose that describes it

The tree is 321 files and 324,580 lines at 0.7.123: one flat package plus `sectors/`, `ui/` and `tools/`. `Game.java` is the seam every system meets at, 16,372 lines and forty-two banner sections, and on 18 September four mechanics that already had the shape of a class left it with their text intact and their behaviour byte-for-byte unchanged — the households' car market as `Motoring`, the boutiques and the kitchens as `LuxuryCounter`, who is at risk of offending as `Offending`, what the city eats as `CityBasket` — each called from the same line of the month it always was, with every moved getter kept on `Game` as a delegation so that no caller changed. The currency reform stayed, because it redenominates twenty-two subsystems through `Game`'s own fields and that is the seam doing the seam's job. The investor, the foreign borrowing and demographics are bigger and entangled, and each would be a plan of its own.

Nobody reads those files whole. `tools/` reads the sources as text and writes `docs/`: a code map with one row per file and one page per file listing its banners and every method with its line; `dials.md`, every `static final` with its value and the sentence above it, 2,862 of them; `month-order.md`, the month as a numbered list of statements with where each call goes, which is what section 01 of this page is struck against; and `harnesses.md`, the 9,407 labelled assertions in 98 harness files under their sections and which harnesses name which class — which is how it is known that nothing yet names `LuxuryRetail`, and only `CarCheck` and `BuildingDataCheck` `Automotive`. `Where` finds a member or a banner by name and prints it; `SaveDump` looks inside a save without loading it. And every batch has a sixth step since 18 September, done by a context that did not make the change: a docs pass that makes every comment, header, index and count agree with the code again, because the agent that changed the code has stopped seeing the prose. Its first run found four stranded javadocs and two false headers; its mechanical half is `tools.Stale`, which found 84 orphaned javadocs on its first run and has been at zero firm findings since, 97 soft at 0.7.49 and still none firm at 0.7.64, at 0.7.69 and at every batch's gate to 0.7.123, 114 soft after 0.7.106's docs pass, 119 after 0.7.115's and 122 after 0.7.123's; the half that needs judgement stays with a reader, and four comments whose numbers disagreed with their constants were decided by Jerus — *"the code is correct, the comments are the outliers."*

## 25. Open questions

*Known, measured, and written down rather than discovered later. These are decisions, not defects. Eighty-seven stood here at 0.7.115, the last edition. Two have been answered outright since — a card that passes every gate, which has the investors' interest test as its last gate since 0.7.122, and where the Earth's file lives, the asset of a GitHub release since the commit after 0.7.122 — and two that the batches raised were answered inside the period (under the table); eight have moved and are rewritten, the next format among them, which 0.7.120 bumped and raised the floor with; and the batches from 0.7.116 to 0.7.123 opened nine more — ninety-four, reconciled against those batches' own lists on 11 October. Eighty-two stood here at 0.7.106; one was answered outright by 0.7.115, the money gate, by Jerus's decision A in 0.7.112 and 0.7.113, and part of another, a bump that refused no older save, in 0.7.108, two that those batches raised were answered inside their period, four moved, and the batches from 0.7.107 to 0.7.115 opened six more. Sixty-eight stood here at 0.7.69; two were answered outright by 0.7.106, both in 0.7.106 — a new city's lake and what Insane owes for its ground — with parts of several more, twelve moved, three of them under new names, and the batches from 0.7.70 to 0.7.106 opened sixteen more. Sixty-six stood here at 0.7.64; by 0.7.69 one had been answered, the saves made while fields were shared, which the grid converts, six had moved, and the grid batches had opened three more. Fifty-nine stood here at 0.7.54; none of them was answered outright by 0.7.64, though the gravest thing the scale study found, a land price that ran away at five and ten billion, was, and the land, water, map and fuel batches from 0.7.55 to 0.7.64 opened seven more. Fifty-three stood here two editions before that, three were answered by the price model, and the batches from 0.7.24 to 0.7.49 opened nine; more that they raised were answered inside the period, and are under the table too.*

| Question | What is measured |
| --- | --- |
| The city's size is hypersensitive to a small steady drag | Seven *hundredths* of a point added to the sick rate, with no crime at all, ends two seeds **9% smaller**; at a thousandth of crime's strength another ends 16% smaller. It predates every recent batch, and it means an eight-seed median can hide or invent a 10% effect. **The first thing to look at next.** |
| A bank with no lending business | **Half answered, and the other half closed by measurement.** On the default seed on 22 September the bank lends $13.2bn of $77.9bn deposited and runs at 69% of its capacity, on 28 September it ended with $131M lent of $293bn deposited, at 13%, on 1 October with $1k lent of $260.5bn, at 6%, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, with $234.7B lent of $162.3T, at 35%. Since 0.7.0 its spare cash earns the policy rate at the central bank rather than the world's 2% abroad, which changes what idle money pays and not how much of it there is. Nothing borrows below what the money costs the lender now, and over sixteen seeds failures went 5.0 → 0.0 median, recapitalisation $3.8bn → $0, months run at a loss 44–58% → 3–14%. The intended next step — a real intermediary funding domestic investment out of domestic savings — was measured and dropped: the bank lends **1.87% of its deposits** at home and runs at 31–49% of the capacity it already has. The city's savings are on the order of two hundred thousand times what its productive sector wants to borrow. It is demand-limited, not funding-limited, and deposit-gathering cannot change that. The open question is what a city this rich should be able to *do* with the money. |
| Cities that empty out, and nothing notices | Over sixteen seeds, nine had a population drawdown of more than half — median worst 57%, deepest 77% — and it is present in the control build too, so it is not new. Every one of those runs reports "Nothing. Every month passed the audit." The money conserves, the books foot, and a city loses three people in four with no finding raised. **The audit has no measure of a city shrinking**, nor of one running away the other way: on a Lean founding in 0.7.13, seed 0 ended owing $476.6T with 43.9% of its people out of work, and the playtest raised no finding. |
| Savings that cannot be spent | Read off a real screen, slot 3, month 2305, a city of 1,003,081. The 1,361 households in *out of work, EI run out* are each \$390 a month short, have **\$201,363 put by** — 516 months of cover — and have defaulted. **The reading is settled and the fix is not made**: the draw-down path is wired, and the discharge fires anyway because `discharge()` tests the *wage* against subsistence and never looks at savings — a bug in the opposite direction, and why a city with no poor people in it manufactures bankruptcies. It belongs with the supply work. Alongside it: orphan bands three orders of magnitude apart on a 2,300-month steady state. The prisoners' \$70 student loan that stood here was the balance they carried in — nothing collects a student loan except from a working family — and since 0.6.9 the freeze is the prisoner's own, no instalment and no interest. |
| The landlock predicate does not clear | `Game.isPrivateInvestmentLandLocked()` reads true at month 12 with 1,974,000 sq ft still free, and is still true at month 300. `landBlockedSectors` does not appear to be emptied, so the inbox notice "your businesses have nowhere to build" is very likely firing on cities with plenty of ground. The summary deliberately does not use it. |
| The households' trillion | **Half answered, and the half that is left is a supply question.** The hoard was diagnosed on 17 September — foreign coupons compounding abroad at 1.58% a year, \$2,649bn of them against \$584bn of every wage ever paid — and it was given somewhere to go: the coupon paid home, a wealth term in the plan, cars, boutiques and kitchens. Net worth oscillates now instead of climbing (432 → 137 → 128 → 214 months of GDP), and the default seed ends on 22 September with the households holding US\$197bn abroad against \$73.8bn at home, on 28 September US\$356bn against \$60.6bn, on 1 October US\$337bn against \$51.6bn, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, US\$287bn against \$63.6T, prices having risen 1,213-fold, where one seed used to hold US\$1.1tn against \$105bn. What is left: a quarter of every plan is never delivered and the undelivered quarter is the hoard, because the city cannot sell its households what they already want to buy; and `MARGINAL_PROPENSITY` has no life-cycle behind it — a fifth of discretionary income saved for ever, by everybody, at every age, is the third leak and the only one entirely untouched. |
| A lockup | The smallest prison is 300 cells for $360M; a city of 15,000 needs about twenty cells. No seed of that size built one, so 2,100–2,900 people were caught over 333 years and every one of them walked — and the cities are ten times the size now: 59,189 caught on the default seed on 22 September, all of them walking, with three stations covering 46% at the end. On 28 September the advisor built jails at last, four of them standing at the end with 344 people inside, and still 35,279 of the 79,592 caught over the run were not held; on 1 October it built none again, and all 69,581 caught walked, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, all 62,638. A 40-cell lockup, or cells in the headquarters, is what is left to decide. |
| Rent per cell should follow the door | The housing match bills landlords by unit size and puts a pensioner in the smallest flat that fits; the household books still charge families and the retired the city's *average* door. So **Senior living alone** is the one cell in trouble in every seed — −\$46 to −\$294 a month for the first decade, \$8,970 owed at the ceiling, locked out — and since the sixth band, **Elder living alone** beside it is the one to watch first when senior care is short. The people outside the families already pay their own door share; families and pensioners do not. |
| Full general care is worth less than it was | A fully served adult used to die at 0.15% a year. They now die at 0.232% — the halved base rate plus a sliver of illness — because the ×3 swing is gone. The halving does not make up for the good end. The lever is the halving, not the ring. |
| The investment planner ignores every ratio | In most sectors it costs a new building at nameplate capacity — real estate is the exception and the pattern to copy; since 0.7.18 every planner that builds posts asks whether the city could staff them, which is a gate, not a cost. It also under-builds shops, and it has never built a college, so the student machinery is only exercised in a harness — and, since 0.6.9, in a playtest that is told to build schools (`-Dplaytest.schools=true`). |
| The supply wall | Why can the shops fill only three quarters of a plan in a city with a hundred billion of unspent demand standing in front of them? Retail's binding constraint is coverage times the operating rate, and the operating rate in the default playtest is about half. On the default seed on 22 September the shops fill **77% of the queue they could serve at all**, running at 77%, and the city gets 4.2% of the groceries it asks for, on 28 September 54%, running at 54%, and 2.5%, on 1 October 56%, running at 57%, and 2.6%, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, 44%, running at 44%, and 5.7% of the baskets it asked for at the shelf's price, 79% of the city short at the end; whatever is not delivered is banked, by construction, because the settle has nowhere else to put it. The kitchens are a second door and took median hunger from 36% to 22%. The dearer basket — a rich household buying a dearer basket rather than more of them, since nobody eats twice — is the only consumption item left, and Jerus's call was to take it through the new sectors first. Since 0.7.43 what is asked for is baskets at a price rather than a want thirty times what the shops serve, so the gap is no longer inflated by a want nobody would pay for, and what is short is split into the priced out and the shelves left short ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)). |
| Who is playing | The playtest's advisor built five wind farms and two cemeteries for 176,000 people over three centuries, not because it ranks constraints badly but because the loop skips six to a hundred and twenty months between looks, averaging fifty-four — deliberately, the length a person actually clicks. So **every number the harness has ever reported was measured in a city in crisis from neglect**. A second player, `-Dplaytest.player=attentive`, checks in yearly with the same advice: over eight seeds **418,948 people against 148,479, $2,125M a month against $544M**, hunger 18% against 43%, sickness 7.8% against 23.1% — and a labour ceiling the neglected city never reached, at 89% fill. The default is bit-identical to before the flag, so every ensemble in the record stays comparable. And one that cannot be explained: over 600 months the *neglected* city ends bigger and richer than the attentive one while being sicker and hungrier, and over 4,000 the ordering reverses decisively. Something about the early game. And the stand-in player falls behind on police late in a run: that, through crime and migration, is why the default city ended a few percent smaller on 0.7.11, and in 0.7.14's runs every seed that ended with police coverage of 40% or more had 5 to 19 points more unemployment. |
| Bounded world demand | An unbounded export market at a fixed floor means the single best export is built for ever and nothing else ever is: 179 Fabrication Works and zero Machine Works over a run, then nineteen Locomotive Works and two hundred and forty Commercial Vehicle Plants the day those could be sold abroad. The narrow fix was to say the world does not buy vans or wagon sets; the general fix touches four sectors and would change every existing city, and it is still its own batch. |
| Shells, and a banned firm | A sector with no plant can keep a dust of debt and a pantry it can neither use nor sell for up to 3,200 months, defaulting on its interest every month — 78–96% of all the defaults for want of cash on 0.7.12, and little money, 1,276 of 1,535 on the default seed on 28 September, 616 of 663 on 1 October, and 657 of 1,616 on 5 October, at 0.7.49. Nothing winds it up, where a real company in that state is liquidated. And a banned firm with an empty till cannot restock, because the ban shuts the working-capital line the rules keep open for everyone else. Since 0.7.113, its investors asked the whole cost, Materials' longest spell as a shell went from 257 months to 488, from month 860, and its longest run of defaults from 83 to 298, 264 of them banned: the one figure the whole cost made worse, which the iron batches of 0.7.120 and 0.7.123 did not reach: at 0.7.123 Materials went under whole eleven times over the playtest and ended it 353 months into a run of losses. |
| Output does not read its inputs | A maker's output does not read the inputs it bought, so holding its inputs to what it can pay for would make goods out of nothing — on 0.7.12's runs it would have skipped $393B of inputs with the same output — and a maker's inputs are bought whole for that reason. A production recipe would be a sixth throttle beside the five ratios (Jerus: *"Buy inputs whole, todo"*). |
| Where the companies' spare cash goes | By `OutwardInvestment`'s rule, mostly abroad: after 0.7.12's eight default runs the companies held $6.7T abroad against $1.7T in their tills, and 26–32% of the bonds; on the default seed on 28 September they ended with $928bn abroad against $233bn in their tills, on 1 October with $837bn against $209bn, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, with $386.4T against $98.7T. And the household cells' rebalancing on the book barely fires, $0.47M offered over eight runs, because a cell short of money has usually sold in its waterfall already. |
| The young bank, and a plant that loses money before interest | Under every failure 0.7.8 left, one sector held 30–73% of the book, and since 0.7.12 concentration is priced rather than capped (answered below). What still fails the bank is the young one, on the $32M of capital its founding branch brings, before month 1,000, when Manufacturing or Automotive goes under; a plant retired at material price can take a sector past the line within months, and on autopilot seed 7 a $44M backstop met a $21M bank. The last change of 0.7.12 took the autopilot's failures from 4 to 9, and that was not traced. The single-industry multiplier the price uses is Basel III's 1.25, set for large financial institutions, and is kept and flagged. Branch openings between the minimum and the target were 35% of the default runs' openings on 0.7.11, and left open the old trap of recapitalising a bank by opening branches; since 0.7.19 a branch opens only for its customers and their fees, and the default cities of 1 and 5 October opened none past their charters in 4,005 months, but the band itself has not been measured again. The row that stood here, *a plant that loses money before interest is still lent for*, now meets a price off the curve at the leverage the plant would leave the sector at (0.7.8) and a door shut past the default point (0.7.12); it has not been measured again since 0.7.2. |
| The default curve's one number | `BusinessDebtManager.ASSET_VOLATILITY` 0.25, the spread of fortunes among a sector's firms, from the Merton and KMV literature's 20–35% and not tuned to any result: at 0.20 the curve is steeper, fewer defaults under the line and more past it, and at 0.35 flatter. Jerus's to settle. |
| The bank's target sits at its cap | `Bank.MAX_BUFFER` binds in every seed: the worst year a bank lives through was 38–109% of its weighted book on 0.7.8's runs, so its target is 16.5% throughout and covers a sixth of it. On the default seed on 28 September the worst year on record was 12.06% of the book, on 1 October 22.24%, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, 33.40%, the target 16.5% each time. |
| The quarter prices the shortfall desk past the default point | The shortfall desk lends on the month's leverage while the price reads the quarter, which was Jerus's choice, so over 0.7.8's default eight 1,435 of its loans were priced past the default point, 73% of them Luxury Retail in the high month of its restock. Pricing the shortfall desk on the month, or on the lower of the two, would stop it, and it is his call. On 28 September 16 loans were written past the default point over the run, on 1 October 16 again, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, 44. |
| Deposits are not on the bank's books | The bank counts the city's savings as deposits for its capacity without holding them, the one stated simplification in its header. It is the root of the worst stress finding of 0.7.7 — held at 10%, a recovered bank paid savers its chosen 3.5% over the world's 2%, the households brought US$2.7bn home into a city of about 2,000, and prices ran to 5.64 times founding before they unwound — and the reason the Balance sheet page carries deposits as a memo line. Putting them on the books moves the bank's three statements, the audit's pools, every payment between a household and a business and the central bank's interest on reserves, and it is its own batch (Jerus: *"Memo now, own batch later"*). |
| The city keeps its bank | A resolved bank's stake falls only as it sells new shares (Jerus: *"New issues only"*), so the city keeps its bank for decades: a median 58.8% twenty-five years after a default resolution, and 91–100% in the autopilot and held setups (0.7.14); the default seed of 1 October, resolved in month 664, still held 65.0% twenty-five years on and 62.2% at the end, and that of 5 October, resolved eight times from month 2,678, held 69.3% twenty-five years after the first and all of it at the end. A sell-down like the United Kingdom's out of NatWest, by placements, a trading plan and directed buybacks from 2015 to 2025, is Jerus's if he wants one; the player can sell the rescue book by hand, since 0.7.39 from the bank's page under the fund. Beside it: the fund never pays for a rescue, by his word, and at a 300% dial all 66 months on advances were resolutions' while the fund held about $500B; it can pass 10% of a company without buying when that company's buybacks shrink the shares under it; and TARP's $25B cap is left out, because nothing converts it into this game's money. |
| The landlords' test is per building | So a landlord whose profit is under its mortgages' principal borrows the difference from the shortfall desk — $1.46B on one seed of 0.7.11 — and the 10% city's insurance losses came from the same place. And a landlord with an empty till can wait on its 15% down payment: 250 months on 0.7.12's seed 5, with households there going without a home for 161 of them. |
| Size-level slack in the housing retirement rule | A distressed landlord sold 5,800 of 13,272 homes in seven months because the rule asked whether the segment had spare doors and the slack was spread over four sizes. Guarded — nobody sells a door while somebody has nowhere — not fixed. Whether a given set of households fits a given set of doors is a packing question and no comparison of totals answers it. |
| Every planner assumes the ground is free | The fields plan off the crop market, the houses off the jobs, the fabricators off the steel price, the railway off the freight nobody is carrying, and none of them can see that they are bidding for the same land. The rule that stopped the farms crowding out housing is a patch on one sector, not a mechanism, and the railway and the assembly plants are the hungriest for ground the game has had. A land market the planners bid into. Since 0.7.107 the player can hold ground for the ones that need it, at a price the player names ([zoning](#18-land)): a hand on the problem, not the mechanism. |
| Converting for land does not push the currency | The 0.7.6 brief asked that whatever pressure the exchange puts on the rate when the treasury buys dollars apply to land too, and there is none to apply: a treasury purchase of dollars is the financing item below the line, which the pressure never reads, so buying reserves has never moved the rate and `ForeignCheck`'s section 14 asserts an equality with nothing. Right for reserves, whose dollars stay in the country; arguably wrong for land, which the world sold the city and was paid for in dollars the city had to buy, so a city that spends a decade buying ground sees no weakening for it. The fix is small — count the dollars paid abroad for land as an outflow the pressure reads, for converting or for both — and it is Jerus's call. |
| A third of meals out, and two businesses that cannot fail | `MOST_MEALS_EATEN_OUT` is a third and nothing measures whether that is the right number; on the best seeds a quarter of the city eats out and the kitchens build to the cap. Restaurants finish seven seeds of eight with zero write-downs at 2.00% credit, the profile of Retail and Agriculture, the sectors that have never gone under — a business that cannot fail is not much of a decision. Luxury Retail is the opposite, going under more often than anything but Mining and Materials, its two buildings never sized against a city's luxury budget, and **it still has no harness of its own**: every bootstrap fault the kitchens hit had already been paid for there, and only `CarCheck`, since 0.7.47, and `BuildingDataCheck`, since 0.7.90, name `Automotive`. |
| A car's loan is a bridge | Jerus wanted a car to cost something to keep, which gives *cut back expenses* something to cut and makes a financed car a real commitment, and since 0.7.49 it does: $2.00 of the world's fuel a journey, forty a month, imported — since 0.7.62 off the refiners' tanks first, since 0.7.78 at wholesale and since 0.7.83 at the pump — weighed by the owners against the fare and by a buyer in a car's full cost ([transport](#21-transport--vehicles)). What is left is a car loan with a term, if the credit cycle is meant to be felt rather than merely recorded: today's loan is repaid out of spare cash within a month or two. |
| The railway's allowed return is a constant | A regulated network's allowed return follows the cost of its money; here `TARGET_RETURN` is 1.2% a month whatever the credit desk charges, and the link runs the other way — dear money keeps the band wide. Alongside it: the railway settles at 38–43% of the lorry rate in the ensemble and has been seen quoting 99% of a lorry, which leaves shippers barely better off; and rail haulage does not reduce a sector's van need, while Construction draws its materials on demand and so reads as moving nothing. |
| Small orders wait behind large ones | Bromilow's weights give a big building the bigger crew, and Jerus's rule when he left it was that small orders waiting is accepted (0.7.17). What it looks like to a player: a new city that orders its depots beside a coal plant gives them a fiftieth of the plant's crew, and `ForeignCheck`'s founding sat at about 1,000 people for fifteen years; in his city the lead-time gate refused Industry for 94 sector-months and Materials for 99 behind his 47 care complexes. **The first thing to try on the PC.** And nothing caps a site's crew at the pace a building could go at alone, Bromilow's K, so since 0.7.22 an order the player sets can hand the city's whole share to its first site. |
| Unemployment moves twice as much | Since the builders lay off the crews their work does not need (0.7.17), unemployment moves about twice as much from month to month: the 95th percentile of the default eight's monthly move went from 0.81 points to 1.93, and the schools city's from 0.64 to 1.53. |
| A city short of hands | When the best-paid fill moves workers at once and the wage walks after them, a city short of hands pays first: Jerus's year-149 city ran a deficit of $9.87B in the first year against $5.10B, and was in surplus from the third (0.7.18). A young town that waits for staff builds late and then fast — `MonetaryCheck`'s town, without its re-cause, opened its Boutique and Diner at month 16 rather than 5 and doubled through the window — and the ensembles' median does not show it. A default city is short of college workers all its life, at a median college fill of 0.57. The 7.5% of unskilled arrivals is Ontario's figure, to be replaced by a Canada-wide one. And Food Processing, whose own banner once measured an 80% floor as wrong for plants of four posts, was held on staffing in all 120 months of his city; whether that is the intended cost is Jerus's. The rule that a band nobody can fill takes no posts is dormant: it binds only for a band with no way in, and anything that closes arrivals to a band in play would wake it (0.7.18). |
| The builders' tax at its edges | Three consequences of the rules as the law has them (0.7.19). A House mostly bears its tax, being worth more with its plot than the rental rebate's $450,000. An oversupplied city's landlords sell empty buildings, because their rents are rebated and their repairs taxed: the free-tuition city of `EducationCheck` sold 53 of its 120 Low-Rise; Jerus: *"Leave as the law has it"*. |
| The city held at 25% | The stress city held at a 25% dial is smaller since 0.7.17, with households left with nowhere in every seed, and two of its collapsed seeds reload with differences in the sixth to eighth significant figure that are not traced. Since 0.7.19 it collapses, 428 people at the median against 8,168, because it had lived on the deposit cap's strain and the window, both removed on purpose. Jerus: *"Let it fail"*; it stays a stress case whose findings are watched, not a city required to recover. Its drift in the paper and the bonds predates 0.7.19 and is not fixed. |
| A demolition's edges | Since 0.7.106 a quarter of a demolished building's material comes back, the middle of the 20 to 30% the US EPA found recovered in 1996 (answered under the table), a citation the batch quoted from memory, with no network, for Jerus to confirm (EPA530-R-98-010); by weight, and mostly downcycled, so by value it is still generous. Beside it, buying out the builders' own depots pays a large business loss and takes their capacity with it; FAR's settlement costs and Ontario's injurious affection are left out by choice, having no figure in the model; and the player's own demolitions are drawn in the red the game keeps for failures. Jerus's calls. |
| What the short lines lost | Text in three layers moved the long paragraphs behind an (i), and the mockups' popover wording dropped some clauses: Construction's *"the only sector in the city with a liability of that shape"*, the tax dial's *"every sector's and every band's move rides whichever base is its own"*, and the Government's *"a bridge that hides its own gap is not a bridge"*, kept where there are movements (0.7.21). Whether any comes back is Jerus's call; this page could carry them. The founding panel's name field shows no focus ring, only the caret. |
| A young city's growth swings | The header's GDP tile reads real growth over twelve months from month 24, and a young city's swings hard — minus 66% at month 30, plus 10% at month 70 — because its first year's output is mostly its own orders (0.7.21). The tile shows the model's figure; its tooltip could say why. |
| The decision log's edges | The log has no cap and is saved whole, and the playtest's advisor adds a line for each tax or paper call; the advisor's own steps of the policy rate are not in it, because it moves the rate by a setter the log does not watch; full screen covers the toasts and the inbox, by a call made while Jerus slept; and a wrapped legend can push the overview strip under the window's edge in full screen (0.7.23). |
| Four small things about the CSV | Left for Jerus by 0.7.16: an episodes CSV, not built, because the list is short and its worst figure is in a different unit for each kind of episode; full precision, not taken, so that the CSV and the text always agree; a friendlier line when a CSV is open in Excel and cannot be written; and an Excel set to a comma decimal, which opens a comma CSV as one column. English-Canadian Windows is fine. |
| What no harness looks at | The screens are in `ui/`, which the suite leaves out, and cannot run in the cloud, so they are checked by eye on the PC. Since the redraws every screen works out its figures and words in methods that draw nothing, and the model reads they rest on are held — the sector pages by `SectorFlowCheck` and `BuildCardCheck`, their old lines by `SectorBooksCheck`, Policy's previews by `PolicyPreviewCheck` and the rule's at each strictness by `CentralBankCheck`, City History's by `ChartCheck`, the Bank's arithmetic by `BankCheck`, the map's by `MapCheck`, and every new getter after a load by `ReadPathCheck` — but not their drawing, and the words were composed only by the implementers' probes on a 600-month and a 2,400-month city. What has been seen there: 0.7.10's founding screen, which Jerus checked on 24 September; every tab once in a new city, and Build, People, History and the inbox in his city of a million, on the play-through of 0.7.19 on 30 September; 0.7.20's own fixes the same night, bar three things the remote session could not reach — Esc, the header's price tooltip and a toast; 0.7.24's frame and Build; 0.7.32's Finances and 0.7.33's Bank on 1 October; and what Jerus played of 0.7.39, which found what 0.7.40 and 0.7.41 fixed. Still to look at, every batch's list in its record: 0.7.4 to 0.7.23 as the last edition listed them, bar what has been drawn anew since; the cards, the land office, People and Household money, Services, Infrastructure, Sectors and Government (0.7.25 to 0.7.31); the buttons, the ladder's broken *later* and the Sectors list's one line (0.7.34); Trade, Policy and City History (0.7.35 to 0.7.37); the small charts' lanes, the fare's dial card and the drawer's cover and parity colours (0.7.38); the fund as a brokerage (0.7.39); Build › Funding, the typed ask, the charts that no longer creep and served everywhere (0.7.40, 0.7.41); the anchor on the header and on Money, Promises' Food page, THE SHELF, WHO GOES SHORT and History's new series (0.7.45); the leverage chart, Construction's materials and a 0.7.45 save loaded (0.7.46); Automotive, the Real Estate hold, the property offset's (i) and Government's trailing year (0.7.47); THE WITHDRAWAL and the fund's marks (0.7.48); Transit's riders by reason, the fare card's fuel, Government's transit lines and People's and Trade's fuel (0.7.49); a chart under the pointer as months land and as its page is torn down (0.7.50); and Build's three-line cards, *Build all three* held for land or on credit, and Services' gate with its posts (0.7.51); and THE RULE card's strictness ladder under the target's, the words that follow its thumb, at 1,389 × 868, and NEEDS YOU's PRICES row off Standard (0.7.52); and a city past 2.1 billion people on every screen that counts it, its money in quadrillions (0.7.53, 0.7.54); THE WORLD on the founding panel (0.7.56); the office's interim nine of forty (0.7.57, gone since); the Desalination Plant's card, the no-coast page and Services' amber limit line (0.7.59); the land office round its map, Expand at 60 frames a second, the hover card, and Build's LAND FREE and its pages' Buys (0.7.61); the Oil Well and Oil Refinery cards, the oil no-deposit page and fuel on Trade (0.7.62); and the map drawn from what the city has, a new city's bank alone on bare ground, and *Buy the cheapest* (0.7.64); and the grid's office and map — the places as rows, the chips' counts, the empty place's row, the size's blocks, every area in m² or km² and every ground price a m², the shortcut naming its place, the faint block lines, the hatch cut round the city's ground, the place numbers, a converted save's first look, and Expand panned at 60 frames a second on a big city (0.7.67 to 0.7.69); and the road cards' life and land bars, the Gravel Road card's paving block and the construction page's *N paving · no stop* (0.7.70); the three centres' cards and their words (0.7.71); the map's network, track and yards and its legend's Railway (0.7.72) and its gravel bridges (0.7.77); Build's AUTOMATIC BUILDING, its chip and its two notices (0.7.73, 0.7.77); every business's and the bank's Summary and Statement, the equity in columns, the debt by kind and every building at every gate, drawn here only through a mirror in Java2D (0.7.74, 0.7.75); the Oil Refinery's card, Trade's petrol and the railway's diesel (0.7.76); and the oil's and the map's from 0.7.78 to 0.7.92, drawn here only through mirrors in Java2D — the fifteen units' cards and their lines, Refining's page and its held-back crude, the Filling Station's card, Retail's forecourt lines and Trade's price at the pump, the Oil page's dry ground, lift and At sea lines, oil storage, the ports and the no-coast page's quay, the oil platforms and pipelines, THE RULE's loose steps' words, AUTOMATIC BUILDING's limit and its toggle, the land office's opening zoom, and the map painted from the street plans, its runs and ramps, its packed buildings dimmed and its legend's notes; and from 0.7.93 to 0.7.106 the Oil page's two pools and its At sea lines, the refinery's picture and its strip, the oil page's tiles, wells, chart, units and products and the reserve's Fill and Release, the campus, the works on the shore, the oil at sea and the boats on their lanes at 60 frames a second, Build's power card over its life and the no-deposit page's pay-back line, automatic building's payback in the inbox, Government's four lines and its Fuel duty, Policy's Fuel page, Refining's run and the crude units' pills, Build's care ring with its priced out, the demolition card's 25%, the water card's words and the founding screen's Insane tooltip — drawn here, where at all, through mirrors in Java2D; and from 0.7.107 to 0.7.115 Policy › Zoning's ground, its zones' pages and its forest law, the hub's fifth card, Build's LAND FREE and the land office's zoned line, NEEDS YOU's zoned words, City History's sand flags, a refused save's line on the slot list and the investors' whole-cost words on Sectors, composed by the implementers' probes, 95 of zoning's strings measured to fit at 1,389 × 868; and from 0.7.116 to 0.7.123 the founding panel on the real Earth — its chips, the search, Random spot, the globe turning and zooming to 150 m, and its card — the map's far view on the Earth and its hover's place and geology, the build card's interest words and the Sectors screen's sixth column, the Electric Arc Furnace's, the Iron Mine's and the integrated route's seven cards, Trade's *Iron ore* and *Scrap*, Iron & Steel's page and its *Old metal* lines, and the load screen's refused slots, drawn here only as the globe's pixels and composed by the implementers' probes, the hover's lines and the card's interest words measured to fit; one place name of 7,342, *Tarabulus*, has a letter the game's face lacks. Every screen that keeps a set of opened lines — the Bank, Sectors and Government — keeps them through a month; the rest snap shut on the month's redraw. |
| A small call from 0.7.4 | Whether the inflation target should be staged and applied with the rate, rather than taking effect at once as the ceiling does. The other call that stood here, the bank on the profit tax page, was answered in 0.7.36: WHO PAYS lists it, taxed at Retail's rate, in arrears. |
| The term premium is Jerus's to settle | `DebtManager.TERM_PREMIUM_10Y` … `50Y` at 0.50, 0.90, 1.15, 1.35 and 1.50 points were set to have a curve at all, and the shape — linear from a year to ten, linear between the entries, flat past fifty — is the implementer's reading of the brief. The world's curve reads the same table, so the numbers price dollar paper too. |
| The "spread is gone" sale can hardly ever fire | The households' yield is read off today's curve, which sits on the dial, and the deposit rate is, since 0.7.7, the share of the dial the bank chooses, so the paper nearly always out-yields deposits and the sale does not happen in a real run; `HoldersCheck` exercises it by handing it a zero yield, a fixture standing next to its condition. And 0.7.2 saw it fire anyway: in `BankCheck`'s settle month the deposit rate rose past the paper's yield, 6.825% against 6.726%, and the desk bought $1,080k back. Whether the rule should read the coupon locked in at issue is Jerus's. |
| The currency's new numbers are untuned | `ForeignAccounts.RATE_PULL` 4 and `CapitalFlows.MAX_SPREAD` .25 are both marked in the source as Jerus's numbers to settle. Four was chosen because six gave the loop a gain of 1.44 and sent one seed to its guard; it buys two thirds of the support a credible real rate used to buy. And the rate term acts from month one, before the trade pressure is allowed to, which predates the batch. Since 0.7.42 beside them: `EXPECTED_REVERSION` .15, how fast investors expect a currency away from parity to come back, and the anchored drift at credibility times the target, both the design study's ([the currency](#16-prices-the-currency--the-world)). |
| The exchange rate goes NaN in a city with no trade | A founding left without the advisor goes NaN at month 26, on 0.7.2 and 0.7.3 alike: `pressure()`, `absorption()` and `realRateDifferential()` read NaN first, and the currency's guards pass it through, because a clamp hands a NaN straight on. Found by the 0.7.3 batch and not traced to the root. |
| Should the defence answer only a crisis? | The founders' billion went on structural deficits, not crises (0.7.2): every default seed sold more than half of it and six all but 1%, while the playtest's advisor bought it back with the treasury's cash — one seed sold US\$1.29B of a US\$1B vault, and held at a 50% dial US\$625B. On the default seed on 22 September half of it was gone by month 726. Since 0.7.10 the founders leave US\$25M, and on 28 September half of that was gone by month 753, on 1 October by month 40, and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, by month 38. A defence that waited for a run would need a rule for what a run is; the hot money's panic, a fragile position and a shock, is the nearest the model has. |
| Interest on reserves compounds without limit at a held extreme rate | Held at 30% or 50%, M0 reaches 10^8 to 3×10^14 $B while prices stay near one: spare cash earning the rate in new money that becomes spare cash, and the households' savings, earning it too, reach 10^7 to 10^14 years of income. And the central bank's equity ended below zero on every default seed measured through 0.7.3, mostly the loss carried from paying interest on reserves: minus $1.1B to minus $3.3B on 0.7.2's eight, minus $2.39B on the default seed on 22 September. On 28 September, at a dial whose median over the run was 0.44%, that seed's ended at $32.1M — the vault it counts as its asset, less $1.48M of loss carried — on 1 October, at a median of 0.46%, at $13.9M, less $4.94M; and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, at a median of 3.18%, at $221.7B, less $173.2B. |
| Nothing limits the city's own paper at home | The price of the city's paper stops at the dial plus ten points and the term premium; the bank buys whatever the households leave, funded at a window with no cap; debt service is a promise, paid past the advances ceiling; and only abroad does a window shut. So a city can compound its paper without limit: Lean seed 0, rolling twenty-year paper for cash, ended owing $476.6T (0.7.13); held at 25% the city borrows from its bank to buy the bank's preferred, $962T of it with the advances peaking at $20.4 quadrillion, which Jerus kept (*"Keep as built"*), and five of eight Insane seeds spiral on the same missing limit (0.7.14); and the holdings dial at 100% makes the central bank the buyer when nobody else is without limiting what the city sells (0.7.15). A market limit — a buyer's refusal, or a debt-service rule at home — is Jerus's to design. |
| The dear-care city is hungrier | `HealthCheck`'s line (0.7.12): read over a year, the city charging fifteen times the founding fees was 8.4 points hungrier than the free one on 28 September, against a tolerance of five; 77 points on 0.7.17's tree and 39 on 0.7.18's, 40.0 on 1 October, 10.1 on 5 October with hunger counted in baskets, and 19.7 at 0.7.99. Since 0.7.100 a builders' depot stands with the poor city (Jerus's A14), whose first depot had still been on site when the fee was set: the gap fell to 5.4, 0.1 priced out of a basket and 5.3 short on the shelf, still red by 0.4; and since 0.7.102 it passes, at 0.7.103 by −1.8, 3.2 priced out and −5.0 on the shelf, on the shelves' timing, the fee's rule unchanged. His three ways stand open: read the money half alone, which moves the premise; take the line as it reads; or have a fixture keep the shelves. Of its hungry as 0.7.12 traced them, a quarter were priced out of care and a fifth billed care their household row had already paid for — the documented shortcut in `HouseholdBalance` — and nearly half had money for food after their fixed bills and still planned less, which is untraced and the first thing to trace. |
| The price model's three fails | On sixteen seeds under five policies the price model passed 22 of 25 criteria (0.7.44, which stands for 0.7.45), and three fail, each for a reason measured ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)): a 0% dial held from month 600 runs at 7.07% a year, because the city meant to be slack was taking off — keep the window and read it beside the month-1,800 hold, 3.16%, or move it to a mature city; a 0% dial in a hot young city gives a burst and never an accelerating rate, which the wage curve's lack of a growth term rules out — change the premise or add the term the design study rejected; and a boom holds year-on-year inflation over 10% for 12 or 13 months against a limit under 12, as the shelf runs from its floor to its cap, 30–50% in six to twelve months, about 11% on the index. Beside them, the anchor's own numbers are the design study's and Jerus's to confirm: credibility won in 60 months and lost in 24, from 0.25 to 0.95 and seeded at 0.80, a point's tolerance and four more for a full miss; the satiation at half again over the floor; the elasticity of .4; luxury's weight held to 15%; the real hurdle floored at a quarter of the rate; and the voucher's test at half of what a household has after its fixed bills. On the final model trust bottomed at 0.76 over 125 months held, so a red PRICES row had to be caused by hand. 0.7.49's sixteen ran at 2.22% under the autopilot, and its hot spells still fail. On the world's land, scored like for like, the ensemble passed 22 of 26 criteria at 0.7.62 and again at 0.7.64, the hot spells among the four that fail. On the block grid it passed 21 at 0.7.67, a fifth failing and seed 14 collapsing under its test player, and 23 once the player was mended: the boom's longest spell over 10% passes at four months at most, and so does the high rate's inflation against its twin, and three fail — the 0% dial held from month 600, at 4.48% with a peak of 17.95% a year; the hot young city's burst; and the high rate's unemployment, because its AUTO2 twins now run more people out of work, 15.1% from month 600 to 1,200 against 10.4% at 0.7.67, so the 15% rate shows as people leaving rather than as people idle. At 0.7.71, its roads chosen over their life and childcare resized, it passed 23 again, the same three failing. At 0.7.99 the boom's spell went red again, seeds 8 and 13 spending 13 and 16 months over 10% after month 120. Since 0.7.100 two premises are restated as the model claims them (Jerus's A27; [the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)): the hot young city passes, asked for a burst that persists and does not accelerate; and the slack city, held at 0% from month 1,800 and read against its twin, reads red, 1.41 points a year over it with a spell of 13 months, its currency drifting weaker against its twin's all window, 1.51 times at twenty years in seed 0, where the design's uncovered interest parity was to stop a held 0% compounding — model or premise, Jerus's. At 0.7.106 the ensemble passes 22 of 26, the boom's spell, the slack city, a high-rate criterion by three seeds and the shock's population by seven people red. At 0.7.113, every order asked the interest on its whole cost, it passes 24: the high rate's seeds over a point fall from three to one and the shock's city reaches 15,332 people where it reached 13,726, at least three quarters of its baseline's now, both green, while the boom's longest spell over 10% runs a median 20 months against 14, and the slack city 1.80 points a year over its twin against 2.07, both still red. Not tuned. At 0.7.120, iron at the world's price, it passes 20 of 25, the hot young city's second criterion having no burst to judge: that city's burst rises in its second half, 1.83 points over its first where 0.51 had passed, and the high rate's seeds over a point go back to three and its towns under three quarters of their baseline, the steel chain gone (the steel jobs under a high rate, below); at 0.7.123, 21, the boom's spell, the slack city, the hot young city's rise and the high rate's seeds red. |
| Grocers at their floor lose money | The shelf's floor is its opening price at the expected level or its stock's cost and half again, and the margin over cost does not pay the shops' staff at operating rates of .3 to .65: seed 12 of the ensemble lost $0.5–1.1M a month from month 490 and seed 9 $2.1M at month 700, selling shops at a loss in a boom, and `Retail.estimatedMonthlyProfit()` counted no wages until 0.7.106, which counts a shop's and a station's posts at today's wages in the investors' test (Jerus's A18), so the grocers no longer borrow for shops whose margin does not pay their staff; the floor itself still pays none. Wages in the floor were measured to empty the shelves, 81% hungry, so the answer is Jerus's. And the floor's catch-up, half the gap a month for a shelf under it, hides shortages: of the autopilot's months with the clearing price over 1.2 times the floor, 41% had the shelf within 1% of the floor, and seed 9 from month 728 had a clearing price two to fifty-five times the floor with the shelf on it. |
| A held high rate pushes rent up | Through the landlords' mortgage interest, by Jerus's 0.7.11 rule, *"keep it"*: with the lender reading the real rate since 0.7.44 the mortgaged stock is larger, and in the diagnosis's run a dial held at 15% for ten years sent rent up 38–57% in three seeds. The ensemble's high-rate criterion passed with two seeds over a point. |
| The fare's cap is a tax on the car-less | Since 0.7.49 the car-less in reach ride at any fare, so a dearer fare loses owners and keeps them, and revenue rises almost in line with the fare: at the \$50 cap the 2,400-month city takes D\$97.6M a month, a pass 27.6% of an unskilled household's take-home, and its households hold about 114 months of take-home, so nothing stops it for years. The fare card says who is paying it; whether the cap should be lower, or the car-less's fare means-tested, is Jerus's. |
| One car a household, and fuel outside the index | A household holds one car at most, which is what leaves 73% of the 2,400-month city's workers without one of their own and puts a couple's second earner on the bus. And the households' fuel, a real import since 0.7.49, a good the city can refine since 0.7.62, petrol since 0.7.76, at wholesale since 0.7.78 and bought at the pump since 0.7.83, is in no part of the price index, so a weak currency that dears every drive moves no measured inflation. Both are the transit batch's calls, left for Jerus. At wholesale and at the pump's 1.32 times it, a drive's fuel is under half the default fare, so no owner takes the bus on cost alone; the ones who ride are the jam's. Since 0.7.103 a fuel duty is the player's to set, nothing by default, and moves owners toward the bus as it rises. |
| A reloaded city's first month | Since 0.7.46 a save carries what a reloaded city had read as nothing or struck again, and the playtest's twin parts nowhere; but in the 2,400-month research city 12 of 229 series still differed a month after a load, by at most 8.3e-5, the residual nobody had traced. A reloaded city drifted a little in its first month at 0.7.27 too, 112,810 people against 112,812. Since 0.7.63 two figures only the month sets are saved — the ratios each sector's month was run at, and the graduates waiting for the census to carry their loans — and city600, city2400 and Jerus's city, each reloaded at twelve points two months apart, play on to the bit in every pool the money audit reads and in their people, where city2400 had come back 0.23 units adrift and Jerus's 7,447 short. Whether every one of the 229 series now agrees was not measured again. And since 0.7.74 the statements read what only the month in memory has — the interest by instrument and the debt by kind (0.7.74), how each kind moved and the stock's revaluation (0.7.75) — so a reloaded business shows its debt as one line for a month and its debt's movements as not counted for two, and the page says so; and the bank's sheet after a load re-reads its deposits, moving $131.9M between two of its borrowings' lines in the test player's city at month 364, its totals and its year ago unchanged. Since 0.7.102 the investors' last word crosses a save and the not-counted rule reads a mark of its own; since 0.7.103 a stack emptied keeps its place across a save, where a city saved with every gravel road paved had parted from its twin within months; and since 0.7.106 a load puts back the central bank's lines and the fund's transfer, which a refresh before the first month had read as nothing. Two remain: Jerus's autosave at month 416 loses 535.74 to *Not accounted for* in its first month after a load, as it did before; and the city's repairs, its arrears paid down and the reserve's crude, 0.7.102's lines, are not put back in the month's accounts until the month runs, which matters only if something refreshes the books first. |
| A newer save in an older build | The save format guards a newer city opened in an older build, and since 0.7.45 the house practice has been to append to an array and leave the number where it is — at 30 until 0.7.57 moved it to 31 for the land, which an older build would have read wrongly, and at 31 since through the water rights, the drivers' fuel and the graduates: a 0.7.45 build handed a 0.7.49 save refuses its cells, its care and the households' statement whole, at widths it does not know, which is the very downgrade the number exists to catch. The standing rule asks only that an older save load in a newer build. Whether the format should have moved is Jerus's. Since then it has moved where an older build would load wrongly, as the rule asks: 32 for the grid (0.7.67), 33 for each company's paid-in capital (0.7.75), whose wider register a format-32 build refuses whole, and 34 for petrol and diesel (0.7.76), which a format-33 build would drop; 35 for the oil in two pools (0.7.93), 36 for the old world's ground (0.7.99), 37 for scrap split from ore (0.7.120) and 38 for a city on the real Earth (0.7.121). And since 10 October Jerus's rule is that an older save need not load until the game is published, a bump refusing one cleanly; but the loader refused only a format newer than its own or older than 21, so a bump alone refused no older save, until 0.7.108 gave the loader its floor, which a bump raises, and which 0.7.120 raised to 37 ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)). What stands is the other way, a newer save in an older build, which the number guards and an appended array still slips past. |
| The fund's two marks | Over the default withdrawal the fund sold its market book at fair value, as its design said, and in a small city nobody bid there; since 0.7.102 the withdrawal's part is asked at the desk's bid (answered under the table). What stands: the rule's 70/30 mix reads the last trade while the fund's worth reads its mark, so a stale share is valued two ways in one fund; and at 0% the default city ends 13% smaller, the transfer being real revenue there. |
| A city buys its ground in many small offers | Since 0.7.67 an offer is one block by two of the city's level, or two by four, so the offers bought average 2 to 3% of the city at every size, and the design counts 195 to 344 purchases to Jerus's old city's size and 512 to 785 to ten billion people, where the lanes took 411 to 444; a new city's are 0.0288 km² each, where its forty bands had run from 0.0093 to 0.167. The playtest kept its ground ahead with 200 offers over its run, 153.13 km², where 0.7.64's bought 85 for 18.01. Measured at 0.7.58, the 1% unit and buying only when full together halved the city in its middle centuries; the test player has kept its ground ahead since. Whether it is too many clicks before a city reaches its size is Jerus's; *Buy the best N* buys many at once, at exactly what they would cost one by one. |
| The playtest's city never finds iron | The playtest's player needs iron from month 13, and buys a field only once the mines it could staff would pay its price back at the market's rate (since 0.7.67): to 0.7.98 its first was West 2 at month 359, six sites for US$37.05M out of the cash. Since 0.7.99, a tenth as many fields each ten times bigger, no offer near its city ever holds iron — at 0.7.99 it looked 202 times and found none listed, the default world's nearest field 12 km out and in a lake — so it stands no mine and no oil well all run, buys its ground elsewhere, 25.90 km² of it lake and river, and ends 13.5% smaller, 545,179 people against 630,290, its GDP $1.9T a month against $2.5T. Whether the default world should hold iron nearer, or the player reach farther for it, is Jerus's, asked on 10 October and not tuned. The pay-back question itself is the game's since 0.7.101: Build's no-deposit page says under its Buy whether the cheapest field pays back for a city this size ([land](#18-land)). At 0.7.123 the bigger city's ground, bought for room, took in 56 iron sites and 93 oil sites by its end, Iron Mining sinking a mine on one of them and the oil sector two wells, the first at month 3,932; its player's own iron rule still found no field listed, in 201 looks. |
| A drawn good pays the boundary price | The materials the builders draw, the households' cars and since 0.7.62 the fuel pay the price at the city's boundary and no rail charge when the railway carries their stream, so in Jerus's old city, whose railway carries all the goods stream, the drivers' fuel came to 0.888 of 0.7.49's bill rather than the 1.137 of the world's price level, fuel's lorry freight having left the band. It is the house's pattern for every draw and was not changed with fuel. |
| The copies still shrink | `ScaleCheck`'s copies of a city K times over are quoted its ground since 0.7.55, and build, but lost about 0.85% of their people a month at 0.7.55: a city's founding care and police endowments do not scale with the copy, so a town of 3,449 copied a thousand times has a thousandth of its senior care, and its seniors' pull on arrivals falls to nothing. With both endowments scaled the copy grew. Whether a copied city should carry them is a question of what a copy is for. |
| Small things the land batches found | A live city's allocation can sit 45,000 sq ft, a Commercial Bank's lot, under its buildings' footprint, so its reload, which derives the allocation from what stands, is fuller than the city it was saved from (0.7.58); a sidecar written before a month's later purchases is redrawn at every load, as slot 3's was, written on 88 purchases where the save holds 133 (0.7.64); an offer nobody buys — on 0.7.58's lanes, the ones that ran into a lake — stands for a thousand months and more at a younger city's size and price, which the places keep, and the office could say an offer's age or list stale ones again (0.7.58); `ScaleCheck`'s fixture month holds every premise only from 527 to 565 under the mended test player, so a re-baseline may need the months scanned again (0.7.67); and `ScaleCheck`'s copies run their utilities unstaffed, power and water at their fallbacks, which no assertion reads (0.7.58). |
| Places that wait | A place waits empty while the free ground along its side is all in the side's other offers, and lists once there is room; but a player buying for value leaves water standing and fills its sides unevenly. On the design's runs a best-value player had up to 0.40 of the 24 places empty on average over its purchases, and one buying evenly 0.01 to 0.02, with up to 5.1% of the city enclosed water at times, which stays offerable. The office says so in the row and no assertion fails; it is a risk the design named and left. |
| An exact count on a huge city | Since 0.7.67 an offer's ground is counted plot by plot when it is listed, at every size. The design measured the first count of a large offer at 0.3 to 0.5 s on one core in blocks of 30.72 and 61.44 km and derived 8 to 31 s in blocks of 245.76 km; the count now keeps whole tiles and spreads a large rectangle over the cores, `LandCheck`'s 2,116 tiles in 130 ms on two, but no harness counts on a city that size as played — its huge fixtures are records scaled by hand — so whether the office pauses after a purchase in a city of billions is to be seen on the PC. |
| A road's life, and the lines' | Gravel had been the cheaper road to keep a trip, every road's repairs being the house's 1% of its price: city2400's advice went from paved to gravel on it, 18.30 D$k a trip against 18.60. Since 0.7.103 each road has its own, 3% a year for gravel, 2% paved and 1.25% a highway, the Canadian Infrastructure Report Card's rates, which Jerus checked (answered under the table). What stands is the rest: the life is charged to every road candidate, a line's crews less its fares among it, so city600's advice went from a Light Rail Line to six Elevated Highways and Jerus's slot 3's from a Bus Network to four Gravel Roads at 0.7.70 — one unit, or no ranking. Paving, played only by `RoadCheck` at 0.7.70, is the default playtest's too since: 87 gravel roads in 14 orders at 0.7.99, and 10 in 2 at 0.7.106, its player ordering roads by need. |
| Old daycares, ten times the places | A save holds its buildings by id, so since 0.7.71 a Home Daycare loads as a Small Childcare Centre, ten times its places and its posts. Jerus's autosave at month 416 comes back with 629 of them: 50,521 places for 6,845 children where it had 5,233, 12,580 posts against a labour force of 11,087, its unskilled fill falling from 1.00 to 0.39, $67.3M a month in wages where it paid $13.2M, and their ground 1.83 km² where it was 0.35, 0.53 km² more than the city owns. A year on it has 31,924 people against 0.7.70's 25,764, but its cash is $153.6M under nothing where it was $5.7M over, and general care is 74% served against 91%. The advice gives such a city no childcare card, so nothing adds to it; demolishing about 538 keeps 91, the 7,481 places the advice sizes its need to. Whether old daycares should convert by places instead is Jerus's. Since 0.7.120 a save that holds a Home Daycare is older than the floor and does not load at all ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)), so the question waits for the day old saves must load again. |
| Should the test player build childcare? | The default test player builds none and never has: at 0.7.70 its city held none at month 4,000 for 11,862 home buildings. With its rule on (`-Dplaytest.childcare`, the advice's card whenever NEEDS YOU lists childcare) its city ends at 308,988 people against 477,358, 86% of its children in care at month 4,000. A choice about the default player, and so about every reading taken from it, left to Jerus. |
| A city whose buildings outgrow its ground | Since 0.7.71 Jerus's autosave owns 79,108,283 sq ft and its buildings use 84,764,200, its resized childcare centres among them, so its free ground reads nothing and it is 5.66 million sq ft short. The map deals its two districts 812 plots more than they hold, and its roomiest tile draws 348 of its 787 buildings on no plot (0.7.72); automatic building's first order there buys the whole deficit with its own ground, $432.8M of land for a $45.8M road, on the funding page's bond (0.7.77), because it counts what is short from the ground owned less the ground used (`AutoBuilder.lacks()`); and Build's no-land page, which counts from the free ground and stops at nothing, offers ground that does not cover the building and asks again. Since 0.7.101 automatic building buys only an order's own ground, and a city over its ground buys none and holds every order for ground: his city, 0.525 km² over, holds them at any limit. Whether such a city should buy its deficit once, or new ground, and what Build's page should offer, are Jerus's. |
| A refinery that loses money | Since 0.7.76 a refinery is planned for a plant's worth of the city's petrol and diesel, about four times as early as it was for fuel, and none it builds pays. Its estimate clears the interest test at 0.22 to 0.75% of its cost a month; once it supplies the market, petrol and diesel strike under the import price the estimate read, it runs at 0.4 to 0.76 of nameplate for want of vans and power, and the 79.5% of its run that is gas, naphtha, jet fuel and fuel oil fetches the export price, worth less than its crude. In the playtest eleven were ordered and eleven shed, each losing money all its life, nominally from D\$644M over the first's 132 months to D\$14.4B over the last's 30, and 99.7% of the drivers' and the railway's fuel came from abroad. Its fix was to be the next batches', and they came: wholesale prices for petrol and diesel (0.7.78), grades, the refinery's units and a planner for what its slate is worth (0.7.79 to 0.7.82). The question stands the harder for them. At wholesale a medium crude's slate is worth less than its crude before a post is paid, and the playtest built none; the spread planner weighs a crude unit with the units its cuts would feed, and on imported crude the Oil Refinery with its Small Lube Plant lost 0.15 to 0.57% of its cost a month in every year of the playtest, while the Crude Unit's packages, earning 0.11 to 0.39% a month in the research cities, ask 59 million litres of petrol and diesel the city lacks, where those cities lack under 1.4 million and the playtest's at most 22.8 million; a refinery a player stands on imported crude is sold after two years of losses, its lube plant six months later. Three answers followed from 0.7.93 to 0.7.106: the slate ships what the city does not take (0.7.98), where the crude was bought and its products idled; the world takes lubricants only to 1% of the crude (0.7.103); and the crude units run only the barrels that pay (0.7.105), so a refinery on imported crude by lorry or rail stands and one by tanker runs ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). Jerus's city at month 8,474, five Crude Units and an Oil Refinery on imported crude, lost \$2.49B in two years before them and \$190M after, its refiners subsidised so that no loss is counted and nothing is sold, and his own fourteen Crude Units on site, 96% built, wait in a queue its builders cannot work. Whether a city should be able to stand a refinery its barrel does not pay for, and on what terms, stands. |
| What the statements found | Since 0.7.74 every flow that moves a business's equity and reaches no statement is named outside the trading result, twelve from 0.7.75 and nine since 0.7.102, when what its borrowing cost it up front went inside, expensed over each debt's life (answered under the table, with the sheet read at the close): the city's subsidy and arrears, the interest on its bank balance, the coupons it is paid, the interest abroad rolled into its holdings, an overdraft forgiven, the loans and the bonds its lenders wrote off, and the theft. None of them is taxed or in what its dividend is struck on, so the interest a business earns is never taxed; whether any should be is Jerus's. And forty years for a mortgage's premium, its amortization, is his to confirm: a fifth a year, the *Income Tax Act*'s, ran the landlords at a loss for a year and a half. |
| Automatic building's calls | Automatic building (0.7.73) keeps NEEDS YOU's own line and its margin on top, so at 15% a network holds at least 153% served; and since 0.7.77 it buys its orders' ground, Jerus's *"no you do need to buy land"* read as it must, which he may have meant the other way. Since 0.7.101 the first of a kind, the limit's default and its debt, the walk and the ranking over a building's life, and since 0.7.104 the budget made smarter, are answered; their own calls stand. The payback reads *"extra tax revenue"* as all the city takes in a resident past all it spends a resident, because the tax lines alone, against the other services' running, built a village's school from its founding cash and stalled it for 500 months. The life's demand reads the city's own trend over its last life, so a city months old reads its founding growth as a life's: a town of 31 at month 4 is covered as 789 residents, and a first school can pay back in a founding month and be bought from the founding cash, as Jerus's A4 asked — whether a founding month's growth should read so is his. The left panel's Debt/GDP is the bonds and bills over a scaled year and the limit all the city owes over the year recorded, so his month-416 city reads 250% on one and 274% on the other: one figure, or both. And on his month-8,473 city the advice now ranks coal first for power, and wind on his month-416 one. All Jerus's to confirm. |
| The map's loose ends | The network's went with it in 0.7.88 — lanes every two plots off the streets that read as teeth at six pixels a plot, a road tile cut by a river dealt road its hub's bank could not hold, and a patch touching the rest only at a corner (under the table). The street plans have their own, as 0.7.92 measured them. Buildings packed without a street at the city's edge, 148 in Jerus's city, are Wind Farms and Assembly Plants his full districts have no cells for, which only more ground, or lots and streets in the model itself, would place; road the streets cannot carry, 183,991 of his plots, is counted in the legend and not drawn; 1,863 plots of his railway's track have no ground for its lines until the islands come; 69 cut estate cells keep their streets and hold nothing; and every district's plan needs the plans before it, so a screen at a big city's edge waits on the worker, about a second for a band of 128 districts. `PlanCheck`'s 40 ms bound on the dense screen's slowest district missed about half its runs alone on the cloud's two cores through 0.7.93, the compiler still at work on the planner seconds into the run, and 0.7.94 made the plan steady. `MapCheck`'s timing labels — a screen and the view's path in 80 ms, a month's change in 5 — go red when other work holds the machine's processors, as they did through 0.7.77's gate and in that edition's own run, 82.3 ms on the view's path at ten thousand times, and want an idle machine to be judged on; since 0.7.100 the month's bound reads the main thread's CPU, 10 of 10 alone, though the screen ratio, on the wall clock, failed 3 of 10 at a load of four at 0.7.102. And since 0.7.99 a dense district over one of the new iron clusters can leave a street piece walled in by mines and buildings, which `PlanCheck`'s one network would fail — no fixture stands there yet; and a new default city's far views mark only the fields within its offers' reach, so it sees no deposit at all, its nearest iron 12 km out. |
| A city with no filling station | Since 0.7.83 the drivers buy their petrol at the pump, and past what the stations can sell at the queue's 18% over wholesale. A station is three posts, two of them for workers without a diploma, and in Jerus's two saves and his old city none was built in two years for want of a spare hand, so their drivers pay the queue's price on every litre. Diploma posts only, or another rule, are his. Since 0.7.106 a station's test counts its staff's wages as well, so in the playtest, with that change alone, the first station waits from month 75 to month 105. |
| A well's second life | A worn-out well is drilled again on its site at the full hundred barrels a day while the field has oil (0.7.84), and the 10% a year and the ten-barrel retirement are the research's estimates; whether a field's later wells should start lower is Jerus's. |
| How far the world is, and how strong a port | The sea's freight shares are the research's rule at 5,000 km (0.7.86), where its rail-against-lorry ratios bracket the railway's quotes; at 2,000 km they would be about twice. And a port is strong: the playtest at 0.7.86 built 23 General Cargo Terminals, $70M each for 0.45 Mt a year, and ended 38% larger, 87% of its boundary tonnes by sea. Which distance is the world's, and whether a port should be worth that much, are Jerus's. |
