| The calls the redraws made | Each screen batch made its own calls and wrote each down, and the most visible wait on Jerus: the road's red line at 111% served, where the networks go red at 100%; two served figures for care, Build's unclamped and Services' held at 100%; the order bar's price a little under the press when the yard makes a later order dearer; a run funded only up to an order the city would refuse; the one parity rule at 25% and 50% either side; the fund's hand naming any price, with no upper limit, and profit and loss its only verdict colours; the Bank's small charts that do not pan; the floor in founding money on City History and in the year book, with no series of it in today's money; the HELD button's line that names a door its press reaches only through the refusal page; and the bank's capital ratio recorded clamped at 1,000%, which a young bank's draws as a flat line. |
| Care on a deficit | Since 0.7.104 care is essential to automatic building, held only by the limit, the money and the ground, so it is built ahead of a village's revenue: in four of the eight auto-built seeds a village stands at 2,000 to 3,600 people for some 400 months, seed 0 at month 200 spending 1,947k a month on health against 2,118k of tax and running about 1.24M a month into deficit, its homes at 539 and then 728 for 300 months, and no school or station pays back while each resident costs more than it pays; all eight end at 1.5 to 2.1 million. Weighing childcare and senior care for their payback too, measured on four seeds, or holding an essential service's count while the city spends past what it takes in, would keep them moving; neither is built. Jerus's. |
| The run swings | Since 0.7.105 the crude units run only the barrels that pay, moving a quarter of nameplate a month at most (`RUN_PACE`, the brief's example, not measured). In Jerus's city the margins sit within 3% of nothing and the city's own tonnes move the railway's price, so over 24 months the run went to nothing, came back to 79% of nameplate and fell again; and the city's take the run reads is the investors' forecast, which misses the railway's diesel, so the diesel step comes early. A damping is Jerus's call. And the barrel is the campus's average, one crew at one rate: keeping the units full at a cut run would be realer, but every nameplate read — the tanks, the planner, the room — would then part from the run's. |
| Two pools, one field | Since 0.7.93 a field keeps no oil of its own, so the platforms on the sixteen shallow fields of Jerus's city also lift its nineteen deep fields' 7.26 Mt; and an older save's one pool was charged to the ground, floored at its tonnes, none to the sea, so his city has its sea's 11.49 Mt back. Both are readings for him to confirm. His investors order a jacket at once, and his builders give it about 1.2 of its 3,600 points a month, 26 sites owing 3.1 million: rush it, or add builders. |
| Roads by need, and a young town | Since 0.7.103 the test player orders the advice's own card for the road, sized for the advice's horizon and slack, while it looks every 6 to 120 months, so its young town runs short of road between looks, 70 to 73% from month 265 to 617, and the ensemble's young towns are smaller — AUTO2's median at month 600 5,118 people against 6,609 — while its old ones end larger, 257,632 at month 2,400 against 230,564. A slack for the player's absence, or leave it: Jerus's. |
| The whole cost's edges | Since 0.7.113 every order the investors weigh carries the interest on its whole cost, but a landlord's homes keep the mortgage lender's test, which reads the payment, and a home bought outright is asked nothing: 186 of the 648 home orders the landlords placed in the playtest at 0.7.113 were paid outright. A twin asking every slice of a home the interest on its whole cost at the insured rate left households with no home at months 260 and 261 and reached 200,000 people at month 2,573 against 2,315; the landlords' hurdle is Jerus's rule of rent at zero profit, and the recommendation is to keep it. And the till's part of a slice is priced at the slice's one rate, a bond's blended rate where a bond is cheaper: priced at the sector's own rate instead, the playtest was the same to month 614 and parted on one order after, ending at 535,686 people. Both are Jerus's to confirm. |
| Zones are amounts, not places | The model has no positions, so a zone holds an amount of ground and the map does not tint it yet (0.7.107, 0.7.109). The land office's going price still reads what is allocated against what is owned, so ground the zones hold makes nobody else's dearer, which would matter if zones grew large; PRICE GIVEN UP counts only what the zones hold, the price given up on ground already sold in a zone being recorded nowhere, which would be a new saved field; and WHAT IS BITING has no zoning card, where a zone short of what it wants would be one. The batches' calls are Jerus's to confirm, each with its flip: the books at the going price and only the roll at the zone's; zoned ground traded at the zone's price both ways, and a zone taken off forgetting what it sold; short zones sharing the free ground alike rather than first come; how building clears the forest; the law's two ladders where the study drew one bar with two thumbs; and the dials' steps. |
| A refused load rebuilds the world first | A load the floor refuses (0.7.108) builds a blank world before it reads the save, as a newer build's refused load always has, so from the pause menu the city in play would be replaced by an empty one though nothing loads. The load list cannot reach it, a refused slot's Load button being off; only code can. Since 0.7.120 every save Jerus had made is such a save. |
| Jerus's cities, refused | Since 0.7.108 a bump that makes an older save load wrongly raises the floor with it ([saves](#23-time-saves--logs)), and 0.7.120 was the first: scrap split from ore in a way an older save would read wrongly, so by the house rule the format and the floor went to 37, and every city Jerus had saved, slots 1 to 9 among them, stopped loading in that build and every one since, each staying on its file, the slot list naming the build that still opens it, 0.7.119 or older. He was told on 10 October at 23:20 and has not answered; the default was the bump. Keep it so, or revert the iron batch's merge and have it come back with the conversion written: his to say. |
| The steel jobs under a high rate | Iron at the world's price (0.7.120) took away the steel chain that had kept a city's posts through a 15% rate — Heavy Industry's 330 to 440, Manufacturing's 400 or so and Automotive's up to 500, on three seeds traced — and the high rate's criteria went red: three seeds a point over their twins where two are allowed, and its towns' population 4,148 against a bar of 4,805, three quarters of 0.7.113's, its unemployment at month 720 31.6% against 18.4%, one seed 60% out of work at month 690. The integrated route (0.7.123) does not bring them back: those towns hold 2,000 to 7,000 people at months 600 to 720, too few for any of its works, and their runs are 0.7.120's to the byte, the population criterion passing since only because its baseline is 0.7.120 itself. Under the autopilot every seed holds Iron & Steel posts at some point, first at months 1,068 to 1,989, but only in spells, 400 to 840 posts at most for 28 to 464 of 2,400 months, three seeds holding any at month 2,400. Nothing was tuned. The recommendation is to accept it as built, the route needing a bigger city than those towns; it is Jerus's ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). |
| Mills that undersell themselves | Iron & Steel values a works' output at the import price for as much as the city imports and at the export price past it, the spec's rule, kept as written (0.7.123). A Large Mini-Mill makes 125,000 t a month, so once one stands it covers the city's imports and steel's local price falls toward the middle of its band, demand over demand and supply; the mill earns less than it was weighed at, runs at .6 to .8, short of power and vans, and pays interest past what it clears, and some are lost and ordered again. The planner sees neither the price falling nor the rate. A price after its own supply, for the processing sectors and not the refiners, would make mills that hold; it is a model change and Jerus's, and the recommendation is to keep the spec's rule until he says ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). |
| A works weighed with its lorries | Since 0.7.123 Iron & Steel weighs a works with the vans its tonnes need, their running in what it earns and their price in its whole cost, which the spec did not: without it the probe's first build was a Pelletising Plant on imported ore whose 2,538 vans cost 64% of the plant, lost within months, and over the run Iron & Steel went under whole seventeen times, with it once. The study's four cases still leave the lorries out. Jerus, the morning it shipped: *"for i4 the lorries, ill answer it shortly"*, in a note of his own, a batch after the planned ones; until then it stands as built, and undoing it is the weighing's two terms. |
| The old steel's rules, and the years | The city's old steel (0.7.123) is a month's pool: what no yard takes goes to landfill that month and is not carried; 85% is recovered from all four sources, the offcuts too; a yard is ordered once the pool past the yards standing is 60% of its intake; and the sellers are paid 70% of scrap's export price, Jerus's figure. Offcuts are 95 to 97% of the pool and the cars never pass 3%. And each new row carries the year it first existed — 1900, the start year, for the yard, the ovens and both blast furnaces, 1952 for the oxygen shop, 1955 for pelletising and 1969 for the large mill, where 1989's thin-slab caster would also do — which nothing reads yet, the recommended shape for what a city may build when, with no list of recipes. The recommendation is to keep all of it; it is Jerus's to confirm. |
| A works that makes its own power | A works whose own power covers its draw is still slowed by the grid's energy ratio, as every plant is, though it buys none of its power from the grid: the ratio reads the city's grid, not the works' own. Since 0.7.123 three works make power, the Coke Ovens and the Blast Furnace more than they draw; none of them stood in any run, so the throttle has never bitten one. On the list since 0.7.112, and not done. |
| The Earth's geology, as built | Four calls of 0.7.117, each recommended and Jerus's to confirm. Z is built as defined, measured on the file, and not the study's figures, whose iron, copper and uranium do not follow from its own table — with its own shares iron's Z is .76 where it printed .888 — so its spots come out under what it printed, Rotterdam's oil ×2.58 and not ×2.99, the Yilgarn's iron ×2.89 and not ×3.55. The hand table corrects 68 provinces beyond the 219 it was asked to place, each row saying why. Z leaves out the ground south of 60 degrees, where East Antarctica, a shield under ice, would take about a sixth of the reachable world's iron. And oil's Z is over the land with the sea of shelves, basins and rifts on top, which adds 51.6% to the land's oil, where a Z over both would keep the total and cut the spots' oil by a third. A geologist's eye on the table's 287 rows is worth having ([the real Earth](#18-land)). |
| The Earth's sea and rivers, as built | The sea's depth on the Earth (0.7.121) is the generated world's rule with the distance from the coast for the heights the file does not carry, so platforms stand within about 58 km of a coast, and Rotterdam's North Sea is 16 m deep 40 km out where the real one is about 30; with no depth at all no platform could stand anywhere on the Earth, and Rotterdam's oil is mostly offshore. Heights in a later Earth would replace it. The far view's rivers (0.7.119) are thinned by width as the view widens, where the study asked for every river a pixel wide, which drew Siberia 45% fresh water; its forest is dithered, the void drawn past the rim while the model's ground there stays sea, and the hover names a place alone, no country. Each is recommended as built, and Jerus's to confirm ([the real Earth](#18-land)). |
| A home's card | The card's interest gate (0.7.122) is not asked of a landlord's home, which shows a dash, because the investors ask a home the mortgage lender's test instead, its income over the mortgage's payment 1.20 times. The card does not ask that test, so it cannot say when the lender would refuse a home; a door on the game around the lender's decision would let it, as the interest test's door does for the rest. The recommendation is to keep the dash until that door is built. |
| The Earth's file, in the player's words | Since the commit after 0.7.122 the Earth's file reaches `data/` by itself, `get-earth.bat` fetching it from the release `earth-1` before the game starts; but the founding screen's words and a refused load's still tell the player to put `earth-1.bin` there by hand. They are not false, and which words a player should read is Jerus's. And when the repository goes private for Steam the release's address will need a sign-in; the Steam build is to carry the file itself. |
| Onboarding | The game never states the goal or teaches its causal order — land, housing, people, jobs, industry. Every confusing thing a new player hits is that order being violated. Still the only thing that gates shipping. |

> **Why easy money barely inflated** — Jerus's question of 4 October, and the three rows it answered: **the index's base period**, a basket weighted from one month two years in, is a basket struck on the trailing year and chained every ten years since 0.7.43; **the shelf's floor doing a price's job**, a founding constant, is struck at the price level the city expects since 0.7.42, and the shelf clears on money between it and a cap since 0.7.43; and **the shelf priced by coverage, not by money**, is priced by what households would spend at each price, with the counter and the table in the index. Raised and answered inside the period: **transit's bill, paid by nobody**, is paid by the treasury as a promise since 0.7.49, and **G without the schools and transit** carries both; **a busy month read as a year** on Government's *of GDP* is the trailing year since 0.7.47; **a load that read the month as nothing** — Trade's flows, care's fees by kind, the Food page's count, Construction's materials, the railway's first month — reads it since 0.7.46; **the epidemic that never ended**, 2,213 months in the 2,400-month city, is gone since 0.7.46, an epidemic named only on Health's outbreaks; **a band paid today's floor read as having room**, because pinning compared with the founding floor, until 0.7.47; **History's graduates**, zero by construction, are the gains since 0.7.46; **a car that cost nothing to run** burns fuel since 0.7.49; **the Bank tab's branch verdict**, which could disagree with its figures near the line, is the investors' planner's since 0.7.33; **the bank on the profit tax page** is on WHO PAYS since 0.7.36; and **a dollar piece on the buyback page**, priced at the city's short rate, is priced on the world's curve since 0.7.32.

> **Answered in the editions before**
>
> **When the first inflation reading should come** — about month 50 in a Standard city, because the basket is fixed after 24 months of shopping and the rate needs a year of readings after that. Jerus: *"Keep the countdown"*: the header reads *rate in ~N mo* until then, and no model figure moved (0.7.20). **The price card's "against what it cost at founding"**, whose 1.00 is the month the basket was fixed: *"Leave it"*. **The other sector pages' money form**: *"With 0.7.21's text cut"*, and every sector page prints the short form since 0.7.21. **BuildMenuCheck's 73 failures**, since 0.7.19, because its price check predated the builders' sales tax: *"Update to the taxed price"*; it checks the taxed price from the rule's own inputs, passes 73 of 73 and runs in the cloud gate (0.7.21). **Whether the city held at 25% must live**, after 0.7.19 removed the deposit cap's strain and the window it lived on: *"Let it fail"* ([the bank](#14-the-bank)). **The bank's branch built 29 posts without the staffing test** (0.7.18): it asks it since 0.7.19, like every other planner. **The five longest paragraphs on screen** are a line and an (i) since 0.7.22. **Settings and Load on a cold start** drew over the empty start-up world's header and panels in 0.7.21, and are over the menu's backdrop since 0.7.22. **City History's lines in red, amber and green** waited for the chart's rebuild, and since 0.7.23 no chart draws a series in a verdict colour.
>
> **Who gets 45%** — the constant and the deposit quote's cap are gone: since 0.7.7 the bank chooses what it passes on, 0.35 of the dial when flush and toward 0.90 at the window, never more than its margin after costs or the savers' share of it. **Who absorbs a failed bank** — the city, since 0.7.14: every common share passes to it and the old owners get nothing, and it pays the hole and the capital to reopen as a promise, its central bank advancing what the treasury lacks. Nothing is declared as coming from outside any more, and the audit's old line for it reads nothing; whether that line goes is Jerus's. **A concentration limit on the bank** — answered by a price, not a limit (0.7.12): Basel's IRB capital, with a correlation that rises with the book's concentration, allocated to each sector and into its rate, took the default setup's failures from 115 to 1. Syndication past Basel's large-exposure limit was tried on the way and deleted (0.7.8); what is left is the young bank, above. **The bubble** — the dealer whose quote climbed with the demand it could not fill is gone (0.7.12). A price is the last trade on a book where nobody is obliged to sell, and on the default seed on 28 September the median last trade stood at 0.99 of fair value and the ninetieth percentile at 1.42; whether a dealer should bid at a quote it does not believe in went with the dealer.
>
> **The treasury rolled its whole debt in one bill** — a single six-month emergency note it repaid with money it did not have and wrote again, for ever. The note is retired: since 0.7.0 the central bank advances the gap at the policy rate, up to a ceiling the player sets, and past it the promises are paid and the rest owed. Term loans are issued at five benchmark maturities on a curve. The rest of that row — long bonds dominated past fifteen years, and rounded to $100M — was not re-measured; the rounding is at least stated on the borrow page now. **The overdraft had no floor** — a founding village given a university went to NaN by month 1,632 — and the advances ceiling is the floor. **The city borrowed below its own central bank's rate**, and the constant that did it is deleted. **The bank never paid for the city's paper**, and it does now. **Wages were indexed a third above the price level they chase** — closed without a fix, because it does not reproduce: `LabourCheck` holds the wage index to the published price index through 240 months of steady inflation, a reform and a reload, and on all eight seeds every one of 144 checkpoints sits at the level the two-year lag implies, wages over the index between 0.84 and 1.12. **The tuition table was calibrated against the wages before the rebalance**, and the price of a place is the player's dial now: at ×3 the trap the header describes is back, at ×1 it is quiet, and the balance call is at the player's hand.
>
> **Is the city too rich against its food?** — answered, and the answer was not the food. Measured against Canada the wholesale price was sane and the shops' markup was sane, but the *poorest* cell held about three times what an average Canadian does per head, and Jerus deferred the question until households carried transport and luxury costs, which they now do. The households looked rich against a basket with two things in it because they *were* rich, for a reason nothing on the page had measured: their savings abroad compounded at the world's 2% with the coupon rolled where it was earned, so net worth climbed to five thousand months of GDP and every household was past satiation on a shelf that was the only thing it could buy. The wealth term, the coupon paid home, cars, boutiques and kitchens gave the money somewhere to go, and the honest hunger measure then showed the shops delivering a fraction of what was asked — the food share was never the question; the supply wall is. **The transit loss** — $5.4M a month at the default fare, carried as a balance problem — was a ride charged once a month; forty journeys a month and it is gone. **The savings that cannot be spent** have their reading: the discharge tests the wage and never the savings. **The fare was collected from nobody**, and is a fee on every rider's statement now. **Nothing about transport was on a screen** — it is a tab with four pages.
>
> **Materials were priced nine times too low** — $18,000 a unit now, every template re-derived, and it found an import bill that had never been paid. **Retail's shelf price was the last unpriced half** — done; hunger sat at 0–1% and the shops delivered 94–96% of what they planned, on a hunger measure that was later found to be reading the shops' own denominator, so those two figures were never the city's (see the supply wall above). **Unemployment** — 12.8–15.5% at the end of eight seeds, against 41.5% when it was the largest open problem.
>
> **The two-hundred-year plateau** — answered by giving the city customers who do not live in it. A city whose every buyer is one of its own people can only grow as fast as it grows; with business services and manufacturing selling abroad, the median run went from 16,834 people with six seeds in sixteen ever taking off, to **127,651 with sixteen of sixteen**, and the price level from 0.799 to 0.975. **Nothing borrows below cost** — one rule closed the bond floor, the business desk and the carry trade at once. **The mills made food out of nothing** — they buy crops now, and the plant's return fell from 6.2% of build cost a month to about 3.9%.
>
> **A laid-off parent orphaned their children** — answered. The children of an adult who leaves work now go with them, at the city's own rate, and live on whatever that household lives on. Worst orphan month on the probe city **2,093.7 → 12.4**; child deaths over one 4,000-month seed **55,546 → 47,503**. **One good called Food fed everybody** — the shelf is thirteen foods, chosen by income, and the good called Food has been retired behind them. **A line that made two things was charged for both twice** — the sector cost methods divided a whole line's payroll, power and inputs by one good's output, which made an oven with two products produce nothing at all, and had been quietly over-costing business services and manufacturing since the day each shipped. Joint costs are split by relative sales value now, and a sector making one good is bit-for-bit what it was.

> **Judge nothing by a single playtest**
>
> Four thousand months of a chaotic trajectory diverge on the first differing decision. The same change measured +18% on one land seed and −28% on another, and a perturbation of one part in a million moves the long-run size of the city by 10%. Vary the seed, and measure the symptom rather than the end state.
